evidence_text: AI-driven multi-omics integration in cancer research and precision oncology. Integrating multi-omics data with Artificial Intelligence offers new opportunities for understanding cancer biology and discovering actionable biomarkers. In this selective review aimed at clinicians and translational researchers, we survey methodological innovations from classical machine learning to deep learning. We synthesize recent innovations, identify persistent technical challenges, and evaluate the landscape of available multi-omics datasets. Ultimately, we propose a strategic roadmap for translating AI-driven integrative models into real-world precision oncology. Introduction  Advances in high-throughput molecular profiling have marked the beginning of the “multi-omics” era. While mono-omics approaches provide high-resolution insights into discrete molecular planes, they may fail to capture the cross-layer regulatory crosstalk and feedback loops driving oncogenesis. The comprehensive characterization of cancer genomes (DNA sequence), epigenomes (chromatin accessibility and modifications), transcriptomes (RNA expression), (phospho)proteomes (protein expression and chemical modifications), and metabolomes (metabolite quantification), offers a more holistic view of cancer biology. This approach allows for the characterization of emergent properties that remain invisible to single-modality analysis. However, the resulting data heterogeneity necessitates more advanced methods capable of synthesizing these large and heterogeneous datasets. Artificial intelligence (AI) encompassing machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL), provides the robust computational framework necessary to mine high-dimensional omics data, reveal latent biological patterns, and extract clinically actionable insights. Recent advances in single-cell sequencing and spatial omics further add to the data richness, enabling deeper resolution of tumor heterogeneity and microenvironment interactions – thereby necessitating advanced AI methods to integrate information across scales  1  .  Precision oncology may stand to gain substantially from such integrative approaches. Indeed, multi-omics data have already been used to redefine cancer subtype classification  2   and discover therapeutic targets  3  . Early successes in using multi-omics deep learning models include the discovery of prognostic (outcome prediction) and theranostic biomarkers (drug response prediction  4  ). They show that AI algorithms are well suited to distill these complex, multidimensional data into actionable knowledge.  While our focus remains molecular multi-omics data integration, this concept extends beyond molecular assays to include radiological and pathological imaging and clinical data, a convergence often termed multimodal integration. Radiomic features extracted from medical images and digital pathology can complement molecular biomarkers (radiogenomics), underscoring the value of integrated analyses  4  . Likewise, electronic health records and clinical variables provide important phenotypic context. To maintain thematic depth, we cite multimodal studies that include multiple molecular omics modalities.  This review provides a comprehensive non-systematic narrative synthesis of the AI-based methods and strategies enabling multi-omics data integration in cancer research. Tailored for clinicians and translational scientists, it offers an overview of the field along with a practical roadmap for their research. We surveyed methodological innovations through a non-systematic search of bioRxiv and PubMed through February 2026, using relevant keywords such as “Cancer + Multi-omics” and “Machine-learning + Multi-omics”, along with more specialized keywords for sub-topic deep-dives, like “Omics + Federated learning”. Selection criteria prioritized peer-reviewed publications demonstrating novel algorithmic architectures, large-scale pan-cancer benchmarks, or prospective clinical validation. We begin by comparing early, late, and intermediate strategies for data integration, providing illustrative examples for each approach. We then discuss key applications in oncology (diagnosis, prognosis, therapy response prediction, and patient stratification), highlighting both cancer-specific case studies and pan-cancer analyses. We summarize the major resources, datasets, and benchmarks that have catalyzed advances in this field. Finally, we examine the challenges that must be addressed to translate AI–multi-omics innovations into real-world clinical practice, and outline future directions for this rapidly evolving domain. Together, these insights provide a roadmap for real-world translation of AI-driven multi-omics into precision oncology.    Multi-omics integration strategies  Integration strategies are often categorized as early, intermediate, or late integration (with some authors also proposing “mixed” or hierarchical approaches)  5  , significantly impacting model performance and interpretability. These approaches are illustrated in Fig.  1 .    Fig. 1   Illustration of early, intermediate and late integration strategies for multi-omics data.  Autoencoders are used as an exemplary architecture. Neurons are represented by colored squares, and neural network layers are depicted by the shapes connecting them. Yellow and blue represent two distinct omics modalities, while green represents a learned joint representation.                    Early integration  Often called feature-level integration, it combines all omics data at the input stage, feeding for instance a simple concatenation of RNA and protein levels to a model. This approach is able to capture all cross-omic interactions within a single model. However, concatenating these disparate molecular layers frequently generates large, sparse matrices that exacerbate the “curse of dimensionality”, a limitation particularly detrimental in small cohorts or datasets with missing modalities. Dimensionality reduction or feature selection is thus usually applied in conjunction with early integration to ensure model generalizability. We will discuss these methods when introducing classical machine learning.    Late integration  Also called decision-level integration, it keeps data types separate until the final stage, by training independent models on each omic dataset, or different model types, and then combining the outputs (predictions) of those models. The combination could be an average of predicted risk scores, or a majority vote for classification. Late integration is an ensemble approach. Its advantage is that each model can be optimized for a given data type (for instance, a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) on imaging data and a random forest on genomic data) and one can easily identify which modality contributes the most to the final decision, making its prediction more explainable. Moreover, this approach is very robust to missing modalities if each model is based on one omics modality at a time. However, late integration misses opportunities to learn cross-omic feature interactions during model training (e.g., a gene mutation significance might only be realized in the context of an expression change or proteomic marker).    Intermediate integration  Often called joint or mid-level integration, it refers to methods where each omic is first processed (or reduced) separately, and then integrated at an intermediate stage of model building. In practice, this could mean learning lower-dimensional representations for each omic (e.g., latent features) and then concatenating or further integrating these representations for downstream prediction. The intermediate approach attempts to retain each modality’s most salient information while avoiding the noise and dimensionality issues of raw early integration. Its explainability may be more complex, but it usually performs well, and we will see through various examples that it is more frequently used in modern models.    Integration with biological knowledge  An orthogonal strategy is to integrate data at the level of biological entities or pathways. Rather than fusing raw features, one can map different omics to common descriptors – for example, mapping DNA mutations, RNA expression and protein abundance to the genes or pathways they involve and then integrating at that level. Tools like DeepKEGG  6   use this approach, integrating multi-omics features according to known pathways to predict cancer outcomes, thereby improving interpretability and reducing noise. Graph-based or network-based data integration (mentioned earlier under Graph Neural Networks - GNNs) may similarly use known interaction networks as a scaffold for combining omics, effectively performing an integration that respects molecular relationships. These methods can be seen as intermediate integration informed by prior knowledge.  In summary, no single integration strategy suits all problems. For instance, researchers have used and compared both early-integration and joint/late- integration autoencoders to extract integrated features predictive of cancer outcomes  7  . Recent trends favor more flexible architectures that can adaptively do both separate and joint modeling of omics – for example, using attention mechanisms to let the model learn how much to rely on each data source for a given prediction  8 , 9  . Let’s now discuss these key concepts and approaches.     Methodological frameworks  The landscape of AI for high-throughput molecular data has shifted from simple feature aggregation toward integrative synthesis, driven by algorithmic innovation and increased computational capacity. While ‘classical’ machine learning provided a foundation for mono-omics and early multi-omics projects, modern deep learning architectures serve as the computational substrate required to model the non-linear interactions between different omics layers. Most recently, the field has adopted attention-based frameworks, notably Transformers, to capture complex dependencies across diverse biological datasets, providing a more robust framework for multi-omics applications. Table  1  provides a comparative overview of AI approaches developed in the last decades for cancer multi-omics integration, and Fig.  2  visually illustrates their architectures.    Table 1   Key analytical approaches for multi-omics data integration      Approach  Key principles  Strengths  Limitations       Machine learning algorithms     The following advanced statistical methods were first developed to integrate multi-omics data. They are often used as baselines for more modern architectures.    Regularized regression   Penalizes the loss function to produce simpler regression models and prevent overfitting.  - LASSO: selects features.  - Ridge: reduces the impact of correlated features.  - ElasticNet: combination of LASSO and Ridge regression.    A common benchmark for multiomics integration  81  .  Can also be used as a first feature-selection approach for other models.   Suffers from the “curse of dimensionality” in multi-omics settings. Feature selection and dimensionality reduction is often required.    Random forest and gradient boosting methods  Ensembles of learned decision trees for classification or regression tasks with categorical and/or continuous input data.   Handle heterogeneous inputs.  Provide feature importance (“gain”) for basic interpretability.  Gradient boosting methods (e.g., XGBoost, CatBoost  82  ) often outperform random forest, especially with categorical data.   Gradient boosting methods sometimes require more computation power than random forest, and may need careful tuning to avoid overfitting.    Joint & individual variation explained - JIVE  Deterministic joint dimensionality reduction across multiple omics layers to separate shared and omic-specific sources of variation.   Identifies shared and omic-specific variation, providing biologically interpretable insights  Requires less computational power than MOFA below.   Its deterministic framework makes it less adaptable to noisy datasets than MOFA introduced below.    Multi-omics factor analysis – MOFA  Probabilistic joint dimensionality reduction across multiple omics layers to separate shared and omic-specific sources of variation.  A strong baseline for sample clustering. The learned factors can be interpreted as molecular drivers or shared/omic-specific sources of variation.  A single omics modality can be overrepresented in the learned features. Newer integration methods frequently outperform MOFA, which is often used as a standard comparison point.     Deep learning algorithms     The following deep learning algorithms are based on Neural networks. This technology has enabled more powerful multi-omics models, as they can inherently handle high-dimensional inputs and capture complex nonlinear relationships. They are often considered “black-box” models, as their interpretability is more limited than that of classical machine learning approaches described above.    Autoencoders and variational autoencoders  83    Generative models that use an encoder-decoder structure to learn a condensed probabilistic representation of input data.  Widely used for dimensionality reduction, visualization, clustering, classification, and data generation.  Their relatively simple neural network structure may limit performance.    Graph neural networks (GNNs)  84     Nodes can be omic features (eg. genes) in a knowledge-based interaction graph, or samples, to compute similarity.  For gene network discovery, sample clustering or classification.    High performance by leveraging molecular network topology.  Straightforward explainability if the structure is pathway-guided, or when using saliency maps  85  .   Knowledge-based graphs are not always available.    Attention mechanisms and transformers   Attention: the weight of inputs is based on the context for each sample.  Transformer: multi-head attention models capturing different nuances of long-range feature interactions.   Often higher performance due to context-awareness.  Require large datasets and substantial computing power.    Generative adversarial networks (GANs)  Pitting a generator and discriminator against each other to learn complex cross-omics relationships.  Effective for data denoising and missing data imputation across omics.  Generated or denoised data usually requires further classification or analysis by other models.     Combined and larger models     Combined approaches  For instance, combine the straightforward interpretability of GNN and high performance of transformer-based models  In representative benchmarking studies such as MOGONET  9   and DeepKEGG  6  , cross-cohort classification accuracy (ACC) on TCGA datasets improved by 5–15% using graph-transformer hybrids.  Combined models may also combine limitations. In the case of GNN - transformer hybrids, a knowledge graph, large training dataset, and high computing power are required.    Foundation models  Large attention-based models trained in a self-supervised manner on very large and broad datasets, then fine-tuned for specific tasks.  Foundation models have a potential to support various downstream multi-omics tasks  86  , similar to GPT-style models in natural language processing.  Current examples mainly focus on single-omics and single-cell data; still far from the scale and robustness of foundation models seen in natural language processing or computer vision (e.g., DINO  87  ). In bulk multi-omics integration, TMO-Net  86   is an early step, even though it is not attention-based and has only been trained on localized tumors from TCGA.        Fig. 2   Illustration of the general architectures of key deep-learning frameworks for omics data analysis as described in Table  1 .  Auto-encoders compress inputs into a latent space via reconstruction loss. Graph Neural Networks aggregate node data from topological neighbors to learn embeddings. Transformers employ a series of blocks with multi-head attention to model complex feature dependencies. Generative Adversarial Networks pit a generator creating synthetic samples from noise against a discriminator trained to distinguish real from generated data.                   In brief, no single architecture consistently dominates across cancer types or omic layers. Performance appears primarily constrained by data completeness, biological priors, and interpretability requirements rather than by algorithmic novelty. Let’s introduce key datasets and resources used in the field.    Key resources and benchmarking datasets  The progress in AI for cancer multi-omics has been propelled by the availability of large multi-omics datasets and databases. The most widely used one is The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) due to its large scale, diversity in tumor types and modalities, along with its long-standing history. Other initiatives have emerged to provide complementary datasets, for instance of rare cancers, metastatic samples, or new omics modalities. Table  2  summarizes some of the key resources widely used in the field.    Table 2   Key data resources fueling AI multi-omics research      Resource/dataset  Description & contribution      The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA)  88    ~20,000 primary tumor and matched normal samples across 33 cancer types, with genomic, transcriptomic, epigenomic, and some proteomic data. A primary training and benchmarking ground for countless AI models, enabling pan-cancer analyses. It includes very few metastatic samples primarily from melanomas, and tumors mainly come from Western populations.    International Cancer Genome Consortium (ICGC)/ICGC-ARGO  89    Global initiative aggregating whole-genome sequencing and other omics (mainly transcriptomics) for tens of thousands of cancers. The upcoming ICGC-ARGO aims for 100,000 tumor genomes with clinical data across more diverse populations, including Japan, China, Korea, and Saudi Arabia.    Genomic Data Commons (GDC)  90   and cBioPortal  91    Platforms that host and provide access to cancer genomics and multi-omics datasets with unified standards. cBioPortal in particular offers visualization and basic analysis tools for integrated data.    Clinical Proteomic Tumor Analysis Consortium (CPTAC)  An NCI program generating deep proteomic and phosphoproteomic profiles on TCGA tumors and others, adding a proteogenomic layer to the genomic data for several cancer types (breast, colorectal, lung, etc). Data are available via the Proteomics Data Commons (PDC) and have been used in proteogenomic AI studies.    Metastatic tumor datasets  A vast majority of public datasets are composed of primary tumors. For certain questions, including metastatic samples is highly recommended. Priestley et al.   92   from the  Hartwig  Medical Foundation paired 2520 metastatic and normal tissue and performed WGS. The pan-cancer META-PRISM cohort offers matched RNA-seq and WES data  93  . The POG (Personalized OncoGenomics) program assembled transcriptome, whole-exome and clinical data for 570 cancers, 77% from metastatic sites, and 82% previously treated  94  . The MET500 cohort is composed of transcriptomes and exomes from 500 metastatic tumors  95  . Other studies focus on smaller cohorts of specific tumor types, like Hepatocellular Carcinoma  96  . However, these studies are often restricted to one or a few cancer centers within a single country.    National genomics programs for precision oncology.  National plans have emerged to produce and analyze multi-omics data to personalize rare or difficult-to-treat cancers. They assemble at the same time rich multi-omics cancer cohorts. The German NCT/DKFZ MASTER program for advanced or rare cancers  97  , and the French PFMG2025 for advanced or rare cancers and cancers of unknown primary  98  , are examples of such initiatives. These datasets are however reserved for clinical use or selected research programs, and are by definition biased towards a single country.    Cancer Cell Line Encyclopedia (CCLE)  29  /DepMap  99    A compendium of hundreds of cancer cell lines with multi-omics characterization - mutations, gene expression, copy number, epigenomics, and drug sensitivity data. DepMap (Dependency Map) integrates these with CRISPR/RNAi gene essentiality screens. These resources allow development of AI models linking multi-omics features to drug response in preclinical models, which can then inform patient predictions.    MOSAIC Atlas (Multi-Omics Spatial Atlas In Cancer)  46    The MOSAIC consortium is assembling a large multimodal spatial and single-cell atlas, integrating molecular and spatial heterogeneity with clinical and bulk omics data.    Single-Cell Atlases (e.g., Human Cell Atlas, Mouse Cell Atlas)  While focused on single-cell data, these atlases now often include multi-omic data - scRNA-seq + scATAC-seq from the same cells, etc. They are driving development of AI methods for single-cell multi-omics integration, like graph-based and contrastive learning approaches, which can eventually be applied to bulk tumor data (e.g., deconvolving bulk tumors using single-cell references).       These datasets and platforms have enabled model training, validation, and comparison across studies.     Researchers are now calling for a dedicated multi-omics benchmark suite – analogous to ImageNet  10   in computer vision – to facilitate systematic evaluation of integrative models on a variety of tasks. Progress towards this goal includes MLOmics  11   that provides curated ML-ready datasets derived from TCGA, and compares the standardized performance of different methodologies. For building cohorts by fusing heterogeneous datasets, MINDS (Multimodal Integration of Oncology Data System) is a robust framework. These advancements in data infrastructure are pivotal for transitioning AI models into clinical and research applications, that we will now introduce.    Application areas  Integrating multi-omics with AI promises to improve various aspects of cancer care: from earlier detection and diagnosis to refined patient stratification and personalized treatment selection. Here we highlight major application areas, with examples of how multi-omics AI has been applied, while referring to previously introduced concepts and studies.   Cancer diagnosis and early detection  Multi-omics approaches are being investigated to enhance diagnostic accuracy and even enable early cancer detection from minimally invasive samples. For instance, blood-based liquid biopsies that combine gene and protein markers have shown promise in detecting cancer in asymptomatic individuals. A notable example is the CancerSEEK test, which integrated circulating tumor DNA mutations in 16 genes together with 9 circulating protein biomarkers to detect eight common cancer types at early stages. The analysis is then based on an ML model able to predict both the presence of cancer cells but also their tissue of origin. Such multi-modality blood tests achieved sensitivities of ~70% across eight cancer types with few false positives, outperforming single-modality screening. However, they are not high-throughput approaches, as they use targeted sequencing and protein quantification  12  . As technology continues to advance, we anticipate AI could fuse data from novel diagnostics such as cell-free DNA methylation, circulating tumor cells, and metabolic signatures. This would enable the simultaneous screening of multiple cancer types from a single assay, similar to liquid biopsies currently undergoing clinical trials  13  .    Resolution of pathologically ambiguous cases  A typical example is cancer of unknown primary (CUP). Multi-omics AI models could help predict the tissue of origin or subtype by comparing the tumor’s integrated molecular profile to reference profiles from cancers of known primary sites. An example is the single-omics RNA-seq based tissue of origin classifier TransCUPtomics  14  , now implemented in the French national molecular tumor board for CUPs  15  . A second example is the case of rare and heterogeneous cancer types, where single-omics classification tools are used on a regular basis, like the DNA methylation-based classifier for central nervous system (CNS) tumors  16   now explicitly referenced by the WHO Classification of Tumors of the CNS  17  , or for sarcomas  18  . As seen earlier, some companies and academic groups have developed molecular classification assays that combine genomic mutations and expression signatures to classify cancers; these have shown accuracy improvements over single-omics assays in validation studies.    Prognosis and outcome prediction  A major application of multi-omics integration is to predict patient outcomes (survival, recurrence risk, metastasis) more accurately than traditional clinical or single-omic markers. Multi-omics signatures can serve as composite prognostic biomarkers. For instance, multi-omics AI models outperformed single-omics ones in classifying tumors into prognostically significant patient groups in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC)  19  , lung adenocarcinoma  20  , and breast cancer  21  . Multimodal models combined genomic, histopathological, radiomic, and clinical features of ovarian carcinomas to significantly improve risk stratification  22  . Pan-cancer prognostic models have emerged as well, leveraging large databases like TCGA to predict survival risk scores, effectively learning both cancer-general and cancer-specific prognostic features. For instance, the CustOmics framework leads to a more precise survival prediction than single-omic models  23  . Tran et al. wrote a comprehensive review and compared the performances of such approaches  24  . It seems however important to note that most large multi-omics datasets used for model training and testing include a limited number of metastatic samples (Table  2 ) decreasing their validity when applied to metastatic cases, despite these being the most lethal forms of cancer.    Therapeutic response prediction and drug discovery  Combining multi-omics allows more nuanced predictions of therapy response, which is crucial for personalized treatment: a tumor with a given DNA mutation might respond to a targeted inhibitor only if the downstream pathway (assessed by RNA/protein) is activated. Multi-omics AI models can learn these conditional dependencies and improve decision-making. These are more often trained in a supervised manner, which means that the model knows the response to the treatment, and learns predictive patterns. One area of intense interest is immunotherapy response prediction  25  . For example, an AI model integrating exome and RNA-sequencing was able to better predict responders in melanoma immunotherapy trials than any single feature alone. It also used Shapley values (SHAP) to identify response biomarkers, in an explainable AI approach  26  . Pathology can also be integrated for tumor response prediction. For example, Sammut et al. combined digital pathology with genomics and transcriptomics to predict breast cancer neo-adjuvant therapy response, with more precision than models based on either pathology or genomics alone  27  . In precision medicine trials, multi-omics helps match patients to therapies: The WINTHER trial used gene expression (microarray) and DNA alteration data (targeted NGS panel of 236 genes) to guide therapy selection for refractory cancers, showing signal for a clinical improvement when a drug target was detected  28  . In drug discovery, on the preclinical side, massive pharmacogenomic screens (like the Cancer Cell Line Encyclopedia  29   and the Genomics of Drug Sensitivity in Cancer, GDSC project  30   have used multi-omics profiles of cancer cell lines to train ML models that predict drug sensitivity. These models can then be applied to patient tumor multi-omics data to nominate potentially effective drugs or drug combinations. For example, a graph-based model integrated various omics data and essentiality networks to predict synthetic lethal interactions, pointing to drug combinations that could selectively kill tumor cells  31  . AI-driven integration is also enabling computational drug repositioning - identifying existing drugs that might work in defined patient subsets - by linking multi-omics tumor signatures to known drug response profiles  32  . In unsupervised settings, multi-omics tumor clustering and its biological interpretation can also help propose therapeutic strategies. Indeed, squamous cell carcinomas resemble one another across tissues of origin, suggesting shared treatment approaches  33  . In glioblastoma, this approach identified one subgroup of patients with elevated metabolic enzyme expression and metabolite levels, suggesting an increased sensitivity to metabolic inhibitors. In the same way, basal-like/mesenchymal characteristics samples with high immune infiltration and PDL-1 expression were also identified, suggesting a potential sensitivity to immune checkpoint inhibitors  34  . However, it is important to note that the current validated applications, such as whole-genome sequencing-based targeted therapy, often focus on single-omic data, and rare cancers or advanced treatment lines. First-line treatments for the most common cancers continue to be selected based on clinical and pathological data, and seem more complex to outperform with AI drug discovery models.    Personalized predictive models and digital twins  The focus shifts from training universal cohort-wide models, toward the fine-tuning of AI systems on a single patient’s multi-omics profile. This could, for instance, simulate how a given patient might respond to various therapies, in an approach related to digital twins  35  . Recent research is exploring this concept of patient-specific modeling using Bayesian modeling  36   or reinforcement learning, to compare and select an optimal treatment policy for each patient based on their omics. Early examples include models that, given a patient’s omics (only a few selected features) and mid-treatment imaging data, recommend adaptive therapy adjustments in radiation oncology  37  . However, current models function primarily as simulations based on data snapshots. The development of true digital twins that update continuously during a patient’s treatment remains a future goal.  We have demonstrated that ML models can effectively leverage multi-omics data to address fundamental challenges in cancer research and clinical practice. The nature of the data, and the structure of the model, must be adjusted according to the question being addressed, as illustrated in Table  3 . These examples underscore that cancer-specific studies can dive deep into the nuances of one cancer type (often revealing fine-grained subtypes or mechanisms) while pan-cancer analyses leverage breadth to identify overarching principles and shared biomarkers. Despite these promising demonstrations, it bears emphasis that the vast majority of the applications surveyed above have not yet been implemented in routine clinical practice. As recently highlighted in the context of spatial omics in breast oncology, standardised workflows, data interoperability, and prospective clinical validation remain critical prerequisites before such approaches can be meaningfully integrated into oncological decision-making  38  . Consequently, the following sections review the current technical limitations and proposed solutions, followed by a discussion addressing clinical research challenges to precision oncology translation.     Technical challenges and future directions  Many of these challenges and limitations are active areas of research and overcoming them will define the next stages of the field.   Batch effects and confounders  Batch effects mainly reflect the variability of data generation methods, including differences in sample preparation (e.g., frozen versus fixed tissue), extraction protocols for RNA or DNA, the production of NGS libraries, and the sequencing technologies themselves, which can lead to misleadingly optimistic performance if not explicitly controlled. A landmark example is the presence of technical artifacts in TCGA germline data. Buckley et al.  39   demonstrated that Whole-Genome Amplification (WGA), which was disproportionately applied to certain cohorts (e.g., ovarian cancer and acute myeloid leukemia), led to an artificially increased burden of loss-of-function indel calls. Without rigorous control for data-generation protocols, an AI model could inadvertently learn to associate WGA-induced noise with specific cancer types or patient outcomes. Several methods have been proposed to limit their effect such as (1) training vs test data splits by acquisition center (e.g., leave-one-center-out or external cohort validation) rather than random sample-level splits to estimate realistic generalization; (2) harmonization at the measurement level using established tools, such as ComBat  40   for array/normalized data, or ComBat-seq  41   for RNA-seq counts; and (3) systematic audits for measured confounders such as age or prior treatment, including covariate–batch association tests, and sensitivity analyses. It is however crucial to ensure that harmonization has not removed true biological signal, for instance by visualizing distributions and running downstream biological checks before and after correction. While harmonization ensures that the available data is technically consistent, it does not account for the inherent incompleteness of clinical datasets.    Missing data  Multi-omics data can suffer from missing values. It is common that not all modalities are measured for every patient. AI models must therefore be designed to either impute missing modalities or maintain robustness despite their absence. Various strategies have been explored, like cross-modal imputation using deep generative models (using one or more omics to predict another), at the risk of generating statistically plausible but biologically inaccurate data (imputation bias)  42  . Another approach is to define the structure of the model with this in mind. For instance, explicit modality masking allows the model to predict from arbitrary subsets of modalities  43  . The Mixture-of-Experts (MoE)  44   is another strategy, where different models (experts) are trained depending on the available modalities, and in the prediction phase, samples are routed to the most informative experts when a modality is absent. In a single-cell multi-omics framework, this approach is robust and accurately predicts missing modalities by cross-modal generation  45  . Finally, researchers should perform systematic ablation (“drop-one-omic” and single-omic tests) on held-out data to quantify the marginal utility of each omic, and to report the resulting performance degradation. These measures can provide both operational robustness to incomplete assays and transparent reporting of how missingness affects predictive accuracy. Successfully implementing these models requires more than mathematical innovation, it demands a physical and computational framework capable of handling such complex tasks in real-time.    Bioinformatics and IT infrastructure  Integrating multi-omics data into clinical workflows requires robust bioinformatics infrastructure. Clinical labs need pipelines to collect, process, and integrate multi-omics data in a timeframe compatible with treatment decisions (a matter of weeks). Some institutions have started building “data lakes” where genomic, transcriptomic, and proteomic data for a patient are stored in unified databases accessible to analysis tools, like the MOSAIC atlas project for multi-omics spatial omics  46  . Moreover, data analysts and powerful computing clusters are not available in every hospital. Centralized bioinformatics structures that process data from multiple cancer centers may therefore be necessary to form population-scale cohorts.    Scaling to population-level  It is indeed essential to overcome the aforementioned “curse of dimensionality”, and to resolve the full spectrum of molecular and phenotypic tumor heterogeneity. Although TCGA provides thousands of samples, larger world-wide datasets for multi-omics may only emerge through widespread clinical implementation or shared initiatives. Efforts like the AACR Project GENIE  47   and various national precision oncology programs are working to generate more multi-omics data on clinically treated patients, which will be crucial for AI model training and validation. Lastly, the high cost of these technologies remains a major barrier to data generation. This is particularly true in regions where they are not widely available, and in clinical settings where multi-omics profiling is not part of routine care and must therefore be financed by research laboratories or by patients themselves. To overcome these geographic and institutional barriers, Federated Learning (FL) has emerged as a strategic solution: Federated learning  48   allows model training across multiple institutions’ data without physical pooling due to privacy and data governance regulations. It has been studied for single-omic in oncology  49   and multi-omics in other fields  50  . It might become important to leverage data at scale while preserving patient confidentiality. Efforts are underway to federate multi-omics analyses across research centers, using AI to adjust for batch and site differences so that a model trained in one hospital works in another. Even with access to massive, multi-centric datasets, the ‘black-box’ nature of the resulting models remains a significant barrier to clinical adoption, as physicians require transparent reasoning to justify treatment changes.    Interpretability and knowledge integration  The black-box nature of deep models is a barrier to clinical adoption. There is a push toward explainable AI (XAI) in multi-omics. Inherently interpretable pathway-guided architectures, like DeepPathNet  51  , embed known pathways in the model structure, so that the output can be interpreted in terms of pathway activation. Another approach is Concept Bottlenecks, where the model learns to predict specific concepts (e.g., inflammation pathway activation) and then use them to make the final prediction  52  . Other XAI methods that can be applied to various deep learning models include Integrated Gradients  53  , DeepLift  54  , or SHAP values  55   previously introduced. They quantify which input features are most important for a given output, and can provide visual analytics that allow clinicians and researchers to explore the model’s reasoning – such as interactive networks highlighting which multi-omics features drive a prediction. It is however key to differentiate the predictive correlations that these models learn (e.g. “mutation of gene A correlates with expression of gene B”) from causal relationships (e.g. “mutation of gene A causes expression of gene B”) which requires additional investigation to be established. To this end, causal AI for multi-omics  56   is gaining traction, by moving beyond correlations and leveraging single-cell perturbation data, such as in Perturb-CITE-seq  57  , to link specific genetic perturbations to transcriptomic and proteomic outcomes and infer actual causal relationships, thereby rendering interpretation more straightforward.    Generalizability and reproducibility  A model trained on one cohort may not directly transfer to another due to technical differences and population heterogeneity. Yates & Van Allen note reproducibility as a key challenge – simpler models sometimes generalize better than complex ones if data are limited  58  . The community is addressing this by assembling larger diverse datasets that could be used for external validation (Table  2 ). Ultimately, multi-omics AI models might need to be adapted to specific contexts (e.g., a model fine-tuned for a certain hospital’s assays). Continuous learning frameworks, where models are updated with new data while maintaining validation performance, will be crucial as more data accumulate. There is also the aspect of computational reproducibility – ensuring that code and models are published openly. The best practices are summarized as the FAIR principles (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable and Reusable)  59  . Most multi-omics AI studies now share their code on GitHub or provide notebooks, and journals are encouraging or mandating this. Best practices include containerization or workflow encapsulation (e.g., via Docker  60  ) and the explicit reporting of random seeds for stochastic algorithms. This will help others reproduce and build upon results, accelerating progress. As we establish these standards for current multi-omics assays, the field continues to evolve, introducing high-resolution modalities that present entirely new dimensions of complexity.    Emerging data types and modalities  The definition of “multi-omics” keeps expanding. We now have spatial transcriptomics  61   that combines expression with 2D location data, and sometimes corresponding digital pathology slides, single-cell multi-omics  62   where multiple modalities are measured in the same cell, microbiome omics  63   such as metagenomics and meta-transcriptomics of microbes, etc. Each presents new integration challenges, and these biomarkers may not be transferable to more accessible modalities (e.g., a spatial-transcriptomics-defined immune cell distribution in a tumor may be complex to implement in classical pathology slides). Single-cell multi-omics integration is a burgeoning subfield in oncology. Methods like totalVI  64   and multi-omics autoencoders are used to integrate single-cell RNA and ATAC data  65  , or RNA and epitope data (CITE-seq) from the same cells. These methods will inform bulk tumor analysis, for example by enabling models that account for tumor microenvironment composition via deconvolution algorithms, or that integrate patient bulk data with reference cell signatures. However, this translation must account for “signal dilution”, where rare clones identified at single-cell resolution become undetectable in bulk averages. Spatial omics integration with imaging is another frontier  66  : AI models are being crafted to integrate pathology images with spatial transcriptomics, and more recently protein expression (DBiT-seq  67  ) effectively merging molecular data with histology in three dimensions. This could revolutionize how we understand heterogeneity within a tumor and how we guide biopsy and treatment decisions regionally. Future integrative AI approaches will likely incorporate spatial and temporal dimensions, using longitudinal multi-omics to model tumor evolution, treatment resistance  68  , and relapse  69  . These methods are already becoming central to cancer research. However, the clinical translation of these technologies may be constrained by their high cost, limited availability in cancer centers, and the complexity of data analysis. They are therefore often used as fine-grained biomarker discovery approaches, to be transferred to more accessible data modalities in subsequent steps.    Overall  The primary challenges of the field include addressing data accessibility and standardization, as comprehensive multi-omics profiles are rarely routine in clinical practice, developing robust bioinformatics infrastructure for timely clinical data processing, and ensuring model generalizability across diverse patient cohorts. Current efforts to tackle these limitations include international consortiums for data generation. Furthermore, efforts in XAI are crucial to increase clinician trust by moving beyond black-box correlations and providing pathway-based biological interpretability of model predictions. These ongoing developments, coupled with the integration of emerging data modalities like spatial and single-cell multi-omics, are rapidly advancing the computational foundation. The ultimate measure of success for these tools, however, is their impact on patient care, which necessitates successful real-world clinical translation. We will now detail the nature, achievements, and challenges of AI multi-omics across key clinical domains.     Real-world clinical translation  Translating multi-omics AI advances into routine clinical practice remains an ongoing challenge, even though notable progress has been made. A few AI-driven multi-omics tests are beginning to impact clinical decision-making in certain settings. For example, in oncology trials and tumor boards, it is becoming more common to review not just genomic sequencing data but also transcriptomic results for each patient  15  . AI-based decision support systems have been developed to assist molecular tumor boards: one prototype evaluated the use of multiple omics approaches, mainly at the single-cell level, to inform therapeutic response  70  . They propose treatment strategies considering multi-omics evidence. For example, a candidate drug identified through genomic profiling is prioritized only if transcriptomic data verify the expression of the target. Unlike mono-modality AI, no integrated multi-omics algorithm for cancer detection or treatment is FDA/EMA-approved for routine clinical use as of early 2026. These currently function primarily as laboratory developed tests in research settings. One of the main causes of this, beyond the novelty of such approaches, is the lack of prospective validation clinical trials.   Prospective validation  Prospective validation of AI-driven multi-omics decision-making is the gold standard for establishing generalization potential – hence the importance of clinical trials. Thus far, most multi-omics AI models have been developed on retrospective data from mainly non-metastatic tumors (e.g., TCGA) and tested in silico, raising the question of their external validity. To be implemented in clinical practices, the next phase is to embed these models into clinical trials where diagnoses or therapy choices are informed by the model, and evaluated based on patient outcomes, as done with some single-omic tools  14  . Pilot studies are underway: the WINTHER trial mentioned earlier, while not using a complex AI, demonstrated the feasibility of integrating gene expression with genomics for therapy choice in a prospective manner. Although the trial failed to meet its primary endpoint for Progression-Free Survival (PFS), its limitations (including a restricted gene panel, RNA microarrays, a low 35% therapy matching rate, and the absence of a control arm) offer critical lessons for designing more effective multi-omics clinical trials  28  . Regulatory approval necessitates demonstrated clinical benefit, such as improved survival endpoints like PFS or the “gold-standard” Overall Survival. Alternatively, a tool may prove its non-inferiority by matching current survival outcomes while providing added benefits such as reduced toxicity or lower costs. Another realistic outcome is the decision-impact of multi-omics tools, by measuring the proportion of patients whose treatment strategy was modified, or the reduction in time to treatment decision. A typical trial could be randomized (e.g., Molecular Tumor Board (MTB) + AI vs MTB alone), or more pragmatic (e.g., stepped-wedge approach comparing patients outcomes before and after model’s use  71  ). Finally, enrichment designs can be employed to specifically enroll patients most likely to benefit from a biomarker identified by the AI, maximizing the statistical power to detect a therapeutic effect. The field would benefit from publishing negative results too, or models that failed to generalize, in order to accelerate learning regarding the causes of translational failure. Overall, the gap between the rising number of high-performing AI models always outperforming their predecessors, and the few clinical trials validating them at the bedside has to be bridged.    Multidisciplinary collaboration  Developing clinically useful multi-omics AI requires oncologists, biologists, data scientists, and regulatory experts working together. One strategy is to involve clinicians early in AI development to focus on models that answer pressing clinical questions instead of doing integration for integration’s sake. To do so, and to promote the use of AI based tools in clinical practices, the integration of AI courses into medical education  72  , as in MD-PhD curricula and for already certified clinicians, seems essential.    Regulatory and ethical considerations  Multi-omics data often include germline genetic information raising privacy and legal concerns. They are high-dimensional enough that patient identification is a risk if data are shared inappropriately. Federated learning previously introduced may be a solution, by conserving data ownership and privacy while allowing the training of AI models  48  . Another approach is to exploit the generative capabilities of modern AI models to create synthetic data, thereby addressing the under-representation of specific populations, and increasing dataset size  73  . An ongoing and frequently raised question by patients concerns the return of their multi-omics results. Indeed, while patients have rights regarding their medical data, the interpretation of multi-omics data is complex and rarely clinically validated  74  . Ensuring compliance with data protection laws and obtaining informed consent for AI analysis of comprehensive molecular data is essential. On the regulatory side, AI models that assist in diagnosis or treatment are considered medical devices (software as a device) and thus subject to regulatory approval. Agencies like the FDA and EMA have shown willingness to consider complex diagnostic algorithms, as seen with some AI pathology and genomic tests, and issued guidance on AI in medical devices: FDA’s “Good Machine Learning Practice for Medical Device Development: Guiding Principles”  75   and EMA’s “Reflection paper on the use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in the medicinal product lifecycle”  76  . They emphasize the need for transparency, performance validation, and monitoring for bias. The FDA also provides guidelines for model retraining after approval: “Predetermined Change Control Plan”  77  . Moreover, a multi-omics AI model could inadvertently encode biases, for instance, if training data over-represents certain ancestries or tumor subtypes. The TCGA dataset is indeed composed of predominantly localized tumors from Western populations, and models trained with it may be less accurate for other patient groups. Careful curation of training data and post-market surveillance of AI recommendations is needed to ensure equitable performance. Finally, the substantial computational power required to train and utilize large AI models contributes to a significant carbon footprint. This underscores a strategic shift toward resource-efficient architectures, and the pragmatic advantage of fine-tuning pre-trained foundation models over de novo training.    Interpretability and trust  These are critical points if AI tools are to be accepted by clinicians, as they are understandably cautious about acting on a “black box” AI recommendation, especially one derived from thousands of molecular features. Therefore, XAI techniques are being employed to accompany predictions with interpretable explanations  78  . For example, a multi-omics survival model might highlight that a patient’s poor prognosis prediction is driven mainly by a high proliferation gene expression signature and a certain protein marker being elevated, information that oncologists can interpret and verify against their knowledge. Given the distribution of “importance” among numerous features, using functional annotation tools such as gene ontology enrichment analyses to rapidly interpret what types of genes are used by the model can be an efficient summarizing method. These approaches are often a trade-off between completeness and readability of interpretability outputs. They also have intrinsic technical pitfalls, as they can still overlook correlated features, masking biologically relevant signal, be subject to attribution instability, where importance scores change when the model is trained multiple times, or learn from batch-correlated features (batch leakage  39  ). A survey among oncologists emphasizes that improving the interpretability of AI models is essential for clinical adoption  79  , suggesting that incorporating known biology such as pathway-based features, and providing user-friendly visualizations of results will help clinicians trust and effectively use these tools. Moreover, quantifying the ‘confidence’ of a prediction with a score, a percentage or a confidence interval, could help clinicians estimate the impact it should have on their decision. Over time, if success stories keep emerging, and AI multi-omics tests outperform standard tests for certain predictions, confidence may be expected to build.    User-friendly reports and AI agents  AI-powered decision support systems in oncology that routinely incorporate multi-omics could manifest as an “omics dashboard” in electronic medical records. It would summarize the patient’s multi-omics profile (with top pathway drivers, key molecular alterations, and confidence bounds when available) and highlight actionable insights (e.g., “high FGFR3 expression and mutation – consider FGFR inhibitor” or “mismatch repair deficient signature – candidate for immunotherapy”) like the one previously introduced in a melanoma multi-omics tumor board  70  . AI agents are a new class of models that can actively retrieve information and interact with external tools such as coding environments. They may provide biological insights in research settings; for example, AI-HOPE  80   translates researchers’ natural language queries into executable code and performs integrative analyses on clinical and genomic data, returning results such as stratified survival analyses. These models may also open new avenues for generating reports that include treatment recommendations - and their justification - potentially grounded in multi-omics integration. Conclusion  Overall, integrating cancer multi-omics with AI has yielded biological insights and predictive capabilities unattainable with single data modalities. We are witnessing rapid progress in methods, accumulating evidence of their utility in research settings. The rapid expansion of multi-omics datasets along with the decreasing cost of sequencing is another encouraging sign for its future clinical implementation. The limitations to clinical translation of these approaches - data, cost, interpretability, and prospective validation – are active research areas, and the potential reward is substantial: more precise, data-driven oncology that leverages the full breadth of molecular information to benefit each individual patient. With ongoing innovation and collaboration, AI-driven multi-omics integration stands to become a cornerstone of precision cancer medicine, bridging the gap from bench to bedside in the era of big data and advanced AI. evidence_text: RegFormer: a single-cell foundation model powered by gene regulatory hierarchies. Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) enables high-resolution profiling of cellular diversity, but current computational models often fail to incorporate regulatory priors, handle data sparsity, or efficiently process long gene sequences. Here, we present RegFormer, a foundation model that integrates gene regulatory networks (GRNs) with Mamba-based state-space modeling, overcoming the scalability and context-length limitations of Transformer architectures. RegFormer encodes each gene through dual embeddings, a value embedding for quantitative expression and a token embedding for regulatory identity, organized within a GRN-guided gene order to capture both expression dynamics and hierarchical regulation. Pretrained on 25 million human single cells spanning 45 tissues and diverse biological contexts, RegFormer achieves superior scalability and biological fidelity. Across comprehensive benchmarks, it consistently outperforms state-of-the-art single-cell foundation models (scGPT, Geneformer, scFoundation, and scBERT), delivering higher clustering accuracy, improved batch integration, and more precise cell type annotation. RegFormer also reconstructs biologically coherent GRNs, accurately models transcriptional responses to genetic perturbations, and enhances drug response prediction across cancer cell lines. By combining regulatory priors with efficient long-sequence Mamba modeling, RegFormer establishes a biologically grounded and scalable framework for single-cell representation learning, enabling deeper mechanistic insight into gene regulation and cellular state transitions.

Illuminating cell states by a comprehensive and interpretable single cell foundation model. Advances in single-cell sequencing have enabled AI-driven foundation models with powerful data representation. However, their practical use is limited by real-world data sparsity, heterogeneity, and poor interpretability. To overcome these, we introduce CellVQ. To enhance generalizability, we incorporate a large-scale single-cell dataset comprising 68 million cells, model parameters totaling 500 million, and challenging pretraining tasks. Notably, we introduce a Single-Cell Discretization (SCD) module that effectively represents cell embeddings, addressing data heterogeneity. For improved interpretability, the SCD module transforms high-dimensional and sparse single-cell data into a "cell code," facilitating recognition and analysis. Additionally, we also present CellVQ-Graph, a plug-and-play tool that integrates CellVQ's features with multimodal data (genes, cell communication, annotations) to build a knowledge graph for biological discovery. Extensively evaluated, CellVQ outperforms strong baselines in all downstream tasks, and also uncovered intriguing biological phenomena with compelling explanations. CellVQ aspires to serve as a truly applicable and generalizable AI tool for the cell biology community. Introduction  Cells, as the fundamental units of life, though tiny, execute a remarkable diversity of essential functions crucial for maintaining human health  1 , 2  . The discovery of cells by Robert Hooke through his microscope captivated scientists, prompting an enduring fascination with their complexity and intricacies, and initiating a quest to uncover the secrets of cellular life. Historically, during the microscopy era, biologists primarily speculated about cells at the microimaging level, where observations were largely confined to their morphology, activity, and interactions. This limitation impeded deeper investigations into the complexities of cellular states. However, with the advent of the post-genomic era, a paradigm shift has emerged toward a molecular understanding of cell states, highlighting the myriad factors that influence them  3  . A significant international initiative, the Human Cell Atlas Project  4  , was launched in 2017 to establish “an open, comprehensive reference map of the molecular state of cells in healthy human tissues.” This project employs single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq)  5 , 6   techniques and has inspired similar endeavors focusing on well-studied animal models  7 , 8   and patient-derived tissue samples  9   across a diverse range of diseases. In addition to RNA sequencing, other omics technologies, such as single-cell ATAC sequencing (scATAC-seq)  10 , 11   for chromatin accessibility and proteomics, have been employed to comprehensively analyze cell states. Concurrently, the availability of sequenced single-cell data has surged to tens of millions, presenting a significant opportunity for the application of AI-based methods in cell biology.  Leveraging large-scale scRNA-seq data, several deep learning-based methods have emerged to learn informative cell representations through pretraining on extensive datasets. For instance, scBERT  12   employs a bidirectional transformer architecture  13   to pretrain on unlabeled scRNA-seq data, subsequently fine-tuning for specific tasks. Similarly, scGPT  14   utilizes a generative pretrained transformer trained on a repository of over 33 million cells, demonstrating robust performance in both generative and representation tasks. scFoundation  15   adopts an asymmetric encoder-decoder transformer to conduct read-depth-aware modeling pretraining on 50 million transcriptomic profiles. Additionally, scPRINT  16   focuses on gene network inference by interpreting the attention matrix generated by its transformer, which is pretrained on 50 million cells. Collectively, these models leverage large-scale single-cell data to learn robust cell representations and exhibit impressive performance across various downstream tasks. Despite these advancements, emerging evidence indicates notable generalizability limitations of these foundation models  17 , 18  . These limitations can be categorized into three primary aspects: (1) Sparsity of Single-Cell Data  19  : In scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq datasets, only a subset of genes or regions is expressed or captured, resulting in a substantial amount of zero gene expression. This sparsity challenges the model’s capacity to extract compact and rich information from high-dimensional data. (2) Heterogeneity of Single-Cell Data  17 , 18  : Single-cell data are generated by various institutes using different sequencing, processing, and normalization methods. This diversity leads to significant variations in the sequenced genes and expression scales, complicating the generalization of single-cell foundation models. (3) Poor interpretability of Foundation Models: These models contain a vast number of parameters and exhibit high complexity. While they are capable of generating informative gene and cell representations, the high-dimensional and continuous nature of these representations renders them challenging for biological scientists to comprehend.  We present CellVQ, a comprehensive and interpretable single-cell foundation model. CellVQ innovatively integrates a Single-Cell Discretization (SCD) module into the single-cell foundation model. This module utilizes a unified cell codebook to transform the cell representation into a cell code and uses an SCD cell embedding derived from the cell codebook to represent the cell corresponding to the code. CellVQ employs an encoder-SCD-decoder architecture, encompassing 511 million parameters and pretrained on over 68 million single-cell data points. The model incorporates multiple pretraining tasks at both the cell and gene levels. At the cell level, the task involves predicting cell properties such as type, tissue, age, sex, and disease. At the gene level, we implement a cell-gene-prompt (CGP)-based Zero-Inflated Negative Binomial (ZINB) prediction task  20 , 21  , which effectively enhances cell representation and captures gene co-expression patterns, and addresses the high sparsity of the data. Notably, our findings and prior evidence  22 , 23   indicate that the SCD module effectively mitigates data heterogeneity and batch effects  24  . By utilizing the unified representation and cell codes from the cell codebook, the SCD module represents cells from different batches, leading to significant enhancements in both generalization and interpretability. Additionally, we introduce a lightweight model, CellVQ-Graph, designed to integrate multi-omic and multimodal data to construct a Graph Knowledge Network (GKN). By leveraging the representations generated by CellVQ, the plug-and-play functionality of CellVQ-Graph facilitates the transfer of insights to diverse real-world datasets, enabling the discovery of biological knowledge through the GKN.  We evaluated the performance of our models across multiple tasks, categorized into prediction and analysis tasks. In the realm of prediction tasks, which encompass cell clustering, annotation, property prediction, gene and drug perturbation prediction, as well as drug response prediction, CellVQ demonstrates significant advancements over other foundation models such as scGPT and scFoundation. For analysis tasks, we integrated CellVQ and CellVQ-Graph into four distinct tasks: cell state discovery, gene discovery, gene regulatory network (GRN) analysis  25 , 26  , and multimodal analysis. These analyses highlight the unique advantages of our models in terms of interpretability. We contend that the introduction of CellVQ and CellVQ-Graph effectively bridges the gap between AI models and biological research, thereby enhancing the understanding of cellular and genetic mechanisms.    Results   Overview of CellVQ  Figure  1  illustrates the comprehensive framework of CellVQ. Figure  1 a depicts the model architecture of CellVQ. For the encoder input, we first append a [Count] token, representing the sum of gene expression values. We then extract expression values from gene expression profiles and randomly sample genes as input for the encoder. The sampling rates follow a uniform distribution  U (0.5, 0.8) to facilitate multi-scale information extraction. These sampled gene expressions are processed through an embedding module comprising three components: gene expression embedding, gene position (gene id) embedding, and gene ontology embedding. The gene expression embedding transforms continuous gene expression scalars into learnable high-dimensional vectors, while the gene position embedding encodes gene identification(gene names, like  DLK1 ,  CLU ). The Gene Ontology embedding module incorporates prior knowledge from Gene Ontology  27   to model gene co-expression, which is updated during training. Subsequently, these embeddings are passed through 12 Transformer layers to refine the gene embeddings, leading to the generation of a cell embedding via a pooling method. We input the gene embeddings into an SCD module to obtain SCD gene embeddings, while the cell embedding is quantized to produce an SCD cell embedding and a cell code, which serves as a data-driven identifier for the cell. The SCD cell embedding is utilized for multiple property predictions to train both the encoder and the SCD module. In the decoder component, we initialize all expression values to zero, allowing the embedding module to focus solely on capturing gene position and ontology information. We replace the decoder embeddings at the corresponding gene positions with SCD gene embeddings as prompts, setting the SCD cell embedding at the “Count” token for the cell prompt. These processed decoder embeddings are subsequently input into six Performer  28   layers and a Zero-Inflated Negative Binomial (ZINB) predictor to estimate the ZINB distribution for each gene expression value. We select predictions for non-sampled genes and a subset of non-expressed genes (equal to or fewer than the non-sampled) to compute the ZINB loss against the corresponding gene expression values, facilitating the training of the entire model. Further architectural details are provided in Section 4.    Fig. 1   The overall framework of CellVQ.   a  The model architecture of CellVQ. Token c denotes the `All Count', which is the sum of gene expression values.  b  CellVQ is applied in six prediction tasks.  c  The integration of CellVQ and CellVQ-Graph.  d  CellVQ and CellVQ-Graph are applied in four analysis tasks. A circle, triangle, and pentagram represent a cell, gene (or chromatin region), and an attribute, respectively.                   Figure  1 b visualizes the six prediction tasks implemented using CellVQ, including cell clustering, annotation, property prediction, gene perturbation prediction, and drug response prediction. All prediction tasks were performed under the zero-shot setting without fine-tuning. Additionally, we provide the comprehensive ablation study of CellVQ in Supplementary Section  1 ; and the results of batch correction tasks to demonstrate that CellVQ effectively resolves data heterogeneity in Supplementary Section  3 . We also showcase the extensive experiments of CellVQ on Cell clustering and cell type annotation tasks, comparing with broader baselines on TS2  29 , 30   datasets in Supplementary Section  2 .  Figure  1 c illustrates the integration of CellVQ and CellVQ-Graph. CellVQ-Graph receives representations from CellVQ and combines these with other omics and modal data, such as scATAC-seq and property annotation data, to construct the graph knowledge network. Figure  1 d presents four analysis tasks: cell state discovery, gene discovery, GRN analysis, and multimodal analysis. In all analysis tasks, we only utilize the embeddings provided by CellVQ pre-training model and train CellVQ-Graph on the corresponding dataset. Comprehensive details regarding the datasets and experiments are available in the Supplementary Sections  12  and  13 .    Representation improvement on cell clustering  The cell clustering task is fundamental to single-cell analysis. By clustering cells based on similar gene expression profiles, biologists can achieve cell type identification, analyze cell heterogeneity, conduct drug response studies, and discover biomarkers. Additionally, the effectiveness of the clustering task serves as a rigorous test of representation quality; superior cell representations yield higher accuracy and clearer visualizations.  To evaluate this, we applied CellVQ to three scRNA-seq datasets, specifically the Pancreas  14  , Zheng 68K  31  , and Segerstolpe  32   datasets, all of which include cell-type annotation labels. We compared results with raw gene expression, GeneCompass  33  , scBERT  12  , UCE  34  , CellFM  35  , scGPT, and scFoundation. For each method, we derived cell representations and employed the K-means algorithm for clustering based on cell type labels. We utilized several evaluation metrics: Accuracy, Normalized Mutual Information  36   (NMI), Adjusted Rand Index  37   (ARI), and Silhouette Coefficient  38   (SIL). Among these metrics, Accuracy, NMI, and ARI assess whether cells of the same type are clustered together, while SIL measures the closeness of samples to their respective clusters and their separation from other clusters. Thus, these metrics provide a comprehensive evaluation of CellVQ’s performance in clustering tasks.  Figure  2 a displays the overall performance of the eight methods across the three datasets. The metrics for CellVQ on the Pancreas dataset are as follows: NMI (0.9424), ARI (0.9492), and SIL (0.4636). For the Zheng dataset, the metrics are: Accuracy (0.5127), NMI (0.6000), ARI (0.3904), and SIL (0.2050). The Segerstolpe dataset yields: Accuracy (0.7401), NMI (0.8720), ARI (0.6824), and SIL (0.6288). CellVQ achieves exceptional performance across all datasets and metrics, particularly in the Pancreas dataset, where Accuracy, NMI, and ARI exceed 0.94, with a SIL of 0.4636. In contrast, other methods report NMI below 0.89, ARI below 0.77, and SIL below 0.34. Furthermore, in the Segerstolpe dataset, CellVQ outperforms other methods across all metrics, leading by 0.23 in NMI, 0.30 in ARI, and 0.5 in SIL. CellVQ enhances bulk-level RNA-seq data representation  Bulk RNA-seq  41   data is generated by extracting RNA from a mixed population of cells, rather than from individual cells, and subsequently sequencing it. This approach provides the average gene expression profile of all cells in the sample, in contrast to single-cell data, which offers single-cell resolution. Although bulk RNA-seq data lacks the cellular heterogeneity captured by single-cell sequencing, it remains essential for numerous practical applications, such as tumor and drug response research, due to its more established and cost-effective experimental and analytical processes. To evaluate whether CellVQ can enhance the representation of bulk RNA-seq data and further demonstrate its generalization capabilities, we applied CellVQ to two drug response prediction tasks: drug response classification and cancer drug response prediction.  The goal of drug response classification is to predict the sensitivity of a patient or cell to a specific drug based on various biological characteristics, such as gene expression. CellVQ enhance gene representation for perturb-seq data  Perturb-seq  46   is a high-throughput experimental technique that integrates CRISPR-based gene perturbation  47   with scRNA-seq. This method enables researchers to systematically investigate the effects of gene perturbations on gene expression at the single-cell level, thereby facilitating a deeper understanding of cellular functions, gene interactions, and biological pathways.  To evaluate whether CellVQ enhances gene-level representation and captures gene co-expression during pretraining, we applied CellVQ to three perturb-seq datasets: Adamson  48  , Norman  49  , and Dixit  46  , focusing on gene perturbation prediction tasks. We combined CellVQ with an advanced model known as GEARS  50   for predicting single-cell-resolution perturbations. Gene Regulatory Network Analysis with CellVQ-Graph  Studying gene-gene interactions is a critical step in understanding GRN  26  . These networks regulate gene expression levels and timing, thereby influencing cellular function and behavior. Investigating GRNs is essential for elucidating biological processes, understanding disease mechanisms, and developing therapeutic strategies.  We propose that CellVQ-Graph serves not only as a valuable tool for studying gene interactions through its graph attention module but also visualizes these interactions at the cell state level via the CellVQ SCD module. To validate this, we applied the CellVQ-Graph model to the human pancreas cell dataset, focusing on Acinar cells.  Figure  8 a displays the gene-gene interactions predicted by the CellVQ-Graph for an acinar cell. We encoded the genes from the acinar cell and obtained their corresponding codes by SCD module, as SCD module can also embed the gene embeddings into a code. Two genes are defined as connected if they share the same code. We selected highly expressed genes in acinar cells to visualize their interactions, as shown in Fig.  8 a. The gene regulatory network predicted by CellVQ-Graph is biologically meaningful. For instance, CellVQ-Graph predicts an interaction between the  PRSS1  and  CTRB1  genes.  PRSS1  encodes trypsinogen, a major digestive enzyme in the pancreas, while  CTRB1  encodes a trypsin inhibitor that regulates the activity of pancreatic digestive enzymes and prevents their premature activation in alveolar cells. The expression and function of these genes are interdependent; overexpression of  PRSS1  may result in insufficient inhibition by  CTRB1 , thereby increasing the risk of cellular injury. The importance of these genes in the Gene Ontology database is rated at 0.5, indicating a significant biological relevance. Multi-modal analysis with CellVQ-Graph  For cell state identification, manual annotations such as cell types and tissue characteristics are critical informational factors that contribute to the construction of cell states. However, prior research has predominantly concentrated on analyzing scRNA-seq or scATAC-seq data, often neglecting the influence of these properties. To address this gap, we introduce a scalable approach that employs a language tokenizer which introduced by BioGPT  89  . It include 42,383 tokens and can convert the text of single cell properties describtion into one or a seires of tokens, effectively embedding these properties within a unified graph framework. This enables a comprehensive examination of how these annotated properties influence cell states.  To evaluate the significance of these properties, we validated CellVQ-Graph using a sampled pretraining dataset comprising 10,000 cells, categorized into 167 cell types, sourced from 30 different tissues and involving 465 donors. This dataset enables us to consider various properties, including tissue type, disease state, age, and sex, and to investigate their respective influences on cell states.  Figure  9 a–d depict the distribution of attention weights for Tissue, Disease, Age, and Sex across nine distinct states. Our analysis reveals that tissue annotations are the most influential factors among these properties, with attention weights ranging from 0 to 0.25 and an average attention weight of 0.12 across the states. Additionally, Fig.  9 e illustrates a strong correlation between cell distribution and tissue types, indicating that cells sharing the same tissue tend to cluster together in specific areas of the visualization. Discussion  In this paper, we address the significant limitations of current single-cell foundation models, namely their restricted generalizability for heterogeneous and sparse data, as well as their lack of interpretability. These limitations severely hinder the application of single-cell foundation models in real-world scenarios. We introduce our models, termed CellVQ and CellVQ-Graph. CellVQ is a single-cell foundation model comprising 513 million parameters, integrating a transformer encoder, a vector quantization module, and a performer decoder. It is pretrained on 68 million single-cell data points across multiple pretraining tasks. CellVQ-Graph serves as a lightweight and plug-and-play algorithm for CellVQ, effectively leveraging its representations for biological analysis and discovery within single-cell multi-omic and multi-modal datasets.  We applied CellVQ and CellVQ-Graph across various tasks, categorized into prediction and analysis. In the domain of prediction tasks, which include cell clustering, annotation, property prediction, gene and drug perturbation prediction, as well as drug response prediction, CellVQ demonstrates significant advancements over other foundation models, such as scGPT and scFoundation.  For analysis tasks, we integrated CellVQ and CellVQ-Graph into four distinct objectives: cell state discovery, gene discovery, GRN analysis, and multimodal analysis. These analyses underscore the unique advantages of our models in terms of interpretability. We assert that the introduction of CellVQ and CellVQ-Graph effectively bridges the gap between AI models and biological research, thereby enhancing our understanding of cellular and genetic mechanisms while facilitating drug discovery.  Looking ahead, we aim to expand CellVQ to support multi-omics pretraining. Currently, due to limitations in data scale, CellVQ has only been pretrained on a large-scale scRNA-seq dataset and fine-tuned on a scATAC-seq dataset. In the future, we plan to establish a comprehensive dataset that integrates scRNA-seq, scATAC-seq, and multiple annotations for each single cell. Subsequently, we will design a model that can effectively leverage all modal data to achieve improved representational capacity and enhanced interpretability. As prior works supported  16 , 91  , ZINB predictor effectively addresses data sparsity by combining a zero-inflation model with a negative binomial distribution. It first models additional zeros through the zero-inflation component, enabling the model to capture the high proportion of zeros in real data rather than treating them solely as outcomes of the negative binomial distribution.
