Introduction Precision medicine aims to provide personalized therapy tailored to individual patient characteristics [ 1 , 2 ]. In particular, tumors exhibit extensive genetic and phenotypic heterogeneity [ 3 – 5 ], leading to diverse drug resistance mechanisms and complicating treatment outcome prediction [ 6 – 8 ]. Advances in single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) technologies enable transcriptomic profiling at single-cell resolution, making it possible to identify different cell states and characterize intratumoral heterogeneity in detail [ 9 – 12 ]. The ability to profile thousands of individual cells from a single tissue sample has enabled the construction of large public single-cell databases, which has facilitated the development of foundation models. For example, scGPT [ 13 ] is pretrained on over 33 million cells using a generative workflow tailored for non-sequential omics data, enabling simultaneous learning of cell and gene representations via a transformer-based architecture. scRobust [ 14 ] leverages a self-supervised learning strategy that integrates contrastive learning with gene expression prediction. It also introduces a novel cell augmentation technique to better capture comprehensive gene-level representations. scFoundation [ 15 ] scales to 100 million parameters and utilizes over 50 million expression profiles for pretraining. It employs an asymmetric architecture optimized for scRNA-seq data and incorporates a read-depth-aware pretraining objective to enhance training efficiency and cross-depth generalization. These foundation models take single-cell gene expression profiles as input and generate latent cell embeddings that capture biologically meaningful cellular states learned from large-scale pretraining datasets. Because these embeddings are learned from large-scale pretraining datasets, they can provide more generalizable feature representations than models trained on a single dataset alone, thereby improving downstream tasks such as cell-type annotation, gene regulatory network inference, and perturbation response prediction. Despite large-scale single-cell databases, single-cell datasets with drug response labels have remained limited due to technical challenges. In contrast, bulk transcriptomic datasets such as Genomics of Drug Sensitivity in Cancer (GDSC) [ 16 ] and Cancer Cell Line Encyclopedia (CCLE) [ 17 ] have provided comprehensive drug sensitivity profiles across thousands of cancer cell lines. Recent studies have leveraged bulk datasets to infer drug response at the single-cell level, employing domain adaptation and transfer learning. For instance, scDEAL [ 18 ] extracts features from both bulk and single-cell datasets and utilizes the maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) loss to minimize domain shift between the two modalities. SCAD [ 19 ] considers bulk and single-cell data as source and target domains, respectively, performing domain adaptation via adversarial training using a discriminator. SSDA4drug [ 20 ] adopts a semi-supervised few-shot transfer learning approach, utilizing domain adversarial training with limited labeled samples in the single-cell domain. Although these approaches aimed to reduce the distributional gap between bulk and scRNA-seq, they did not demonstrate that transformed bulk RNA-seq confers the advantages of scRNA-seq, such as single-cell resolution analysis and the ability to leverage single-cell foundation models. Some cell-type deconvolution methods [ 21 – 25 ] are designed to estimate cell-type proportions or infer cell-type-specific gene expression profiles from bulk RNA-seq data. These methods typically rely on reference single-cell data with cell-type annotations and assume sufficient correspondence between the bulk and reference single-cell datasets, such as matched or closely related tissue contexts. In addition, their applicability can be limited when the reference single-cell data contain only a small number of cell types or lack reliable cell-type annotations. These requirements make such approaches less suitable for the single-cell drug response prediction setting considered in this study, where many datasets do not provide detailed cell-type annotations and often differ in experimental conditions, tissue contexts, or drug perturbation settings. Moreover, deconvolution methods are not primarily designed to transform each bulk RNA-seq profile into single-cell-like profiles that can be directly used as input to pretrained single-cell foundation models. In this study, we propose scStyling, a quantile-based transformation framework that maps bulk RNA-seq profiles into single-cell-like expression profiles. We refer to the transformed bulk profiles as scStyleBulk. The goal of scStyling is to reduce the distributional discrepancy between bulk and scRNA-seq profiles, thereby enabling bulk RNA-seq data to be more effectively used with pretrained single-cell foundation models without additional model training. Unlike cell-type deconvolution methods [ 24 , 25 ], scStyling does not require cell-type annotations or explicit estimation of cell-type proportions to generate single-cell-like profiles from bulk RNA-seq data. By transforming bulk RNA-seq profiles into scStyleBulk, scStyling enables the effective use of bulk data in single-cell foundation models. Consequently, these models would extract more informative biological representations from bulk RNA-seq data, leading to improved downstream predictive performance. Across 18 test datasets, applying scStyleBulk to pretrained models generally yielded better performance than benchmark methods. In addition, the transformed profiles enabled pathway-level analysis using single-cell-informed representations, revealing biological signals that were not readily detectable from the original bulk profiles. Taken together, these results suggest that scStyling provides an effective framework for bridging bulk and single-cell transcriptomic data and expands the utility of pretrained single-cell foundation models to bulk RNA-seq profiles. Materials and methods Datasets Bulk data collection and preprocessing For the training dataset, we collected bulk transcriptomic and drug response data from the Genomics of Drug Sensitivity in Cancer (GDSC)[ 16 ]. RMA-normalized basal gene expression profiles and IC50 values were downloaded from the GDSC bulk download portal ( https://www.cancerrxgene.org/downloads/bulk_download ). The final GDSC dataset comprised 15,381 genes across 961 cancer cell lines with available drug response labels. Single-cell data collection and preprocessing We assessed the generalizability of our framework using 18 single-cell test datasets covering 13 drugs across diverse cancer types and treatment conditions. These datasets were derived from seven studies obtained from the GEO repository [ 26 ]: GSE110894  [ 27 ]: Murine acute myeloid leukemia cells treated with I-BET-762 GSE112274  [ 28 ]: PC9 cell lines treated with Gefitinib GSE117872  [ 29 ]: OSCC patient-derived cell lines treated with Cisplatin GSE140440  [ 30 ]: PC3 cell lines treated with Docetaxel GSE149383 and GSE149215  [ 31 ]: PC9 cell lines treated with Erlotinib and Etoposide GSE108383  [ 32 ]: 451Lu and A375 cell lines treated with PLX4720 GSE157220  [ 33 ]: Pan-cancer drug screening data Data preprocessing was conducted using the Scanpy Python package [ 34 ]. Total counts were normalized across cells using sc.pp.normalize_total and subsequently log-transformed with sc.pp.log1p. The resulting preprocessed data served as the test set for model evaluation, whereas these preprocessing steps were not applied to scStyling. Gene selection was carried out using two strategies: the highly variable gene (HVG) and the common gene approaches. Specifically, sc.pp.highly_variable_genes was applied to select the top 2,000 HVGs, while in the common gene approach, we retained genes shared between bulk and single-cell datasets. A summary of all datasets is provided in Supplementary Table  S2 . Cell type annotation scRNA-seq datasets with cell type annotations were obtained from the CELLxGENE portal [ 35 ]. For each predefined cell type, differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were identified using the rank_genes_groups function in the Scanpy Python package [ 34 ]. In the target scRNA-seq dataset, cells were clustered using the Leiden algorithm, and DEGs were extracted for each cluster in the same manner. We assigned cell type labels to target clusters by comparing their DEG sets with those of the predefined cell types. Specifically, for each cluster, we computed Jaccard similarity scores [ 36 ] and annotated it with the most similar cell type. scStyling Overview scStyling is a quantile-based transformation framework designed to address the distributional mismatch between bulk RNA-seq and scRNA-seq data. Our approach requires two input datasets: target bulk RNA-seq data to be transformed and reference scRNA-seq data that provides the template for the transformation. scStyling consists of two main stages: (1) simulating single-cell gene expression distributions using a zero-inflated negative binomial (ZINB) model [ 37 ], and (2) mapping bulk gene expression data to the ZINB-simulated single-cell distributions through quantile-based distribution alignment. An overview of the scStyling is illustrated in Fig.  1 . Fig. 1 Overview of scStyling and drug prediction. A Workflow of scStyling. A target bulk RNA-seq profile and a reference single-cell RNA-seq profile are used, with only the genes shared between them retained. The scStyling consists of two phases: first, Zero-Inflated Negative Binomial (ZINB) modeling is applied to the reference single-cell data; second, the bulk data are aligned to the simulated single-cell distribution via a mapping module (quantile-based transformation), yielding the transformed bulk data referred to as scStyleBulk. B Mapping module. ZINB-simulated single-cell profiles are used to construct gene-wise empirical cumulative distribution functions (eCDFs). For each gene, bulk expression values are Z-normalized, converted to standard normal CDF values, and then mapped onto the corresponding intervals of the single-cell eCDF, thereby aligning bulk profiles with single-cell distribution. C Workflow of drug response prediction. Bulk and single-cell RNA-seq profiles are first prepared. Bulk profiles are optionally transformed into scStyleBulk via scStyling, and embeddings can optionally be extracted using a single-cell foundation model. A prediction model is then trained to predict binary drug response (sensitive/resistant) using either the embeddings or the original RNA-seq data as input ZINB parameter estimation using scRNA-seq data scRNA-seq data are characterized by high sparsity, overdispersion, and the presence of outliers [ 38 , 39 ]. To model these characteristics, we adopt the Zero-Inflated Negative Binomial (ZINB) distribution, which is widely used in scRNA-seq data analysis [ 40 , 41 ]. The ZINB model accounts for biological overdispersion through its negative binomial component and models technical variability, as well as excess zeros, via a zero-inflation component [ 37 , 40 ]. In our framework, this modeling facilitates more consistent gene-wise transformations by providing a unified statistical baseline. Formally, the ZINB models the probability of an observed count x as arising from two components: (i) a zero-inflation component that accounts for the excess zeros frequently observed in single-cell data, and (ii) a negative binomial component that captures the biological variability in non-zero counts [ 42 , 43 ]. The probability mass function (PMF) is given by: 1 where denotes the probability mass function of the negative binomial distribution with mean μ and dispersion parameter θ , x is the observed gene expression count, and π represents the probability of an excess zero due to dropout. Since the ZINB model requires non-negative count data as input [ 42 ], we do not apply typical preprocessing steps such as library size normalization (e.g., scaling to ) or log transformation (e.g., ). Instead, we perform parameter estimation directly on the integer read count. For each gene, we estimate the parameters by minimizing the negative log-likelihood (NLL) of the ZINB model using the L-BFGS-B algorithm [ 44 ], which supports bound-constrained optimization. We initialize parameter values by sampling from empirically chosen uniform ranges: , , and . The estimated parameters are then used to simulate single-cell gene expression profiles under the ZINB model. Quantile-based transformation For each gene i , we compute its empirical cumulative distribution function (eCDF) using ZINB-simulated single-cell expression values. The eCDF characterizes the expression distribution of gene i in the single-cell context. To align bulk expression values with these distributions, we then standardize each bulk value of gene i to have zero mean and unit variance: 2 where k denotes the index of a bulk sample, and and are the mean and standard deviation of gene i across all bulk samples. Then, the standardized values are transformed into quantile scores using the standard normal cumulative distribution function Φ : Finally, each quantile score is mapped to a discrete expression value by locating the corresponding interval in the gene-specific eCDF : 3 where denotes the sorted set of unique single-cell expression values for gene i , is the number of unique values, is the index of the corresponding interval, and by convention. The resulting transformed bulk expression profiles are referred to as scStyleBulk . Drug response prediction We apply transfer learning to predict drug responses at the single-cell level by training on bulk data and testing on single-cell datasets, thereby transferring drug response knowledge. For model inputs, two types of representations are used: (i) raw gene expression values and (ii) embeddings derived from large-scale foundation models trained on single-cell data (Fig.  1 C). Specifically, three foundation models–scRobust [ 14 ], scGPT [ 13 ], and scFoundation [ 15 ]–are utilized to exploit their capacity to encode biologically meaningful single-cell representations. For foundation model-based experiments, gene expression profiles are first provided as inputs to the pretrained foundation models, and their cell embeddings are used for downstream drug response prediction. This experimental setting enables assessment of whether scStyleBulk provides a more suitable input representation for foundation models than raw bulk expression values. The extracted embeddings are subsequently used as inputs to three benchmark prediction methods: a simple classifier, SCAD [ 19 ], and scDEAL [ 18 ]. Hyperparameter optimization is performed using five-fold stratified cross-validation on bulk RNA-seq data, with 80% of the data used for training and 20% for validation in each fold. For the simple classifier, a grid search is conducted over learning rates , hidden layer dimensions , batch sizes . For SCAD and scDEAL, hyperparameters are tuned via random search with 50 configurations per model. The best-performing models on the validation sets are then evaluated on single-cell datasets as external test sets. Model performance is assessed using F1-score, area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC), and average precision (AP). Benchmark models For the simple classifier, we implement a neural network consisting of a single hidden layer with ReLU activation and a sigmoid output layer to perform binary classification between sensitive and resistant classes. The training objective is the binary cross-entropy (BCE) loss, defined as: 4 For SCAD [ 19 ], the framework consists of a DNN-based feature extractor, drug response predictor, and domain discriminator. The feature extractor is trained on both bulk RNA-seq data (source domain) and scRNA-seq data (target domain), while the drug responses are not used for training. The domain discriminator encourages the feature extractor to generate domain-invariant representations via adversarial training. Finally, the drug response predictor is trained on domain-invariant features to infer drug sensitivity, using the BCE loss. For scDEAL [ 18 ], the framework consists of a DAE [ 45 ]-based feature extractor and a DNN-based drug response predictor. scDEAL aligns single-cell RNA-seq profiles to bulk RNA-seq distributions using Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) loss [ 46 ]. After alignment, the predictor is trained on the bulk distribution and predicts drug responses using the aligned scRNA-seq profiles. Unlike the simple classifier and SCAD, the scDEAL predictor employs cross-entropy (CE) loss as its objective function: 5 Results scStyling improves predictive performance for single-cell drug response We evaluated the effectiveness of scStyling in drug response prediction across 18 single-cell test datasets, where each test dataset was used as its corresponding reference single-cell dataset (Supplementary Table  S2 ). To this end, we compared two settings: models trained on raw bulk data and models trained on scStyleBulk data (Fig.  1 C). Three drug response prediction models—a simple classifier, SCAD [ 19 ], and scDEAL [ 18 ]—were assessed. Unlike the simple classifier, which does not account for distributional mismatch between bulk and single-cell data, SCAD and scDEAL employ domain adaptation techniques to align the distributions of the two datasets. All three models were evaluated using four types of input: bulk expression and embeddings derived from scRobust [ 14 ], scGPT [ 13 ], and scFoundation [ 15 ]. For scFoundation, embeddings were generated from genes shared between the bulk and single-cell datasets, following the same procedure as the model [ 15 ]. In contrast, inputs for scRobust, scGPT, and bulk data were restricted to the HVG2000 gene set. Table  1 and Fig.  2 show that most models trained on scStyleBulk outperformed cases using raw bulk data. The corresponding heatmaps of AUC and AP are provided in Supplementary Fig.  S1 . The use of scStyleBulk led to consistent performance improvements over the bulk expression data, with average gains of 0.04 in F1 score, 0.052 in AUC, and 0.033 in AP. Embeddings extracted from foundation models using scStyleBulk also improved performance by 0.04 in F1, 0.05 in AUC, and 0.04 in AP compared to embeddings extracted using raw bulk data. In particular, the simple classifier using scStyleBulk embeddings as input yielded the highest performance among the three benchmark models, with improvements of 0.125 in F1, 0.111 in AUC, and 0.086 in AP. In contrast, SCAD and scDEAL sometimes exhibited reduced performance when scStyleBulk embeddings were used as input, likely because their distribution alignment overly adjusted profiles that had already been transformed into scRNA-seq–like representations. The x-axis represents different modeling scenarios, where () denotes input data types and * denotes the use of embeddings from the corresponding foundation model; the y-axis shows drug–cell line pairs The gefitinib (PC9) dataset represents a highly imbalanced case, with 37 sensitive and 470 resistant samples. When using bulk expression data in PC9, the simple classifier with foundation model embeddings showed limited performance, yielding AUC values of 0.451–0.695 and AP scores of 0.071–0.217 across all models. In contrast, the use of scStyleBulk resulted in substantially improved performance, achieving AUC values of 0.810–0.959 and AP scores of 0.354–0.603, thereby providing more discriminative representations (Supplementary Fig.  S1 ). To comprehensively evaluate model performance, we performed rank-based analysis, and statistical testing was conducted using results from five-fold cross-validation. Because scDEAL consistently underperformed in F1 score, we excluded it from this analysis. The simple classifier and SCAD with foundation models were trained on bulk and scStyleBulk data, resulting in 16 cases. For each dataset–metric pair, cases were ranked from 1 to 16, and their average rank was taken as the final performance score (Supplementary Table  S3 ). The simple classifier with scGPT embeddings trained on scStyleBulk data ranked first with an average rank of 6.204 ( p < 0.005 , Cohen’s d > 0.61 ), consistent with its best performance in average scores (Table  1 ). The SCAD without foundation models using scStyleBulk data ranked second overall with an average rank of 6.407 ( p < 0.03 , Cohen’s d > 0.28 ), also consistent with its second-best performance in average scores. SCAD with scRobust embeddings, while ranking 4th overall, exhibited the significant statistical improvement when using scStyleBulk ( p < 0.001 , Cohen’s d > 0.74 ). Notably, all of the bottom five rankings were occupied by models using the bulk expression, with average ranks ranging from 9.111 to 11.056. These results demonstrate that scStyleBulk substantially improves prediction performance, particularly when combined with foundation models. Ablation study Impact of ZINB-Based eCDF estimation In scRNA-seq data, some cells have unusually large read counts or dropout events for certain genes partly due to technical variation such as sequencing depth, capture efficiency, and batch-specific effects. To reduce the influence of these artifacts, we leveraged eCDFs estimated from ZINB-simulated expression values, instead of the empirical distribution of the observed single-cell data. To evaluate the effect of using ZINB-simulated reference distributions, we additionally generated scStyleBulk using the empirical distribution of the observed single-cell data and compared its performance with that of the original ZINB-based approach. Across the 18 test datasets, the use of ZINB-based eCDFs resulted in slightly better drug response prediction performance than the empirical distribution-based approach (Supplementary Fig.  S3 ). The performance difference between the ZINB-based and empirical-distribution-based approaches was modest. One possible explanation is that extreme count values or severe zero inflation may not be prevalent in many of the test datasets, allowing the empirical distribution of the observed single-cell data to approximate the expression distribution reasonably well. Therefore, the benefit of using ZINB-simulated reference distributions may become more apparent in datasets with stronger sparsity, more pronounced count outliers, or larger technical variability. Impact of reference dataset selection To assess the effect of reference single-cell dataset selection on drug response prediction performance, we conducted cross-reference dataset experiments. Specifically, for each of the 18 drug-response datasets, we generated scStyleBulk profiles by using each available single-cell dataset as the reference dataset for scStyling, and then evaluated the resulting prediction performance. The results are summarized as a heatmap in Supplementary Fig.  S4 , where the x-axis represents the reference single-cell dataset used to transform bulk (GDSC) into scStyleBulk profile and the y-axis represents the test dataset used to evaluate the prediction model. Overall, prediction performance varied across different training-reference dataset combinations. Contrary to our initial expectation, using the same dataset for both model training and reference-based scStyling did not necessarily yield the best performance among all combinations. This result may reflect the inherent difficulty of the drug response prediction task, where the optimal reference distribution is not always determined solely by dataset identity. Nevertheless, using the matched training dataset as the reference generally showed reasonably good performance across most cases (Supplementary Table  S5 ). Comparison of scStyleBulk with single-cell-level baselines To establish an upper-bound baseline for single-cell drug response prediction, we considered a setting in which a classifier was directly trained and evaluated on single-cell transcriptomic profiles with drug response labels using five cross-validation. However, in the GSE149383 dataset, cells were clearly separated according to drug response labels in the UMAP representation (Supplementary Fig.  S5 , left). This separation was largely attributable to the label assignment scheme: single-cell transcriptomic profiles collected at day 0 were labeled as sensitive, whereas profiles collected at later time points (days 1, 2, 4, 9, and 11) were labeled as resistant (details in Supplementary file of ‘Definition of drug response labels across single-cell datasets’). Therefore, we tested the both cases with and without batch correction by ComBat [ 47 ]. Without batch correction, the classifier achieved high predictive performance, with an F1 score of 0.944 (Supplementary Fig.  S6 ). However, this result was likely inflated by the strong confounding between drug response labels and sampling time points. After batch correction, the F1 score decreased substantially to 0.524, and the UMAP visualization showed markedly reduced separation between treatment groups, with substantial mixing of cells across labels (Supplementary Fig.  S5 , right). Using the same training–test split, we generated scStyleBulk profiles from bulk RNA-seq data using either uncorrected or batch-corrected reference single-cell data. The resulting scStyleBulk profiles were used to train classifiers, which were then evaluated on the identical held-out test set. As shown in Supplementary Fig.  S6 , the classifiers trained on scStyleBulk profiles using uncorrected and batch-corrected reference data achieved F1 scores of 0.579 and 0.539, respectively. Although these values were lower than the performance of the classifier trained on uncorrected single-cell profiles (F1 score: 0.944), they were slightly higher than the batch-corrected single-cell baseline (F1 score: 0.524). Notably, the performance difference between the two scStyleBulk settings was modest, suggesting that scStyleBulk is not highly sensitive to batch correction of the reference single-cell data. These results indicate that scStyleBulk achieves performance comparable to the batch-corrected single-cell baseline. Evaluation of bulk-to-single-cell alignment by scStyling To evaluate whether scStyling successfully aligns bulk profiles with the single-cell expression space, we compared the transformed profiles (scStyleBulk) against ground-truth single-cell profiles. For that, we employed the Segerstolpe dataset [ 48 ], which consists of bulk (E-MTAB-5060) and single-cell (E-MTAB-5061) transcriptomic profiles from identical donors. Specifically, the Segerstolpe dataset consists of 2,209 single-cell profiles from six healthy donors and four patients with type 2 diabetes (T2D), as well as seven bulk RNA-seq samples from three healthy donors and four patients with T2D. To focus on the diabetic cell types, we analyzed 886 alpha, 270 beta, 197 gamma, and 114 delta cells. Since scRNA-seq and bulk RNA-seq from the same sample are rarely available in real-world applications, it is important to evaluate scStyleBulk using both internal (same-sample) and external (different-sample) single-cell references. For clarity, we denote these two settings as scStyleBulk-Internal and scStyleBulk-External profiles. For the Segerstolpe dataset, we employed the Xin dataset  [ 49 ] as the external reference. Moreover, to test whether scStyling merely imposes single-cell expression patterns regardless of an input bulk RNA-seq, we designed a control experiment. In this setting, we generated perturbed scStyleBulk-Internal profiles by gene-wise shuffling of the Segerstolpe bulk data before transformation using the Segerstolpe single-cell reference. As shown in Fig.  3 A–D, UMAP visualizations were performed by cell types in the reference single cell, scStyleBulk-Internal, scStyleBulk-External, and perturbed scStyleBulk-Internal profiles. In all cases, the reference scRNA-seq data were well clustered by donors, where we marked the centroid of each donor cluster for a representative donor-specific point. Most scStyleBulk-Internal and -External profiles were positioned near their corresponding donor-specific single-cell clusters, demonstrating that scStyling effectively extracts sample–specific features from bulk RNA profiles. Furthermore, profiles from the same donors were closely aligned regardless of the reference dataset, indicating that scStyling’s performance is robust to the choice of reference. As expected, perturbed scStyleBulk-Internal profiles did not align with any single-cell clusters, confirming that scStyling does not artificially enforce bulk profiles to match single-cell profiles. After transforming bulk RNA profiles into scStyleBulk profiles, it is essential to assess whether they retain cell type–related information. To this end, we applied scStyling to 136 bulk lung cancer cell line profiles from the GDSC dataset, using the adenocarcinoma subset of the Human Lung Atlas [ 52 ] from CELLxGENE [ 35 ] as the reference. The reference dataset consisted of 42,523 single cells annotated into 41 distinct cell types, with unclassified cells excluded. UMAP visualization showed that scStyleBulk preserved the cell-type-level structure observed in the reference single-cell data (Fig.  3 E). Specifically, scStyleBulk profiles exhibited clustering patterns and spatial arrangements that were broadly consistent with those of the reference single-cell profiles, reflecting biologically meaningful relationships among cell types. For example, ‘epithelial cell of alveolus of lung’ and ‘epithelial cell of lower respiratory tract’ were located close to each other in the UMAP spaces of both the reference single-cell and scStyleBulk profiles (Fig.  3 F). To further quantify the preservation of cell-type-level structure, we calculated pairwise Euclidean distance matrices between cell-type centroids in PCA space for both the reference single-cell and scStyleBulk datasets, and visualized the resulting matrices as heatmaps (Fig.  3 G). The heatmaps showed broadly similar patterns between the two datasets: similar cell types in the reference single-cell data tended to remain close to one another in the scStyleBulk space, whereas more distinct cell types remained separated. These results suggest that scStyleBulk retains cell-type-level relationships that are broadly consistent with those observed in the reference single-cell data. We next examined whether cell-type-specific gene expression patterns were also retained after transformation. The mast cell-specific marker MS4A2 was highly restricted to mast cell clusters in both reference and scStyleBulk profiles (Supplementary Fig.  S7 A). In contrast, COL1A2 , which is broadly expressed across multiple cell types, exhibited similar expression patterns between single-cell and scStyleBulk profiles (Supplementary Fig.  S7 B). These results indicate that scStyling could preserve cell-type-specific transcriptomic signatures. Identifying drug response–associated pathways through scStyling As bulk RNA-seq captures an average transcriptomic signal, the detection of pathway activities associated with drug response is limited. For the pathway analysis at the single cell resolution, we applied scStyling to transform clinical bulk RNA-seq profiles into multiple scStyleBulk representing distinct cell types (Fig.  4 ). Pseudo-bulk reconstruction from scStyleBulk profiles To assess whether scStyleBulk retains bulk-sample-specific transcriptomic information, we performed a pseudo-bulk reconstruction analysis. Although scStyling applies a gene-wise distributional transformation independently to each gene, the transformation is performed across the entire genes of each bulk sample. Therefore, scStyleBulk profiles may preserve multi-gene expression patterns that reflect heterogeneous contributions from multiple cell types or cellular states. Under this assumption, if the scStyleBulk profiles can be aggregated to reconstruct expression patterns similar to those of the original bulk RNA-seq profiles, it would provide indirect evidence that the transformed profiles retain bulk-level transcriptomic signatures beyond individual gene-wise distributions. Thus, we examined whether the transformed scStyleBulk profiles could be aggregated to recover pseudo-bulk profiles resembling the corresponding original bulk RNA-seq profiles. For each bulk sample and each gene, we first identified ten scStyleBulk profiles with the highest transformed expression values for that gene. These profiles were considered representative of cell states or cell types in which the corresponding gene is highly active or informative. We then used the z-score of the gene in the original bulk sample to determine the number of representative scStyleBulk profiles included in the reconstruction, with higher z-scores assigning a larger number of profiles. Specifically, the number of selected profiles was mapped to a range of 1 to 10 according to the gene-wise bulk z-score. After repeating this procedure across all genes, the selected scStyleBulk profiles were aggregated to construct a pseudo-bulk profile. To compare the reconstructed pseudo-bulk profiles with the original bulk data, the pseudo-bulk profiles were first normalized to counts per million (CPM). Both the original bulk and CPM-normalized pseudo-bulk profiles were then standardized using gene-wise z-score normalization. The reconstructed pseudo-bulk profiles showed moderate but non-trivial similarity to the original bulk profiles, with Pearson correlations ranging from 0.53 to 0.58 (Supplementary Table  S1 ). In addition, when the original bulk and reconstructed pseudo-bulk profiles were projected into a shared UMAP space, the reconstructed pseudo-bulk profiles were broadly co-localized with the corresponding original bulk profiles, occupying similar regions of the transcriptomic manifold (Supplementary Fig.  S10 ). These results do not indicate exact reconstruction of the original bulk profiles or recovery of cell-type mixture proportions. However, they suggest that scStyleBulk retains sample-specific transcriptomic information from the input bulk data in a single-cell-like representation space. Thus, despite being formulated as a gene-wise distributional transformation, scStyling can preserve bulk-level transcriptomic signatures that may reflect contributions from multiple cell types or cellular states. Conclusion In this study, we introduce scStyling, a novel framework that statistically maps bulk RNA-seq profiles onto scRNA-seq profiles, and the transformed bulk data is referred to as scStyleBulk. scStyling effectively mitigates distributional discrepancies between bulk and single-cell distributions, facilitating more reliable cross-domain knowledge transfer and improving the compatibility between bulk data and single-cell foundation models. We evaluated our approach across 18 independent single-cell test datasets for drug response prediction. Prediction models trained with scStyleBulk consistently outperformed those trained on bulk data profiles. Using embeddings of scRobust, scGPT, and scFoundation using scStyleBulk data, the models consistently achieved superior performance, demonstrating the effectiveness of scStyling. Notably, when the SCAD model was trained with embeddings of scRobust using scStyleBulk, it achieved the highest Cohen’s d values ( p < 0.001 , Cohen’s d > 0.74 ) across all test datasets while exhibiting lower standard deviations compared to bulk-based embeddings (Supplementary Table  S4 and Supplementary Fig.  S2 F). This suggests that scRobust’s contrastive learning strategy is poorly suited for averaged bulk expression profiles. In contrast, scStyleBulk captures inter-sample heterogeneity, providing representations more compatible with scRobust’s learning framework. Beyond predictive performance, we demonstrated that scStyling recovers single-cell-level information from bulk transcriptomic data. Using paired bulk and single-cell RNA-seq data from the same patients (E-MTAB-5060 and E-MTAB-5061), we observed that scStyling could capture patient-specific features. scStyling preserved cell type-specific expression patterns and facilitated identification of cell-type-related pathways. Importantly, these biological signals were entirely obscured in untransformed bulk data, underscoring the effectiveness of scStyling. Therefore, scStyling provides an effective bridge between bulk and single-cell profiles, enabling single-cell resolution of bulk data and enhancing compatibility with single-cell foundation models. Our pseudo-bulk reconstruction analysis further suggests that scStyleBulk retains bulk-sample-specific transcriptomic information while representing it in a single-cell-like form. Thus, scStyleBulk should be viewed as a bulk-informed single-cell-like representation, rather than as batch-effect-corrected bulk data or a deconvolution output. By reducing the distributional mismatch between bulk RNA-seq profiles and pretrained single-cell foundation models, scStyling can facilitate biologically informative embedding extraction and may support broader downstream analyses, including pathway-level analysis and conventional prediction tasks. evidence_text:
Leveraging single-cell foundation models for accurate survival outcome prediction.

Motivation

Foundation models trained on large-scale single-cell transcriptomes can capture rich molecular representations of cellular states, yet their potential for cancer survival prediction from bulk RNA-seq data remains largely unexplored.

Results

We applied the single-cell foundation model scFoundation to derive patient-level embeddings across 25 cancer types from TCGA and systematically evaluated their prognostic value under both cancer-specific and pan-cancer settings. To leverage complementary information, we developed an Embedding-Gene-Survival Prediction (EGSP) model that integrates foundation model embeddings with gene expression and clinical variables. EGSP achieved a mean concordance index (C-index) of 0.724 across cancers and exceeded 0.8 in seven cancer types, consistently outperforming single-modality models and existing multi-omics survival approaches. Comparative analyses showed that embeddings derived from pretrained scFoundation weights exhibited lower redundancy with gene expression while retaining complementary prognostic signals relative to pan-cancer fine-tuned embeddings. Explainable AI analyses further revealed that prognostic embeddings capture interpretable biological programs related to tumor differentiation, immune activity, and tumor-intrinsic growth, enabling transparent survival prediction at both cohort and patient levels. Overall, single-cell foundation model embeddings provide biologically meaningful and partially non-redundant survival signals that substantially improve bulk RNA-seq-based prognostic modeling.

evidence_text: PathOmCLIP: Connecting tumor histology with spatial gene expression via locally enhanced contrastive learning of Pathology and Single-cell foundation model Tumor morphological features from histology images are a cornerstone of clinical pathology, diagnostic biomarkers, and basic cancer biology research. Spatial transcriptomics, which provides spatially resolved gene expression profiles overlaid on histology images, offers a unique opportunity to integrate morphological and expression features, thereby deepening our understanding of tumor biology. However, spatial transcriptomics experiments with patient samples in either clinical trials or clinical care are costly and challenging, whereas histology images are generated routinely and available for many legacy prospective cohorts of disease progression and outcomes in well-annotated cohorts. Inferring spatial transcriptomics profiles computationally from these histology images would significantly expand our understanding of tumor biology, but paired data for training multi-modal spatial-histology models remains limited. Here, we tackle this challenge by incorporating performant foundation models pre-trained on massive datasets of pathology images and single-cell RNA-Seq, respectively, which provide useful embeddings to underpin multi-modal models. To this end, we developed PathOmCLIP, a model trained with contrastive loss to create a joint-embedding space between a histopathology foundation model and a single-cell RNA-seq foundation model. We incorporate a set transformer to gather localized neighborhood tumor architecture following contrastive training, which further enhances performance and is necessary to obtain robust results. We validate PathOmCLIP across five tumor types and achieve significant performance improvements in gene expression prediction tasks over other methods. PathOmCLIP can be applied to many archived histology images, unlocking valuable clinical information and facilitating new biomarker discoveries.

evidence_text: RegFormer: A Single-Cell Foundation Model Powered by Gene Regulatory Hierarchies Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) enables high-resolution profiling of cellular diversity, but current computational models often fail to incorporate regulatory priors, handle data sparsity, or efficiently process long gene sequences. Here, we present RegFormer, a foundation model that integrates gene regulatory networks (GRNs) with Mamba-based state-space modeling, overcoming the scalability and context-length limitations of Transformer architectures. RegFormer encodes each gene through dual embeddings, a value embedding for quantitative expression and a token embedding for regulatory identity, organized within a GRN-guided gene order to capture both expression dynamics and hierarchical regulation. Pretrained on 26 million human single cells spanning 45 tissues and diverse biological contexts, RegFormer achieves superior scalability and biological fidelity. Across comprehensive benchmarks, it consistently outperforms state-of-the-art single-cell foundation models (scGPT, Geneformer, scFoundation, and scBERT), delivering higher clustering accuracy, improved batch integration, and more precise cell type annotation. RegFormer also reconstructs biologically coherent GRNs, accurately models transcriptional responses to genetic perturbations, and enhances drug response prediction across cancer cell lines. By combining regulatory priors with efficient long-sequence Mamba modeling, RegFormer establishes a biologically grounded and scalable framework for single-cell representation learning, enabling deeper mechanistic insight into gene regulation and cellular state transitions.

evidence_text:
Scupa: single-cell unified polarization assessment of immune cells using the single-cell foundation model.

Motivation

Immune cells undergo cytokine-driven polarization in response to diverse stimuli, altering their transcriptional profiles and functional states. This dynamic process is central to immune responses in health and diseases, yet a systematic approach to assess cytokine-driven polarization in single-cell RNA sequencing data has been lacking.

Results

To address this gap, we developed single-cell unified polarization assessment (Scupa), the first computational method for comprehensive immune cell polarization assessment. Scupa leverages data from the Immune Dictionary, which characterizes cytokine-driven polarization states across 14 immune cell types. By integrating cell embeddings from the single-cell foundation model Universal Cell Embeddings, Scupa effectively identifies polarized cells across different species and experimental conditions. Applications of Scupa in independent datasets demonstrated its accuracy in classifying polarized cells and further revealed distinct polarization profiles in tumor-infiltrating myeloid cells across cancers. Scupa complements conventional single-cell data analysis by providing new insights into dynamic immune cell states, and holds potential for advancing therapeutic insights, particularly in cytokine-based therapies.

Availability and implementation

The code is available at https://github.com/bsml320/Scupa.
