evidence_text: Universal and transferable attacks on pathology foundation models using microscopic perturbations. The advent of foundation models initiated a paradigm shift in pathology and optical microscopy. However, these powerful systems also introduce vulnerabilities, making them susceptible to adversarial attacks. To shed light on these potential threats, here we introduce Universal and Transferable Adversarial Perturbations (UTAP) for pathology foundation models that reveal critical vulnerabilities. Optimized using deep learning, UTAP comprises a fixed and weak microscopic noise pattern that, when added to a pathology image, systematically disrupts the feature representation capabilities of foundation models. Therefore, UTAP induces performance drops in downstream tasks that utilize foundation models, including misclassification across a wide range of unseen data distributions. We demonstrate two key features of UTAP: (1) universality: its microscopic perturbation can be applied across diverse field-of-views independent of the dataset that UTAP was developed on, and (2) transferability: its perturbation can successfully degrade the performance of various external, black-box pathology foundation models-never seen before. These indicate that UTAP is not a dedicated attack associated with a specific foundation model or microscopy image dataset, but rather constitutes a broad threat to pathology foundation models and their applications. We evaluated UTAP across various state-of-the-art pathology foundation models on multiple datasets, causing significant drops in their performance with visually imperceptible microscopic modifications to the input images using a fixed noise pattern. The development of these potent attacks establishes a benchmark for model robustness evaluation, highlighting a need for advancing defense mechanisms to ensure the safe/reliable deployment of AI in pathology and optical microscopy.

Delineating tumor microenvironment (TME) heterogeneity enables improved prognosis and tailored treatment strategies. In this study, we propose a Multi-step Multi-modality Ensemble Survival (MMES) model for gastric cancer prognosis based on HE-stained histological images and multiplex immunohistochemistry (mIHC) data.

Methods

The MMES model employs a multi-step approach to decompose the complex overall survival (OS) prediction task into smaller, manageable subtasks, enabling the use of lightweight models at each stage. To integrate multi-modal information, the model leverages a pathology foundation model to extract tissue texture features from HE-stained images and utilizes hypergraph neural networks (HGNN) to capture spatial distribution pattern of immune-related molecules from cell-hypergraphs constructed from mIHC data. The MMES model was trained and tested using data of 456 gastric cancer patients across five batches of tissue microarrays (TMAs) from multiple centers. We further expanded the input of the MMES model from TMAs to HE-stained whole slide images (WSIs) of 354 patients in The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) gastric cancer cohort.

The integration of multi-modal data further enhances the robustness of survival prediction, achieving a 5.4 % higher C-index compared to the average performance of single-modality modeling strategies. Notably, the risk score generated by the MMES model serves as an independent prognostic indicator for gastric cancer patients. Beyond this, results on TCGA data show that the risk score extracted from WSIs is also a strong independent prognostic marker.

Conclusion

The MMES model, through multi-step modeling and the effective integration of HE-stained images and mIHC data, demonstrates significant potential as a reliable and independent prognostic tool for gastric cancer, with promising future applications in WSI-scale multimodal data analysis.

The placenta forms a critical barrier to infection through pregnancy, labor and, delivery. Acute placental inflammation in the membranes, diagnosed as Maternal Inflammatory Response (MIR), has short-term, and long-term consequences for offspring health. Digital pathology and machine learning can play an important role in understanding placental inflammation. The goal of this work is to develop machine learning models to predict pathologist-classified MIR stages from based on whole slide images (WSI) and establish early benchmarks.

We used digitized histopathology whole slide images (WSI), the UNI foundation model and the Multiple Instance Learning (MIL) framework to predict MIR from WSI images. To assess the relationship between local and systemic inflammation, we also attempt prediction of white blood cells count (WBC) and maximum fever temperature (Tmax). To analyze model performance, we built a classifier to identify inflammation in individual patches extracted from whole slide images.

Results

We were able to classify MIR with a balanced accuracy of up to 88.4% with a Cohen's Kappa (κ) of up to 0.758. Discussion

MIR staging is reasonably well predicted using MIL on WSIs. We show a weak but statistically significant correlation between histologic findings and maternal systemic inflammation. These findings could be used to improve reliability of classification and prediction of neonatal outcomes.

The density of stromal tumour-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) is a prognostic factor for patients with triple-negative breast cancer and reflects their immune response. Computational TIL assessment has the potential to assist pathologists in this labour-intensive task, because it can be quick and reproducible. However, computational TIL assessment models heavily rely on detailed annotations and use complex deep learning pipelines that pose challenges for model iterations and clinical deployment. Here, we propose and validate a fundamentally simpler deep learning-based model that is trained in only 10 min on 100 times fewer pathologist annotations.

We collected whole slide images (WSIs) with TIL scores and clinical data of 2340 patients with breast cancer, including 790 patients with triple-negative breast cancer, from three cohorts in three countries (one each in the USA, UK, and Netherlands) and three randomised clinical trials in the Netherlands. Morphological features were extracted from WSIs using a pathology foundation model. Our model, label-efficient computational stromal TIL assessment (ECTIL), directly regresses the WSI TIL score from these features. We trained ECTIL on a single cohort from The Cancer Genome Atlas (n=356, ECTIL-TCGA), on only triple-negative breast cancer samples from four cohorts (n=400, ECTIL-TNBC), and on all molecular subtypes of five cohorts (n=1964, ECTIL-combined). We computed the concordance between ECTIL and the pathologist using the Pearson's correlation coefficient (r) and computed the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) using the pathologist TIL scores split into the clinically relevant TILs-high (≥30%) and TILs-low (<30%) groups. ECTIL-TCGA showed concordance with the pathologist over five heterogeneous external cohorts (r=0·54-0·74, AUROC 0·80-0·94). ECTIL-TNBC showed a higher performance than ECTIL-TCGA on the PARADIGM cohort (r 0·64, AUROC 0·83 vs r 0·58, AUROC 0·80), and ECTIL-combined attained the highest concordance on an external test set (r 0·69, AUROC 0·85). Multivariate cox regression analyses indicated that every 10% increase of ECTIL-combined TIL scores was associated with improved overall survival (hazard ratio 0·85, 95% CI 0·77-0·93; p=0·0007), which was independent of clinicopathological variables and similar to the pathologist score (0·86, 0·81-0·92; p<0·0001).

In conclusion, our study showed that ECTIL could score TILs on haematoxylin and eosin-stained, formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded WSIs in a single step, attaining high concordance with an expert pathologist. Without using deep learning-based segmentation and detection pipelines, ECTIL attained similar hazard ratios to the pathologist's score in an overall survival analysis independent of clinicopathological variables. In the future, such a computational TIL assessment model could be used to pre-screen patients for prospective de-escalation trials in patients with triple-negative breast cancer or as a tool to assist pathologists and clinicians in the diagnostic investigation of patients with breast cancer. Furthermore, our model is available online under an open-source licence, allowing translational researchers to validate and use ECTIL in future studies in breast or other cancers.

Cracks in the Foundation: How Data-Hungry and Sensitive to Domain Shift are Vision Foundation Models for Computational Pathology?

Background

Vision Foundation Models (VFM) have emerged as a promising approach for computational pathology, offering scalable feature representations that may reduce labelled-data requirements and improve robustness to variation in tissue preparation and digitisation. However, VFM decoder and dataset size requirements as well as the performance under real-world domain shifts remain unclear.

Methods

We evaluated six contemporary VFMs on a protocol-variant Prostate Cancer (PCa) dataset comprising 37 683 tissue microarray spot images from 10 412 patients. The dataset includes six controlled domain shifts arising from differences in staining duration, section thickness, scanner type, and sampling location. Two clinically relevant downstream tasks were examined: ISUP grading and 5-year relapse prediction. We compared two decoder architectures, quantified dataset-size requirements using a saturation analysis (45–5727 samples), and assessed cross-domain robustness using out-of-domain test sets.

Findings

Larger VFMs consistently outperformed smaller models in peak accuracy and robustness metrics. Contrary to expectations of data efficiency, all models showed strong dependence on training-set size, requiring at least 1000 samples to approach stable results. All VFMs showed notable degradation under protocol-level domain shifts, with performance reductions of 4 to 13 percentage points in both cancer grading and relapse prediction, although larger models exhibited somewhat greater robustness. Furthermore, KNN-based probing performed substantially worse than a decoder-based approach across all architectures.

Interpretations

Despite their strong representational capacity, current VFMs do not yet provide reliable domain generalisation or data-efficient performance in computational pathology. Decoder design remains essential, and substantial amounts of labelled data are still required to achieve clinically meaningful accuracy. Further advances in pre-training strategies, decoder architectures, and domain adaptation methods will be crucial for translating VFMs into robust clinical tools.

Research in context

Evidence before this study

This study focuses on pathology foundation models, which offer promising improvements in performance, data requirements, and robustness to domain shifts for computational pathology. To identify relevant studies, we searched in Google Scholar for research published before 1 April 2025. We searched for studies introducing novel foundation models trained on pathology images, or reviews comparing those models in terms of performance or robustness. The search terms used were ‘computational pathology’, ‘benchmarking’, ‘review’ and ‘foundation model’, as well combinations of these terms. We found that many studies focus on increasing the complexity of pathology foundation models while using increasingly extensive and heterogeneous pre-training datasets. Various benchmarking studies demonstrate the superior performance and robustness of more recent and larger foundation models. However, these studies have limitations in their evaluation datasets. Either they cover only a domain shift due to a different scanner device, or they have small sample sizes. We also identified a research gap regarding the requirement for large datasets to train a decoder based on a pathology foundation model for a specific downstream task.

Added value of this study

The goal of this study was to evaluate the necessity of large downstream task datasets and the domain shift robustness of multiple pathology foundation models. For this purpose, we used our internal protocol-variant prostate cancer dataset, which provides a controlled evaluation setup as multiple domain shift types have been intentionally and separately introduced for different sub-datasets. Our saturation analysis revealed that at least 1000 samples were necessary to achieve good performance. Furthermore, our findings show that none of the evaluated foundation models are robust against all of our domain shifts, though larger models generally perform better.

Implications of all the available evidence

This study reveals that increasing the capacity of pathology foundation models improves performance and robustness. However, we demonstrated that all models exhibit some degree of performance degradation for certain domain shifts and require substantial datasets for training on downstream tasks. These limitations demonstrate that pathology foundation models do not fully address the issues of robustness and data requirements.

evidence_text: Multiple instance learning on tile level-pathology images provides accurate and interpretable classification for breast cancer molecular subtypes Accurate breast cancer molecular subtyping is critical for treatment decisions, yet standard methods such as immunohistochemistry and gene expression profiling are costly and labor intensive. Deep learning classification approaches using Hematoxylin and Eosin-stained whole slide images are an active area of research. However, many existing methods rely on large, high-quality annotated datasets where tumor regions are manually outlined for segmentation. This process is costly, does not scale well, depends on expert pathologists, and may ignore relevant tumor microenvironment features or reflect subjective labelling decisions. Here, we present an annotation-free, weakly supervised pipeline and web-based tool for breast cancer molecular subtyping using a computational pathology foundation model. A total of 1433 WSIs from three public cohorts (TCGA-BRCA, CPTAC-BRCA, and the Warwick HER2 cohort) were tiled into 224×224 patches without overlap at 20× magnification. Tile-level embeddings were extracted with a foundation model, and slide-level representations were obtained by mean pooling. We evaluated one-vs-rest classifiers including cosine similarity, logistic regression, and attention-based multiple instance learning. On a held-out test set of 287 WSIs, calibrated logistic regression achieved a macro F1 score of 0.75 using slide embeddings, while attention-based MIL reached 0.83 using tile embeddings. Luminal A and Basal subtypes were predicted reliably, whereas Luminal B remained challenging. These results demonstrate accurate and interpretable breast cancer subtyping without tumor annotations, and we provide a web server to support pathology diagnostics.

evidence_text: Robust integration of weakly anchored spatial multi-omics Spatial multi-omics holds great promise for dissecting complex biological processes, though inherent technical constraints continue to limit its widespread adoption. Currently, most studies therefore measure distinct omics features on separate tissue sections, necessitating spatial diagonal integration. An emerging practical solution is to leverage hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) images as an integration anchor, given their ubiquity, low cost, and compatibility across tissue preparations. However, this anchor is frequently compromised in real-world settings by variations in H&E staining style, absence of reliable histological landmarks, and mismatches in spatial resolutions across omics modalities. To address this, we introduce SpaWeaver, a computational framework that couples a pathology foundation model with a graph Transformer and a latent feature aligner module, providing a highly robust solution for weakly anchored spatial omics data diagonal integration. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SpaWeaver exhibits superior robustness against isolated or synergistic weak-anchoring factors. The spatial multi-omics profiles generated by SpaWeaver link molecular features originally separated on two sections, unlocking diverse downstream analyses once exclusive to co-assayed spatial multi-omics data, including niche-aware cell–cell communication inference and multi-omics resolved cell state. In this study, it unveils tumor-distance-dependent fibroblast–CD4□T-cell signaling in human colon adenocarcinoma and identifies a hypoxic glycolytic tumor state with pyknotic nuclei in human ovarian cancer. Overall, our approach bridges readily accessible single-omics measurements across weakly anchored tissue sections, enabling unified spatial multi-omics characterization and system-level tissue analysis.

In addition, the predictive value of other immune cell subsets, including plasma cells, neutrophils, histiocytes, and melanophages, remains unclear. We organized the Panoptic segmentation of nUclei and tissue in advanced MelanomA (PUMA) challenge to evaluate whether the spatial localization of TILs and other immune cell subsets on melanoma H&E slides collected before start of treatment was associated with treatment outcomes. Algorithm performance was evaluated on a hidden test set, after which top-ranked algorithms were applied to pre-treatment metastatic whole-slide images from a large, multicenter cohort of patients with advanced melanoma treated with first-line ICIs (n = 1102). Automatically quantified tissue features and immune cell subsets were then associated with clinical outcomes. Top-performing algorithms improved detection of immune cell subsets through pathology foundation model features, multi-stage tissue-context learning, and class-specific architectures, although accuracy for rare classes remained limited. Across challenge participants, TIL density showed the most consistent association with treatment response and survival. Associations for stromal TILs were weaker, while plasma cells, histiocytes, melanophages, neutrophils, necrosis and blood vessels did not show independent associations with outcomes. Overall, the PUMA challenge advanced immune cell detection in melanoma histopathology and showed that intratumoral lymphocytes are most consistently associated with treatment response and survival.

The clinical promise of computational pathology increasingly depends on foundation model-based pipelines, yet the morphological concepts encoded by these systems remain poorly understood. We address this gap with a concept-level visualization framework using class visualizations (CVs) and activation atlases (AAs) in a pathology foundation-model setting across colorectal tissue and multi-organ cancer tasks. Synthetic data generation emerges as a strategy to mitigate data scarcity in digital pathology, where complicated tissue and cellular features are correlated with cancer diagnosis. The synthesis of such visuals, however, suffers from limited inter class diversity and scarcity of cellular annotations. Current methodologies struggle with capturing the broad spectrum of pathology features, causing unpredictable objects and defected fidelity. Moreover, discrepancies in image resolution across developmental and operational phases can amplify the distribution shifts, undermining the precision of diagnosis. To address these challenges, we introduce TOpology guided PathOlogy Foundation Model (ToPoFM), a visual foundation model designed for the synthesis of high-resolution pathology images with cellular-level control. Our approach integrates a topology-informed cell arrangement generator to steer large language models for crafting synthetic cell arrangements. We correlate cell arrangement guidance with diffusion model for pathology content generation, then further implement a random sliding inference strategy, merging discrete low-resolution samplings into single high-resolution representation. Our model requires only small patches for training. The efficacy of ToPoFM is demonstrated through extensive experiments, complemented by expert validations, showing high fidelity on data synthesis. Additionally, we underscore the utility of our generated imagery as an augmentation tool, enhancing the performance of downstream tasks, including cancer subtype classification and segmentation.

Detection of basal cell carcinoma on whole-slide images from Mohs micrographic surgery using weakly supervised learning.

Background

Mohs micrographic surgery (MMS) is the gold standard for treating aggressive basal cell carcinoma, but its success depends on expertise in intraoperative interpretation of frozen sections.

Objective

To develop weakly supervised, multiple instance learning framework using a pathology foundation model for automated basal cell carcinoma detection in MMS frozen sections.

Methods

An internal data set of 995 frozen MMS whole-slide images was slide-level labeled as tumor (512) or no tumor (483). Furthermore, tumor regions in the test set were annotated. Whole-slide images were tiled and encoded with Prov-Gigapath features for a weakly supervised multiple instance learning framework. The performance was evaluated as binary slide-level classification and in attention maps showing the localization of the tumor regions prior to validation on 2 external data sets.

Results

The model showed near-perfect diagnostic performance, achieving 97.0% accuracy, and an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.998 on the internal data set. Furthermore, attention maps visualized diagnostically relevant regions, enhancing model interpretability (Intersection-over-Union = 0.41 ± 0.046 [Dice 0.58 ± 0.046]). External validation confirmed robust performance (90% to 92% accuracy, area under the receiver operating characteristic curve: 0.92-0.95).

Limitations

The absence of tumor region annotations on external data sets.

Conclusion

These findings support the feasibility of artificial intelligence-assisted analysis of MMS frozen sections and justify prospective studies evaluating its integration into clinical workflows.

High-sensitivity pan-cancer AI assessment of lymph node metastasis via uncertainty quantification. The histological heterogeneity of primary tumors across the pan-cancer spectrum poses a formidable barrier to accurate lymph node metastasis assessment, often causing AI systems to make "overconfident errors" on rare variants that lead to missed diagnoses. To address this, we present UPATHLN, a unified diagnostic platform that synergizes a pathology foundation model-based encoder with a decoupled uncertainty estimation mechanism. We developed and validated the system using a large-scale multicentre dataset of 26,229 lymph nodes from 14 distinct primary origins. In internal validation, UPATHLN achieved an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.986. Crucially, the uncertainty module functioned as a decisive fail-safe: by flagging potential false-negative predictions for mandatory pathologist review, it intercepted all missed diagnoses, securing 100% conditional sensitivity across both the development and independent test cohorts-even for tumors from seven unseen primary origins. Concurrently, this mechanism reduced the review burden on negative lymph nodes by 73.2%. Ultimately, UPATHLN sets a new benchmark for safety-critical AI, demonstrating that explicitly modeling uncertainty is key to unlocking reliable, workload-efficient diagnostics at the pan-cancer scale. Introduction  Cancer remains a leading cause of death worldwide  1  , primarily driven by metastasis  2 , 3  . Lymph nodes (LNs) are critical anatomical checkpoints in cancer progression  4  , serving as initial metastatic sites and immune regulatory hubs orchestrating host-tumor interactions  5  . Accurate assessment of lymph node metastasis (LNM) status is therefore paramount for prognostic assessment and therapeutic decision-making across diverse cancer types  6  . However, current clinical management relies primarily on crude quantitative approaches—predominantly pN staging  6  —which fail to capture crucial biological features such as lymph node ratio (LNR), metastatic tumor burden, and diverse spatial growth patterns of metastatic cells within LNs. Recent evidence explicitly links elevated LNR to decreased survival rates and shortened recurrence-free intervals  7  , while highlighting how spatial distributions of metastatic cells can modulate the immune microenvironment, potentially facilitating immune escape  8  . Despite these insights, pathologists now face an unprecedented surge in LN specimens due to rising cancer incidence  9  , rendering such detailed, multi-dimensional analysis practically unfeasible in routine workflows.  Deep learning has rapidly advanced pathological diagnosis, with numerous artificial intelligence (AI) systems gaining regulatory approval. However, existing AI approaches for LNM detection  10 – 15   typically follow cancer-specific paradigms. This fragmentation hinders widespread clinical adoption by necessitating multiple, disparate systems  16 , 17  , conflicting with the need for operational efficiency and unified diagnostic standards. Moreover, tumor heterogeneity manifests as a “long-tail distribution”  18 , 19  , where common metastatic patterns coexist with diverse rare variants. Standard deep learning models often struggle with these outliers, prone to “overconfident errors” where the system makes incorrect predictions with high certainty on out-of-distribution data. The reliable detection of these rare but clinically significant variants is crucial for patient safety  20 , 21  , yet remains challenging even with large datasets. While emerging foundation models  22 – 27   offer powerful representational capabilities, their effective application across the pan-cancer spectrum requires substantial annotation resources. Thus, there is an urgent need to transcend these limitations and establish a unified, robust, and safe diagnostic framework capable of not only high sensitivity but also reliable failure awareness across all cancer types.  To address these challenges, we developed UPATHLN, a unified, uncertainty-aware AI platform integrating a pathology foundation model with uncertainty-guided active learning and robust uncertainty estimation (Fig.  1 ). Trained and validated on an extensive multi-center, multi-cancer LN dataset, this study demonstrates UPATHLN’s capacity for highly sensitive and safe pan-cancer LNM detection with robust generalization. Ultimately, this study represents a critical step towards establishing a unified, trustworthy diagnostic standard for AI-assisted pathology. Results   Establishment of the UPATHLN platform and active learning optimization  To establish the UPATHLN platform, we curated a large-scale, multi-center pan-cancer dataset comprising 26,229 lymph nodes (LNs) from 8294 whole-slide images (WSIs) across 2738 patients, spanning tumors from 14 distinct primary organs. The dataset was rigorously partitioned into a development cohort and an independent test cohort, with seven rare primary origins strictly held out as unseen primary-origin holdouts to evaluate generalization to previously unseen origins (SFig.  1 ). Rather than relying on static training, we optimized the platform using an uncertainty-driven active learning strategy. Misclassified tiles were enriched in the high-uncertainty (HU) tail of the tile-level uncertainty-score distribution (SFig.  4a ). Accordingly, we summarized tile uncertainties into a slide-level ambiguity score and ranked candidate WSIs for expert review (SFig.  3 , “Methods”). Through five rounds of human-in-the-loop iterations, this active optimization substantially improved discriminative performance on the internal validation set, increasing the tile-level AUC from a baseline of 0.953 (95% CI: 0.932–0.974) to 0.986 (95% CI: 0.976–0.996), with consistent gains in both PPV and NPV (Fig.  2b–d ).  To rigorously attribute this high performance to architectural design rather than data accumulation alone, we benchmarked the final model against alternative architectures trained on the identical dataset generated from the final iteration. The multiscale architecture significantly outperformed both the single-scale UNI baseline (AUC = 0.928, 95% CI: 0.910–0.946; DeLong test,  P  < 0.0001) and the ImageNet-pretrained feature extractor (AUC = 0.918, 95% CI: 0.901–0.935; DeLong test,  P  < 0.0001; SFig.  4b ). Discussion  This study addresses the limitations of current organ-specific AI paradigms by presenting UPATHLN, a unified, uncertainty-aware framework for pan-cancer LNM diagnosis. While previous deep learning approaches have validated LNM detection in organ-specific cohorts, they often operate as “black boxes,” lacking the safety mechanisms required for broad clinical adoption  20  . By devising a specialized Multiscale cross-attention framework to effectively contextualize features from the pathology foundation model, UPATHLN establishes a robust clinical safety net. Notably, this architectural design demonstrated a definitive “fail-safe” capability in a large-scale independent cohort: the uncertainty mechanism successfully intercepted all initially missed metastases, securing 100% conditional sensitivity. This achievement marks a significant advancement: moving from algorithms that prioritize raw accuracy to safety-critical systems that effectively mitigate the risk of FNs in metastatic screening.  The parallel uncertainty estimation branch underpins the technical integrity of this safety profile. Classical uncertainty estimation methods—such as uncertainty-prediction model co-training  28 , 29  , multiple model ensembles  30  , or repeated dropout strategies  28 , 31  —increase computational burden and often flag large unnecessary regions for manual reassessment. By contrast, our independent bypass architecture provides precise localization of diagnostically uncertain regions without compromising inference speed. This decoupled mechanism acts as a reliable diagnostic filter, specifically designed to handle the inherent biological heterogeneity of metastatic disease. It respects the ambiguity of “long-tail” rare variants and non-neoplastic confounders (e.g., anthracotic pigment), routing these cases strictly within the system’s competence boundaries. This “rescue effect” ensures that algorithmic limitations do not translate into diagnostic errors, maintaining high reliability even when encountering complex morphologies that typically confound conventional models.  Furthermore, we successfully navigated the data annotation bottleneck that typically constrains the scalability of foundation models. By coupling high-level feature representations with an uncertainty-guided active learning framework, we efficiently captured a comprehensive spectrum of metastatic morphologies across 14 cancer types without necessitating exhaustive annotation. This strategy proved vital for addressing the diverse patterns of metastatic pathology. Consequently, the system maintained robust performance even on LNM samples from primary sites entirely unseen during training. This demonstrates that uncertainty-driven learning provides a practical, scalable pathway to generalize pathology AI, enabling adaptability to domain shifts and rare cancer types lacking large-scale training data.  UPATHLN reconciles the critical tension between rising diagnostic volumes and the demand for granular prognostic assessment. By safely automating the exclusion of 73.2% of negative LNs, the system liberates pathologists to focus on complex cases. Crucially, this efficiency renders detailed “multi-dimensional analysis”—specifically the precise quantification of tumor-to-lymph node area ratio  12   and spatial distribution patterns—feasible in routine practice. Moving beyond crude pN staging, UPATHLN provides the quantitative depth required for modern precision oncology that is practically impossible to achieve manually.  Despite these advances, several limitations should be acknowledged. First, this study is retrospective, and all training/validation data were sourced from hospitals in China; therefore, real-world deployment requires prospective multi-center evaluation and external validation across diverse populations, institutions, and scanning protocols. Second, although many artifacts are appropriately flagged as high uncertainty, future work could incorporate dedicated artifact-suppression or quality-control modules to further reduce review burden without compromising safety. Third, while the pipeline is designed to be compatible with different pathology foundation models, we only evaluated UNI and did not empirically compare performance against alternative encoders.  Collectively, UPATHLN advances pan-cancer LNM screening by introducing a risk-aware architecture that balances automation with expert oversight. The synergy between its decoupled uncertainty “fail-safe” and active learning framework ensures robust performance and scalability under heterogeneous clinical conditions. This approach not only streamlines routine triage but also provides a quantitative basis for assessing metastatic burden, potentially informing prognostic insights beyond standard pathological staging.    Methods   Dataset collection and cohort definition  We established a large-scale, pan-cancer dataset combining clinical data from three independent medical centers, with heterogeneous clinical workloads and patient populations, enabling evaluation across varied real-world settings. The primary clinical cohort included 2738 patients (8294 WSIs, 26,229 LNs) covering 14 distinct solid tumor types (SFig.  1a ). We applied specific exclusion criteria to ensure data quality: WSIs exhibiting severe artefacts—such as tissue folding covering >20% of the area, significant out-of-focus blurring, or extreme staining inconsistencies—were removed prior to analysis. In addition to the clinical cohort, we utilized an annotated gastric cancer dataset from our previous work  12   (GLN21) and the publicly available breast cancer dataset from the CAMELYON16 challenge  11   (BLN16) for model initialization.  Crucially, to prevent data leakage, we employed a strict patient-level splitting strategy, where all WSIs and LN sections from the same patient were assigned exclusively to a single cohort. As illustrated in the study design flow (SFig.  3 ), the clinical data were stratified into two independent cohorts. The development cohort consisted of 683 patients (2547 WSIs, 9729 LNs) from 7 common cancer types and was further subdivided to support the active learning workflow (SFig.  1b ). The multi-center multi-cancer test cohort comprised an independent set of 2055 patients (5747 WSIs, 16,500 LNs), serving as the held-out standard for final performance evaluation (SFig.  1c ). To rigorously assess the model’s generalization capabilities, the test cohort was stratified into two groups: the 7 cancer types encountered during training and a distinct set of 7 cancer types (thyroid, pancreas, bile duct, kidney, prostate, penis, and anus). Crucially, samples from these rare origins were strictly excluded from the training pipeline, ensuring that their evaluation represents a true test of the model’s ability to generalize to completely unseen primary origins. For LN counting, pathologists manually reviewed the slides to identify spatially distinct LNs; serial sections of the same node, if present, were identified based on morphological continuity and excluded from the total count to ensure each observation represented a unique LN.  This retrospective, multi-center study was conducted in accordance with relevant guidelines and regulations and the Declaration of Helsinki. The study protocol was approved by the Ethics Committee of Changhai Hospital (CHEC2024-276), the Ethics Committee of the Second People’s Hospital of Wuxi (2024Y-125), and the Ethics Committee of the 960th Hospital of the People’s Liberation Army (2024-087). The requirement for informed consent was waived because of the retrospective design and the use of anonymized data.    Lymph node contour recognition  To increase the training accuracy of LN metastasis detection models, we first developed an LN contour recognition model. The WSIs of LN tissue include not only LNs but also muscle, extraneous fat, and cancer nodules. The presence of these nontarget tissues can adversely affect the accuracy of metastasis detection.  Our model comprises two stages: initially, the YOLOv8-s model is employed for LN detection due to its high efficiency and rapid localization capabilities. The detected regions are subsequently input into the nnUNet  32   model for segmentation to remove impurities from the LN periphery.  We processed images using 1024 × 1024 pixel tiles at 1× magnification and utilized a 256-pixel sliding window for segmentation. The YOLOv8-s model was trained with default parameters, using the annotated contour coordinates as ground truth labels. The nnUNet model was similarly trained with default settings, using the bounding box of annotated regions to cut tiles at 0.25× magnification and employing annotated contours as masks.  During inference, a staged strategy was employed: YOLOv8-s model-predicted coordinates were used to cut local tiles, which were then input into the nnUNet model to obtain precise contour masks. These masks were mapped back to the full 0.25x thumbnail based on relative coordinates. For overlapping sliding windows, an averaging method was used to smooth boundaries.  We annotated 200 WSIs with 721 LNs from various tumor types for the YOLOv8-s model and nnUNet model training. After initial training, predictions of unannotated WSIs in the development cohort were manually reviewed. We reviewed 918 WSIs (comprising 3528 LNs) and reannotated 132 WSIs with incorrect predictions. Then, the YOLOv8-s model was retrained on a combined dataset of the initial 200 annotated WSIs and the 918 manually reviewed WSIs (total 1118 WSIs; randomly split into 80% training and 20% testing). Ultimately, the YOLOv8-s model achieved a recall rate of 0.994 (95% CI: 0.990–0.998) for LN detection.  Since nnUNet requires contour-level annotations, we used the initial 200 WSIs along with the 132 fully corrected WSIs (comprising 1245 LNs) for retraining. Finally, the nnUNet model achieved a mean Dice score of 0.934 (95% CI: 0.923–0.945) for LN contour segmentation. A manual review of inference results from the development cohort confirmed the ability of the two-stage model to accurately delineate LN contours and exclude non-LN tissues. This process provides high-quality input data for subsequent metastasis detection. As illustrated in SFig.  2a , we effectively identified and extracted LN contours from complex pathological images, facilitating high-quality input for further metastasis detection. Some missed LN diagnoses are due to atypical morphology (e.g., indistinct capsules) or small nodal size (SFig.  2b ). In clinical applications, missed LN identification is rare, so it does not increase the workload. Pathologists can easily add annotations during the review process. As missed diagnosis cases continue to be collected, this situation will become increasingly rare. The annotation and review process was conducted by two senior pathologists with over 15 years of experience: Y.C. and C.Q.    Data preprocessing for the classification model  Following the extraction of LN contour regions from WSIs, we tiled tumor metastasis areas on the basis of annotations to train the classification model. Given that accurate diagnosis of some LN metastases requires multiscale observations, we applied multiscale tiling to the annotated dataset. This process involved extracting image tiles of size 256 × 256 pixels at both 10x and 4× magnification, as shown in Fig.  2a . The center coordinates of tiles at both scales were aligned to ensure consistent observation of the same region at different resolutions.  By integrating the LN contour mask with the tumor mask, we cropped regions of interest into tumor and nontumor areas. At 10× magnification, a sliding window of 64 pixels was used to divide the region into extractable tiles, with each grid classified on the basis of the proportion of the tumor area annotated by doctors. Specifically, if more than 25% of a grid area was annotated as a tumor, the tile was labeled positive; otherwise, it was labeled negative. To ensure category balance, if the number of tiles in any category exceeded 100 within a WSI, we randomly selected 100 tiles. This sampling strategy maintained balanced categories at the tile level.    Feature extractor  In this study, we utilized UNI  23  , a Vision Transformer (ViT-Large  33  ) foundation model pre-trained on over 100,000 HE-stained WSIs, as a frozen feature extractor. UNI was selected as it represented a leading solution for pan-cancer feature representation at the time of study implementation. Importantly, our proposed multiscale architecture is designed to be foundation-model agnostic. While UNI was employed here as a representative high-performance encoder to validate our framework, the system is compatible with and can readily incorporate other emerging pathology foundation models  22 , 24 – 27  . For feature extraction, we processed image tiles of size 256 × 256 pixels at both the 10× and the 4× magnification levels and randomly cropped them to 224 × 224 pixels. The resulting feature matrix for each tile maintains a shape of (196 + 1, 1024), where 196 represents the length of the patch-tokens, and 1 represents the class token.    Multiscale feature fusion and classification module  By extracting features from the same local region at different magnification levels and then fusing them, the model can capture both global and local pathological morphological features, better locating and identifying tumor areas. Specifically, we adopted the cross-attention module proposed by Zhou et al.  34   to multiscale image feature fusion. As shown in Fig.  2a , the entire cross-attention module consists of two cross-attention blocks and two self-attention blocks. The cross-attention blocks learn the intrinsic connections of multiscale image features by dynamically weighting features from different spatial scales. During training, the parameters of the UNI pretrained ViT-Large feature extractor were fixed, and no backpropagation optimization was performed. We used ColorJitter from Torchvision for transformation with the following parameters: maximum increments of 0.1 for brightness, 0.2 for contrast, 0.2 for saturation, and 0.15 for hue. The tiles were also randomly flipped and rotated by 15°. To address the imbalance between positive and negative samples, we perform balanced sampling of positive and negative samples at the initialization of each epoch. We calculated the loss via cross-entropy between the predicted probabilities and the true labels and optimized it via adaptive moment estimation with weight decay (AdamW) during training, with a weight decay of 0.05 and a batch size of 64. The learning rate was managed via a cosine annealing schedule, starting at 1e-4, peaking at 5e-4 and ending at 1e-6 over 40 epochs. All training and testing were performed on six NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPUs.    Uncertainty estimation module  Deploying deep learning models across multi-center pan-cancer cohorts inevitably introduces challenges related to histological heterogeneity, variable data quality, and out-of-distribution inputs that essentially differ from the training distribution. In such scenarios, enforcing deterministic predictions often leads to high-confidence errors. To address this, we incorporated a parallel uncertainty estimation module into our diagnostic framework. The primary objective of this module is to quantify the reliability of region-level predictions, serving a dual purpose: guiding model optimization through active learning during development and acting as a trigger for pathologist review during clinical inference.  Diverging from conventional approaches that rely on computationally expensive ensembles or require joint training with classification objectives (which may destabilize the primary task)  28 – 31  , we implemented a sequential optimization strategy. Specifically, the uncertainty branch is trained as an independent architectural bypass only after the multiscale classifier parameters are frozen. This design ensures that the uncertainty mechanism is specifically calibrated to the fixed decision boundary of the main model. Consequently, this approach enables precise confidence estimation without compromising the original diagnostic performance, while incurring negligible computational overhead.  Specifically, we implemented this module by adapting the uncertainty estimation algorithm for pretrained models proposed by Kirchhof et al .   35  . As shown in Fig.  2a , using the same feature  F  as the classification model input, we passed it through the uncertainty estimation module comprising three fully connected layers with 512 hidden units and LeakyReLU intermediate activations, outputting a single value normalized by the Softplus function to ensure positivity. We used mean squared error (MSE) loss, comparing the uncertainty module’s predictions with labels derived from the classification model’s forward propagation loss, computed at runtime with backpropagation disabled. Crucially, this design provides an intuitive measure of reliability: a high predicted loss indicates that the model anticipates a likely error on the input, thereby flagging it as a “High Uncertainty” (HU) region for pathologist review.  The loss function is defined as:   8     L  uncertainty   =   1  N    ∑   i  =  1   N        u  i   −   L   pred  i       2      where    u    is the uncertainty module’s predicted value and      L    pred      is the loss from the classification model’s forwards propagation.  The training process employed the same data and sampling strategy as those of the classification module. We used the AdamW optimizer with a weight decay of 0.05 and a batch size of 64. The learning rate followed a cosine annealing schedule, starting at 1e-4, peaking at 5e-4 and decreasing to 1e-6 over 10 epochs.    Uncertainty-driven active learning strategy  To address tumor heterogeneity and optimize annotation efficiency, we implemented a human-in-the-loop, uncertainty-driven active learning framework structured into five distinct iterations (Fig.  1d  and SFig.  3 ). To facilitate this process, the clinically derived development cohort (683 patients) was partitioned into two functional subsets via random patient-level sampling: a large unlabeled candidate pool of 594 patients (2245 WSIs, 8832 LNs) available for selection, and a strictly held-out internal validation set of 89 patients (302 WSIs, 897 LNs). Notably, the internal validation set was comprehensively annotated at the lesion level prior to the active learning process. This set remained fixed throughout the study and served as a reliable ground truth to monitor model convergence and determine hyperparameters without biasing the training process.  The training workflow commenced with an initialization phase (Iteration 1), where the baseline model was trained solely on the fully annotated initialization datasets (GLN21 and BLN16) to establish foundational detection capabilities. Subsequently, we conducted four consecutive rounds of uncertainty-driven refinement (Iterations 2–5). In each round, the model performed inference on the unlabeled candidate pool to compute tile-level uncertainty scores      u    i      (derived from the uncertainty module). WSIs were then prioritized for expert review according to a slide-level diagnostic ambiguity score. Data annotation and establishment of ground truth  To satisfy the distinct requirements of model development and independent validation, we implemented a two-tier annotation strategy conducted by senior pathologists with over 15 years of experience (Y.C., C.Q., J.L., C.B., and M.S.).  For the development cohort, pathologists performed exhaustive region-level annotations on WSIs selected for the expanded training set and the internal validation set. This involved delineating precise boundaries for all LNs and contouring all internal metastatic foci. This process ensured that the model received high-granularity supervision for distinct metastatic morphologies, including macro-metastases, micro-metastases, and isolated tumor cells (ITCs). During active learning iterations, regions flagged as HU were specifically reviewed and corrected (C.Q., J.L., C.B., and M.S.) to provide high-quality supervision for challenging examples.  For the independent test cohort, we established a rigorous diagnostic standard to evaluate clinical safety. Instead of pixel-level contours, we focused on the definitive metastatic status of each LN. Two senior pathologists (Y.C. and C.Q.) independently reviewed all WSIs. Discrepant cases were adjudicated by a consensus panel. To resolve diagnostic ambiguity in morphologically challenging cases, we performed confirmatory immunohistochemical (IHC) staining (CAM5.2 and AE1/AE3) on 52 challenging cases to determine the final ground truth (SFig.  12 ). This process ensured a non-ambiguous “Positive/Negative” label for every LN in the test set.    Statistical analysis  The detection (YOLOv8-s) and segmentation (nnUNet) models were implemented with probability thresholds of 0.25 and 0.50, respectively. For the classification model, the binary decision threshold was set at 0.50. The uncertainty threshold for each iteration was determined empirically using the Internal Validation Set. To balance the trade-off between the volume of regions flagged for review and FP predictions, we selected the threshold at the intersection point where the average High Uncertainty area per slide (HUavg) equalled the average False Positive area per slide (FPavg) (SFig.  13 ). Isolated positive predictions approximately the size of one tile (3600 μm²) were excluded from analysis owing to resolution constraints.  To comprehensively evaluate the system, we defined detection and classification targets at three distinct levels. Tile-level performance measures the fundamental classification accuracy of individual 256 × 256 pixel image patches, where a tile is labeled positive if tumor tissue comprises >25% of its area. Lesion-level (Region) performance evaluates the model’s ability to correctly localize and classify contiguous metastatic areas (including macro-metastases, micro-metastases, and ITCs) within the LN tissue, distinct from simple tile-level accuracy. LN-level performance serves as the primary clinical unit for N-staging; an LN is considered positive if the model identifies at least one metastatic lesion within the nodal area.  We defined specific metrics to assess the safety and efficiency of the proposed human-AI collaborative workflow. Conditional classification sensitivity evaluates the classification performance specifically on all LNs successfully localized by the detection module. For performance evaluation, regions flagged as HU (highlighted in yellow in the prediction heatmaps) were considered positive for sensitivity calculations, as these areas require pathologist review in clinical practice. To quantify workload, we defined the Review Burden Rate on Negative Cases (RBR-N) as the proportion of true-negative LNs that required high-magnification manual review. An LN contributes to this burden if it contains any region predicted as False Positive (FP) or High Uncertainty (HU).  Bootstrap analysis (1000 iterations) was performed to calculate 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for all performance metrics. AUCs were compared using DeLong’s test (two-sided). evidence_text: Calibration-Aware Patient-Level Prediction of Source-Defined MSIMUT Status in Colorectal Cancer from Whole-Slide Histopathology Images Using Foundation-Model Embeddings. Background/Objectives: Microsatellite instability (MSI) is clinically important in colorectal cancer, but definitive assessment requires molecular or immunohistochemical testing. This study developed a leakage-safe, calibration-aware patient-level framework for predicting a source-defined MSIMUT category from hematoxylin-and-eosin whole-slide-derived patches using fixed Phikon foundation-model embeddings. Methods: The TCGA-derived colorectal cohort comprised 360 patients, including 65 source-defined positive and 295 MSS cases, represented by 192,312 pre-extracted patches. Patch embeddings were aggregated using mean, max, and mean-plus-max pooling, and downstream classifiers were evaluated under patient-level cross-validation with calibration, threshold, decision-curve, clinicopathological, source-provenance, and patch-count sensitivity analyses. Results: In the primary random patient-level evaluation, logistic regression with mean-plus-max pooling achieved a mean ROC-AUC of 0.915 and PR-AUC of 0.809. Fully nested Platt calibration yielded pooled out-of-sample ROC-AUC 0.913, PR-AUC 0.796, Brier score 0.073, calibration slope 1.037, and calibration-in-the-large 0.023. Within the internally cross-validated mean-plus-max framework, an exploratory sensitivity ≥ 0.95 operating point yielded sensitivity 0.969, specificity 0.393, and negative predictive value 0.983. Provenance reconstruction identified source-partition-dependent patch-count structure. In a source-TRAIN to source-TEST holdout, mean-plus-max ROC-AUC decreased to 0.788, while patch count alone was near chance in source-TEST (ROC-AUC 0.517) and explicit patch-count addition did not improve discrimination. Conclusions: These findings support the methodological feasibility of fixed foundation-model embeddings for internal MSI-related pre-screening research, while showing that apparent performance is sensitive to source structure. Independent multicenter validation with clinically adjudicated MSI-H/dMMR endpoints remains necessary before clinical application. 1. Introduction Microsatellite instability (MSI) is a molecular phenotype resulting from deficient DNA mismatch repair and the consequent accumulation of insertion and deletion errors within repetitive genomic regions [ 1 , 2 ]. In colorectal cancer, MSI is associated with a distinct hypermutated tumor biology and has important implications for prognostic assessment, therapeutic stratification, and response to immune checkpoint blockade [ 1 , 3 ]. Although MSI is defined at the molecular level, MSI-high tumors may also exhibit recognizable histomorphological and immune-related characteristics on routine hematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-stained sections, including prominent lymphocytic infiltration, mucinous differentiation, architectural heterogeneity, and variation in the tumor microenvironment [ 1 , 3 , 4 ]. This relationship between molecular status and tissue morphology makes MSI a particularly relevant target for computational pathology, in which routinely acquired histological images can be analyzed as high-dimensional biomedical data. In current clinical practice, MSI or mismatch repair status is generally assessed using polymerase chain reaction-based microsatellite testing or immunohistochemistry for the mismatch repair proteins MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, and PMS2 [ 1 , 3 ]. These established approaches remain essential for definitive biomarker assessment but require testing beyond routine morphological examination. By contrast, H&E-stained slides are already generated as part of standard histopathological workflows and may contain image-level correlates of the underlying molecular phenotype. Computational analysis of these routinely available images has therefore been investigated as a potential pre-screening approach for identifying patients who may benefit from prioritized confirmatory testing [ 4 , 5 ]. Such methods should not be considered replacements for validated molecular or immunohistochemical assays, but rather as complementary strategies that may support prioritization within existing diagnostic pathways. The digitization of histopathological slides has enabled artificial intelligence methods to extract clinically relevant information from whole-slide images. Landmark work by Kather et al. demonstrated that deep learning could predict MSI directly from H&E-stained histological images of gastrointestinal cancers, establishing an important proof of concept for image-based molecular biomarker inference [ 5 ]. Subsequent studies and reviews have expanded this evidence base and further demonstrated the potential of computational pathology for MSI prediction [ 4 , 6 , 7 ]. However, the published literature also shows substantial heterogeneity in cohort composition, class prevalence, image preprocessing, model architecture, validation design, reference standards, and clinical framing [ 4 , 6 , 7 ]. The central question has therefore progressed beyond whether MSI-associated information is present in histomorphology to how this information should be represented, validated, and interpreted to support reliable, transparently evaluated, and potentially transferable patient-level inference. Methodological rigor is particularly important in whole-slide image analysis because individual patients may contribute multiple slides and thousands of correlated image patches. If these observations are partitioned without preserving patient-level independence, related samples may occur in both the training and evaluation sets, creating information leakage and producing optimistically biased performance estimates [ 8 ]. Moreover, discrimination alone does not fully characterize the potential relevance of a biomarker prediction model. Although the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC-AUC) summarizes the ability of a model to rank positive and negative cases, it does not establish whether predicted probabilities are appropriately calibrated, whether operating thresholds suitable for a proposed use can be identified, or whether model-guided action may offer net benefit relative to default strategies [ 9 , 10 , 11 ]. Evaluation should therefore extend to class-imbalance-sensitive metrics, uncertainty estimation, probability calibration, threshold-dependent performance, and decision-analytic assessment. Robustness to variation in the amount of available tissue information is also relevant because whole-slide images may differ substantially in tissue area and patch burden. Accordingly, an unresolved methodological need is a patient-level framework that combines strict leakage control with calibration, operating-point analysis, decision curve evaluation, and representation-robustness assessment. Task-specific end-to-end deep-learning pipelines can require substantial computational resources, extensive model optimization, and careful management of cohort-dependent effects [ 6 , 7 , 8 ]. Pathology foundation models provide a modular alternative by learning transferable representations from large and heterogeneous histopathology collections [ 12 , 13 , 14 ]. In an embedding-based workflow, image patches are processed using a fixed pretrained encoder, after which the resulting feature vectors can be aggregated into slide- or patient-level representations for downstream prediction. This separation of representation learning from task-specific classification reduces the need for repeated end-to-end retraining and allows the effects of representation design, classifier selection, calibration, and robustness to be examined within a common feature space. Within such a framework, deterministic mean and max pooling provide a transparent means of testing whether pretrained embeddings retain sufficient globally distributed and locally salient information without introducing an additional trainable attention mechanism. The resulting representations can then be evaluated using comparatively simple downstream models, improving analytical traceability and facilitating representation-level interpretation. Nevertheless, latent embedding dimensions should not be assumed to correspond directly to specific microscopic structures, and an embedding-based workflow does not eliminate the computational burden of patch extraction and foundation-model inference. Against this background, the present study developed and internally evaluated a calibration-aware, leakage-safe, and decision-support-oriented framework for patient-level prediction of the source-defined MSIMUT category using a publicly available TCGA-linked colorectal cancer patch archive derived from routine H&E-stained whole-slide images [ 15 , 16 ]. The source repository defines MSIMUT as microsatellite unstable or highly mutated; accordingly, this category was treated as the positive analytical endpoint and was not assumed to be equivalent to a uniformly assay-confirmed MSI-H/dMMR outcome. The verified cohort comprised 360 patients, and patch-level features were extracted using the fixed Phikon pathology foundation model [ 17 ]. Mean pooling, max pooling, and their concatenation were evaluated for constructing patient-level representations, and multiple downstream classifiers were compared under strict patient-level separation. Evaluation extended beyond conventional discrimination analysis by incorporating repeated patient-level validation, bootstrap-based uncertainty estimation, leakage-safe nested probability calibration, threshold-based screening assessment, decision curve analysis, pooling-strategy comparison, patch-burden sensitivity analysis, and representation-level interpretability. The objective was to determine whether fixed Phikon-derived histopathology embeddings could support informative patient-level prediction that remained stable across alternative internal patient-level partitions, without end-to-end retraining, while explicitly characterizing probability behavior, operating-point trade-offs, potential decision-analytic relevance, and representation robustness. 2. Materials and Methods 2.1. Study Design, Data Source, and Cohort Assembly This retrospective computational pathology study investigated patient-level prediction of microsatellite instability-related status using a publicly available colorectal histopathology patch dataset derived from hematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-stained whole-slide images. The patient was prespecified as the fundamental analytical unit because individual cases could contribute multiple correlated image-derived observations. Maintaining patient-level independence was intended to preserve the clinical interpretation of the prediction task and to reduce the risk of information leakage and optimistically biased performance estimates [ 6 , 8 ]. Accordingly, patient-level separation was maintained throughout representation construction and model evaluation. The overall study workflow is summarized in Figure 1 . Figure 1 Overview of the patient-level MSI prediction workflow. Whole-slide-derived histopathology patches and their source-defined MSIMUT/MSS labels were obtained from a publicly available TCGA-derived colorectal cancer dataset. The pre-extracted image patches were encoded using the original Phikon pathology foundation model and aggregated into patient-level representations. Candidate classifiers were evaluated under patient-level validation, and the selected model subsequently underwent uncertainty estimation, leakage-safe nested probability calibration, threshold-based assessment, decision curve analysis, robustness evaluation, and representation-level interpretation. Whole-slide-derived colorectal histopathology patches were obtained from a publicly available colorectal-only JPEG derivative [ 18 ] of the FFPE image dataset originally published by Kather et al. [ 16 ] and generated from TCGA diagnostic slides. The distributed archive was organized into source-defined MSIMUT and microsatellite-stable (MSS) categories. TCGA patient identifiers encoded in the patch filenames were extracted programmatically to reconstruct patient-level groups and to preserve the association between each patch and its source case. The source-provided category labels were used as the reference outcome for supervised prediction; no local relabeling or additional pathological annotation was performed. Patient-level groups were retained when the archive contained image patches with an extractable TCGA case identifier and a corresponding source-defined category label. No new participants were recruited, no intervention or specimen collection was undertaken, and no identifiable patient information was analyzed. Following reconstruction and verification of the patient-level groups, the final analytical cohort comprised 360 patients, including 65 patients in the source-defined MSIMUT category and 295 patients in the MSS category. The positive category therefore represented 18.1% of the cohort, resulting in a class-imbalanced prediction problem. The approaches used to preserve class distribution during validation and to evaluate performance under class imbalance are described in the subsequent methodological sections. The verified cohort was held fixed throughout all representation construction, model evaluation, and robustness analyses, ensuring consistency between cohort definition and reported performance [ 6 , 8 ]. No independent external validation cohort was available for the present study. Accordingly, all discrimination, calibration, threshold, decision-analytic, subgroup, and sensitivity analyses should be interpreted as internal evaluations of the TCGA-derived cohort. Additional internal sensitivity analyses were designed to examine potential site- and clinicopathological confounding within this cohort, but they were not considered substitutes for independent multicenter validation across different institutions, staining protocols, scanners, specimen-processing workflows, or patient populations. Source Patch Dataset and Patch-Level Feature Extraction Image analysis was based on a publicly available colorectal histopathology patch collection published by Kather et al. [ 16 ] and subsequently distributed as a colorectal-only JPEG archive [ 18 ]. The original image resource was derived from formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded diagnostic whole-slide images in The Cancer Genome Atlas. According to the source documentation, tumor-containing regions were detected automatically, resampled into 224 × 224-pixel patches at a spatial resolution of 0.5 µm per pixel, and color-normalized using the Macenko method [ 16 ]. The locally used archive contained 192,312 JPEG patches, comprising 75,039 patches in the source-defined MSIMUT directory and 117,273 patches in the microsatellite-stable (MSS) directory [ 18 ]. Provenance reconstruction showed that the upstream resource had been distributed in predefined TRAIN and TEST partitions with class-specific patch-count structures shaped by upstream dataset construction. The source TRAIN partition contained 46,704 MSIMUT and 46,704 MSS patches; according to the source documentation, this patch-level balance reflected random reduction of the more numerous MSS training patches [ 16 ]. The reconstructed source TEST partition contained 28,335 MSIMUT and 70,569 MSS patches. These counts refer to image files reconstructed from the available source filename manifest and matched to the 360-patient analytical cohort. At the patient level, these partitions comprised 260 TRAIN patients (39 MSIMUT and 221 MSS) and 100 TEST patients (26 MSIMUT and 74 MSS), with no patient overlap. Because the pooled derivative archive combined patients originating from these differently structured source partitions, absolute patient-level patch burden could encode upstream dataset-construction characteristics in addition to the amount of available tissue. This possibility was therefore examined explicitly through source-partition-specific patch-count analyses and a reconstructed source-holdout sensitivity analysis described below. The archive was supplied as a colorectal-only image collection, and no additional filtering by TCGA project, tissue-source site, or other source-related metadata was applied before patient-level representation construction. Because the analysis used pre-extracted patches rather than reprocessing the original whole-slide images, the original tiling stride and overlap configuration could not be determined from the available source documentation. The source repository defines MSIMUT as microsatellite unstable or highly mutated [ 16 ]. In the present analysis, this source-defined category constituted the positive class, whereas MSS constituted the negative class. TCGA case identifiers embedded in the patch filenames were extracted programmatically and used to associate each patch with its source patient and to establish the patient-level identifier framework subsequently used for linkage to TCGA/GDC metadata. This procedure reconstructed 360 non-overlapping patient groups, comprising 65 patients in the source-defined positive category and 295 patients in the MSS category. No patient identifier occurred in both categories. Each patch was retained only as an intermediate image-derived observation, whereas the patient was preserved as the indivisible analytical unit throughout downstream dataset partitioning, model development, and performance evaluation; patches originating from the same patient were never distributed across training and test subsets. No additional image augmentation or histology-specific stain normalization was applied during feature extraction because the distributed JPEG patches had already undergone source-level color normalization. Patch-level features were extracted using the original Phikon pathology foundation model, loaded through the Transformers interface using the model identifier owkin/phikon [ 17 ]. Each patch was opened in RGB format and processed using the corresponding AutoImageProcessor. The encoder was maintained in evaluation mode, and feature extraction was performed without gradient computation, task-specific fine-tuning, or end-to-end retraining. For each patch, the classification-token representation from the final hidden state was retained as a fixed 768-dimensional latent histopathology embedding. The embeddings were converted to 32-bit floating-point arrays and saved separately for each patient. Implementation used the corresponding AutoImageProcessor and AutoModel interfaces, with the encoder operated in evaluation mode under torch.no_grad() during patch-level inference. These fixed patch-level embeddings constituted the inputs for the deterministic patient-level aggregation procedures described in Section 2.3 . The reconstructed patient identifiers were retained unchanged across downstream analyses and provided the linkage key for the source-related metadata analyses described separately below. The use of fixed pretrained pathology embeddings as transferable representations is consistent with broader general-purpose foundation-model approaches in computational pathology [ 19 ].
