Artificial intelligence (AI) and its computer algorithms, including those of machine learning and deep learning, have been transforming the oncology field. Generative AI (Gen AI) and general AI technologies, which can be adapted to various tasks based on diverse inputs, are being increasingly utilized in healthcare applications. Foundation models, driven by Gen AI and general AI technologies, have enthralled the medical world, representing the next generation of large-scale AI tools in medicine that are trained on massive amounts of data and will make a major impact due to their versatility, high performance, personalization enhancement, and assistance of healthcare workers. That said, it is undeniable that there are multiple obstacles that these algorithms must overcome to be successfully utilized in the field. In this review, we first present a brief background and a history of the recent rise of Gen AI and foundation models. Next, we explore their applications in the diagnosis and treatment of cancer, specifically in radiology, pathology, precision medicine, personalization of care, and surgical oncology. Then, we discuss some of the limitations that could hinder general and Gen AI's clinical translation.

Contrastive Language-Image Pretraining (CLIP) models, which are pretrained on natural images with billions of image-text pairs, exhibit strong zero-shot and cross-modal capabilities. The emergence of diverse pathological foundation models has empowered computational pathology tasks within the field of oncology, including tumor subtyping, cancer prognosis, biomarker prediction, gene expression prediction, and so on. However, variations in model architecture and data sources hinder consistent downstream performance and complicate centralized training. Specifically, the lack of data sharing makes retraining foundation models with pooled data infeasible. Here, we propose the Meta-Encoder, a unified framework that integrates features from multiple pathological foundation models to generate a comprehensive representation, achieving superior performance in downstream cancer detection tasks compared to single foundation models. For high-dimensional tasks such as multiplex protein and gene expression prediction within tumor tissues, the attention-based strategies of our Meta-Encoder framework demonstrate substantial advantages over single models, offering an optimal balance of performance and efficiency. By harnessing the complementary strengths of multiple foundation models, the Meta-Encoder enhance the molecular characterization of pathology images, thereby advancing precision oncology.

Comparative Analysis of Deep Learning Approaches for Histopathology-Based Survival Prediction in Hepatocellular Carcinoma.

Background

Accurate prognostic stratification in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) remains challenging due to substantial tumor heterogeneity. Deep learning (DL)-based approaches, particularly convolutional neural networks (CNNs), have been widely applied for prognostic prediction using histopathological images. Recently, pathology foundation models combined with multiple-instance learning (MIL) have emerged as a promising alternative. In this study, we aimed to provide a comparative evaluation of conventional CNN-based and foundation model-based approaches for HCC prognosis prediction, with a focus on tissue selection strategies and cross-dataset generalizability.

Methods

We compared a patch-level CNN approach with a foundation model-based MIL approach for overall survival (OS) prediction from hematoxylin and eosin-stained whole-slide images. A total of 256 patients from Seoul St. Mary's Hospital (SSMH) and 334 patients from the TCGA dataset were included. Models were trained using either all tissue regions or tumor-only regions under five-fold cross-validation. Model performance was evaluated using the concordance index (C-index), Kaplan-Meier analysis, and time-dependent receiver operating characteristic analysis. Cross-dataset validation and combined-dataset training assessed generalizability.

Results

In the SSMH dataset, the CNN model performed better with tumor-only regions (C-index 0.8308) than with all tissue regions (0.7498). In contrast, the foundation model-based MIL approach showed stable performance regardless of input regions (C-indices: 0.8701 and 0.8752). Similar stability was observed in the TCGA dataset (0.7744 and 0.7722). Cross-dataset validation showed reduced performance, indicating limited generalizability. Combining datasets did not lead to performance improvement. Subgroup analyses showed prognostic information beyond histologic grade, and feature visualization revealed relevant histopathologic patterns.

Conclusions

A foundation model-based MIL approach provides robust and interpretable prognostic modeling in HCC. DL-based prediction offers complementary information beyond conventional clinicopathological variables. Future efforts integrating multimodal data and improving generalizability will be essential for clinical translation.

evidence_text: Generative Artificial Intelligence and Large Language Models in Clinical Oncology. Cancer remains a major global health challenge, and the increasing availability of multimodal biomedical data has created unprecedented opportunities for precision oncology. Recent advances in generative artificial intelligence (AI), particularly large language models (LLMs), have enabled new approaches for integrating heterogeneous data sources, including electronic health records, medical imaging, pathology, genomics, and clinical text. However, current studies remain fragmented across specific tasks, cancer types, and model architectures, and a comprehensive synthesis of how generative AI can support the entire oncology continuum is still lacking. This review provides an overview of generative AI in clinical oncology, covering LLMs, generative adversarial networks, diffusion models, and multimodal foundation models. We summarize their methodological foundations and discuss applications in cancer diagnosis, prognosis prediction, treatment planning, patient management, and clinical trial optimization. Particular attention is given to multimodal data integration, synthetic data generation, clinical reasoning, and decision support, together with current challenges related to interpretability, reliability, data privacy, regulatory governance, and real-world implementation. By consolidating recent technological advances and clinical evidence, this review highlights future priorities toward safe, trustworthy, and clinically deployable intelligent oncology systems. Emerging agent-based architectures and human-AI collaborative workflows may further expand the clinical utility of generative AI in oncology.

evidence_text: AI agents in cancer imaging: Concepts, advances, and clinical perspectives. Medical imaging serves as a critical source of evidence for cancer diagnosis, treatment, and follow-up. However, most existing medical imaging artificial intelligence (AI) systems still operate on predefined tasks and inputs, limiting their ability to address the evolving needs of clinical practice and research. AI agents use foundation models as central engines for reasoning and orchestration. They organize analytical processes according to task objectives, invoke external tools and data resources, and adapt subsequent actions based on intermediate results. They may therefore facilitate a shift in cancer imaging AI from isolated model applications toward continuous workflow support. This review outlines the fundamental principles, system components, and evaluation approaches for AI agents from a cancer imaging perspective and summarizes representative advances in image interpretation, clinical decision support, and research workflows. Current evidence suggests that agents can connect previously fragmented imaging, clinical, and knowledge resources, thereby potentially improving the continuity and traceability of complex tasks. Nevertheless, clinical evidence for AI agents remains limited, as most studies have been conducted in controlled settings and have yet to demonstrate consistent value in real-world clinical workflows. Clinical translation is further constrained by the computational demands and potential error propagation inherent in multistep execution, as well as by the dependence of agent performance on specific tools, data environments, and workflow configurations. Future research should move beyond task-level performance toward system-level validation, with particular emphasis on whether agents can reliably organize information, interpret findings, and collaborate effectively with clinicians. Such evidence will be essential to clarify their practical role in cancer imaging care and research.

Neuroblastoma is a leading cause of childhood cancer mortality, presenting persistent management challenges due to its biological heterogeneity and the limited accessibility of molecular profiling in routine practice. Here we present NEVA (NEuroblastoma Vision-language AI), a multimodal foundation model designed to address these barriers. Unlike conventional approaches that rely on frozen encoders and multiple instance learning, NEVA implements a pathologist-inspired hierarchical workflow with end-to-end optimization. By integrating interpretable attention maps that localize histologically relevant regions, NEVA establishes a scalable framework for neuroblastoma risk stratification and clinical decision support.

Sequential question answering AI for hierarchical gastric pathology diagnosis. Artificial intelligence in digital pathology has evolved from task-specific models to multimodal foundation models. However, clinical adoption remains limited by a misalignment between model design and the hierarchical, conditional nature of diagnostic reasoning. In complex domains, such as gastric pathology, diagnosis requires navigating strictly dependent steps where downstream tasks are only clinically valid given specific upstream findings. Regardless, current computational approaches often treat diagnostic tasks in isolation, obscuring these critical dependencies. Herein, we present AUGUST (Adaptive Unified Gastric diagnosis Using Sequential Tasks), a sequential question-answering framework designed to mimic the stepwise reasoning of pathologists. AUGUST explicitly models diagnostic dependencies by iteratively generating task-specific questions conditioned on prior findings, projecting whole slide images into context-aware representations, and producing answers constrained to clinically valid pathways. We evaluated AUGUST on 23,072 gastric whole slide images spanning 19 hierarchical tasks and 79,924 question-answer pairs. In both fully autonomous and human-in-the-loop settings, AUGUST outperformed state-of-the-art multiple instance learning, pathology-specific vision-language, and foundation models on a wide range of datasets and tasks. Our results demonstrate that AUGUST has superior hierarchical consistency and diagnostic accuracy across coarse-, fine-, and grading-levels. Introduction  Digital pathology has progressed rapidly with advances in artificial intelligence (AI). Early works focused on task-specific deep learning models analyzing digitized whole slide images (WSIs)  1  . These models have been successfully applied to various tasks, such as tumor detection  2  , subtyping  3  , and prognosis prediction  4  , lesion classification  5  , and pathologically significant feature detection  6  . More recently, the field has shifted toward multimodal foundation models (FMs) that learn shared representations across WSIs and complementary clinical data, including pathology texts/reports  7 , 8   and genomic profiles  9  . By leveraging large-scale pretraining, these models can transfer across datasets and tasks, support cross-modal retrieval, and in some settings, zero-shot or few-shot inference  10 , 11  .  Despite these advances, the clinical adoption of AI in pathology remains limited. A central challenge lies in the misalignment between AI model design/evaluation and clinical workflows. Although recent approaches increasingly adopt FMs, trained on large-scale datasets from multiple sources, they are often optimized and evaluated for isolated, independent tasks (e.g., tumor classification, segmentation, or biomarker prediction) on relatively narrow test sets  7 , 8 , 12 , 13  . In routine practice, however, pathology reasoning is multi-label and hierarchical, with conditional dependencies: upstream findings determine which downstream assessments are clinically valid (e.g., tumor grading is only meaningful when carcinoma is present), and multiple co-occurring lesions frequently require multi-label interpretation. Treating lesions either independently or collapsing them into a single prediction obscures these dependencies and provides limited assurance that model outputs will remain coherent and reliable in real-world diagnostic settings.  This misalignment is particularly pronounced in gastric pathology. Gastric cancer remains a leading cause of cancer incidence and mortality worldwide  14  , with most patients diagnosed at advanced stages and facing poor outcomes  15  . In routine practice, a single gastric biopsy may simultaneously reveal co-existing gastritis, dysplasia, and early carcinoma, each requiring distinct clinical management decisions  16  . This diagnostic complexity, compounded by the fact that most patients present at advanced stages, demands a form of AI reasoning that is hierarchically coherent and contextually adaptive. For instance, gastritis is evaluated for chronic inflammation and neutrophilic activity, each of which can be graded as mild, moderate, or marked (severe). Consequently, gastric diagnosis is inherently multi-label, hierarchical, and context-dependent. Moreover, Helicobacter pylori ( H. pylori ) is a key etiologic factor associated with progression toward carcinoma  17  , further underscoring the need for models that respect conditional diagnostic structure.  However, most existing AI models are not designed to explicitly address the hierarchical and multifaceted nature of gastric pathology  18 , 19  . Current approaches largely fall into two categories: multiple instance learning (MIL)-based models and vision-language model (VLM)/large language model (LLM)-based models. MIL-based methods aggregate thousands of patches into a single slide-level representation and commonly employ task-specific prediction heads to predict multiple diagnostic targets. In parallel, VLM- and LLM-driven approaches have popularized the Pathology Visual Question Answering (VQA) paradigm, spurred by the development of large-scale datasets such as PathVQA  20  , PMC-OA  21   and PathGen  22  . These datasets have enabled models to generate report-like, multi-label outputs or answer open-ended textual queries from a slide-level embedding. Beyond patch- and slide-level inference, LLM-based approaches have also been explored for automated clinical report generation, demonstrating the broader potential of prompt-driven AI in clinical documentation  23  . Although both MIL- and VQA-based approaches can encourage shared representation learning, they typically treat targets/labels or isolated QA pairs as independent and lack explicit mechanisms to integrate diagnostic dependencies or enforce hierarchy-consistent predictions. While traditional pathology VQA models successfully map visual features to textual descriptions, they do not inherently emulate the sequential, conditional logic required to navigate complex diagnostic trees. These limitations motivate the development of alternative AI frameworks that explicitly model dependency-aware reasoning for real-world gastric pathology diagnosis.  To address these challenges, we propose AUGUST (Adaptive Unified Gastric diagnosis Using Sequential Tasks), a sequential question-answering framework for hierarchical gastric pathology diagnosis across a broad range of diagnostic tasks that closely mimics pathologists’ reasoning process (Fig.  1 ). Unlike multi-task MIL or VLM/LLM-driven label generation, AUGUST formulates gastric diagnosis as a sequential, clinically grounded question-answer process in which the diagnostic decision evolves over successive steps. Given a WSI, AUGUST iteratively creates the task-specific question conditioned on prior findings (context-aware questioning), constructs a task-relevant WSI representation conditioned on the question (question-conditioned WSI projection), and generates an answer constrained to the current diagnostic pathway (pathway-constrained answering), which in turn determines the next downstream task to pursue. This stepwise and adaptive process produces hierarchy-consistent predictions, ranging from coarse determinations to fine-grained subtyping and grading, in a clinically coherent order. By aggregating the full sequence of decisions, AUGUST generates a structured pathology report summarizing diagnostic findings across hierarchical levels.  Fig. 1   Overview of the AUGUST framework.   a  AUGUST mimics hierarchical reasoning used by pathologists via a multi-turn conversational interface with chain-of-though-style context.  b  Hierarchical and conditional dependency structure of gastric pathology diagnosis. Tasks are organized into three levels (coarse, fine, and grading), indicated by purple, teal, and pink brackets, respectively. A dashed bracket denotes a multi-label task.  c  Summary statistics of the coarse-level label distribution across all datasets.                       We evaluate AUGUST on a combined set of four distinct WSI-level gastric pathology datasets, comprising 23, 072 WSIs with up to 19 distinct diagnostic tasks that are organized into three hierarchical levels, including coarse-, fine-, and grading-level tasks. Tasks are formulated as hierarchically conditioned prompts, yielding 79, 924 question-answer pairs. Using these curated datasets, we benchmark AUGUST against state-of-the-art MIL-based methods, as well as pathology-specific FMs and VLMs under two evaluation scenarios: a fully autonomous hierarchical question-answer (Auto-QA) scenario and a human-in-the-loop question-answer (HITL-QA) scenario. In the Auto-QA setting, AUGUST performs end-to-end hierarchical diagnosis, with downstream predictions conditioned on upstream model outputs, thereby capturing strict dependency and error propagation in realistic autonomous workflows. In the HITL-QA setting, hierarchical inference proceeds sequentially from coarse to grading levels, with each upstream prediction influencing subsequent tasks. Whenever an upstream decision differs from the ground truth label, the ground truth label replaces the model’s prediction before propagating to the next diagnostic level. This process emulates an AI-assisted workflow in which expert pathologists confirm or correct intermediate findings before rendering final diagnostic judgments. Together, Auto-QA and HITL-QA settings represent two realistic deployment scenarios: fully autonomous screening to support high-throughput pathology workflows, and HITL collaboration to enhance the stability of AI-driven diagnoses. Notably, AUGUST natively supports both fully autonomous and collaborative workflows without any model modification. Across various datasets and diagnostic levels, AUGUST achieves consistently strong performance and improved hierarchical consistency over state-of-the-art baselines, demonstrating the importance of conditional reasoning for accurate and reliable gastric pathology.  More broadly, this study addresses a critical unmet need in computational pathology: AI systems that frame disease diagnosis as a conditional, multi-step reasoning process rather than a set of isolated predictions. By aligning model inference with the hierarchical structure of clinical diagnosis, AUGUST has the potential to improve diagnostic coherence, support reliable triage and characterization of high-risk lesions, and facilitate trustworthy AI integration into routine pathology practice.    Results   Hierarchical gastric diagnosis framework  AUGUST implements a unified, agent-like framework (Fig.  1 a) for hierarchical gastric pathology diagnosis, covering coarse-, fine-, and grade-level predictions (Fig.  1 b) within a single framework. It was trained on an internal dataset (GastUJB-Train), which consists of 6 913 WSIs and 27, 069 question-answer pairs, covering three coarse-level tasks, eleven fine-level, and five grade-level tasks (Fig.  1 c and Figure  S1 ). Coarse-level tasks include global properties such as  proximal / distal  stomach  location ,  H. pylori  infection status, and broad  condition  category ( inflammatory disease / benign tumor / dysplasia / cancer ). Fine-level tasks refer to subtype-level decisions, covering more specific  location  assignments ( body / cardia / fundus ,  antrum / prepylorus ) and detailed  inflammatory  or  benign / cancer  subtype classifications. Grading-level tasks address severity scales or histologic grades, including  dysplasia  severity (DYS Grading),  chronic inflammation  grading (Chronic Grading),  neutrophilic activity  grading (Activity Grading),  adenocarcinoma  grading (ADC Grading), and  lymphoma  grading (Lym Grading). The training followed a three-session training curriculum (Section “Results”): (1) Cross-domain alignment, using 6 913 WSI-caption (a list of all associated labels) pairs to ground visual features in diagnostic concepts; (2) Visual instruction tuning, using the 27,069 question-answer pairs with 6 913 WSIs to acquire task-specific diagnostic behaviors; and (3) Multi-turn VQA, which restructured the same WSIs and question-answer pairs into chain-of-thought (CoT) sequences, enabling the model to conduct hierarchical, conditional, and context-aware reasoning across progressive diagnostic steps. During inference, AUGUST operates autonomously in a coarse-to-fine manner. It first conducts three coarse-level classifications ( location ,  H. pylori , and  condition ), and then dynamically selects subsequent questions based on the accumulated question-answer history. Moreover, AUGUST supports HITL diagnosis, in which upstream predictions can be replaced with ground truth labels (i.e., confirmed or corrected by expert pathologists) before proceeding to downstream tasks. We evaluated the trained AUGUST on four separate validation cohorts (Fig.  1 c), including an internal validation set GastUJB-Test (5 166 WSIs with 21,396 question-answer pairs) and three multi-institutional external validation sets, including GastAIHub (6, 360 WSIs with 16,644 question-answer pairs), GastCODiPAI (3 642 WSIs with 12,971 question-answer pairs), and GastADC22 (991 WSIs with 1844 question-answer pairs). GastUJB-Test covers the same task set and hierarchy as GastUJB-Train, while the remaining validation sets include varying subsets of tasks across hierarchical levels. To benchmark AUGUST, we compared it against three model families: five MIL-based methods, two pathology-specific VLMs, and two pathology-specific FMs (Section “Results”). Both MIL models and VLMs were trained on GastUJB-Train to facilitate direct diagnostic capability comparison. In contrast, given their extensive pre-training on large-scale WSI data, FMs were evaluated in a zero-shot classification setting to assess out-of-the-box adaptability. Collectively, these comparisons quantify gastric diagnosis performance with and without specialized, hierarchy-aware diagnostic modeling.    AUGUST improves overall gastric diagnosis performance  We first evaluated AUGUST’s end-to-end structured report generation capability for gastric diagnosis under the Auto-QA protocol. AUGUST conducts fully autonomous hierarchical gastric diagnosis by sequentially answering clinically grounded questions and aggregating the resulting predictions into a structured pathology report (Fig.  1 a and Fig.  S2 ). Since errors at higher levels propagate to dependent tasks, this protocol, therefore, represents a rigorous evaluation of fully automated deployment, jointly assessing report-level correctness and hierarchical consistency. We quantified report quality using five evaluation metrics, including BLEU 1 , BLEU 2 , BLEU 3 , BLEU 4 , and ROUGE  L  , and compared AUGUST against three baseline families. For concise visualization and comparison, we mainly report a single best-performing model from each family (Best MIL, Best VLM, and Best FM). These representative models were selected by averaging report generation metrics within each family, resulting in ABMIL, SlideChat, and PRISM being chosen as Best MIL, Best VLM, and Best FM, respectively.  Across datasets and evaluation metrics, AUGUST consistently outperformed the three representative baseline models (Fig.  2 ). On the internal GastUJB, AUGUST obtained the highest score on every evaluation metric (91.91 BLEU 1 , 86.79 BLEU 2 , 83.84 BLEU 3 , 82.29 BLEU 4 , and 92.32 ROUGE  L  ). These correspond to substantial improvements over the baselines, with grains of +4.56 to +20.14 (BLEU 1 ), +1.32 to +22.31 (BLEU 2 ), +0.99 to +19.36 (BLEU 3 ), +2.01 to +27.08 (BLEU 4 ), and +3.64 to +19.69 (ROUGE  L  ). We observed the same trend on the three external validation sets (GastAIHub, GastCoDiPAI, and GastADC22). On GastAIHub, AUGUST achieved the highest scores for both BLEU 1−4  (94.38/89.70/86.34/82.83) and ROUGE  L   (91.80), exceeding the three baselines by at least +7.77 (BLEU 1 ), +5.48 (BLEU 2 ), +5.43 (BLEU 3 ), +4.23 (BLEU 4 ) and +5.10 (ROUGE  L  ). Consistent with this, AUGUST also obtained the best BLEU and ROUGE scores on both GastCODiPAI and GastADC22, indicating robust generalization across external datasets. Radar plots further visualize these consistent improvements (Fig.  2 a). AUGUST formed the outer envelope across most metrics and datasets, whereas the three representative baselines showed consistently smaller polygons. Comparing the three representative baselines, Best MIL was generally superior to other two baselines. Best VLM was comparable to Best MIL on BLEU 1  (unigram-level lexical overlap), but lagged on higher-order BLEU and ROUGE  L  , suggesting weaker multi-phrase consistency and global report fidelity. Best FM performed worst across metrics, highlighting the limitations of the alignment-based report generation.  Fig. 2   Performance of structured gastric diagnosis report generation.   a  Radar plots and  b  heat maps comparing AUGUST with three representative baseline models using BLEU 1−4  and ROUGE  L   scores.                       To ensure that the comparison with SOTA models (MIL models, VLMs, and FMs) was not confounded by differences in domain-specific optimization, we re-evaluated these baseline models after training them on GastUJB-Train under the identical optimization settings (e.g., epochs, learning rate scheduling) as AUGUST. Since VLMs include an LLM decoder, they were trained using our three-session training curriculum on the question-answer dataset. In contrast, FMs and MILs, which do not contain an LLM decoder, were trained using WSI–label pairs. As detailed in Tables  S9 – S16 , FMs benefited from this matched optimization. For example, the Best FM (PRISM) exhibited consistent improvements across both internal (+0.466 on GastUJB) and external validation sets (+0.529 on GastAIHub, +0.466 on GastCODiPAI, and +0.625 on GastADC) under Auto-QA. Likewise, the Best VLM (SlideChat) improved performance, with gains of +0.158, +0.142, +0.012, and +0.013 across GastUJB, GastAIHub, GastCODiPAI, and GastADC, respectively. However, the Best MIL (S4MIL) showed overall degradation under the AUGUST training setup, with performance declining on three of the four datasets: GastUJB (−0.019), GastCODiPAI (−0.164), and GastADC (−0.033); only GastAIHub yielded a localized gain (+0.230). This degradation may reflect a mismatch between the AUGUST training configuration and the learning characteristics of MIL-based models. Unlike FM and VLM architectures, which are underpinned by large-scale pre-trained representations, MIL models typically function as task-specific classifiers with relatively limited learning capabilities. As a result, they may benefit less from the optimization settings of AUGUST and may be more susceptible to overfitting under the prolonged training schedules. Trained from a relatively limited initialization, making them more susceptible to overfitting under the extended training schedule used in our setup. Despite these gains among FMs and VLMs, AUGUST continued to outperform all retrained competing models across every evaluation dataset, achieving F1 scores of 0.780, 0.780, 0.703, and 0.625 on GastUJB, GastAIHub, GastCODiPAI, and GastADC, respectively. These results confirm that AUGUST’s superiority is not merely a byproduct of domain-specific training exposure but stems directly from its specialized architectural design for hierarchical gastric WSI diagnosis.  Overall, AUGUST excelled at generating accurate and hierarchically consistent structured gastric diagnosis reports across both internal and external validation sets, supporting robust fully automated deployment under the Auto-QA setting. Further details are provided in Table  S1 .    AUGUST improves individual gastric diagnostic tasks  While the quality of structured reports captures overall diagnostic correctness, it does not isolate performance on individual diagnostic tasks. We therefore examined AUGUST at the task level under the Auto-QA setting by analyzing per-task performance across coarse-, fine-, and grading-level tasks. This task-centric evaluation provides a more granular view of diagnostic behavior under the same hierarchical workflow and facilitates direction comparison to baseline models at each diagnostic step. For conciseness, we compared AUGUST against Best MIL (ABMIL), Best VLM (WSICaption), and Best FM (PRISM) using F1 scores. As shown in Fig.  3 a, AUGUST consistently achieved strong task-level performance across all four cohorts, with detailed results provided in Tables  S2  and  S3 .  Fig. 3   Performance of task-level gastric diagnosis under Auto-QA.   a  Bar plots display per-dataset F1 scores.  b  Box plots summarize the distribution of F1 scores for each dataset.  c  Radar plots visualize multi-task performance for (left) the internal GastUJB and (right) the three external datasets.  d  Task-wise F1 heatmaps show performance for all coarse-, fine-, and grading-level tasks, with color intensity indicating F1 score (0–1). Two-sided paired bootstrap tests were used to calculate the statistical differences between AUGUST and the top-performing alternative model, with  P  denoting the  p  − value. In  a , data are presented as means with 95% CI estimated using the bootstrap method ( n  = 1 000 replicates).                       On the internal GastUJB dataset, AUGUST achieved an average F1 score of 0.780 (95% CI: 0.743–0.816) and delivered the highest performance across all external datasets, with F1 scores of 0.780 (95% CI: 0.760–0.799) on GastAIHub, 0.703 (95% CI: 0.685–0.722) on GastCODiPAI, and 0.625 (95% CI: 0.597–0.653) on GastADC22, with each comparison against the top-performing alternative model reached statistical significance ( p  − value < 0.0001). Aggregated across all datasets and tasks, AUGUST obtained an overall average F1 of 0.722 (95% CI: 0.696-0.747), exceeding the best baseline within each family (Best MIL: 0.614; Best VLM: 0.508; Best FM: 0.132).  AUGUST also exhibited markedly improved stability across tasks, with higher medians and narrower dispersion than baselines (Fig.  3 b). For example, on GastUJB, AUGUST attained the highest median F1 of 0.802 with an interquartile range (IQR) of 0.163, followed by Best MIL at 0.735 median F1 with 0.226 IQR, whereas Best VLM and Best FM showed substantially lower median F1 scores of 0.638 (IQR: 0.422) and 0.078 (IQR: 0.214), respectively. Similar trends were found on the external sets (GastAIHub, GastCODiPAI, and GastADC22).  We further examined head-to-head task-level diagnostic capabilities using radar plots (Fig.  3 c) and heatmaps (Fig.  3 d). Radar plots (Fig.  3 c) provide a geometric view of multi-task competence across coarse-, fine-, and grading-level tasks. AUGUST formed a large, comparatively uniform polygon spanning the majority of coarse- and fine-grained diagnostic axes, suggesting consistently strong performance across diagnostic tasks. In contrast, baseline models exhibited dented and irregular shapes that reflect selective failures. Specifically, Best MIL showed deficits in  inflammatory disease  subtyping tasks on the internal GastUJB, and in  cancer -related tasks (marked as ’CC’ in Fig.  3 c) on external cohorts, while Best VLM and FM collapsed further toward the center, particularly on fine-grained diagnostic tasks, suggesting limited ability to capture the full diagnostic spectrum. Moreover, task-wise F1 heatmaps (Fig.  3 d) confirmed these findings at higher resolution. AUGUST dominated across coarse-, fine-, and grading-level tasks, with the majority of cells exhibiting high F1 scores, whereas baseline models showed fragmented performance, with pronounced degradation at finer diagnostic levels. This highlights their persistent difficulty in resolving histologic details and subtype structures in the absence of a hierarchy-aware training and inference approach. The heatmaps also revealed systematic differences among baseline models. Best MIL remained competitive on coarse-level tasks, but its performance varied at the fine- and grading-level tasks, with noticeable drops for some  dysplasia  and  cancer -related tasks. Although Best VLM maintained moderate coarse-level performance, its performance deteriorated rapidly on fine- and grading-level tasks, with several tasks approaching near-zero F1. Best FM showed the least stability, frequently yielding low scores on multiple tasks across hierarchical levels. Additionally, we evaluated Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curves for AUGUST and the best family models, with Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC) and 95% CI (Figs.  S11 – S16 ). Across these ROC curves and AUCs, AUGUST showed consistent and superior performance on coarse- and fine-level tasks such as general location,  Helicobacter pylori , condition,  cancer  subtypes, while it slightly underperformed on certain grading tasks, particularly  adenocarcinoma  grading and  dysplasia  histology grading.  Furthermore, as investigating all baseline models, we found that models within the same architectural family tended to exhibit similar ranks across datasets (Table  S4 ), suggesting that these limitations are largely architectural rather than driven by isolated model choices. In particular, both VLM (SlideChat and WSICaption) and FM (PRISM and TITAN) families performed poorly across tasks and datasets, indicating that large-scale pretraining models alone cannot reliably induce pathology-specific, hierarchy-aware reasoning required for comprehensive gastric diagnosis. Importantly, these task-level advantages were consistent across internal (GastUJB) and external (GastAIHub, GastCODiPAI, and GastADC22) evaluations. Despite substantial differences in data distributions, class compositions, and data sources, AUGUST exhibited stable performance patterns and preserved its relative advantage across cohorts, while baseline models showed larger performance degradation and greater variability. For example, on the  condition  classification (’Cond’ task in Fig.  3 d), AUGUST obtained an F1 score of 0.879 on GastUJB, compared to 0.876, 0.827, and 0.506 for Best MIL, Best VLM, and Best FM, respectively. Human-in-the-loop supervision enhances hierarchical gastric diagnostic performance  To assess the effect of HITL supervision in hierarchical gastric diagnosis, we evaluated AUGUST and all baselines under the HITL-QA setting. The three top-level diagnostic tasks, including  location ,  H. pylori  infection status, and  condition , were evaluated identically to Auto-QA, as they have no prerequisite conditions. For all subsequent tasks, HITL-QA intervenes in the autonomous procedure by replacing upstream predictions with ground truth labels at each step before proceeding downstream (Fig.  4 ). This breaks hierarchical error propagation during evaluation, facilitating independent assessment of each downstream task without cascade effects. This setting reflects a realistic computer-aided workflow in which a pathologist validates or corrects upstream decisions before the model is applied to finer-grained assessments. We analyzed HITL-QA from two complementary perspectives: (1) task-level diagnostic performance when downstream predictions are conditioned on ground truth upstream decisions, thereby separating per-task capability from cascade error propagation; and (2) the intervention rates (i.e., how often upstream predictions must be corrected to match ground truth), which quantifies the degree of expert intervention that would be required in practice. AUGUST and competing models struggle on specific tasks  Across all 36 tasks (19 on GastUJB, 9 on GastAIHub, 6 on GastCODiPAI, 2 on GastADC22), AUGUST achieved top or near-top scores on the majority of tasks. Nonetheless, performance remained reduced on a small subset of fine- and grading-level tasks. To better understand these errors, we analyzed Auto-QA F1 scores across all four cohorts from two perspectives: (1) Universal challenges shared across architectures and (2) Model-specific failures (Fig.  3  and Tables  S2  and  S3 ).  Despite their overall performance differences, AUGUST and all baseline models struggled on rare fine-level lesion detection and grading-level tasks under distribution shift. On the internal GastUJB, fine-level  inflammatory disease  tasks such as  glandular atrophy  (AUGUST 0.357 F1 vs. Best MIL 0.000, Best VLM 0.000, Best FM 0.077),  ulceration  (0.577 vs. 0.450, 0.000, 0.058), and  erosion  (0.689 vs. 0.271, 0.213, 0.000) exhibited lower performance than most other tasks. Grading-level tasks showed a related sensitivity to dataset shift. For  cancer - adenocarcinoma  grading, performance was moderate on GastUJB (0.728 F1 vs. Best MIL 0.699, Best VLM 0.458, Best FM 0.000) but declined on external cohorts, including GastAIHub (0.619 vs. 0.525, 0.365, 0.000), GastCODiPAI (0.646 vs. 0.628, 0.427, 0.000), and GastADC22 (0.607 vs. 0.445, 0.173, 0.000). These consistent absolute drops across models indicate that severity assessment is intrinsically more sensitive to dataset shift than coarse-level tasks such as  location  or  H. pylori  infection status.  To elucidate the mechanisms underlying this performance degradation on rare lesions, we conducted a granular error analysis of the model. Assessment of training versus test accuracy (Table  S17 ) revealed a pronounced generalization gap, indicative of overfitting to data-scarce classes. Although AUGUST achieved near-perfect training accuracy (100%) on rare subcategories such as  xanthoma ,  gastritis cystica polyposa , and  squamous cell carcinoma , its test performance declined substantially, yielding accuracies of 40.0% ( xanthoma ) and 25.0%  gastritis cystica polyposa  on GastUJB, respectively, and 1.01% ( neuroendocrine tumors ) on GastAIHub. This disparity underscores the fundamental challenge of learning robust representations when the absolute number of available training samples is too small to capture the natural morphological variance of the disease. Furthermore, we performed low-dimensional projections of the latent feature space using UMAP   24   (Figs.  S18 – S20 ), demonstrating that minority lesions lack discriminative morphological representations across internal and external datasets. To understand how these representational ambiguities impact sequential decision-making, we evaluated case-level prediction trajectories across the diagnostic hierarchy (Fig.  S21 ). Overall, AUGUST demonstrated superior reasoning stability across all cohorts, maximizing consistently correct diagnostic pathways ( R  ⇒  R ) and minimizing persistent downstream failures ( W  ⇒  W ) compared to alternative architectures. Nevertheless, this trajectory analysis also delineated the mechanics of error propagation when the model encounters data-scarce classes. Since downstream predictions are explicitly conditioned on upstream clinical context, any initial misclassification, frequently driven by the aforementioned morphological ambiguity, forces the model down an incorrect diagnostic pathway. Although AUGUST mitigates cascading errors more effectively than the baselines, an upstream inaccuracy inevitably establishes a flawed contextual premise. Consequently, rare lesions remain disproportionately vulnerable, as an initial diagnostic error systematically misdirects the subsequent hierarchical assessment.  Beyond these shared challenges, different models exhibited distinct failure patterns that were not apparent from average F1 alone. Best MIL showed strong performance on several tasks on the internal GastUJB (e.g., 0.891 ~ 0.904 F1 on  cancer  subtyping and 0.945 F1 on  chronic inflammation ), but left some rare fine-level tasks essentially unsolved (e.g., 0.000 F1 on  glandular atrophy ) and showed noticeable degradation on grading and  H. pylori  detection across external validation cohorts. Best VLM demonstrated moderate coarse-level performance on GastUJB but exhibited larger variability across cohorts, with notably lower grading scores on GastADC22 (0.173 F1 on  adenocarcinoma  grading vs. 0.607 for AUGUST). Best FM exhibited the most limited overall performance, with multiple near-zero tasks on GastUJB and consistently low scores on the external validation cohorts, suggesting that large-scale pretraining alone does not reliably translate to pathology-faithful fine-grained decision making under hierarchical dependency. Moreover, GastADC22, which focuses exclusively on  condition  and  cancer - adenocarcinoma  grading, provided a focused evaluation of grading robustness. AUGUST maintained strong performance on both tasks (0.768 and 0.607 F1), while Best MIL obtained reduced grading performance (0.697 and 0.445 F1), Best VLM degraded further (0.416 and 0.173 F1), and Best FM collapsed to 0.000 F1 on both tasks. These results suggest that  cancer -enriched cohorts can disproportionately challenge fine-grained severity estimation.    AUGUST supports visually grounded and interpretable diagnosis  Model interpretability is essential for clinical adoption in computational pathology, where “black-box” decision-making can obscure diagnostic rationale. To assess whether AUGUST’s hierarchical predictions are visually grounded in plausible tissue evidence, we produced and examined post-hoc saliency maps using gradient-weighted class activation mapping (Grad-CAM)  25  , which highlights image regions that most strongly influence the model’s predictions. Figure  7  shows four representative WSI examples with Grad-CAM saliency maps, spanning multiple fine- and grading-level tasks. For each example, we provide three high-attention close-up regions along with the corresponding question-answer pair to facilitate clinical inspection. We note that saliency maps for anatomical  location  or  inflammatory disease  findings are excluded, as they often correspond to diffuse or globally distributed histologic patterns, for which focal saliency visualization is less informative. Qualitative review by an experienced pathologist indicated that the highlighted regions generally demonstrate diagnostically relevant morphology that contribute to specific predictions. For instance, in a  fundic gland polyp  case (Fig.  7 a), the saliency map highlights polypoid architectures with characteristic mushroom-shaped morphology that distinguishes these lesions from flatter lesions. In a  dysplasia  grading case (Fig.  7 b), the highlighted regions capture mild architectural atypia that is distinct from relatively regular glandular structure. In gastric  cancer  cases (Fig.  7 c–d), regions of high-activation consistently correspond to malignant tissue rather than background artifacts or normal glands. Conversely, visual interpretability provides critical insight into the model’s failure modes by revealing where attention diverges from diagnostically relevant morphology. We visualized representative misclassifications across coarse- and fine-grained tasks (Fig.  S17 ). For example, when misclassifying a ground truth  hyperplastic polyp  as an  inflammatory polyp  (Fig.  S17 a), the model’s attention is broadly distributed across generic polypoid structures rather than localizing on the characteristic hyperplastic glandular architecture. Similarly, in a case of false-negative  cancer  detection (Fig.  S17 b), high-activation regions completely fail to capture the infiltrative features indicative of malignancy. In grading errors, such as overestimating  low-grade dysplasia  as  high-grade  (Fig.  S17 c), saliency is misdirected toward structurally ambiguous tissue regions rather than definitive low-grade architectural changes. These examples demonstrate that interpretability tools not only validate correct predictions but also directly expose the specific representational vulnerabilities, such as morphological ambiguity or feature misalignment, that precipitate clinical errors. Although Grad-CAM provides only a coarse, post-hoc analysis and does not establish causal evidence, these examples support that AUGUST’s predictions are grounded in visually plausible tissue regions, strengthening its suitability as a transparent decision-support framework for gastric pathology diagnosis. To further evaluate the clinical reliability of AUGUST, we analyzed false negative rates (FNR, %) for major disease categories across multiple hierarchical tasks (Table  S7 ). Lower FNR indicates improved sensitivity by measuring how often clinically significant findings are missed. Across all task-level evaluations, AUGUST achieved the lowest average FNR under both Auto-QA and HITL-QA, decreasing the mean FNR to 32.04% and 25.49%, respectively, compared with 37.10% and 29.84% for Best MIL. This advantage was broadly distributed across tasks, with AUGUST yielding the lowest FNR in 14 of 20 Auto-QA tasks and 10 of 20 HITL-QA tasks. The reduction was particularly notable for several critical clinical findings, including  H. pylori  positive status on GastAIHub (13.06% vs. 42.04%) and condition-level cancer on GastAIHub (26.61% vs. 41.75%). Moreover, HITL-QA further reduced the overall FNR of AUGUST from 32.04% to 25.49%, suggesting that expert verification of upstream decisions effectively mitigates the propagation of missed downstream diagnoses. Nevertheless, FNR remained relatively high for some difficult subclasses, such as  dysplasia  on GastAIHub, implying that rare or highly challenging categories remain an important source of diagnostic error despite the overall gains.    Ablation study reveals the impact of training and conditioning strategies  AUGUST utilizes a three-session training curriculum (Session 1: Cross-domain alignment, Session 2: Visual instruction tuning, and Session 3: Multi-turn VQA) and clinically grounded conditioning. To quantify the contribution of each training session, we conducted ablation studies on four validation sets (GastUJB, GastAIHub, GastCODiPAI, and GastAD22) and evaluated under both Auto-QA and HITL-QA. Fig.  S3 a-b summarizes these results. Across all datasets and both settings, the full AUGUST model consistently outperformed ablated variants, indicating that its gains arise from complementary design choices. The largest degradation occurred when both Session 2 and 3 were excluded, on average, dropping F1 scores from 0.751 to 0.554 in Auto-QA and 0.772 to 0.595 in HITL-QA. The addition of Session 2 partially recovered performance but remained substantially inferior to the full model. These results highlight that multi-turn question-answering (Session 3) is essential for learning dependency-aware hierarchical diagnostic behavior. Data augmentation also contributed substantially to model robustness. Without data augmentation, AUGUST experienced performance declines to 0.613 for Auto-QA and 0.721 for HITL-QA on average. This observation suggests that exposure to diverse visual perturbations improves generalization and robustness against class imbalance and dataset shift.  To further assess the architectural contributions of AUGUST, we evaluated the impact of the LLM backbone and the hierarchical constraint mechanism through additional ablation experiments across the same four validation sets under both Auto-QA and HITL-QA settings (Fig.  S4 a–b). Across all datasets and both evaluation settings, the full AUGUST model consistently outperformed other models, confirming that the LLM module and hierarchical constraints act as complementary components. The largest degradation occurred when both components were simultaneously removed, with average F1 scores dropping from 0.751 to 0.559 in Auto-QA and from 0.772 to 0.666 in HITL-QA. The impact was particularly severe on GastCODiPAI, where the joint removal caused a catastrophic decline from 0.746 to 0.394 in Auto-QA. Removing the LLM module alone reduced average F1 to 0.586 in Auto-QA and 0.661 in HITL-QA, whereas removing the hierarchical constraint alone yielded comparable degradation at 0.581 and 0.667, respectively. These parallel performance drops indicate that neither component alone is sufficient to sustain full diagnostic performance, and that both contribute independently to the model’s robustness. Collectively, these results validate the design rationale behind AUGUST: integrating an LLM backbone with clinically structured hierarchical constraints is essential for reliable and generalizable gastric diagnosis.  Moreover, we evaluated the effect of incorporating  H. pylori  infection status as contextual information for downstream predictions. The inclusion of  H. pylori  infection status yielded consistent improvements across all datasets (Fig.  S3 c). For example, without  H. pylori  infection status, the overall average F1 decreased from 0.755 to 0.717. Notably, the benefit of  H. pylori  infection status was comparable under both Auto-QA (+0.053 F1) and HITL-QA (+0.047 F1) settings, with higher performance was obtained with HITL-QA. This result supports the clinical motivation for explicitly modeling  H. pylori  infection status as a dedicated task and using it as etiologic context, providing informative constraints that improve downstream diagnostic discrimination.     Discussion  This study addresses a persistent mismatch between computational pathology models and real clinical practice in gastric pathology. Routine diagnosis is multi-label, hierarchical, and conditional, whereas most AI systems are designed, trained, and evaluated as independent, single-step classifiers. AUGUST aims at bridging this gap by formulating gastric diagnosis as a sequential, hierarchical question-answering process that mirrors how pathologists progressively refine decisions from coarse determinations to subtyping and grading. In a real-world deployment scenario, AUGUST would function as a back-end decision-support module interfaced with the hospital’s Laboratory Information System (LIS) or Picture Archiving and Communication System (PACS). Upon slide digitization, WSIs can be automatically routed to the model for hierarchical inference. By explicitly modeling diagnostic dependencies during both training and inference, AUGUST provides a clinically aligned framework for end-to-end structured report generation as well as for stepwise decision support. Moreover, the structured diagnostic reports generated by AUGUST follow the formatting conventions of clinical pathology reports, allowing the model’s outputs to be directly incorporated into existing electronic medical record (EMR) systems without requiring manual reformatting and thereby supporting seamless integration into routine clinical practice. Should an institution require a more descriptive report or a different structural format, AUGUST’s flexible, LLM-driven architecture can be readily customized to generate tailored clinical narratives and adapt to specific institutional reporting templates.  This work makes four primary contributions. First, we formalize gastric pathology diagnosis into a hierarchical decision-making process spanning three diagnostic axes, including  location ,  H. pylori  infection status, and pathologic  condition , and further organize  location  and  condition  into coarse-, fine-, and grading-level tasks, capturing the progressive and conditional refinement used in routine practice (Section “Results”). Second, we curate and benchmark across four multi-institutional cohorts with substantial distribution shift in specimen types, label coverage, and class prevalence (Section “Results”), enabling robust external validation beyond the single institutional training set. Third, we introduce a multimodal, hierarchy-aware diagnosis framework that couples (1) context-aware questioning, which selects the next diagnostic step conditioned on prior findings, (2) question-conditioned WSI projection, which constructs task-relevant representations conditioned on the current question, and (3) pathway-constrained answering, which generates task-specific answers consistent with the current diagnostic pathway and determines which downstream task to pursue next, thereby producing a structured report from the full sequence of diagnostic decisions. Fourth, we establish evaluation protocols for both fully autonomous deployment (Auto-QA, with hierarchical error propagation) and clinically realistic collaboration (HITL-QA, with expert validation), facilitating systematic analysis of cascade errors and downstream task capabilities.  Under the Auto-QA setting, AUGUST achieves stronger report-level and task-level performance among all baselines across both internal and external cohorts. This consistent advantage suggests that explicitly modeling clinically aligned decision ordering and conditional refinement improves end-to-end diagnostic capability beyond what can be obtained by optimizing disconnected subtasks. Ablation results further confirm the effectiveness of AUGUST’s stepwise reasoning, in which removing multi-turn VQA training substantially degrades performance, indicating that the performance gains arise from dependency-aware reasoning rather than template learning alone. In contrast, baseline models show selective degradation, most prominently on fine-grained subtyping and grading, suggesting their difficulty in resolving subtle histologic cues when prerequisite context is not explicitly incorporated. Although AUGUST enhances fine-grained subtyping and grading, Auto-QA remains inherently sensitive to error propagation, as early mistakes can cascade to downstream steps and further decrease fine- and grading-level performance. This underscores the need to improve upstream robustness and/or incorporate HITL validation for reliable practical deployment.  The HITL-QA setting isolates downstream competency from error propagation by replacing upstream predictions with ground truth labels at each step, emulating a workflow in which a pathologist confirms or corrects high-level decisions before proceeding to finer-grained assessments. Across cohorts, HITL-QA consistently improves performance relative to Auto-QA, quantifying the practical value of expert intervention in hierarchical diagnosis and highlighting that cascading errors substantially limit fully autonomous performance (Fig.  6 ). Moreover, AUGUST remains the top-performing approach under HITL-QA, indicating that its gains are not solely driven by the hierarchical, stepwise procedure but also by stronger per-task capacity across multiple diagnostic levels. At the grading-level tasks, however, the narrowed performance gaps or competitiveness of specific MIL-based models suggest that certain tasks may benefit from complementary architectures, motivating hybrid designs that combine stepwise reasoning with specialized computational modules.  Conventional, non-hierarchical AI models simultaneously generate predictions over 40 diagnostic categories. As these models lack clinical logic, downstream predictions may not correspond to upstream findings. This can cause frequent out-of-context alerts, introducing unnecessary cognitive load and contributing to alert fatigue. In contrast, AUGUST’s hierarchical gating mechanism inherently mimics the logical, step-by-step diagnostic workflow of gastric pathology diagnosis, directing the model through a clinically plausible pathway. This enables pathologists to focus on contextually relevant tasks, rather than reviewing a broad set of potentially irrelevant predictions. By substantially reducing unnecessary and out-of-context alerts, AUGUST may improve the overall efficiency and effectiveness of gastric diagnosis. Moreover, AUGUST’s stepwise framework provides an auditable diagnostic trajectory that makes upstream-to-downstream error propagation visible and traceable, i.e., identifying exactly which upstream decision caused unnecessary downstream evaluations. In practical deployment, this transparent audit trail can support quality assurance, structured review, and root-cause analysis by localizing failure modes and identifying high-impact branch points.  Although AUGUST demonstrates clear performance advantages, its intervention rate under the HITL-QA protocol remains substantial at approximately 30%, despite being lower than that of the baseline models. We note that this should not be interpreted as an isolated limitation of AUGUST, but rather as an indication of the inherent complexity and clinical realism of the hierarchical evaluation setting used in this study. In contrast to prior work that has often focused on simplified, single-step diagnostic tasks, potentially overstating the feasibility of autonomous diagnosis, our results demonstrate that no current AI system is yet capable of fully autonomous and clinically safe gastric WSI diagnosis. Although AUGUST reduces the intervention burden relative to baselines, this margin alone may not eliminate expert workload. Instead, it underscores that human oversight remains strictly necessary for safe deployment. In this context, the practical value of AUGUST’s stepwise, hierarchical framework lies in its ability to naturally integrate this required intervention, effectively preventing the propagation of upstream errors to downstream diagnostic tasks.  For clinical deployment, AUGUST requires careful workflow integration. While hierarchical systems can increase the risk of automation bias if users over-trust upstream findings and implicitly accept downstream predictions without verification, excessive requests for expert intervention can cause alert fatigue, increasing cognitive burden and potentially contributing to diagnostic errors. In high-throughput settings, the most realistic deployment scenario is an autonomous pre-read (Auto-QA) in which the model generates a complete structured report end-to-end, followed by expert review of the final output rather than step-by-step interaction. For HITL use, the system should minimize expert intervention while ensuring diagnostic quality by supporting low-friction usage patterns, such as exception-based review (e.g., uncertainty-triggered evaluation) or checkpoint verification restricted to a small number of high-impact decisions (e.g., cancer vs. non-cancer and coarse condition category). To support these workflows and mitigate both automation bias and alert fatigue, user-centered interfaces should be carefully designed to incorporate: (1) uncertainty-aware mechanisms that measure and display confidence for each decision point, (2) direct links to supporting visual evidence (e.g., representative regions of interest), and (3) explicit mechanisms to override upstream decisions and automatically recompute downstream predictions along the corrected pathway. Furthermore, safe clinical adoption should be accompanied by structured user training that explains the model’s hierarchical reasoning and branching logic, highlights known failure modes (e.g., rare lesions or grading), warns against over-reliance on AI (e.g., treating model’s outputs as second-reader suggestions), and incorporates periodic feedback and audit cycles to monitor real-world performance drift and maintain calibrated usage over time.  Baseline comparisons clarify the strengths and limitations of existing model families for hierarchical gastric diagnosis. Overall, MIL models were superior to pathology-specific VLMs and FMs on most diagnostic tasks, and in some tasks (e.g.,  cancer - adenocarcinoma  grading) matched or even exceeded AUGUST. This is likely because they are explicitly optimized with task-specific classification objectives and dedicated classification heads. However, MIL models implicitly capture shared representations across diverse tasks and lack an explicit mechanism for conditional decision making. As a result, they cannot directly enforce clinically meaningful hierarchical dependencies beyond what is learned implicitly. In contrast, although VLMs were trained on GastUJB-Train and can leverage question-answer supervision, they still underperformed MIL models, suggesting that large multimodal generation capacity alone is insufficient for pathology-faithful, hierarchy-consistent gastric diagnosis. FMs evaluated in a zero-shot setting performed the worst overall, indicating that large-scale WSI pre-training does not reliably translate into correct, fine-grained, dependency-aware gastric diagnosis without targeted fine-tuning/adaptation, task-aligned training objectives, and hierarchy-aware inference strategies.  This study has several limitations. First, both training and validation datasets exhibit data and class imbalance, and rare subtypes remain challenging. Targeted data curation, imbalance-aware training strategies, and pathology-faithful data synthesis may help to improve performance on rare categories without sacrificing performance on common cases. Second, although external validation indicates robustness, real-world variability can be broader. Future work should expand prospective multi-site validation and explore domain adaptation or fine-tuning strategies to better accommodate distribution shifts. Third, while question-answer prompting improves accuracy and reliability on gastric diagnosis, the prompt templates are manually designed. Automating prompt construction would improve scalability and facilitate transfer to other organs and disease settings. Fourth, WSIs may contain multiple concurrent lesions. In this study, we assign a single coarse-level  condition  label based on the lesion of highest clinical significance, which simplifies evaluation but may under-represent multi-lesion complexity. Extending AUGUST to explicit multi-label  condition  reporting and evaluation would better reflect routine clinical practice. Fifth, Grad-CAM saliency maps were used to visually verify that AUGUST’s attention aligns with relevant histopathological features (Fig.  7 ). These visualizations, however, remain qualitative and do not provide a formal quantitative assessment of whether the highlighted regions correspond to expert-annotated pathological evidence. Although systematic localization analysis and quantitative validation against expert annotations would further strengthen the interpretability and clinical reliability of the model’s predictions, such evaluation would be challenging in practice because it would require large-scale expert annotation across numerous diagnostic categories, and quantitative comparison with Grad-CAM saliency maps is itself nontrivial owing to their diffuse and threshold-dependent nature. Sixth, the current hierarchical diagnosis relies on hard thresholding, which can pose limitations in cases with ambiguous predictions or borderline decision boundaries. Integrating an uncertainty-aware mechanism into the hierarchical reasoning framework would provide a more robust and clinically reliable approach by allowing the model to explicitly identify low-confidence predictions and better account for uncertainty propagation across dependent diagnostic steps. Seventh, AUGUST requires comparatively greater computational resources (Table  S20 ), which may limit its practicality in some real-world settings. Future optimization efforts will be necessary to improve its efficiency and facilitate broader clinical adoption. Last, while we demonstrated the capability of AUGUST across multiple cohorts, true clinical utility requires validation beyond retrospective benchmark performance. Fully establishing the clinical utility necessitates prospective, multi-reader multi-case clinical studies with a dedicated clinical user interface. Future research should directly evaluate diagnostic time-savings and error reduction, intervention frequency, workload reduction, user trust and acceptance, and the broader dynamics of human-AI collaboration in practice.    Methods   Structure of hierarchical gastric diagnostic tasks  Gastric pathology diagnosis is inherently a multi-step, conditional decision-making process. To align with this workflow, we organize gastric diagnostic tasks into a hierarchical structure rather than a collection of independent, single-step classifications. We first decompose gastric pathology diagnosis into three broad axes: (1) the anatomical  location  of the tissue, (2)  H. pylori  infection status, and (3) the pathologic  condition , encompassing the lesion type and severity. This decomposition mirrors how pathologists integrate anatomic context, etiologic information, and morphologic interpretation to reach a final diagnosis. Tissue  location  is an anatomical attribute that is largely independent of pathological alteration and primarily provides spatial context for interpretation and management. Although  H. pylori  infection status can be viewed as part of the  condition  category, it serves as a key etiologic driver  26   of the pathological cascade spanning from gastritis to adenoma and gastric cancer and is linked to specific microscopic features. For example, chronic inflammation and neutrophilic activity are frequently observed in  H. pylori -associated gastritis, making infection status highly informative for interpreting inflammatory lesions. Accordingly,  H. pylori  infection status is identified as an independent task and used as contextual information for  condition  prediction. This separation introduces a clinically grounded inductive bias, allowing the model to capture conditional diagnostic dependencies in which the plausibility of specific  conditions  is constrained by  H. pylori  infection status.  Since the three diagnostic axes ( location ,  H. pylori , and  condition ) possess the distinct clinical roles and label structures, we define a separate task hierarchy for each.  H. pylori  status is a single-step binary decision (positive vs. negative) and is therefore modeled as a coarse-level task. In contrast,  location  and  condition  require progressive diagnostic refinement and are organized into three hierarchical levels (coarse, fine, and grading). For  location , the coarse-level prediction identifies whether the tissue originates from the  proximal  or  distal  stomach. Subsequently, the fine-level prediction specifies the anatomical subsite:  cardia ,  fundus , and  body  for  proximal  stomach, or  antrum  and  prepylorus  for  distal  stomach. For  condition , the coarse-level task includes four categories, representing increasing pathological severity:  inflammatory disease ,  benign tumor ,  dysplasia , and  cancer . Since multiple pathological alterations often coexist within a single tissue fragment, we assign a single  condition  label per sample based on the lesion of highest clinical significance (e.g.,  cancer  supersedes  inflammatory disease  when both are present), consistent with routine diagnostic practice.  We define fine- and grading-level tasks within each coarse  condition  category. For  inflammatory disease , the fine-level tasks follow the Sydney classification system and include four core components, including  chronic inflammation ,  neutrophilic activity ,  glandular atrophy , and  intestinal metaplasia  (excluding  H. pylori , which is modeled as an independent task), along with two additional findings, i.e.,  erosion  and  ulceration . Fine-level prediction of  inflammatory disease  is defined as a multi-label task-the only one in our overall task formulation-due to their frequent co-occurrence. Accordingly, the corresponding labels are grouped with a dashed bracket in Fig.  1 b.  Chronic inflammation  and  neutrophilic activity  contain grading-level severity labels ( mild ,  moderate , or  marked ); however, these grading-level annotations were not consistently documented across all samples, resulting in substantial missing or unreliable labels. To avoid introducing noise, we exclude these grading-level predictions from evaluation and report only the corresponding fine-level predictions.   Benign tumor  encompasses non-neoplastic or low-risk polypoid gastric lesions that are often removed for clinical reasons such as bleeding risk, interval growth, or the need for definitive histopathologic assessment. This category includes  fundic gland polyps ,  hyperplastic polyps ,  inflammatory polyps ,  granulation tissue-type polyps ,  xanthomas , and  gastritis cystica polyposa . Although these lesions are biologically benign and generally distinct from malignant tumors, they often require endoscopic excision based on clinical judgment. In this study, we consolidate them into a single diagnostic task.   Dysplasia  corresponds to lesions classified as gastric adenomas (tubular or tubulovillous adenomas), which represent a pre-malignant stage in the progression toward gastric cancer. Because clinical management depends heavily on the degree of epithelial atypia, we formulate  dysplasia  as a grading-level task with three grade labels, including  indefinite  for dysplasia,  low-grade dysplasia , and  high-grade dysplasia .   Cancer  includes a series of two fine-level tasks and two grading-level tasks. At the fine-level, cancer is first categorized into  carcinoma ,  lymphoma , and other  malignant tumors .  Carcinoma  is then further subtyped into  adenocarcinoma ,  squamous cell carcinoma , and  neuroendocrine tumor . For  adenocarcinoma , we define a grading-level task based on histological differentiation. Although five grades can be annotated, such as well differentiated, moderately differentiated, poorly differentiated, poorly cohesive, and signet ring cell carcinoma, the latter three categories (poorly differentiated, poorly cohesive, and signet ring cell carcinoma) are often difficult to distinguish reproducibly in routine practice. Accordingly, we merge these three categories into a single category denoted as poorly cohesive, yielding a three-grade differentiation task:  well differentiated ,  moderately differentiated , and  poorly cohesive . For  lymphoma , we define additional grading-level task that classifies lesions as  extranodal MALT  or  non-MALT lymphoma . Figure  1 b summarizes the full task taxonomy and hierarchy. Dataset  We employ four gastric pathology datasets, including GastUJB, GastAIHub, GastCODiPAI, and GastADC22, in this study. All slides from these datasets were digitized as H&E-stained WSIs at 20x magnification. A comprehensive summary of the dataset statistics is provided in Fig.  S1 .  GastUJB is an internally curated gastric pathology dataset collected at the Catholic University of Korea Uijeongbu St. Mary’s Hospital between 2014 and 2023. The dataset contains a total of de-identified 12, 079 WSIs and is partitioned into 6 913 training slides (GastUJB-Train) and 5 166 test slides (GastUJB-Test) while ensuring patient-level independence. GastUJB offers the most comprehensive coverage of gastric diagnostic categories and hierarchical labels in this study and therefore serves as the primary cohort for defining our diagnostic taxonomy and for evaluating fine-grained tasks. Since some categories are intrinsically over- or under-represented in routine practice, we do not enforce equal class ratios between train and test sets. Nevertheless, the split was designed to prevent excessive class imbalance while preserving the overall distributional characteristics of the cohort. GastUJB will be publicly released alongside this study.  The remaining three datasets are used exclusively for external validation. They originate from various institutions and exhibit distribution shifts in slide characteristics, label availability, and task coverage relative to GastUJB.  GastAIHub is derived from an AI-Hub ( https://www.aihub.or.kr/ ) collection of gastrointestinal endoscopic biopsy WSIs provided by five medical institutions (four university hospitals and one clinical pathology foundation). The original collection contains 12,006 WSIs. By retaining only gastric biopsy slides and excluding slides that are not compatible with our diagnostic taxonomy, such as gastric non-epithelial neoplasms other than lymphoma (e.g., melanoma, GIST, leiomyoma, and lipoma), as well as those with missing or unreliable diagnostic information, we remain with 6,360 gastric WSIs. This dataset aligns closely with our diagnostic structure and serves as the primary external benchmark. It includes all three coarse-level categories:  location ,  H. pylori , and  condition . However, it has incomplete coverage of fine- and grading-level tasks, for example, missing fine-level labels such as  fundus  and  prepylorous  in  location  and, in  condition , limited availability of fine-level  inflammatory disease  labels, no  benign tumor  category, and restricted  cancer  subtype and grading labels. Accordingly, it functions as the primary external benchmark for coarse-level and  condition -related evaluations.  GastCODiPAI is derived from the CODiPAI (Collaborative Open Digital Pathology Artificial Intelligence) platform ( https://www.codipai.org/ ), contributed by a consortium of 15 university hospitals. GastCODiPAI integrates two CODiPAI stomach subsets: Stomach Biopsy (STBX), consisting of 2995 endoscopic biopsy specimens, and Stomach Endoscopic Resection (STER), comprising 647 tissue samples obtained through endoscopic mucosal or submucosal resection, resulting in a total of 3642 WSIs. This dataset provides complete fine-level anatomical  location  labels, making it well suited for assessing the detailed location prediction under external distribution shift. Its  condition  labels are restricted to high-risk gastric lesions, comprising  dysplasia  and  adenocarcinoma .  Dysplasia  is annotated with only two grades (low vs. high) and does not include indefinite category, and  cancer  only includes  adenocarcinoma  cases with three differentiation labels.  GastADC22 (PatchGastricADC22)  27   is a dataset composed exclusively of gastric adenocarcinoma cases. It contains 991 surgical gastric WSIs, each from a distinct patient, and each WSI is accompanied by histopathological captions extracted from the corresponding diagnostic reports. In this study, we re-annotate all WSIs to align with our diagnostic taxonomy. Similar to GastCODiPAI, it includes  adenocarcinoma  cases with three differentiation labels.  Since both GastAIHub and GastCODiPAI provide only two dysplasia grades (low vs. high), predictions of  indefinite  for dysplasia are mapped to  low-grade dysplasia  when computing evaluation metrics to ensure consistency. The three-grade  adenocarcinoma  differentiation task is the only grading-level task that is available in all three external datasets (GastAIHub, GastCODiPAI, and GastADC22).    Preprocessing procedures for WSIs  Following the procedure outlined in CLAM  28  , we preprocess each WSI by first identifying tissue regions and then extracting image patches. Specifically, each slide is loaded at a downsampled resolution and converted from RGB to HSV color space to facilitate automated tissue segmentation, yielding a binary foreground tissue mask. Using the resulting tissue regions, we tessellate the foreground into non-overlapping patches of size 512 × 512 pixels at 20 × magnification, adhering to the standard preprocessing convention established by the UNI  29   model. Rather than applying a separate stain normalization step, all slides were processed through the same tissue segmentation pipeline, and patch-level representations were extracted using UNI  29   with consistent normalization. Because all baseline methods relied on the same precomputed frozen features and identical data splits across institutions, any variability arising from differences in slide preparation, staining protocols, or scanner characteristics was controlled uniformly across all compared methods, ensuring a fair and consistent experimental evaluation.    AUGUST architecture  AUGUST is a hierarchical multimodal decision-making framework designed to mirror the clinical workflow of gastric pathology diagnosis (Fig.  1 a). Given a WSI, AUGUST first encodes local morphology into patch-level features and aggregates them into a slide-level representation. It then answers a sequence of clinically grounded questions in a stepwise CoT fashion by iterating three coupled operations: (1) context-aware questioning, where the next clinically grounded from the diagnostic hierarchy conditioned on previously predicted findings (or answers); (2) question-conditioned WSI projection, where the slide-level representation is projected into the language model space using the current question embedding; (3) pathway-constrained answering, where the LLM generates an answer to the current task using the question embedding and question-conditioned slide-level representation, and the resulting prediction determines which downstream task to pursue next. This stepwise and adaptive process produces hierarchy-consistent predictions from coarse determinations to fine-grained subtyping and grading in a clinically coherent order. By aggregating the full sequence of predicted labels, AUGUST generates a structured pathology report summarizing diagnostic findings across hierarchical levels.
