Malignant epithelial states drive immune dysfunction in ampulla of Vater carcinoma.

Background

Ampulla of Vater (AoV) carcinoma is a rare malignancy arising at the junction of intestinal and pancreatobiliary epithelium. Its heterogeneous clinical behavior and histological diversity have hindered therapeutic advances, and the cellular basis of this heterogeneity remains unclear. We aimed to construct a single-cell transcriptomic atlas of AoV carcinoma, with a focus on identifying epithelial subtypes and their interactions with the tumor microenvironment (TME).

Methods

We performed single-cell RNA sequencing on eight primary AoV tumors and four matched normal tissues. Comprehensive clustering and transcriptomic analyses identified cell-type composition, epithelial heterogeneity, and tumor-immune interactions. Findings were validated using deconvolution of bulk RNA-seq data from 62 AoV carcinoma patients. Results Malignant epithelial cells were categorized into four distinct subtypes: Int-Wnt, PB-KRAS, Int-Hypoxia, and Cycling stage. PB-KRAS cells exhibited stem-like transcriptional programs and high genomic instability. Deconvolution analysis of bulk RNA-seq data from the independent AoV cohort revealed that enrichment of the PB-KRAS subtype correlated with tumor recurrence and poor survival. Our immune profiling analysis discovered a significant association between PB-KRAS subtype and GZMK+ CD8+ T cells, which are in a pre-dysfunctional state, alongside SPP1+ macrophages exhibiting immunosuppressive traits. Spatial transcriptome data further supports the immunosuppressive natures of TME around PB-KRAS subtype malignant epithelial cells in AoV carcinoma.

Conclusions

Our study presents a single-cell atlas of AoV carcinoma, highlighting the molecular diversity of malignant epithelium and its association with the immune microenvironment. The PB-KRAS subtype emerges as a stem-like, immunosuppressive tumor state associated with poor prognosis, providing insights for future therapeutic targeting. Background Ampulla of Vater (AoV) carcinoma is a malignancy arising from the ampulla of Vater, the anatomical convergence of the common bile duct, pancreatic duct, and duodenum. This unique anatomical location gives rise to both histological and molecular heterogeneity, reflecting contributions from intestinal and pancreatobiliary lineages. AoV carcinoma is often categorized into intestinal and pancreatobiliary subtypes, which exhibit distinct prognostic and therapeutic characteristics [ 1 , 2 ]. However, this binary classification does not fully account for the molecular diversity and variable clinical behavior observed among patients [ 3 ]. Previous genomic studies have provided important insights into the molecular landscape of AoV carcinoma. Notably, Yachida et al. [ 4 ] identified frequent mutations in the ELF3 gene, implicating it as a potential driver of tumorigenesis. Similarly, Gingras et al. [ 5 ] reported recurrent ELF3 inactivation and widespread dysregulation of the WNT signaling pathway. While these studies advanced our understanding of AoV carcinogenesis, they were based on whole-exome sequencing and bulk transcriptome profiling, which lack the resolution to capture cell type-specific transcriptional programs and the complexity of tumor-microenvironment interactions. As a result, the biological basis of epithelial heterogeneity and the functional contributions of non-malignant cell populations remain poorly understood. Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) offers a powerful approach to address these limitations by enabling high-resolution, cell-type-resolved transcriptomic profiling [ 6 ]. This technology facilitates the identification of cellular subpopulations, and intercellular communication networks that are not accessible through bulk sequencing methods. Despite its potential, scRNA-seq has not yet been applied to AoV carcinoma, leaving fundamental gaps in our understanding of its cellular and transcriptional architecture. Therefore, our study is essential to move beyond bulk-level genomic insights and establish a high-resolution, cell-type-resolved atlas of AoV carcinoma. In this study, we present the first single-cell transcriptomic analysis of AoV carcinoma. Using scRNA-seq on primary tumor specimens, we identify distinct epithelial subtypes characterized by unique oncogenic and reveal their associations with the immune landscape and clinical outcomes. This work establishes a foundational single-cell atlas of AoV carcinoma and provides new insights into its cellular diversity with potential translational implications. Methods Study patients This study included 70 patients histologically diagnosed with AoV adenocarcinoma between September 2005 and March 2023 at Samsung Medical Center (SMC), of whom eight underwent single-cell RNA sequencing and 62 underwent bulk RNA sequencing. Patient demographics and clinical characteristics, including age, gender, tumor stage according to the American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) 8th edition, tumor differentiation, adjuvant chemotherapy administration, and survival data, were retrospectively collected. The study protocol was approved by the Institutional Review Board at SMC (IRB No. SMC-2022–06-076) and conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. All participants provided written informed consent for the future research use of their pathology specimens. Single-cell RNA sequencing Fresh tumor and adjacent normal tissue specimens were obtained from patients with AoV carcinoma before treatment through Endoscopic Retrograde Cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) for scRNA sequencing. Acquired tissues are collected in MACS® Tissue Storage Solution (Miltenyi Biotec., Auburn, CA, USA) on ice and processed to the single cell dissociation immediately. Biopsy tissues are placed on a petri dish with a small volume of enzyme mixture solution (Tumor Dissociation Kit, Miltenyi Biotec.) and minced into small pieces under 1–2 mm with surgical blades. Minced pieces are transferred to gentleMACS TM C-tube containing enzyme mixture solution. By choosing an appropriate program of gentleMACS TM Dissociator, tissue pieces are further dissociated three times with two interval incubations for 30 minutes at 37 °C under continuous rotation using the MACSmix TM Tube Rotator. Resuspended samples are applied to a cell strainer (70 μm) and washed with 10 ml of DMEM/F12 media with 1% FBS. After a centrifugation at 400xg for 5 minutes, cells were resuspended in an appropriate volume of media and counted with trypan blue staining or acridine orange/propidium iodide staining. Optionally, erythrocytes are removed by red blood cell lysis solution for 10 min before counting. We initiated the cell preparation process by employing the LUNA-FL™ Automated Fluorescence Cell Counter (logos biosystems). Detailed guidelines for cell preparation were sourced from the 10x Genomics Single Cell Protocols Cell Preparation Guide and the Guidelines for Optimal Sample Preparation flowchart. Libraries were meticulously constructed using the Chromium controller in accordance with the 10x Chromium Next GEM Single Cell 3’ v3.1 protocol (10x Genomics). In brief, cell suspensions were diluted in nuclease-free water, aiming to achieve a targeted cell count of 10,000. The diluted cell suspension was mixed with a master mix and subsequently loaded onto a Chromium Next GEM chip, along with Single Cell 3’ V3.1 gel beads and partitioning oil. Within the droplets formed in the chip, RNA transcripts from individual cells underwent unique barcoding and reverse transcription. Pooled cDNA molecules then underwent sequential processes, including end repair, addition of a single ‘A’ base, and adapter ligation. Subsequently, the resulting products were subjected to purification and enrichment through polymerase chain reaction (PCR), ultimately yielding the final cDNA library. To ensure library quality and quantify the purified libraries, we adhered to the qPCR Quantification Protocol Guide (KAPA). Furthermore, library qualification was performed using the Agilent Technologies 4200 TapeStation from Agilent Technologies. The sequenced libraries were processed using the HiSeqX platform from Illumina to obtain the requisite data for our study. Data preprocessing and quality control Raw sequencing data were processed using CellRanger (v7.0.1; 10x Genomics) [ 7 ], with alignment to the GRCh38 reference genome via STAR. CellBender (v 0.2.2) [ 8 ] was applied to each sample to eliminate background RNA contamination. Doublets were detected using Scrublet (v 0.2.3) [ 9 ], with thresholds determined according to simulation-derived scores. we excluded low-quality cells with fewer than 500 detected genes and a mitochondrial gene proportion exceeding 20%. Seurat (v4.3.0) [ 10 ] was used for downstream processing, including normalization, variable gene selection, scaling (regressing out total UMI counts, mitochondrial gene proportion, and cell cycle scores), principal component analysis, and uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) projection. Clustering was performed using the FindNeighbors and FindClusters functions, with dimensionality assessed via JackStraw and ElbowPlot methods. Cell type annotation was conducted using SingleR (v2.0.0) [ 11 ] and further validated through the expression of canonical lineage markers. Major cell types were identified using EPCAM (epithelial cells), COL1A1 (fibroblasts), VWF (endothelial cells), CD3D (T cells), CD14 (myeloid cells), and CD79A (B cells). For more granular annotation of immune and stromal subsets, we utilized the following marker sets: CD4 for helper T cells, CD8 for cytotoxic T cells, FOXP3 for regulatory T cells (Tregs), and NCAM1 and NCR1 for NK cells. Myeloid sub-populations were defined by C1QC (macrophages), LYZ and S100A9 (monocytes), CD1C (dendritic cells), and CPA3 and KIT (mast cells). B cell lineages were further distinguished using CD79A and MS4A1 (B cells), CD38 and CD27 (plasma cells). Subclustering analyses were performed on major immune and stromal compartments following additional doublet removal [ 12 ]. Identification of epithelial subtypes using cNMF To identify transcriptional programs within epithelial cells, we applied consensus non-negative matrix factorization (cNMF) (v0.2) [ 13 ] to the normalized gene expression matrix. The number of components (k) was varied from 2 to 15, and the optimal solution was selected based on silhouette scores and Frobenius reconstruction error. Copy number variation inference To infer copy number alterations at the single-cell level, CopyKAT (v1.1.0) [ 14 ] was applied with default parameters. T cells were used as a reference for normal diploid profiles. CNV scores were computed for individual epithelial cells and summarized across samples to evaluate subtype-specific genomic instability. Transcription factor regulatory network inference Regulatory network analysis was performed using the pySCENIC (v0.12.1) [ 15 ] pipeline. Regulon activity scores were computed from raw UMI matrices to identify transcription factor-target gene modules, and average activity scores were calculated per subtype for downstream comparative analyses. Modular score and stemness estimation The CytoTRACE algorithm (v0.3.3) [ 16 ] was used to infer the differentiation potential of malignant epithelial cells. CytoTRACE computes transcriptional diversity and expression correlation to derive stemness scores, ranging from 0 (fully differentiated) to 1 (highly undifferentiated). This approach enables the identification of less differentiated, stem-like cell states at single-cell resolution. To evaluate functional characteristics of epithelial subtypes, including stemness potential, we calculated gene module scores using AddModuleScore function in the Seurat package. This approach determines the average expression of a specific gene program at the single-cell level, which is then normalized by subtracting the aggregated expression of control feature sets. To ensure a robust baseline, all analyzed features are binned based on their average expression levels, and control features are randomly selected from each bin. This process effectively accounts for technical noise and the influence of overall gene expression profiles. The stemness gene set was constructed using previously reported stemness-associated markers [ 17 ]. Functional enrichment analysis Differentially expressed genes were selected based on adjusted p -values and fold changes. Functional enrichment analysis was performed using EnrichR (v3.2) [ 18 ], employing the hypergeometric test with default parameters to identify overrepresented pathways and biological processes. We employed the hypergeometric test with default parameters to identify overrepresented pathways and biological processes from the MSigDB Hallmark gene set collection. Cell-cell communication analysis Ligand-receptor interaction analysis was conducted using CellPhoneDB (v5.0.0) [ 19 ] to identify potential intercellular communication events between cell types. Significant interactions were inferred via permutation testing using default parameters. Pseudotime trajectory analysis To infer the developmental hierarchy of epithelial subtypes, we performed pseudotime trajectory analysis using the Monocle2 R package (v2.30.0) [ 20 ]. To minimize potential biological variations across patients, we utilized the integrated data generated via the FindIntegrationAnchors and IntegrateData functions from the Seurat package. For trajectory ordering, we selected the top 30 differentially expressed genes from each epithelial cluster. Dimensionality reduction was performed using the DDRTree algorithm. Bulk RNA sequencing and processing For bulk RNA sequencing, formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tumor tissues from an independent cohort of surgically resected 62 AoV carcinoma patients were analyzed. Transcript-level quantification was achieved using RSEM (v1.3.0) [ 21 ], aligned to the GRCh38 genome with GENCODE v33 annotation. Gene-level expression matrices were derived for integrative analyses with single-cell data. Proportions of each subtype were estimated in bulk RNA-seq samples using MuSiC (v1.0.0) [ 22 ]. Xenium in situ hybridization and spatial analysis Surgically resected FFPE tissue samples from AoV tumor patients were profiled using Xenium Prime 5K Human Pan Tissue and Pathways Panel (10x Genomics). FFPE tissue sections (5 µm) were prepared on Xenium slides using Xenium Prime Sample Preparation Reagents. RNA quality was assessed by calculating the percentage of RNA fragments > 200 nucleotides (DV200) extracted from tissue sections, and H&E staining were also used to assess tissue morphology and region of interests by a specialized pathologist before performing the Xenium in situ hybridization. Slides were deparaffinized, rehydrated and decrosslinked, followed by hybridization with Xenium 5K Priming Oligos and probes targeting messenger RNA. Probes were ligated, amplified and washed, with subsequent antibody staining for cell segmentation. Autofluorescence quenching and nuclei staining were performed and slides they were stored in phosphate-buffered saline with tween-20 (PBS-T) at 4 °C. The Xenium Analyzer (version 3.1) was used for imaging, decoding, segmentation and cell assignment, following the manufacturer’s protocols. During the initial quality control and filtering step, cells with a transcript count below 100 were classified as low-quality and excluded from all downstream analyses. For cell type classification, we utilized our own scRNA-seq dataset as the reference. Cell assignment was performed using the FindTransferAnchors and TransferData functions within the Seurat package, employing default parameters. Cells with a prediction score below 0.5 were classified as unknown and excluded from further downstream analyses. Survival analysis The clinical relevance of epithelial subtypes was evaluated using survival analysis. Kaplan-Meier curves were generated using the survival and survminer R packages (v0.5.2). Univariate and multivariate Cox proportional hazards regression models were implemented using the coxph function to assess associations with overall survival and disease-free survival. Statistical analysis All statistical analyses were performed in R. Pair-wise Wilcoxon rank-sum tests were utilized to analyze the proportional differences between groups within each cell type/subset. Significance is displayed as *, p  < 0.05; **, p  < 0.01; and ***, p  < 0.001. For comparisons among multiple groups, the Kruskal-Wallis test was used to determine global significance, followed by Dunn’s test for pairwise post-hoc comparisons with adjustments for multiple testing. Statistical significance for multiple comparisons is presented as adjusted p -values (Padj), indicated as follows: *, Padj < 0.05;, Padj < 0.01; and ***, Padj < 0.001. Pearson correlation was employed to calculate the correlation between the proportions of each pair of cell subsets, and Spearman correlation was used for the co-ecosystem analysis. Results Patient characteristics This study included 70 patients (scRNA-seq: n  = 8 and bulk RNA-seq: n  = 62) with AoV carcinoma. Median age was 61.5 years (range, 36–83 years) and 33 were male (47.1%). Tumor stage (AJCC 8th edition) was I-III in the majority of patients (67/70, 95.7%), with only one patient classified as stage 0 and two as stage IV. During a median follow-up of 9.7 years (interquartile range, 6.4–12.7 years), 27 deaths (38.6%) occurred (Table S1 ). Single-cell transcriptomic profiling reveals diverse cellular composition in AoV carcinoma To investigate the cellular architecture of AoV carcinoma, we performed scRNA-seq on tumors ( n  = 8) and matched adjacent normal tissues ( n  = 4) (Fig. 1 a). After quality filtering, a total of 34,672 cells were analyzed and grouped into 18 clusters, which were subsequently classified into six major cell types based on cell type marker gene expression (Fig. 1 b–c). UMAP visualization revealed that while immune cells were broadly shared across patients, epithelial cell clusters displayed strong patient-specific transcriptional profiles, consistent with the absence of batch effects and reflecting inter-patient variation driven by tumor-specific copy number alterations [ 23 , 24 ] (Fig. 1 d). We further examined the distribution of cell types across individual samples, revealing substantial inter-patient heterogeneity in cellular composition (Fig. 1 e). Some tumors were highly enriched in epithelial or myeloid populations, whereas others showed greater T cell infiltration. These findings highlight the cellular complexity of AoV carcinoma and underscore the diversity of tumor-immune microenvironments across patients. Fig. 1 Single-cell transcriptomic profiling of ampulla of Vater (AoV) carcinoma tissues. ( a ) Schematic overview of the study design. Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) was performed on 8 AoV tumor samples and 4 matched normal tissues. Bulk RNA-seq data from 62 AoV samples were also generated. ( b ) Uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) visualization of major cell types identified in scRNA-seq data. Cells are colored by their annotated cell type: B cell, endothelial cell, epithelial cell, fibroblast, myeloid, and T cell. ( c ) Feature plots showing expression of representative marker genes for each major cell type: EPCAM (epithelial), COL1A1 (fibroblast), VWF (endothelial), CD3D (T cell), CD14 (myeloid), and CD79A (B cell). Expression levels are indicated by color intensity. ( d ) UMAP plot of scRNA-seq data color-coded by individual patient. ( e ) Estimated cell-type proportions in scRNA-seq data across tumor ( T ) and matched normal ( N ) samples for each patient, based on annotation from ( b ). Bar plots display relative proportions of each major cell type Epithelial subtyping reveals distinct transcriptional programs and inter-patient heterogeneity To investigate epithelial heterogeneity in AoV carcinoma, we performed subclustering of epithelial cells. This analysis revealed strong patient-specific clustering patterns (Fig. 2 a), indicating pronounced transcriptional differences between tumors. We then applied consensus non-negative matrix factorization (cNMF) to the epithelial transcriptomes, identifying four robust molecular subtypes (NMF-1 to NMF-4) (Fig. S1 a-b). Although each subtype included epithelial cells from multiple patients, their relative proportions varied markedly across samples (Fig. 2 b). This suggests that, while certain transcriptional programs are shared among tumors, their dominance is highly patient-specific, reflecting substantial inter-patient heterogeneity. Fig. 2 Identification and characterization of transcriptional subtypes in AoV carcinoma. ( a ) UMAP visualization of epithelial cells from AoV tissues ( n  = 8), color-coded by patient sample. ( b ) Proportional composition of four transcriptional subtypes (NMF-1 to NMF-4) in each AoV tumor, identified by consensus non-negative matrix factorization (cNMF) clustering of epithelial transcriptomes. ( c ) Violin plots showing expression levels of well-known marker genes associated with AoV subtypes: CDX2 and KRT20 (intestinal subtype), MUC1 and KRT7 (pancreatobiliary subtype). ( d ) Functional enrichment analysis of each transcriptional subtype, visualized as a bubble plot. The pathways were identified using the MSigDB hallmark gene set collection. The size of each dot represents the statistical significance (-log 10 adjusted p -value), and the color denotes the corresponding transcriptional subtype We further examined the expression of established AoV subtype marker genes across the four subtypes (Fig. 2 c). Intestinal markers ( CDX2 and KRT20 ) were strongly expressed in NMF-1 and NMF-3, whereas pancreatobiliary markers ( KRT7 and MUC1 ) were predominantly enriched in NMF-2. These findings support the biological relevance of the identified subtypes and their alignment with previously described histological features [ 2 , 25 ]. Functional enrichment analysis revealed distinct transcriptional programs characterizing each subtype (Fig. 2 d and Table S2 ): NMF-1 was enriched for Wnt/β-catenin signaling (designated Int-Wnt), NMF-2 for KRAS signaling (PB-KRAS), NMF-3 for hypoxia-related pathways (Int-Hypoxia), and NMF-4 for cell cycle-associated signatures (Cycling). We categorize these four programs as three lineage-driven, differentiated subtypes and one progenitor/functional subtype (NMF-4, Cycling). To further characterize the regulatory landscape underlying epithelial heterogeneity, we performed regulon activity analysis across epithelial cells. This analysis revealed that multiple transcription factor regulons were differentially activated in a subtype-specific manner (Fig. S1 c). MSX1 activity was predominantly elevated in the Int-Wnt subtype compared to the PB-KRAS and Cycling subtypes. HNF1B activity reached its highest levels in the PB-KRAS subtype, showing a significant increase over the Cycling subtype and a strong upward trend compared to the Int-Wnt and Int-Hypoxia subtypes. SIRT6 activity was notably enriched in the Int-Hypoxia subtype, while CDX1 was most active in the Cycling subtype, significantly surpassing the levels in the Int-Wnt and Int-Hypoxia groups (Fig. S1 d). The MSX1 is a known WNT/β-catenin responsive transcription factor implicated in promoting intestinal tumorigenesis [ 26 ]. Similarly, the enrichment of HNF1B in the PB-KRAS subtype is relevant, as its overexpression has been shown to enhance the expression of liver progenitor cell markers and stemness in liver cancer cells [ 27 ]. Finally, the activation of the SIRT6 regulon in the Int-Hypoxia subtype is consistent with its known role in enhancing the stability of HIF-1α, a process linked to epithelial-mesenchymal transition under hypoxic conditions [ 28 ]. These regulon profiles were concordant with the transcriptional programs defined by cNMF, further supporting the molecular distinction among AoV epithelial subtypes. Collectively, these results demonstrate that epithelial cells in AoV carcinoma exhibit diverse transcriptional states driven by lineage-specific and oncogenic programs, with subtype composition varying substantially between tumors. PB-KRAS subtype exhibit distinct genomic instability and stem-like properties To interrogate the degree of genomic instability underlying each epithelial subtype, we first analyzed copy number variation (CNV) profiles inferred from single-cell transcriptomes. Notably, CNV patterns were strongly patient-specific, indicating inter-patient variability in genomic alterations (Fig. 3 a). At the single-cell level, CNV scores were markedly elevated in tumor epithelial cells compared to non-epithelial controls, with the PB-KRAS subtype exhibiting the highest levels of genomic aberrations (Fig. S2 a). To validate these findings at the sample level, we averaged CNV scores across epithelial cells within each sample and compared them across subtypes. This analysis confirmed that the PB-KRAS subtype exhibits the highest CNV burden among all epithelial subtypes (Kruskal-Wallis, p  = 0.00013; Fig. 3 b). These results indicate that genomic instability is unevenly distributed among AoV epithelial subtypes and is particularly pronounced in PB-KRAS subtype. Based on its highest CNV burden, we specifically focused on evaluating the stem-like properties of the PB-KRAS subtype. We first focused on the Cycling subtype. Given its cell cycle-associated transcriptional program and the enrichment of progenitor-associated regulons, such as CDX1 (Fig. S1 d), we hypothesized that it represents a less differentiated, progenitor-like state. To infer the developmental potential across all subtypes, we employed CytoTRACE [ 16 ], a computational tool that infers developmental potential using transcriptional entropy. As expected, the Cycling subtype exhibited high CytoTRACE scores (Fig. 3 c and Fig. S2 b), supporting its identity as a less differentiated, progenitor-like state. Surprisingly, the PB-KRAS subtype, which otherwise presents as a differentiated lineage, exhibited the highest CytoTRACE scores (Fig. 3 c and Fig. S2 b), suggesting unexpected stem-like features. This combination—a seemingly differentiated state with high developmental potential—defines a non-canonical stemness phenotype. This suggests that, unlike the canonical progenitor-like Cycling subtype, the PB-KRAS subtype represents a distinct, highly aggressive stem-like epithelial state that deviates from the typical differentiation pathway. To further examine this possibility, we calculated stemness scores based on a curated stem cell gene signature [ 17 ]. The PB-KRAS subtype exhibited elevated stemness scores that were comparable to those of Cycling cells, while remaining notably higher than the Int-Wnt and Int-Hypoxia subtypes (Kruskal-Wallis, p  = 0.00043; Fig. 3 d and Fig. S2 c). To provide dynamic evidence of this developmental hierarchy, we performed pseudotime trajectory analysis using Monocle2 [ 20 ]. The resulting trajectory delineated a clear lineage progression originating from the Cycling subtype, passing through the Int-Wnt and Int-Hypoxia subtype, and ultimately culminating in the PB-KRAS subtype at the terminal end (Fig. 3 e). Notably, despite its terminal position on the pseudotime axis—which typically denotes a fully differentiated state—the PB-KRAS subtype harbored exceptionally high developmental potential, consistent with its elevated CytoTRACE (Fig. 3 f) and stemness scores (Fig. 3 g). This paradoxical terminal stemness suggests that PB-KRAS cells do not merely follow a conventional differentiation path but may undergo a coordinated transcriptional reprogramming or de-differentiation process, re-acquiring progenitor-like properties at an advanced stage of lineage development. We next sought to determine the potential molecular drivers of this phenotype, focusing on KRAS , the defining feature of the PB-KRAS subtype. Expression of KRAS was significantly upregulated in PB-KRAS subtype compared to the Int-Wnt subtypes (Fig. 3 h and Fig. S2 d), whereas CNV at the KRAS locus showed no significant difference among the subtypes (Fig. 3 i). Consistent with this, correlation analysis at the sample level revealed a moderate positive correlation between CNV score and stemness score ( r  = 0.5, p  = 0.014, Fig. S2 e). Furthermore, the expression of KRAS showed a strong positive correlation with both stemness score ( r  = 0.6, p  = 0.002, Fig. S2 f) and CNV score ( r  = 0.59, p  = 0.002, Fig. S2 g). These findings collectively highlight the robust association of both genomic instability and KRAS expression with the enhanced stem-like properties of the PB-KRAS subtype. Since KRAS knockdown in pancreatic cancer cells is known to reduce stemness characteristics [ 30 ], these observations suggest that the transcriptional upregulation of KRAS , rather than genomic alterations, is the likely contributor to the stemness signature of the PB-KRAS subtype. Among these, the Int-Wnt subtype was the most abundant, followed by Int-Hypoxia and PB-KRAS, whereas the Cycling subtype was relatively rare across samples (Fig. 4 a and Table S3 ). Spatial profiling reveals an immunosuppressive microenvironment in PB-KRAS subtype regions To investigate the spatial relationships between cellular subtypes and the tumor microenvironment, we performed Xenium in situ analysis on two representative AoV carcinoma samples, categorized as intestinal type and pancreatobiliary type based on the consensus judgment of experienced pathologists examining the tumor sections (Fig. 5 f). We first used single-cell RNA sequencing to estimate the major cell types and then mapped their spatial distribution across the tissue (Fig. 5 g). To investigate subtype-specific spatial patterns, we next identified and distinguished specific regions within the tumors, focusing on the AoV-ST1 sample, which are characterized by high proportions of Int-Hypoxia, and the AoV-ST2 sample, which are characterized by high proportions of the PB-KRAS subtype (Fig. 5 h). Importantly, the classification of regions derived from scRNA-seq mapping into Int-Hypoxia high (AoV-ST1) and PB-KRAS high (AoV-ST2) categories showed strong agreement with the initial pathological classification. Visualization of the spatial maps revealed a striking co-localization between the PB-KRAS subtype and Tc-GZMK cells (indicated by triangle-shaped dots), with a denser infiltration observed in the PB-KRAS high sample (Fig. 5 h). Quantitative analysis confirmed this observation: the PB-KRAS high sample exhibited a markedly higher proportion of PB-KRAS cells (among all epithelial cells) and a corresponding elevation in the proportion of Tc- GZMK cells (among all T cells) compared to the Int-Hypoxia high sample (Fig. 5 i). To further validate the spatial association between these populations, we performed a nearest neighbor distance analysis using the Xenium spatial coordinates. Our results revealed that Tc- GZMK cells were located significantly closer to PB-KRAS cells, with a mean minimum distance of 114.3 µm, whereas the distance to Int-hypoxia cells was nearly three-fold higher at 321.4 µm (Fig. 5 j). To visually confirm the presence of the Tc- GZMK population, we performed multiplex immunofluorescence using MACSima Imaging System ( n  = 3 per each group; see supplementary methods). Although this population was relatively sparse, pancreatobiliary subtype enriched samples showed higher infiltration of Tc- GZMK cells, whereas intestinal subtype dominant tumors displayed sparse Tc- GZMK infiltration (Fig. S5 a-b). Quantification confirmed that the proportion of Tc- GZMK cells was significantly higher in Pancreatobiliary subtype compared to intestinal subtype tumors ( p  = 0.0375; Fig. S5 c). These initial findings collectively suggest that the PB-KRAS subtype is associated with a distinctive and highly infiltrated tumor microenvironment. Notably, FGF2 is a well-established mediator known to promote the polarization of tumor-associated macrophages toward a pro-tumorigenic, M2-like state within the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment [ 34 ]. These findings suggest that the PB-KRAS subtype may develop within, or contribute to, a uniquely immunologically conditioned microenvironment enriched in tumor-promoting macrophages and pre-dysfunctional CD8 + T cells. This immune landscape may underlie the aggressive behavior and recurrence-prone nature of this epithelial subtype. Further mechanistic studies are warranted to clarify the functional significance of these immune–epithelial interactions and evaluate their potential as therapeutic targets. Discussion This study presents the first single-cell transcriptomic analysis of AoV carcinoma, offering a high-resolution landscape of its epithelial and immune cell composition. Previous genomic investigations, primarily based on whole-exome sequencing, have significantly advanced our understanding of AoV carcinoma by identifying recurrent alterations such as ELF3 mutations and WNT pathway dysregulation [ 4 , 5 ]. However, these bulk approaches lack the granularity required to resolve cell type-specific programs and microenvironmental interactions. Our single-cell approach addresses these limitations and provides novel insights into epithelial heterogeneity, differentiation states, and tumor-immune crosstalk in AoV carcinoma. Among the four molecular subtypes identified, our data demonstrate that the intestinal subtype itself is not homogeneous but comprises at least two molecularly distinct programs: one characterized by active WNT/β-catenin signaling (Int-Wnt) and another driven by hypoxia-associated pathways (Int-Hypoxia). The Int-Wnt subtype was defined by robust expression of WNT target genes and selective activation of the MSX1 regulon. MSX1 is known to function downstream of WNT/β-catenin signaling, playing a key role in promoting intestinal tumorigenesis. Its loss suppresses ectopic crypt formation in Apc-deficient models, suggesting that MSX1 is a critical mediator of WNT-driven epithelial transformation [ 26 ]. These features suggest that the Int-Wnt subtype retains a proliferative, WNT-responsive phenotype reminiscent of early intestinal neoplasia. In contrast, the Int-Hypoxia subtype displayed prominent enrichment of hypoxia-related gene sets and strong activation of the SIRT6 regulon. This suggests a mechanism involving SIRT6-enhanced stability of HIF-1α, which is known to promote the expression of epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT)-related transcription factors like SNAIL and TWIST [ 28 ]. The resultant overexpression of SNAIL and TWIST leads to suppression of E-cadherin and induction of Vimentin, hallmark events of EMT [ 28 ]. This molecular cascade facilitates increased cellular plasticity and motility, thereby promoting invasive behavior. EMT has been associated with enhanced metastatic potential and poor recurrence-free survival in several cancers, including papillary thyroid carcinoma, and may similarly portend aggressive clinical behavior in the Int-Hypoxia subtype of AoV carcinoma. By uncovering both a WNT-driven and a hypoxia-induced EMT program within the intestinal group, our analysis emphasizes the subtype’s underlying complexity and suggests that these distinctions may carry prognostic or therapeutic significance. The PB-KRAS subtype emerged as a particularly notable finding in our comprehensive epithelial subtyping. This subtype is defined by elevated KRAS expression and a transcriptional program robustly enriched for KRAS signaling. The PB-KRAS subtype exhibited a pronounced degree of genomic instability, carrying the highest CNV burden among all identified epithelial subtypes. Reflecting these substantial genomic aberrations, which are often associated with aggressive and self-renewal-enhancing phenotypes, we were guided to investigate its developmental hierarchy and specifically focused on evaluating its stem-like properties. Strikingly, the PB-KRAS subtype paradoxically exhibited high developmental potential and stemness scores, comparable to the canonical progenitor-like Cycling subtype. This unique combination of an apparent differentiated PB lineage state possessing high developmental potential defines a non-canonical stem-like epithelial state. Unlike the Cycling subtype, which represents a classical progenitor state, PB-KRAS cells achieve stemness through oncogenic signaling. Specifically, we found that the stemness signature was driven by the transcriptional upregulation of KRAS expression, independent of differential CNV at the KRAS locus. This suggests that elevated KRAS expression forces an aberrant, de-differentiated potential within a seemingly mature lineage. This is consistent with prior findings implicating KRAS signaling in the maintenance of stem-like features in pancreatic cancer cells [ 30 ]. Supporting this stem-like phenotype, HNF1B regulon activity was also selectively enriched in the PB-KRAS subtype. As HNF1B overexpression has been shown to enhance the expression of liver progenitor cell markers and stemness in liver cancer cells [ 27 ], this activation suggests a conserved role in supporting KRAS-associated epithelial states. Clinically, the PB-KRAS subtype was associated with significantly worse OS and DFS, as well as a higher incidence of recurrence. These findings collectively suggest that the PB-KRAS subtype program, defined by unique genomic instability and a KRAS-driven non-canonical stemness, represents the most clinically aggressive AoV subtype identified in this study, associated with poor outcomes and inherent therapeutic resistance. In addition to epithelial heterogeneity, our analysis revealed striking differences in the immune landscape across subtypes. PB-KRAS subtype were enriched for a distinct immune microenvironment characterized by abundant GZMK + CD8 + T cells (Tc-GZMK cells) and SPP1 + macrophages. GZMK enriched cytotoxic T cells, recently described as pre-dysfunctional T cells, represent an intermediate state preceding terminal T cell exhaustion [ 31 ]. Their accumulation within the PB-KRAS tumor microenvironment, coupled with spatial proximity to tumor epithelium and signaling through immunosuppressive ligand-receptor pairs (such as TGFB2 , FGF2 , and SPP1 ), strongly suggests active immune remodeling by tumor cells. These specific axes are known mediators of immunosuppressive signaling. For instance, TGF-β is known to suppress CD8 + T cell cytotoxicity by repressing a distinct program of cytotoxic gene responses, thereby limiting the antitumor immune response [ 35 ]. Similarly, FGF2 has been implicated in promoting T-cell exhaustion by regulating the expression of SPRY1 in esophageal tumor-infiltrating T cells, further impairing T cell function [ 36 ]. SPP1 directly suppresses CD8 + T cell proliferation and interferon-γ production, contributing to immune evasion by the tumor [ 37 ]. The co-enrichment of SPP1 + macrophages, previously implicated in promoting immune evasion and supporting tumor progression, further supports the presence of an immunosuppressive TME in PB-KRAS subtype. Importantly, high abundance of Tc-GZMK cells was associated with poor clinical outcomes, reinforcing the relevance of the immune milieu in disease progression. Taken together, our findings suggest that the PB-KRAS subtype defines a biologically aggressive, stem-like epithelial population that may either arise within or actively sculpt an immunosuppressive TME enriched for dysfunctional immune cell states. This epithelial-immune crosstalk may contribute to tumor recurrence and resistance to therapy. In contrast, the Int-Wnt and Int-Hypoxia subtypes are characterized by alternative oncogenic programs and immune environments, with divergent prognostic implications. A key limitation of this study is that the observed association between the PB-KRAS subtype and the immunosuppressive TME is based on correlational multi-omics analysis rather than direct functional validation. It is well established that activating KRAS mutations can actively modulate the immune microenvironment by promoting pro-tumorigenic macrophage polarization, inhibiting T-cell cytotoxicity, and accelerating T-cell exhaustion. Moreover, KRAS-mediated metabolic reprogramming may create a feedback loop where metabolite accumulation induces further genomic instability and mutational burden [ 38 ]. Although our findings regarding the PB-KRAS subtype are highly consistent with these known roles of KRAS signaling, further in vivo studies—such as orthotopic or syngeneic mouse models—and co-culture experiments are necessary to definitively prove the causal role of PB-KRAS cells in shaping this specific immunosuppressive niche. Moreover, while the specific ligand-receptor axes identified in this study, such as TGFB2 and SPP1, represent highly promising therapeutic targets, we acknowledge that their functional significance requires further validation in follow-up translational models utilizing functional blocking with neutralizing antibodies or small molecule inhibitors in patient-derived organoid-immune co-culture systems. These insights have potential therapeutic implications. Targeting the KRAS-HNF1B axis or the immunosuppressive mediators enriched in PB-KRAS subtype may offer novel avenues for treatment. Moreover, immunotherapeutic strategies aiming to restore CD8 + T cell functionality or reprogram tumor-associated macrophages may be particularly effective in this context. Future studies should focus on elucidating the molecular mechanisms underlying epithelial-immune interactions in AoV carcinoma and evaluating their druggability in preclinical models. Additionally, although the multivariate analysis yielded an inflated hazard ratio due to complete separation in our small cohort ( n  = 62), Bootstrap validation (1,000 resamples) confirmed the statistical stability and robust prognostic value of the PB-KRAS subtype. Given the limited number of patients included in the single-cell analysis, validation in larger multi-institutional cohorts will be important to further establish the generalizability and potential clinical utility of the PB-KRAS subtype classification. Conclusions Our single-cell atlas of AoV carcinoma reveals profound epithelial and immune heterogeneity and identifies a clinically relevant PB-KRAS subtype defined by KRAS-driven non-canonical stem-like features and an immunosuppressive microenvironment. These findings provide a foundation for precision classification of AoV carcinoma and suggest novel therapeutic vulnerabilities for high-risk patients. title: Personalizing the treatment of head and neck cancer in vitro: The 3D-OTC model.
xenium_reason: Text indicates reuse of public Xenium data
evidence_text: Personalizing the treatment of head and neck cancer in vitro: The 3D-OTC model. BACKGROUND: Treatment of head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) remains challenging and the survival rates of affected patients remain poor. A three-dimensional organotypic co-culture (3D-OTC) model where patient derived tumor tissue is cultured on human-derived fibroblasts (dermal equivalent, DE) was evaluated regarding its comparability to primary tumor tissue and its applicability in drug resistance testing. METHODS: 3D-OTC models were cultured from n = 10 HNSCC patients for up to 21 days. The growth pattern at the DE was compared to tumor budding of corresponding resection specimens. Furthermore, we immunohistochemically determined the immune cell infiltrate of primary tumor tissue and corresponding 3D-OTC models. Spatially resolved gene expression analysis (“Xenium in situ”) was performed for separate regions of interest within the 3D-OTC specimens and within primary tumor tissue. Up-regulated and down-regulated genes of the 3D-OTC samples were included in gene set enrichment analysis and up-regulated genes between invasive (invading the DE) and non-invasive tumor cells within the 3D-OTC samples were included in drug resistance testing using publicly available databases. RESULTS: The growth pattern observed at the DE was associated with tumor budding in primary tumor tissue. The density of CD3-/CD20-/CD56-positive cells was lower in 3D-OTC samples compared to primary tumor tissue. No such changes were observed for CD68-positive cells and no significant changes in the density of the immune cell infiltrate were detected during the cultivation period. The centroids and dispersion of the gene expression of the 3D-OTC samples did not differ from the corresponding primary tumor tissue. The regions of interest within the 3D-OTC samples showed distinct functional states in gene set enrichment analysis. The comparison of genes up-regulated in invasive tumor parts of the 3D-OTC samples could explain resistance of tumor subclones to certain chemotherapeutics. CONCLUSIONS: The 3D-OTC model morphologically and transcriptomically resembles primary tumor tissue and its biology while preserving the tumor microenvironment. Furthermore, the 3D-OTC model allows the standardized evaluation of tumor tissue by the definition of transcriptomically separate regions of interest and thus, could help to evaluate the impact of personalized therapeutic interventions on the tumor and its microenvironment in vitro.

Single-Nucleus Transcriptomic Atlas Reveals Disease-Associated Cellular States in Human Glomerular Diseases.

Introduction

Glomerular diseases are a major cause of chronic kidney disease and kidney failure worldwide, yet the cellular mechanisms underlying their heterogeneity remain incompletely understood. Single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) enables high-resolution characterization of transcriptional alterations across diverse kidney cell populations.

Methods

We performed snRNA-seq on snap-frozen kidney biopsy tissues obtained from treatment-naïve patients with minimal change disease (MCD), membranous nephropathy (MN), IgA nephropathy (IgAN), and diabetic kidney disease (DKD), together with control kidney samples. In total, 333,938 nuclei from 37 individuals were analyzed to define disease-associated transcriptional programs across kidney cell types.

Results

Upregulated transcripts formed disease-specific programs that were shared across multiple cell types, whereas downregulated transcripts were largely cell type-specific and conserved across diseases. We identified disease-associated cellular states, including a glomerular epithelial population exhibiting a hybrid transcriptional profile shared between podocytes and parietal epithelial cells (PECs); a podocyte subpopulation with endocytosis-related gene expression, correlated with proteinuria severity and treatment response; and expansion of periostin (POSTN)-expressing myofibroblasts, inversely associated with estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) and spatially colocalized with podocyte injury. Each cellular state was independently recovered in external single-cell cohorts.

Conclusion

Single-nucleus transcriptomic profiling of human kidney biopsy tissues reveals disease-specific and shared cellular programs across major glomerular diseases. This resource provides insight into the cellular mechanisms underlying glomerular injury and identifies disease-associated cell states that may contribute to disease progression. Because the kidney is composed of diverse and highly specialized cell populations, disease mechanisms may manifest through cell type-specific transcriptional alterations. Recent advances in single-cell and snRNA-seq have enabled high-resolution characterization of kidney cell populations and injury-associated transcriptional states. 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 These approaches have provided important insights into kidney biology and disease mechanisms, including the identification of rare glomerular cell types such as podocytes that are often underrepresented in conventional transcriptomic studies. 14 However, most single-cell studies of kidney disease have focused on individual disease entities or tissues obtained from nephrectomy specimens, limiting the ability to compare transcriptional alterations across multiple glomerular diseases using diagnostic human biopsy tissues. To address this gap, we performed snRNA-seq on snap-frozen kidney biopsy tissues obtained from patients with 4 major glomerular diseases—MCD, MN, IgAN, and DKD—together with control kidney samples. By integrating transcriptomic profiles across disease groups and controls, we aimed to identify both shared and disease-specific transcriptional programs across kidney cell types and to characterize disease-associated cellular states within the human glomerulus. Methods Ethical Considerations and Patient Consent The study protocol was approved by the institutional review board of Seoul National University Hospital (IRB Nos. H-2203-053-1303 and H-1404-117-575). The study samples were collected from the KORNERSTONE project, a multicenter, prospective cohort study and biobank for glomerular diseases, run under the National Biobank Project of the Republic of Korea. 15 Patients provided informed consent for the collection of the biospecimens, their use in this study, and their use in a public database. The study was conducted under the National Research Project Single Cell Atlas of Immune Disease ( http://www.scaid.org/ ). Kidney Tissue Collection The study subjects were enrolled in the KORNERSTONE project before their first diagnostic kidney biopsy. At our institution, three biopsy cores were typically obtained per patient and first evaluated by an attending nephropathologist for routine clinical diagnostics (light microscopy, immunofluorescence, and electron microscopy). Intact biopsy tissue not required for diagnostic evaluation was immediately snap-frozen at the bedside for biobanking. For snRNA-seq, the remaining cores were used in their entirety; because standard biopsy cores traverse the cortex and may variably extend toward the corticomedullary region, the sequenced material represents mixed cortical regions. We selected patients with preserved kidney function (eGFR ≥ 30 ml/min per 1.73 m 2 ), to minimize disease-nonspecific transcriptomic effects of advanced fibrotic changes. Inclusion required primary MCD with overt nephrotic syndrome, anti-phospholipase A2 receptor antibody-positive MN, IgAN, or DKD without other glomerulonephritis pathologies; patients with urine protein creatinine ratio > 3 g/g (MCD, MN, and DKD) who were immunosuppression-naïve were prioritized to capture active disease. In this study, we included a total of 30 patient kidney samples (from 7 MCD, 6 MN, 13 IgAN, and 4 patients with DKD). Clinical data from the initial visit and treatment initiation were analyzed. For control kidney tissues, we used the normal kidney cortex obtained during radical nephrectomy surgery for kidney cancer. We carefully reviewed the clinical histories to exclude patients with diabetic or hypertensive kidney disease and selected those without proteinuria or obstructive changes in the kidney. To minimize ischemic bias, an intraoperative gun biopsy was obtained from the exposed kidney before renal artery clamping, away from cancerous lesions. Tissues were snap-frozen and delivered to central storage. A total of 7 control patients were included in the study. Results Baseline Characteristics of the Study Subjects We collected data from 37 participants, including individuals with MCD ( n = 7), MN ( n = 6), IgAN ( n = 13), and DKD ( n = 4), as well as a control group ( n = 7). All patient samples were obtained from immunosuppressants-naïve individuals with typical clinical presentations, including primary MCD with overt nephrotic syndrome, anti- PLA2R antibody-positive MN, IgAN, or DKD without another diagnosis. Control kidney tissues were obtained from chemotherapy-naïve patients undergoing nephrectomy for renal cell carcinoma, using noncancerous lesions in cortical tissue. The baseline demographics of the study subjects are presented in Supplementary Table S1 . The mean spot urine protein creatinine ratio for each condition was 8.09 ± 4.87 g/g for the MCD group, 7.98 ± 6.49 g/g for the MN group, 1.05 ± 1.36 g/g for the IgAN group, and 3.68 ± 1.78 g/g for the DKD group. The control group had no proteinuria. The baseline eGFR was 89.8 ± 26.8 ml/min per 1.73 m 2 in the study subjects with typical clinical features. We analyzed a total of 333,938 nuclei from biopsy tissues ( Figure 1 a) and identified 12 main cell clusters, annotated based on known canonical markers, including podocytes, PECs, various tubular cells, endothelial cells, fibroblasts, and immune cells ( Figure 1 b, c). We next examined the distribution of these subtypes across clinical groups and observed pronounced, disease-specific heterogeneity ( Figure 1 d). To validate these annotations, we compared our data with an external dataset from the Kidney Precision Medicine Project. 9 This comparison revealed a high correlation in marker gene expression profiles ( Supplementary Figure S1 A). Furthermore, upregulated differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in our DKD samples showed a similar pattern to those in the Kidney Precision Medicine Project dataset ( Supplementary Figure S1 B). Finally, we performed more detailed subclustering and annotation for each major cell type ( Supplementary Figure S1 C, Supplementary Table S2 ). Figure 1 Study design and single-nucleus transcriptional profiling of kidney biopsy samples from control individuals and patients with glomerular diseases. (a) A schematic showing the overall study design. (b) Human glomerular disease single-nucleus transcriptional atlas ( n = 333,938). UMAP plot showing different cell types identified by snRNA-seq. (c) Dot plot representation of the marker genes for the annotated kidney cell types. The dot size indicates the percentage of relative gene expression for each marker gene. The dot color reflects the average expression level of the specified gene within each cell type. (d) Stacked bar plot showing the per-condition proportions of cell types in each condition. Cell type proportions were calculated relative to the total number of cells within each sample and compared between disease groups and Controls using the Wilcoxon rank-sum test with Benjamini–Hochberg correction. Cell types showing statistically significant differences compared with Controls are marked with white asterisks. (e and g) Heatmap illustrating DEGs (|log2FC| > 0.25, adjusted P value < 0.05) categorized into 16 modules through k-means clustering across various cell types in glomerular disease patients in comparison to those in the control group. (e) Heatmap of upregulated DEGs associated with each glomerular disease. Gene modules specific to each glomerular disease are indicated by the corresponding-colored boxes. (g) Heatmap generated by downregulated DEGs, arranged by cell type. Gene modules specific to each cell type are indicated by the corresponding-colored boxes. (f and h) Bar plots of the −log10( P value) from enrichment analysis of DEGs from different modules, as shown in heatmaps. Pathways represented by upregulated DEGs are colored in orange (f), and those associated with downregulated DEGs are highlighted in sky blue (h). CNT, connecting tubule; DCT, distal convoluted tubule; CDPC, collecting duct principal cell; CDIC, collecting duct intercalated cell; DKD, diabetic kidney disease; Endo, endothelial cell; FIB, fibroblast; IgAN, IgA nephropathy; IMM, immune cell; MCD, minimal change disease; PLA2R MN, phospholipase A2 receptor 1-associated membranous nephropathy; POD, podocyte; PEC, parietal epithelial cell; PT, proximal tubule; TAL, thick ascending limb; tL, thin limb; VSMC, vascular smooth muscle cell. Disease-Dominant, Cell Type-Common, Cell Type-Dominant, and Disease-Common DEGs in Glomerular Diseases Our analysis of DEGs revealed a dichotomous pattern—upregulated DEGs were largely disease-specific but shared across cell types, whereas downregulated DEGs were cell type-specific but common across diseases ( Supplementary Table S3 ). We identified disease-dominant upregulated gene modules enriched in each condition ( Figure 1 e and f; Supplementary Table S4 ). The MCD-dominant module was enriched for transporter-related genes (e.g., SLC13A1 , SLC36A2 ; Module 5). The MN-dominant module included genes associated with epithelial-mesenchymal transition (e.g., SPP1, VIM ) and the interferon response (e.g., HIF1A, IFNAR2 ; Module 8). The IgAN-dominant module was associated with previously reported pathways, including aldosterone-regulated sodium reabsorption (Module 2). In DKD, upregulated modules were associated with differentiation and metabolic processes (Module 15) ( Figure 1 f; Supplementary Table S5 ). Representative genes within each module also showed preferential expression in the corresponding disease group at the sample level ( Supplementary Figure S2 A). Module score analysis confirmed significantly higher in scores in the corresponding disease groups compared with others ( Supplementary Figure S2 B). In contrast, downregulated DEGs exhibited a cell type-restricted pattern shared across diseases ( Figure 1 g and 1h; Supplementary Table S4 ). In podocytes, genes related to the actin cytoskeleton (e.g., IQGAP2 , MICAL2 ) 16 , 17 and cell-cell adhesion were reduced (Module 12). In PECs, genes negatively regulating mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) signaling were downregulated (Module 14). 18 Tubular cells showed decreased expression of metabolic pathways, including fatty acid metabolism, in proximal tubule- and thick ascending limb-specific modules (Modules 1 and 3). 19 , 20 In collecting duct principal cells, the downregulated module included the glucocorticoid receptor and NR4A1 . Endothelial cells demonstrated reduced expression of SPRED2 , with gene ontology analysis indicating negative regulation of the MAPK cascade (Module 9; Supplementary Table S6 ). 21 For each cell type, module scores were significantly lower in diseased samples than in controls, without differences in unrelated cell types ( Supplementary Figure S2 C). Disease-Associated Intermediate Epithelial State Between Injured Podocytes and Activated PECs Subclustering of glomerular cells identified a distinct population positioned between podocytes and PECs on uniform manifold approximation and projection ( Figure 2 a). 22 These cells coexpressed canonical markers of both lineages along with a distinct transcriptional profile ( Figure 2 b, Supplementary Figure S3 A). A pseudotime analysis further demonstrated the transcriptional proximity of this population to both podocytes and PECs ( Figure 2 c). This population was enriched for PEC activation and proliferative signaling programs, including MAPK- and epidermal growth factor receptor-related pathways involving ERBB 2, EGF , FGFR , and CD 24, together with cluster-defining genes such as CASR and PRDM 16 ( Supplementary Figure S3 B and C). 18 , 23 This cluster also showed significant upregulation of genes known to be highly expressed in proliferative PECs ( Figure 2 d). 22 Importantly, the proportion of this cluster was significantly correlated (Pearson's r = 0.35, R² = 0.13, P = 0.031) with clinical severity index that we defined ( Figure 2 e). Marker genes for this cluster were also present between podocytes and PECs in the uniform manifold approximation and projection of the external transcriptomic data for podocytes and PECs ( Supplementary Figure S3 D). 9 Figure 2 Detection of an intermediate epithelial population sharing podocyte and PEC features. (a) UMAP of subclustered cell types belonging to the glomerulus ( n = 13,475) are colored according to subclustered cell type with a hematoxylin and eosin-stained image of the glomerulus. Podocyte and PEC populations were subclustered from the glomerular epithelial compartment, whereas mesangial cells and glomerular endothelial cells were identified through subclustering of the VSMC and endothelial compartments, respectively. (b) Violin plots showing the expression of podocyte and PEC marker genes. (c) Trajectory and pseudotime analysis of podocytes and PECs. The panel illustrates the trajectory in order of subsets of podocytes and PECs. (d) Heatmaps showing the relative expression of genes from previous studies indicating proliferative PECs in each podocyte and PEC subset. 22 (e) Scatter plot of the proportion of Intermediate cells versus renal dysfunction severity. The score is calculated as (proteinuria + 1) × 100 / eGFR, ensuring it rises with increased proteinuria (a marker of kidney damage) and lower eGFR (indicating poorer kidney filtration). The fitted linear regression line with 95% confidence interval (shaded area) is shown. Pearson's correlation coefficient (r), R², and corresponding P value are indicated in the plot. (f) Representative Xenium in situ hybridization images of human kidney tissues from control, and patients having MCD, MN, IgAN, and DKD. Green and red dots indicate NPHS1 , and ALDH1A2, respectively. The dashed box indicates the magnified region shown below. MCD, minimal change disease; (g and h) Immunofluorescent stain images of human kidney tissues from control and patients having MCD, MN, IgAN, and DKD. Podocytes were divided into 3 clusters and annotated using marker genes ( Figure 3 g and Supplementary Figure S4 C). One population was characterized by high expression of genes associated with cubilin and amnionless complex, including LRP2 , CUBN , CLCN5 , and PRKCA , and was therefore designated the podocyte endocytosis state ( Supplementary Figure S4 C and D). 38 A similar transcriptional pattern cluster was also observed in podocytes in independent external single-cell datasets, including in patients with chronic kidney disease ( Supplementary Figure S4 E, F, and G). 9 Compared with conventional podocytes, podocyte endocytosis showed increased PAX2 , 39 and reduced expression of CDKN1C , 40 PODXL, and NPHS2, together with higher proliferation module scores ( Supplementary Figure S4 H and I). Importantly, the proportion of podocyte endocytosis cells significantly increased with baseline proteinuria severity (quasibinomial generalized linear model, β = 0.042, P = 0.001, pseudo-R 2 = 0.226), whereas patients with persistent proteinuria after treatment exhibited higher podocyte endocytosis module scores, suggesting an association between this transcriptional state and poor treatment response ( Figure 3 h and i). Accordingly, the gene module score was significantly greater in the MCD and MN groups than in the other glomerular disease groups and the control group ( Figure 3 j). These findings suggest that the activation of endocytosis-related gene programs in podocytes reflects the severity of proteinuria and may also have prognostic implications. We validated the presence of “podocyte endocytosis” at both the transcriptomic and protein levels through the coexpression of LRP2 and NPHS1 in Xenium in situ and megalin (encoded by LRP2 ) and WT1 in immunofluorescence ( Figure 3 k–l and Supplementary Table S7 ). Additionally, the proportion of podocyte endocytosis tended to be higher in glomerular disease in Xenium in situ and IF ( Supplementary Figure S4 J and K). To further characterize the signaling environment associated with podocyte endocytosis, we performed CellChat analysis across glomerular and peri-glomerular populations. Among the inferred pathways, Bradykinin, complement, and interleukin17 signaling showed preferential communication toward the podocyte endocytosis state ( Supplementary Figure 4 L). Bradykinin signaling originated from multiple glomerular populations, whereas complement and interleukin17 signaling were primarily inferred from juxtaglomerular apparatus cells, PECs, and podocytes. Together, these findings indicate an injury-related signaling microenvironment around podocyte endocytosis cells. Discussion This study presents a single-nucleus transcriptome analysis of human biopsy-confirmed glomerular diseases, comprising 333,938 nuclei obtained from 37 individuals, including 30 treatment-naïve patients with MCD, MN, IgAN, and DKD and 7 controls. By profiling diverse kidney cell populations from diagnostic biopsy cores, our dataset provides a comprehensive view of early disease-associated transcriptional changes across glomerular diseases. Another strength of this study is the inclusion of subjects without substantial GFR reduction, which enabled us to compare cell type-specific transcriptomic alterations in relatively early disease states. Our transcriptome data may enhance the understanding of disease-specific pathophysiologic mechanisms of glomerular diseases, which may lead to the discovery of diagnostic or therapeutic biomarkers and common pathological pathways contributing to the progression of chronic kidney disease. This atlas therefore provides a framework for interpreting cell type–specific transcriptional alterations across major glomerular diseases. A notable observation from our analysis was the distinct pattern of transcriptional regulation across diseases and cell types. Upregulated genes tended to form disease-dominant modules, whereas downregulated genes were largely organized by cell type. This pattern suggests that disease-specific signaling programs activate distinct transcriptional responses, whereas functional impairment manifests through loss of cell type-specific gene expression. For example, the MN-dominant transcriptional signature was enriched for epithelial-mesenchymal transition and interferon-γ response pathways, consistent with immune-mediated injury associated with phospholipase A2 receptor autoimmunity 45 , 46 and IgAN modules with MAPK signaling, consistent with MAPK and/or extracellular signal-regulated kinase activation in mesangial injury. 47 Nevertheless, several upregulated modules also exhibited cell type-restricted patterns that complemented the corresponding downregulated programs within the same cell type. For example, proximal tubule modules paired upregulated transport programs with downregulated metabolic programs, suggesting adaptive tubular hypertrophy; endothelial modules paired vasculogenic activation with loss of MAPK negative regulators. We also identified a glomerular epithelial population exhibiting a hybrid transcriptional profile shared between podocytes and PECs. Podocytes are terminally differentiated cells that undergo structural injury and transcriptional remodeling under stress, whereas PECs retain proliferative potential and can respond dynamically to podocyte loss. The hybrid epithelial population was enriched in diseased glomeruli and showed activation of epithelial stress- and proliferation-associated programs, suggesting epithelial plasticity and remodeling within the injured glomerular compartment. This observation is consistent with previous studies showing that pathological activation of PEC signaling pathways can lead to abnormal PEC proliferation and contribute to glomerulosclerosis. Spatial transcriptomic analysis further supported the presence of these cells within diseased glomeruli. Although the lineage relationships of these cells cannot be resolved from cross-sectional human biopsy data alone, their shared transcriptional features and spatial localization support the existence of an injury-associated hybrid epithelial state in glomerular disease. Our study further identified a podocyte subpopulation characterized by expression of genes involved in protein endocytosis, including the cubilin and amnionless complex components LRP2 and CUBN . 38 , 48 , 49 , 50 , 51 Previous studies have suggested that podocytes may activate endocytic pathways under protein overload to maintain filtration barrier integrity. Consistent with this, the podocyte endocytosis program was associated with increased proteinuria and remained elevated in patients with persistent proteinuria after treatment. Recent work suggesting that antinephrin autoantibodies in podocytopathies induce nephrin internalization and glomerular endocytic activity provides a potential mechanistic framework, and the prominent MCD enrichment may reflect this adaptive or injury-associated response to slit diaphragm dysfunction. 52 The preferential enrichment of Bradykinin, complement, and interleukin17 signaling toward this population further suggests an injury-associated microenvironment, consistent with podocyte dedifferentiation features. These findings suggest that this transcriptional state may represent an adaptive but injury-associated podocyte response with potential relevance to disease severity and treatment response. In addition to epithelial injury programs, we observed consistent activation of stromal fibrotic pathways across glomerular diseases. Trajectory analysis suggested differentiation from fibroblasts to myofibroblasts, accompanied by enrichment of TGF-β signaling and extracellular matrix programs. Notably, the abundance of myofibroblasts correlated with declining kidney function even in patients without severe functional impairment at diagnosis, suggesting that fibrotic remodeling begins early in disease progression. Spatial transcriptomic data further revealed enrichment of POSTN-expressing fibroblasts within diseased glomeruli, supporting the existence of localized fibrotic microenvironments that may promote ongoing glomerular injury. Our data extend previous observations by demonstrating these fibrotic programs at single-cell resolution within human biopsy tissues. Drug2cell analysis further identified candidate compounds targeting disease-associated cellular states, providing a framework for future therapeutic hypothesis generation. The enrichment of distinct pathways in endothelial cells offers potential mechanistic insights into these diseases. For instance, the prominent TGF-β signaling in MN may contribute to the increased glomerular basement membrane thickness characteristic of the disease. 53 Furthermore, the upregulation of major histocompatibility complex molecules in both MCD and MN suggests that endothelial cells may activate antigen-experienced T-cells, implicating T-cell involvement in nephrotic syndrome. 54 , 55 Finally, the elevated interferon signature in MCD could help explain its characteristic steroid sensitivity. 56 There are several limitations in this study. First, glomerular cells comprised a relatively small proportion of total captured nuclei, reflecting the technical challenges of profiling human diagnostic biopsy tissue. Nevertheless, the absolute number of glomerular nuclei ( n = 13,475) was sufficient to identify multiple disease-associated cell states such as podocyte endocytosis. Second, the cohort is heterogeneous with limited samples per disease; however, the use of treatment-naïve diagnostic biopsies allowed us to capture early disease-associated transcriptional programs rarely accessible in human studies and was designed for shared rather than disease-specific classification. Third, our dataset mainly comprises transcriptomic information. Further enhancement by the inclusion of proteomic or epigenetic profiling could expand the insights related to pathophysiologic alterations in glomerular disease. 57 Lastly, control tissues were obtained from histologically normal cortex of nephrectomy specimens rather than healthy donor biopsies; subtle transcriptional alterations from tumor microenvironment effects cannot be fully excluded. To minimize these effects, control samples were collected by intraoperative biopsy-gun before renal artery clamping, mimicking native biopsy acquisition. Future validation with living donor or preimplantation biopsies may further confirm disease-associated programs. In conclusion, we report an extensive snRNA-seq dataset generated from rare and clinically valuable treatment-naïve human kidney biopsy tissues across MCD, MN, IgAN, and DKD. This dataset uniquely captures disease-relevant transcriptomic states of kidney-resident cells at the time of diagnosis, offering a snapshot that is difficult to obtain in other models or settings. Our findings provide novel insights into disease- and cell type-specific alterations in glomerular diseases. As a resource study, this work constitutes a foundational reference atlas that may support future investigations aiming to discover diagnostic markers, therapeutic targets, and mechanistic pathways in human kidney disease. Importantly, because the KORNERSTONE cohort is primarily composed of Korean patients, this dataset also expands the ethnic diversity of currently available kidney single-cell reference resources, which remain heavily weighted toward Western populations. title: Deep spatial transcriptomic profiling of ovarian clear cell carcinoma in the real-world setting.
xenium_reason: New profiling/generation with Xenium is stated
evidence_text: Deep spatial transcriptomic profiling of ovarian clear cell carcinoma in the real-world setting. Ovarian clear cell carcinoma (OCCC) is a rare cancer type of significant relevance to East Asian women harboring critical unmet needs for novel therapeutic options. It is a histological subtype of ovarian cancer with distinct pathological features, molecular profiles, and biological functions. Diverse heterogeneity contributing from histopathological and multiomic molecular features has yet to be translated to guide clinical care. Here, we presented a proof-of-concept study to demonstrate the feasibility of applying deep spatial transcriptomic (ST) profiling of tumor samples from an advanced OCCC patient in the real-world setting, aiming to identify therapeutic options beyond standard-of-care. Matched primary ovarian and metastatic bladder tumor sections were profiled by using GeoMx Digital Spatial Profiling and Xenium In Situ platforms. The spatial architecture and neighborhood niches were identified from GeoMx Cancer Transcriptome Atlas (CTA) and Xenium 5K Human Pan Tissue and Pathways Panel. An immunosuppressive Wnt-activating tumor microenvironment (TME) was identified by GeoMx while a tripartite spatial relationship between SLC2A1+ hypoxic cancer cells, IFIT2+ inflammatory cancer cells, and MMP12+ dendritic cells linking towards metabolism and immune responses was identified by Xenium. Our deep ST profiling findings provided significant biological insights and demonstrated feasibility to make novel discoveries, one patient at a time.

Single-cell and spatial transcriptomics reveal that the CXCL12-CXCR4 axis drives the immune-desert phenotype in small cell lung cancer by recruiting immunosuppressive CXCR4<sup>+</sup> neutrophils and S100A8<sup>+</sup> monocytes.

Background

Small cell lung cancer (SCLC) is a recalcitrant malignancy with limited responses to immunotherapy, largely due to its uniquely immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME). However, the molecular mechanisms driving this phenotype remain incompletely understood.

Methods

We integrated single-cell RNA sequencing and Xenium in situ spatial transcriptomics to analyze the immune microenvironment of five SCLC and four non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) samples. Multiplex immunofluorescence was used to validate cell types and gene expression in the same tissue specimens, and animal models were employed to verify the key mechanistic pathway.

Results

SCLC displayed a distinct immune landscape compared with NSCLC, with increased infiltration of C-X-C motif chemokine receptor 4 (CXCR4)+ neutrophils (via neutrophil extracellular traps) and S100A8+ monocytes (toward an M2-like phenotype), and reduced CD8+ T-cell infiltration. Malignant epithelial cells in SCLC highly expressed CXCR4, regulated by transcription factors ISL LIM homeobox 1 and distal-less homeobox 5, which promoted immunosuppression. The C-X-C motif chemokine ligand 12 (CXCL12)-CXCR4 axis mediated competitive inhibition, impairing T-cell recruitment while enhancing neutrophil accumulation. Monocytes in SCLC shifted toward an M2-like phenotype, weakening antigen presentation. Xenium spatial transcriptomics confirmed colocalization of CXCR4+ neutrophils and S100A8+ monocytes with tumor cells at the tumor-normal interface, while CD8+ T cells were spatially segregated. In vivo experiments showed that CXCR4 inhibition reduced SCLC tumor growth, decreased immunosuppressive cell infiltration, and enhanced CD8+ T-cell accumulation.

Conclusions

The CXCL12-CXCR4 axis, together with immunosuppressive CXCR4+ neutrophils and S100A8+ monocytes, is a key driver of the immune-desert phenotype in SCLC. Targeting this axis holds promise as a therapeutic strategy to remodel the immunosuppressive TME and improve the efficacy of immunotherapy for SCLC.
