KLRB1 (CD161) as a context-dependent prognostic marker in breast cancer: An exploratory analysis of CD4+ memory T cell infiltration: a retrospective multi-cohort study. The prognostic value of KLRB1 (CD161) in breast cancer is debated, and whether CD4+ memory T cell abundance modulates it is unclear. In this retrospective multi-cohort study we integrated The Cancer Genome Atlas Breast Invasive Carcinoma (n = 1088) and Molecular Taxonomy of Breast Cancer International Consortium (METABRIC) (n = 1980) with investigator-generated single-cell RNA-sequencing from 3 patients, public single-cell RNA-sequencing validation (GSE176078), Xenium spatial transcriptomics (19 samples) and multiplex immunofluorescence of a paired primary tumor and metastatic lymph node. Cox regression tested whether xCell-estimated CD4+ memory T cell abundance modifies the KLRB1-overall survival association. Higher KLRB1 expression was associated with favorable overall survival (TCGA hazard ratio [HR] = 0.93, P = .001; METABRIC HR = 0.82, P < .001). The CD4+ memory T cell interaction was significant under median dichotomization (TCGA P = .043; METABRIC P = .014) and after adjustment for age and tumor stage in both cohorts (TCGA P = .033; METABRIC P = .026; pooled HR 1.20, P = .0025); full adjustment for grade and subtype preserved significance in METABRIC (P = .012) but not in TCGA (P = .205). Across 3 single-cell cases KLRB1 was enriched in CD4+ memory T cells; functional profiling identified a cytotoxicity-effector T/NK signature, and TIGIT+ KLRB1+ cells showed no clear evidence of a classical exhaustion transcriptional signature. In Xenium, KLRB1+ cells proximal to CD4+ memory T cells co-upregulated TIGIT (pooled OR = 2.98) and PRF1 (OR = 1.99); multiplex immunofluorescence showed no spatial mutual exclusion. CD4+ memory T cell abundance is a hypothesis-generating candidate context modifier of KLRB1-mediated prognosis. This finding requires external validation in a subtype-stratified cohort, and the present data do not support clinical use. 1. Introduction  Breast cancer is the most common malignancy among women worldwide, with approximately 2.3 million new cases and 670,000 deaths reported in 2022. [ 1 ]  Despite advances in multimodal therapy, a substantial proportion of patients develop recurrence and distant metastasis. The integration of immunotherapy, primarily PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors combined with chemotherapy, has improved outcomes for triple-negative breast cancer, but objective response rates remain limited to 20% to 30% and durable benefit is restricted to a subset of patients. [ 2 , 3 ]  This therapeutic gap underscores the urgent need for biomarkers that capture the functional state of the tumor immune microenvironment and enable more precise patient stratification.  Within the tumor immune microenvironment, natural killer (NK) cells and T lymphocytes constitute the principal effector populations mediating antitumor immunity. [ 4 ]  Among  CD4 + subsets, memory T cells confer durable immunosurveillance, and their intratumoral abundance has been associated with favorable prognosis across multiple cancer types. [ 5 , 6 ]  The balance between effector and exhausted T cell states, governed by transcriptional programs and differentiation trajectories, [ 7 , 8 ]  is increasingly recognized as a critical determinant of clinical outcome. Regulatory T cells (Tregs), characterized by  FOXP3  expression, accumulate within tumors and suppress effector cell functions through secretion of IL-10 and TGF-β, consumption of IL-2, and direct contact-mediated inhibition via immune checkpoint receptors including  CTLA-4 ,  LAG-3 , and  TIGIT . [ 9 ]    KLRB1  encodes cluster of differentiation 161 (encoded by  KLRB1 ) ( CD161 ), a type II transmembrane C-type lectin-like receptor belonging to the NK cell receptor complex on chromosome 12p13. [ 10 , 11 ] 
 CD161  is expressed on the majority of human NK cells, NKT cells, and subsets of  CD4 + and  CD8+  T cells, including tissue-resident memory populations. [ 12 ]  Upon engagement with its ligand  CLEC2D (LLT1 ),  CD161  can deliver both co-stimulatory and co-inhibitory signals depending on cellular context. The functional complexity of this receptor-ligand axis is reflected in contradictory prognostic associations reported across cancer types. Mathewson et al. [ 13 ]  identified  CD161  to  CLEC2D  as an inhibitory checkpoint in glioma, where  KLRB1  knockout in T cells enhanced antitumor immunity in vivo. In hepatocellular carcinoma, single-cell analysis revealed that  CD161 -high  CD8+  T cells exhibited an innate-like, low-cytotoxicity phenotype associated with early relapse, [ 14 ]  illustrating the context-dependent nature of the  KLRB1 / CD161  signal. Pan-cancer analyses have confirmed that  KLRB1  expression correlates with both favorable and unfavorable prognosis depending on tumor type. [ 15 ]   In breast cancer specifically, multiple studies have reported reduced  KLRB1  expression in tumor versus normal tissue, with low expression independently predicting poor survival and altered immune infiltration patterns. [ 16 – 18 ]  Machine-learning-based immune-related gene models have further established  KLRB1  as a prognostic and immune infiltration biomarker in breast cancer. [ 17 , 18 ]  However, whether the prognostic impact of  KLRB1  in breast cancer is modified by the composition of the surrounding immune microenvironment, particularly the abundance of  CD4 + memory T cells, has not been systematically investigated.  The recent development of spatial omics technologies has opened new avenues for interrogating immune cell organization within intact tissue architecture. Xenium in situ sequencing enables subcellular-resolution detection of hundreds of targeted genes. [ 19 ]  Multiplex immunofluorescence (mIHC) provides complementary protein level spatial information, enabling quantitative analysis of cell-to-cell distances, cellular neighborhoods, and their associations with clinical variables. [ 20 , 21 ]  Single-cell profiling of breast cancer has revealed tissue-resident memory subsets associated with improved prognosis [ 22 ]  and immune ecosystems that predict treatment response, [ 23 – 25 ]  while systematic evaluation of tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes supports their prognostic value across breast cancer subtypes. [ 26 – 28 ]   In the present study, we integrated large-scale transcriptomic cohorts (The Cancer Genome Atlas Breast Invasive Carcinoma [TCGA-BRCA] and Molecular Taxonomy of Breast Cancer International Consortium [METABRIC]) with investigator-generated single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) data (three investigator-generated cases: Cases A, B, and C; human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 ( HER2 )-enriched and Luminal B-like subtypes), publicly available scRNA validation, Xenium spatial transcriptomics (19 samples), and mIHC analysis of paired primary and metastatic breast cancer samples to address 3 interconnected questions: whether  CD4 + memory T cell abundance modifies the prognostic value of  KLRB1  in breast cancer; the spatial and single-cell functional states of  KLRB1+  cells; and how  KLRB1 -related immune cell organization differs between primary tumors and metastatic lymph nodes. This is a retrospective, observational, multi-cohort study.    2. Materials and methods   2.1. Study design  The study comprised 5 interconnected analytical layers. First, we performed survival analyses in the TCGA-BRCA and METABRIC cohorts to test whether  CD4 + memory T cell abundance modifies the association between  KLRB1  expression and overall survival (OS). Second, we analyzed investigator-generated scRNA-seq data from 3 breast cancer patients (Cases A, B, and C; clinicopathologic details in Methods 2.4). Third, we validated the single-cell findings in a publicly available scRNA dataset ( GSE176078 ). Fourth, we performed a cross-sample meta-analysis of 19 breast cancer samples profiled by Xenium spatial transcriptomics ( GSE311609 ). Fifth, we performed mIHC on a paired primary tumor and metastatic lymph node from 1 breast cancer patient to characterize the spatial organization of  KLRB1+ ,  FOXP3 +,  GZMB +, and CD107A + cells.    2.2. TCGA-BRCA cohort  TCGA-BRCA transcriptomic data (TPM-normalized RNA-seq) and corresponding clinical annotations were downloaded from the NCI Genomic Data Commons (GDC) Data Portal ( https://portal.gdc.cancer.gov ). Gene identifiers were converted from Entrez ID to gene symbol using clusterProfiler::bitr. Immune cell abundance was estimated using the xCell algorithm [ 29 ]  with the rnaseq = TRUE parameter, generating enrichment scores for 64 immune and stromal cell types plus 3 composite scores (ImmuneScore, StromaScore and MicroenvironmentScore), i.e. 67 features in total. OS was derived from the GDC clinical record: patients recorded as deceased were assigned an event with time equal to demographic.days_to_death; all other patients were assigned a censored observation with time equal to the longest available follow-up among all recorded diagnosis records (diagnoses.N.days_to_last_follow_up). Times were converted from days to months (÷30.4375). The analysis set was defined identically for every survival analysis reported in this manuscript (Table  1  and  Supplementary Table S1 , Supplemental Digital Content 1) as: primary tumor samples with RNA-seq expression data, successful xCell deconvolution, derivable complete OS, and non-missing  KLRB1  expression and  CD4 + memory T cell score. The resulting participant flow was: 1097 expression samples, 1096 with successful xCell deconvolution, 1096 with derivable complete OS, 1089 primary tumor samples (7 metastatic samples excluded), yielding a final analysis set of 1088 patients (544  CD4 + memory T cell low, 544 high; 150 deaths). The nomogram complete-covariate subset comprised 1073 patients (150 deaths). The same definition applied to METABRIC yielded 1980 patients (990 low, 990 high; 1143 deaths). METABRIC confirmatory cohort  METABRIC microarray expression data and clinical annotations were obtained from cBioPortal ( https://www.cbioportal.org ). Duplicate genes were resolved by retaining the probe with the highest median expression. After filtering for complete survival data, 1980 patients were included. Immune cell abundance was estimated using xCell with the rnaseq = FALSE parameter appropriate for microarray data. Because xCell applied to microarray data may underestimate low-abundance cell types, the METABRIC interaction analyses should be regarded as a confirmation of the TCGA discovery rather than as a fully independent validation.    2.4. Investigator-generated scRNA-seq (three validation cases: cases A, B, and C)  scRNA-seq was performed on tumor samples from 3 breast cancer patients (Cases A, B, and C), with matched peripheral blood mononuclear cell (PBMC) samples additionally profiled for Cases A and C. All 3 cases were profiled using the DNBelab C4 platform (MGI/BGI). Clinicopathologically, Case C had an invasive carcinoma of no special type (NST), histologic grade III, with a maximum tumor diameter of approximately 3.0 cm; no definite lymphovascular invasion or perineural invasion was identified. The nipple, skin, base, and surgical margins were free of carcinoma; the right axillary lymph nodes (0/18) showed no metastasis; the interpectoral region showed fibrofatty tissue without tumor involvement. immunohistochemistry (IHC) revealed estrogen receptor (ER) (moderate-strong positive, 80%), progesterone receptor (PR) (strong positive, 90%), AR (moderate-strong positive, 80%),  HER2  (1+, negative), CK14 (negative), P63 (negative),  TRPS1  (positive), P120 (membranous), E-cadherin (membranous), EGFR (negative), P53 (negative, nonsense-mutant pattern), Ki-67 (40%), S-100 (nerve-negative), TOPO-IIα (positive), CKpan (positive), and CD31 (delineating vasculature), consistent with an ER+/PR+,  HER2 -negative, Luminal B-like molecular subtype. Case A had an invasive ductal carcinoma of NST, histologic grade III, tumor size 5.8 × 3.2 × 2.2 cm, with perineural invasion and lymphovascular tumor thrombi; the carcinoma involved the nipple dermis; the right axillary lymph nodes were 6/21 positive for metastasis, and 2 satellite tumor nodules (0.5–0.7 cm) were present. IHC: ER negative, PR negative, AR 2+ (~90%),  HER2  3+, P120 membranous+, E-cadherin+, CK14 negative, P63 negative,  TRPS1 +, EGFR 1+, S–100 nerve+, P53+ (missense-mutant pattern), Ki-67 ~40%;  HER2 -enriched subtype. Case B had an invasive ductal carcinoma of NST, histologic grade II to III; axillary lymph nodes 0/18 and apical lymph nodes 0/2 were negative for metastasis. IHC: ER negative, PR negative, AR 2+ (~80%),  HER2  2 + (FISH-amplified), E-cadherin 2+, P120 membranous+, EGFR 1+, SOX-10 negative, CK14 negative, P53 2+, Ki-67 ~40%;  HER2 -enriched subtype (FISH-confirmed  HER2  amplification). From Case C, 3 libraries were generated. The total cell count of each library was verified from the primary sequencing data: a  CD4 5-unsorted tumor library (14,221 cells), a  CD4 5-sorted ( CD4 5+-enriched) tumor-infiltrating library from the primary tumor (referred to as the “tumor  CD4 5” library; 11,019 cells) and a matched PBMC library (referred to as the “PBMC” library; 5311 cells), enabling joint analysis of tumor-resident and circulating immune populations. The lymphoid-compartment analyses reported below aggregate the  CD4 5-sorted tumor and PBMC libraries. After quality control and removal of low-quality cells, the  CD4 5-sorted tumor and PBMC libraries comprised 16,330 cells, of which 4567 lymphoid cells (3822 T cells and 745 NK cells) were retained for the lymphoid-compartment analyses. Cell-type annotation was performed using canonical lineage markers: CD3E/CD3D for T cells; CD8A/CD8B for  CD8+  T cells;  CD4  for  CD4 + T cells;  FOXP3 /IL2RA/CTLA4 for Tregs; interleukin 7 receptor (IL7R) for memory T cells; NKG7/GNLY/KLRF1 for NK cells.  CD4 + memory T cells were defined as T cells that were  CD4 -positive, negative for CD8A/CD8B, negative for the Treg markers  FOXP3 /IL2RA/CTLA4, and positive for IL7R; this definition was applied identically to all 3 cases.  KLRB1 + cells were defined as cells with detectable  KLRB1  expression (counts > 0). Within  KLRB1 + lymphoid cells,  TIGIT -positive and  TIGIT -negative subsets were defined for stratified analysis. Per-gene odds ratios (ORs) for  KLRB1 + versus  KLRB1 − cells and for  TIGIT + versus  TIGIT − subsets were computed using Fisher exact test; depth-adjusted (sequencing depth) ORs were estimated using a logistic regression model adjusting for log10(total unique molecular identifier [UMIs]) per cell, identical to the main analyses described above. For Cases A and B, the same library preparation and quality control pipelines were applied. Data from the 3 cases were analyzed separately (per-case differential expression and OR estimation) and then summarized for cross-case concordance; no pooled integration of raw counts across cases was performed. Paired  CD4 5-sorted and  CD4 5-unsorted tumor libraries were generated for each of the 3 cases; matched PBMC libraries were additionally generated for Cases A and C, whereas Case B had no matched PBMC library. Across the 3 cases this yielded 8 libraries in total (three  CD4 5-sorted, 3  CD4 5-unsorted, and 2 PBMC libraries). For Cases A and B the paired tumor libraries were analyzed together, as the primary analysis focused on intratumoral T cell states.    2.5. Public scRNA validation ( GSE176078 )  The publicly available breast cancer scRNA-seq dataset  GSE176078  (10x Genomics) was used as an independent validation cohort. [ 30 ] 
 KLRB1 + cell definition and functional gene analysis followed the same principles as for the investigator-generated data; cell-type annotation was taken from the annotation supplied with  GSE176078 .    2.6. Xenium spatial transcriptomics  Nineteen breast cancer samples profiled by Xenium In Situ gene expression (10x Genomics) were obtained from the Gene Expression Omnibus (accession  GSE311609 ). [ 19 , 31 , 32 ]  For each sample, gene expression counts and spatial coordinates were read using scanpy.  KLRB1 + cells were defined as cells with detectable  KLRB1  expression.  CD4 + memory T cells were defined as cells simultaneously positive for  CD4 , CD3E, and IL7R. Because some effector memory T cells may express low levels of IL7R, this definition may preferentially capture central memory  CD4  + T cells. A  KLRB1  + cell that is itself a  CD4  + memory T cell has a distance of zero to the nearest  CD4  + memory T cell and would therefore be classified as proximal irrespective of its spatial context; in the primary analysis the distance from each  KLRB1  + cell to the nearest  CD4  + memory T cell was therefore computed with the cell itself excluded, using the second-nearest  CD4  + memory T cell for cells that were themselves  CD4  + memory T cells. The complete 19-sample analysis performed with the cell included is reported as a sensitivity analysis.  KLRB1  + cells within 30 µm were classified as proximal; those beyond 50 µm were classified as distal. After random downsampling of the distal group to at most the proximal cell count (all distal cells are used when they are fewer than the proximal cells), positivity rates of  TIGIT , PRF1, FCGR3A, LAG3, and HAVCR2 were compared between proximal and distal  KLRB1  + cells using Fisher exact test. Cross-sample meta-analysis was performed using a DerSimonian-Laird random-effects model on log(OR) effect sizes, pooled across samples in which the gene was detectable; the pooled effect sizes reported in the text are back-transformed to ORs for interpretability.    2.7. mIHC and spatial analysis  Formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded tissue blocks of a primary breast tumor and its paired metastatic axillary lymph node were obtained from 1 female patient who underwent surgical resection at the Affiliated Taizhou People’s Hospital of Nanjing Medical University. Four-marker Opal multiplex fluorescence IHC was performed using the following primary antibodies: anti- KLRB1  (clone HP-3G10, 1:200), anti- FOXP3  (clone 236A/E7, 1:100), anti- GZMB  (clone GB11, 1:500), and anti-CD107A (clone H4A3, 1:200). DAPI was used for nuclear counterstaining. Whole-slide scanning was performed on a Vectra Polaris automated quantitative pathology imaging system at 20 × magnification. Cell detection and classification were performed in QuPath, and the centroid coordinates of each classified cell were exported. For each pairwise combination, the observed statistic was the mean nearest-neighbor Euclidean distance from each source cell to the nearest target cell. Two null models that preserve the marginal distribution of the target cells were used, each with 1000 permutations: (i) complete spatial randomness (CSR), in which the target cells were placed uniformly at random within the convex hull of all detected cells; and (ii) a toroidal-shift, in which the target point pattern was translated by a random vector with wrap-around, thereby preserving the internal clustering of the target cells while breaking any source–target association. A two-sided permutation  P  value was computed as twice the smaller tail proportion. The effect size was defined as the ratio of the observed mean distance to the mean of the null distribution, where 1.0 denotes no spatial association, values > 1 mutual exclusion, and values < 1 co-localization.    2.8. Statistical analysis  All statistical analyses were performed in R version 4.5.3 and Python (scanpy 1.12.4). Continuous variables are presented as median with range or mean with standard deviation. Cox proportional hazards regression results are reported as hazard ratios [HRs] with 95% confidence interval (CIs). To further control for potential confounding, we fitted Cox models with progressive adjustment for clinical covariates (age at diagnosis, tumor stage [early vs late], histological grade [grade 1–2 vs grade 3] and molecular subtype [Prediction Analysis of Microarray 50/Claudin-low]) where available in each cohort; cases with missing covariate values were excluded from the corresponding adjusted model. Fixed-effects meta-analysis of the age- and stage-adjusted interaction across the 2 cohorts was performed on the log HR scale. This study is reported in accordance with the STROBE statement for observational studies. Unit of inference for single-cell analyses: all single-cell comparisons were performed between cells within an individual case; cells from different patients were never pooled into a single test. Results are therefore reported as per-case (i.e. patient-level) estimates, and the evidence for generalisability is the directional concordance of these estimates across the 3 cases. Depth-adjusted ORs were estimated using logistic regression with log10 UMI per cell as a covariate. Between-study heterogeneity in meta-analysis was quantified using the I 2  statistic. Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) was applied to control for multiple hypothesis testing where applicable. All hypothesis tests were two-sided. Statistical significance was defined as  P  < .05.    2.9. Data availability TCGA-BRCA and METABRIC data are publicly available from the NCI GDC and cBioPortal, respectively. Xenium data are publicly available from Gene Expression Omnibus under accession number  GSE311609 . The investigator-generated scRNA-seq datasets (Cases A, B and C;  CD4 5-sorted and  CD4 5-unsorted tumor libraries, and matched PBMC libraries where applicable) are available from the corresponding author on reasonable request. All custom scripts used for the data analyses reported in the manuscript are provided as Supplementary Code S1–S4; the numerical supplementary tables are provided as  Supplementary Tables S1–S6 , Supplemental Digital Content 1 (each table in its own Word file, with its table title) and, in machine-readable form, as Supplementary Data (one Excel workbook). Purely figure-production and manuscript-assembly utilities are not included.

evidence_text:
GxP-Ready Single-Cell RNA-seq and Spatial Transcriptomics End-to-End Pipeline for Clinical Research. Single-cell/nucleus RNA-sequencing and Spatial Transcriptomics are powerful tools for investigating cellular heterogeneity and tissue architecture that have deepened our disease understanding. Their broader adoption in clinical and regulated settings, however, is hindered by regulatory requirements related to data integrity, regulatory compliance, reproducibility, and scalability. To address this gap, we developed NNclinSSOAP (Novo Nordisk Clinical Single-cell Spatial Omics Analytical Pipeline)-a modular, GxP-ready end-to-end computational pipeline that combines established single-cell workflows with a new Nextflow pipeline for Spatial Transcriptomics. NNclinSSOAP transforms RNA sequencing and Xenium spatial data into integrated, annotated single-cell objects and spatially resolved tissue maps. Designed to support mechanistic studies and clinical endpoint generation, it enables traceable and reproducible processing of large-scale datasets, scalable for use in HPC environments. Here, we provide a step-by-step demo case for using NNclinSSOAP that can be executed within 1.5 h on a standard laptop. All code and data are available open-source. Introduction  Single-cell/single-nucleus RNA sequencing (sc/snRNA-seq) has revolutionized biological research by enabling the study of gene expression at the resolution of individual cells and nuclei. The technology allows for the identification of cell types, the characterization of cellular heterogeneity within tissues, underlying cell–cell communication, and the understanding of complex biological processes at an unprecedented level of detail [ 1 ]. This granularity can uncover rare cell populations, specific gene expression profiles, and dynamic changes over time [ 2 ]. However, it inherently lacks spatial [ 3 ] information, which is critical for understanding the tissue architecture and the local microenvironment in which the cells reside [ 4 ]. Conversely, Spatial Transcriptomics retains high-resolution spatial information but often lacks the single-cell resolution necessary to discern the complexity of cellular interactions and the interplay of different cell types within tissues [ 5 ].  The multimodal omics approach of combining scRNA-seq and Spatial Transcriptomics addresses their respective limitations and provides a more comprehensive overview of cellular mechanisms in tissue contexts. This enables cellular identity and spatial organization to be established concurrently, which can aid in revealing the mechanisms of action of drugs and understanding disease pathology [ 6 – 8 ].  The use of these technologies and the large data handling requirements that come with them pose challenges for use in clinical settings. Ideally, such data need to be stored and handled in a Good Experimental Practice (GxP)-compliant way and compute resources need to be large enough to handle the data volumes.  This paper addresses these critical challenges, describing the implementation and usage instructions for NNclinSSOAP (Novo Nordisk Clinical Single-cell Spatial Omics Analytical Pipeline)—a GxP-ready pipeline for running sc/snRNA-seq and Spatial Transcriptomics together. Our approach ensures data integrity and facilitates the translation of findings into robust and reliable conclusions for downstream applications, contributing to the standardization and quality control necessary for wider application of sc/snRNA-seq and Spatial Transcriptomics in regulated environments and clinical trial settings. Unlike applications aimed primarily at interactive exploration, NNclinSSOAP is designed as an open-source, configurable pipeline that users can adapt to their own study designs, analysis needs, and compute environments.    Pipeline Overview  The development of this paper was motivated by the need for a combined sc/snRNA-seq and Spatial Transcriptomics workflow in a clinical research and trial endpoint analysis context. While single-cell and Spatial Transcriptomics technologies have become widely used for tissue and disease understanding for hypothesis generation, their application in regulated environments such as clinical trials presents specific challenges related to GxP requirements. Existing workflows, although effective in research settings, often do not address these requirements in a systematic way.  To meet these needs, we designed an end-to-end pipeline that integrates established methods and best practices from the broader community, with adaptations that ensure GxP-readiness and scalability. It was developed to ingest, process, and analyze sc/snRNA-seq and spatial data to generate clinical endpoints and run predefined analysis as per trial analysis plans, while providing a transparent and auditable framework suitable for clinical studies. Because of the number of samples set to be collected from multiple omics modalities, it was clear that the workflow would need to handle large data volumes and support execution in a high-performance computing (HPC) environment. To address these points, we adopted a modular, containerized architecture, enabling compliant storage and processing environments to be connected to the NNclinSSOAP pipeline.  The development process was iterative and collaborative, involving and building on cross-departmental expertise in computational biology, cloud engineering, statistics, and regulatory science. To address diverse data types and evolving analytical requirements, NNclinSSOAP was designed in a modular fashion that allows for straightforward adaptation to new datasets, data modalities, and requirements, providing flexibility and scalability for future research requirements and analyses. It is composed of 3 main components, connected as illustrated in Fig.  1  and described below:    1.  sc/snRNA-seq workflow: Handles the preprocessing, alignment, and quantification of single-nucleus RNA-seq data, leveraging nf-core/scrnaseq [ 9 ] for standardized and scalable data processing.    2.  R library/scripts: Enables advanced postprocessing, quality control, annotation, and statistical analyses of the output from the sc/snRNA-seq pipelines, ensuring robust downstream interpretation.    3.  SpatialXenium: A new Nextflow pipeline developed by us, designed to analyze multimodal data from the Spatial Transcriptomics platform Xenium [ 10 ], and optimized to run on HPCs ensuring efficient handling of large datasets. It ingests spatially resolved gene expression data and performs quality control, normalization, clustering, and spatial niche construction. The pipeline outputs processed Seurat objects (RDS), cluster/niche compositions, top marker genes, and visualizations (Principal Component Analysis [PCA], Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection [UMAP], and spatial plots). Optionally, it performs label transfer, adding cell-type annotation to the visualizations. The submodules that make up SpatialXenium are described in further detail in Box  1 .      Fig. 1.   Overview of how the 3 main components of NNclinSSOAP are connected, with their respective inputs, processing steps, outputs, and compute environments. (A) sc/snRNA-seq workflow. Processes fastq data, outputting, among others, h5ad files together with a multi-qc report and a BCO. The main processing steps include Quality control, Generate reference index, and Generate count matrix. (B) R library/scripts workflow. Processes the h5ad file from (A), outputting an annotated Seurat RDS object. The main processing steps include Quality control, Doublet detection, Multiple sample integration, Seurat object generation, Differential expression analysis, and Cell-type annotation. (C) SpatialXenium workflow. Processes raw Xenium data, outputting Spatial Transcriptomics analyses together with a report and a BCO, optionally taking the RDS object from the previous step to add cell-type labels to the analyses. The main processing steps include Quality control, Data normalization, Dimensionality reduction and clustering, Cell label transfer, and Results visualization.                     Box 1.   Brief introduction to the Spatial Transcriptomics processing steps (submodules)     1.  
 SEURAT_XENIUM 
      •  Orchestrates reading/validating data, quality control, filtering, dimensionality reduction, clustering, and saving results.    •  Can optionally produce a generically named output RDS if  --generic_name  is set to “TRUE”.    
 Key functions 
      •   open_seurat() : Loads Xenium data into Seurat, merging QC metadata.    •   plot_qc() : Generates QC plots (e.g., read count distributions and gene feature counts).    •   filter_genes() : Filters genes based on average quality value (QV) and read count thresholds.    •   run_seurat() : Normalizes data, identifies variable features, and runs PCA/UMAP/clustering.    •   get_cell_markers() : Finds marker genes for each cluster.    •   plot_processed_data() : Visualizes PCA, feature distributions, and UMAP.      2.  
 LABEL_TRANSFER 
      •  Reads the query Seurat RDS, reference RDS, and label column parameters.    •  Calls  transfer_labels()  to annotate the Xenium data.    •  Supports a  --future_mem_limit  parameter to set memory usage for parallel operations.    •  Outputs labeled Seurat RDS and prediction files.    
 Key functions 
      •   create_bygene_df() : Summarizes gene counts across Seurat assays.    •   transfer_labels() : Loads a reference RDS (single-cell data), ensuring matching label columns and overlapping features.    •  Fits a linear model (query vs. reference gene counts), calculates residuals, and identifies anchors.    •  Performs label transfer via  TransferData() , generating predicted labels and probabilities.    •  Filters low-probability cells (“Ambiguous”) and updates Seurat metadata.      3.  
 PLOT_FEATURE 
      •  Loads the Seurat object from RDS.    •  Reads a text file of gene names.    •  Produces and saves UMAP and spatial plots.    •  If no gene list is provided, plotting is skipped.    
 Key functions 
      •  Generates  FeaturePlot  on UMAP for each specified gene.    •  Creates  ImageFeaturePlot  to overlay gene expression on spatial coordinates.     To ensure package version stability and compatibility, we provide users with Docker and Singularity container manifests for the 2 latter pipeline components. This further allows users to build and run NNclinSSOAP in cloud-based containers.  In practice, the “Methods” section in this paper outlines a demo case that enables users to familiarize themselves with NNclinSSOAP and convert raw sc/snRNA-seq and Spatial Transcriptomics data into spatially resolved tissue maps with gene expression and cell-type annotations, through a small number of configuration changes and straightforward execution commands. The steps are divided into 2 procedures (Procedures 1 and 2) for sn/scRNA-seq and Spatial Transcriptomics, respectively. These support local execution on the demo datasets and outline the possibility of deployment on cloud infrastructure for larger datasets.  For usage other than the demo case, several configurable settings are available. These are shown at a high level in Fig.  2 . Importantly, in a clinical setting, the configurations should be set and documented before the pipeline is executed. To see all the options available, please refer to the documentation available in the repository.    Fig. 2.   Overview of user-configurable inputs and review points in NNclinSSOAP. The left panel shows the main workflow components and scripts/modules; the right panel summarizes the configuration files, command-line options, and QC/output review points. Numbers link each configuration or review point to the relevant workflow step. Paths are shown relative to the NNclinSSOAP repository root.                    GxP-readiness  In this manuscript, GxP-readiness refers to the ability of a computational workflow to be deployed within a regulated clinical-research environment in a way that supports data integrity, traceability, reproducibility, auditability, and controlled change management. The term does not imply that the pipeline alone makes an analysis fully GxP compliant. Rather, NNclinSSOAP provides pipeline-level controls that can be combined with an institution’s validated infrastructure, standard operating procedures, access controls, and documentation practices. Relevant expectations for clinical computerized systems and analysis planning include principles described in ICH E6(R3) [ 11 ], ICH E9 [ 12 ], and FDA 21 CFR Part 11 [ 13 ].  NNclinSSOAP implements these pipeline-level controls through a modular architecture, containerized execution environments, and automatic provenance capture. The whirl package provides the functionality of executing scripts in batch and simultaneously getting a log from the individual execution [ 14 ]. Nextflow, an open-source workflow management system [ 15 ], allows each workflow step to be run as a specified module with captured parameters and process metadata, while containers help control software versions and dependencies. The entire workflow is documented automatically in BioCompute Objects (BCOs). They document the intended purpose, inputs, software and version identity, parameter settings, execution details, provenance, and output locations of an analysis, providing a standardized record that can be reviewed, repeated, and archived [ 16 , 17 ]. BioCompute is an FDA-supported standard for regulatory submissions, and can be used during regulated activities and communication with the agency [ 18 ].  In clinical use, the GxP-ready pipeline is intended to be executed after the analysis has been specified in the clinical study analysis plan. Input data, configuration files, and output objects are treated as controlled analysis artifacts. Sample metadata and QC thresholds are defined before execution where possible, the run is executed in a validated or otherwise qualified compute environment, and generated reports, logs, BCOs, and Seurat objects are retained as evidence of what was run.  In our implementation, clinical data storage and access are handled by a compliant Amazon Web Services (AWS) storage service with separate input and output locations and role-based access. For data processing, analyses were performed within a dedicated, GxP-validated compute environment developed in-house as part of the Novo Nordisk secure analytics platform. This environment operates within a cloud-based infrastructure to provide both scalability and regulatory compliance throughout the data life cycle. The flow of inputs and outputs and the environments used is shown in Fig.  1 . Other institutions can reuse the open-source code, containers, and provenance mechanisms that NNclinSSOAP provides, connecting the workflow to their own validated compute, storage, access-control, retention, audit-trail, and electronic-signature processes.  The scope of readiness is therefore layered. Elements that transfer directly with the pipeline include modular workflow definitions, container manifests, configurable analysis parameters, BCO generation, execution logs, and standard outputs for review. Elements that remain institution-specific include formal software validation or verification, training, role-based review and approval of BCOs, controlled versioning and change management of the validated pipeline, secure data retention, audit trails, and any electronic-signature practices. This distinction is important because BioCompute primarily defines what is documented. It does not replace local validation, governance, or standard operating procedures required for full GxP compliance.  Within the pipeline, GxP-readiness is also reflected in how analysis decisions are exposed rather than hidden. QC filters and label-transfer probability thresholds are explicit user-configurable parameters. Cells failing QC are excluded from downstream analysis according to documented thresholds, and low-probability labels are not silently converted into confident cell types. Instead, they are flagged as “Ambiguous” in the labeled Seurat metadata and visualizations and are accompanied by prediction files. This allows downstream users and reviewers to distinguish confident annotations from those requiring caution or manual review.    Applications  NNclinSSOAP was specifically developed for clinical trials incorporating transcriptomics as study endpoints, including sc/snRNA-seq and Spatial Xenium. As a pioneering framework in the pharmaceutical industry, particularly for cardiometabolic diseases, NNclinSSOAP has already been used in 2 mechanism-of-action trials. The first trial, focused on Alzheimer’s disease, incorporated scRNA-seq data as a primary endpoint [ 19 ], and therefore utilized only Procedure 1, which is tailored for single-cell transcriptomics. In contrast, the second trial, a clinical study in kidney disease [ 20 , 21 ], employed both Procedures 1 and 2 as it included both snRNA-seq and Xenium Spatial Transcriptomics data.  By enabling rapid and GxP-aligned data processing, this workflow sets a new standard for transcriptomic analysis in clinical trials. Looking ahead, it is broadly applicable to trials in other therapeutic areas, provided that compatible input data are available. Thanks to Nextflow’s modular architecture, the workflow can be easily adapted to accommodate additional analytical modules in the future.  Notably, the SpatialXenium Nextflow pipeline described in this paper is publicly available as part of the repository and can be integrated into new or existing Nextflow workflows, independently of the broader workflow described in the paper.    Comparison to other methods  There are numerous tools and packages available to facilitate sc/snRNA Transcriptomics data preprocessing [ 22 ]. For sc/snRNA-seq, we used the established nf-core pipeline scrnaseq as part of Procedure 1. Beyond the initial preprocessing steps, downstream processing and analysis of sc/snRNA-seq data commonly leverage widely used packages such as Seurat [ 23 ] that we use as part of our R library. Our SpatialXenium pipeline is wrapped around the Seurat suite relevant for Spatial Transcriptomics data QC, preprocessing, and analytics.  Integrated platforms for combining single-cell and Spatial Transcriptomics exist [ 24 ], but not as workflows aligned with GxP requirements. The purpose of this section is to contextualize NNclinSSOAP rather than to provide a formal benchmarking study. NNclinSSOAP builds on established community methods and combines them into a documented, containerized, and provenance-aware workflow for regulated clinical research settings. The points below therefore focus on workflow structure, traceability, reproducibility, and deployment considerations. Six main features make NNclinSSOAP different to other methods:    1.  Modularity. NNclinSSOAP not only makes it possible to run the underlying sc/snRNA-seq and SpatialXenium workflows separately, but the workflows themselves build on Nextflow modules. This simplifies both using the workflows and adapting them to future needs as well as making them scalable, a key factor in data heavy settings.    2.  GxP-readiness. Using Nextflow for building our workflows enables NNclinSSOAP to be both scalable and reproducible. Combined with BCO-based provenance capture, this supports selected GxP-relevant expectations, particularly traceability, reproducibility, and reviewability. It allows users to connect to a compute environment of choice, without compromising reproducibility, enabling analysis of data volumes at a much greater scale than in the demo case described in this paper. Full GxP compliance ultimately depends on deployment within an appropriate governed environment.    3.  The SpatialXenium pipeline. There is a publicly available pipeline, nf-core/spatialxe, currently under development. It is a flexible image- and coordinate-based reanalysis framework, focused on controlling and improving Xenium data quality through multiple segmentation and spatial-data methods. SpatialXenium differs from this, instead focusing on postprocessing and analysis of Xenium data. It provides users a fully specified, protocol-locked, and easily reproducible end-to-end pipeline, implementing Spatial Transcriptomics analysis from Seurat for Xenium data.    4.  We provide an R library capable of processing outputs generated by nf-core/scrnaseq, supporting standard Seurat workflows and downstream annotation. These scripts offer flexibility, incorporating tools such as Harmony [ 25 ] and RPCA [ 26 ] for multisample integration. For cell-type annotation, automated approaches like Azimuth [ 27 ] or SingleR [ 28 ] are supported, and user-defined reference datasets can be added. For differential treatment effect analysis, we use a pseudobulk [ 29 ] approach by aggregating counts per sample and cell type, followed by statistical assessment using edgeR [ 30 ], which enables robust testing of group-level differences while accounting for biological variability. Alternatively, other statistical methods can be integrated as needed. An overview of this workflow is illustrated in Fig.  1 .    5.  By leveraging the whirl package [ 14 ] to execute the R library, the pipeline produces a BCO along with multiple log files—one corresponding to each R script. The package offers the flexibility to modify certain domains within the BCO and to select specific scripts to run as needed.    6.  The R environment required for running these procedures is provided as a Docker container, ensuring that all necessary packages and dependencies are included and eliminating compatibility issues for the user. This approach allows the entire environment to be reliably loaded and the workflow to be executed as intended. However, one limitation is that package versions within the container may become outdated as new releases are made. Users also have the flexibility to set up and use their own custom environments if preferred.       Experimental Design   Expertise needed for implementation and interpretation  NNclinSSOAP was developed to be used by computational biologists, producing results (e.g., tables and figures) that can be interpreted and understood by medical or biological experts without a data science background. For users following the procedures step-by-step, no expertise is needed and none of the topics below need to be considered. However, some familiarity with single-cell transcriptomics and relevant training in statistical analysis of high-dimensional omics data and running analytics scripts is advisable for a smooth experience and ability to understand the outputs scientifically.  If the workflow outlined in this paper is adapted to another dataset different from the demo, carefully consider the points below. It is also recommended to read the extensive information and instructions provided in the code repository  README.md  and .md files in  /docs . For this, a broad understanding of R, Nextflow, cloud computing, containerization, and single-cell transcriptomics is needed.    Sampling strategy-dependent analysis  The datasets used in Procedure 2 contain a single sample each, one with healthy kidney tissue and the other with cancerous kidney tissue. This case facilitates analysis from the perspective of seeing differences in cell types and gene expression. Depending on a dataset’s sampling strategy, experimental design, and analysis plans, as often preregistered in a clinical trial setting, other relevant analyses and visualizations are possible, e.g., mitochondrial genes, cell cycle genes, biological sex-related genes, batch effect contribution from metadata, etc. For samples taken from the same subject at multiple time points (longitudinal data), it is possible to analyze changes over time. For samples taken at a single time point for multiple subjects (cross-sectional data), it is possible to analyze the homo-/heterogeneity within a population. Combining these 2 strategies creates a clinical trial scenario where NNclinSSOAP can be used to analyze subjects’ tissue characteristics over time as a response to treatment, comparing to a placebo group or among groups at a single time point for disease understanding.    Optional settings and configurations  Beyond the default settings and basic configurations required to run the demo case in the “Methods” section, NNclinSSOAP can be customized through various command line flags and configuration files. Figure  2  provides a high-level overview of these options.  For the sc/snRNA-seq workflow, users can customize the metadata and configuration files to use with their own data, according to the nf-core/scrnaseq documentation:  https://nf-co.re/scrnaseq/4.0.0/docs/usage/ . For improved version control and streamlined collaboration, it is highly recommended to maintain a dedicated Git repository containing all related metadata and configuration files.  Once the nf-core/scrnaseq pipeline has completed, NNclinSSOAP provides users with tools to further analyze and explore their data. Specifically, 3 main R scripts are included for downstream analysis (see Fig.  3 ), each designed with flexibility in both parameters and methods. To customize or modify the pipeline execution, users can edit the associated config file  preprocessing_workflow.yml . These options provide users with extensive flexibility for preprocessing, integrating, and annotating single-cell data within the NNclinSSOAP framework. Note that the RPCA integration method is computationally intensive and may not be suitable for local execution.    Fig. 3.   Summary of sc/snRNA-seq data analysis workflow and results. By default, this file contains the genes needed to reproduce our results on the demo case data. Users should adapt this file if using other datasets, to reflect their genes of interest. Multiple command line options control which cells and genes are included in the UMAP and spatial feature plots, and how strict the filtering is.    Quality control  QC thresholds should be reviewed in the context of each dataset and, where applicable, defined before downstream biological or clinical interpretation. For Xenium data, the relationship between read counts, gene detection, and QV score provides a practical check of assay quality (see Fig.  4 ). A high-quality dataset is expected to retain most informative cells and genes after filtering, with low-quality or control-probe-rich observations limited to a minority of the data. In contrast, a problematic dataset may show a large fraction of observations with low read counts, low QV scores, unusually high read-count outliers, or high control-probe proportions. The selected thresholds are captured in configuration files and execution outputs (see Fig.  2 ), supporting reproducibility and review of the filtering decisions.    Fig. 4. Seurat Spatial Transcriptomics visualization options  The tissue visualizations overlaid with gene expression and cell types generated from running SpatialXenium utilize the Seurat v5 package’s functions  ImageDimPlot() and  ImageFeaturePlot() . These offer a wide range of options beyond what is covered by default in SpatialXenium, enabling extensive control over plot aesthetics and content, including color scales, transparency, cell border properties, molecule overlays, coexpression blending for pairs of genes and grouping cell types. Expected Results  The result of following both procedures is a transformation of raw sc/snRNA-seq data into an integrated and annotated Seurat object, and raw Xenium data into a spatially resolved cell object and map. This can aid in answering clinical questions, giving the user a deeper understanding of the analyzed tissues both at a cellular expression and a structural level, as is the case in the demo case data in this paper, highlighting differences between healthy and cancer kidney tissue.  When the procedures are executed with the supplied demo data using the specified software versions, parameters and settings, deterministic tables and files are expected to be reproducible. Stochastic visualization steps such as UMAP may show minor layout differences while preserving the same biological topology and interpretation. If the paper is followed using a personal dataset, the same types of outputs are expected, but results will differ according to the input data.   Sc/snRNA-seq (procedure 1)  Executing the sc/snRNA-seq workflow (Procedure 1, step 2) generates an nf-core results folder. The demo case dataset has been run with the cellranger aligner [ 31 ], so the results are the standard cellranger outputs. The special addition is the BCO object that has been generated since the plugin is included when running the nextflow pipeline.  In the second part of the workflow (Procedure 1, steps 4 and 5), each script produces a variety of plots and output files, which are organized into dedicated folders—see Box  2  for a summary of the results file structure.    •  Quality Control (QC): QC plots document the standard Seurat workflow, starting from reading the counts matrix and progressing through to the creation of the final Seurat object (see Fig.  3 A to D). A separate folder is generated for each sample’s QC outputs, while the integrated Seurat object is stored in the parent directory.    •  Cell Annotation: This step generates visualizations such as UMAPs displaying annotated clusters and violin plot displaying the annotation scores, along with an updated Seurat object that contains cell type assignments (see Fig.  3 E and F).    •  Differential Expression analysis: For each cell type, the pipeline outputs a normalized counts CSV file, a CSV file with differential expression results, and a volcano and line plot summarizing key findings (see Fig.  3 G and H).      SpatialXenium (procedure 2)  Executing the SpatialXenium workflow (Procedure 2, step 4) produces several key outputs that can be used for clinical interpretation of the tissues analyzed, shown in Fig.  4 . By using Nextflow, reports covering errors, timing and resource usage have automatically been created. An example results file structure is shown in Box  3 . To aid with technical and clinical interpretation, key outputs from Quality Control (QC), gene expression and cell type analysis are described in further detail below:    •  Quality Control: The QC plots (see Fig.  4 A and B) summarize how many genes and reads are captured per cell and how these values are distributed across the dataset. This allows users to identify low-quality cells, technical outliers, or regions with suboptimal capture efficiency before drawing any biological or clinical conclusion, ensuring that downstream patterns (e.g. “immune poor” areas) are not artifacts of poor data quality.    •  Gene Expression: The gene expression visualizations (see Fig.  4 C and D) show how the selected markers from  assets/genes.txt  are distributed both in UMAP space and across the tissue. Clinically, these plots help confirm that canonical markers (for example, tumor, immune, or stromal genes) are expressed in the expected tissue compartments and spatial niches, supporting interpretations such as tumor–stroma interactions, immune infiltration patterns, or localization of specific disease-relevant pathways.    •  Cell Type: The cell-type plots (see Fig.  4 E and F) resulting from the label transfer display the predicted cell types in UMAP space projected back onto the tissue, with cells below the chosen probability threshold set to “Ambiguous”. This makes it clear which assignments are robust enough to support biological or clinical interpretation, which should be treated with caution. In a clinical context, these maps can be used to explore how specific cell types (e.g., cytotoxic T cells, fibroblasts, and endothelial cells) are spatially organized within lesions, margins, or normal tissue, and how this architecture might relate to disease severity or therapeutic response.       Conclusion  NNclinSSOAP offers a GxP-ready framework for scalable processing and analysis of single-cell and Spatial Transcriptomics data for clinical research and trials. Its modular design and automated provenance capture ensure transparent, reproducible, auditable, and fully traceable analyses suitable for regulated environments, e.g., clinical trials. Together, these features provide a practical, unique, and extensible foundation for deploying multimodal transcriptomics across mechanistic studies and clinical trials. Spatial Mapping of the Precancer-to-Cancer Transition in Breast and Prostate. Breast and prostate cancers are both hormone-driven adenocarcinomas that undergo analogous invasion programs. Using lightsheet microscopy on intact tumors, we identified transitional junctions between precancerous and invasive regions. We then developed a multimodal serial-section workflow integrating volumetric reconstruction with spatial transcriptomics. Analysis of 319 spatial assays from 51 cases revealed gene expression features and novel structural insights defining the shift from precancer to invasive disease. In breast cancer, loss of MGP and PLAT was associated with invasive transition and promoted tumorigenesis in functional assays. In prostate cancer, GDF15, ALDH1A3, ANPEP, and FASN were upregulated along invasive progression, and their knockdown in PC-3 cells suppressed proliferation and migration. Enrichment of tumor-associated macrophages (SPP1+ and MS4A6A+) along non-triple-negative breast cancer breast cancer transitions highlights immune involvement as a potential driver of invasiveness.

Significance

Our method of defining precise spatial locations of invasive transition allows for the direct interrogation of transition drivers, presenting new therapeutic targets for the two most prevalent cancers and providing a framework for studying spatially defined mechanisms of tumor progression. See related commentary by Jing and Li, p. 1720. Although they originate in distinct organs, there are notable similarities in their development, progression, and underlying biological mechanisms ( Fig. 1A ; ref. 1 ). Both cancers rely on steroid hormones for growth and development, leading to similar therapeutic strategies targeting hormone signaling ( 2 – 4 ). They also share underlying hereditary genetic mechanisms for cancer initiation, such as alterations in BRCA1 and BRCA2 ( 5 , 6 ), and morphologic similarities, particularly in the organization of their epithelial structures. Both tissues are composed of glandular structures with two primary cell layers, an inner luminal cell layer and an outer basal cell layer, and are responsible for secretory functions (production of milk in the breast and prostatic fluid in the prostate; refs. 7 , 8 ). Figure 1. 3D spatial omic cohort for epithelial transition in breast and prostate cancers. A, Similarities between breast and prostate cancers in terms of sex hormone regulation, genetic predisposition, developmental processes, tissue architecture, physiologic functions, and disease progression timelines. B, Composition of the breast-and-prostate cancer transition cohort analyzed in this study, encompassing stacked 3D and native 3D and 2D cohorts. Left, breakdown of each cohort. Right, assay and case counts for each assay. Stacked 3D cohort: samples with serial sections reconstructed into 3D tumor volumes. This cohort utilizes Xenium, Visium HD, Visium, CosMx, CODEX, and H&E imaging. Native 3D cohort: samples processed with lightsheet microscopy to capture intact 3D structures. 2D cohort: individual sample sections without serial sections. These tissues also share a similar path to tumorigenesis, in which carcinoma typically arises from luminal cells. The surrounding basal layer remains intact during early precancer states, those being ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) in the breast and high-grade prostatic intraepithelial neoplasia (HGPIN) in the prostate ( 9 , 10 ). Luminal cells in both cancers also typically express hormone receptors, such as estrogen receptor (ER) and progesterone receptor (PR) in the breast and androgen receptor (AR) in the prostate. During the transition from precancer to malignancy in both tumor types, the basal cell layer is broken, and neoplastic cells spread into the surrounding environment ( 11 , 12 ). As such, precancerous lesions often have an attenuated basal layer, indicating progression toward loss of this barrier. Additionally, DCIS and HGPIN can both display similar epithelial cell patterns, such as cribriform architecture ( 13 ). Despite the clinical importance of tumor progression, the spatial and molecular dynamics of these transitions, particularly in breast and prostate cancers, remain poorly understood. This is, in part, due to the inability of conventional two-dimensional (2D) single-modality approaches to capture the full complexity of tumor topology and tumor–microenvironment interactions in situ . In this study, we developed a new volumetric approach that combines native three-dimensional (3D) and vertically reconstructed 2D data modalities to investigate malignant transition in breast and prostate tissues. We first imaged 14 tissue blocks from four cases with 3D lightsheet microscopy, providing high-resolution 3D immunofluorescence (IF) data for tissue blocks in their entirety. We report differences between the 3D morphologies of precancerous lesions and invasive carcinoma in both cancer types. To investigate the molecular signatures associated with these transitions, we developed a multimodal 3D serial sectioning approach, combining spatial transcriptomics (ST), multiplex imaging, and histologic staining. We assembled a cohort of 319 assays spanning 51 cases, nine of which were serially sectioned, and imaged with a variety of spatial data types ( Fig. 1B ; Supplementary Tables S1–S3). Additionally, we supplemented our 3D serial section cohort with 69 nonserial sections of Xenium, CosMx, CODEX, Visium, and Visium HD data. This 3D serial section approach enables reconstruction of 3D tissue structures from 2D sections, providing a unified framework for analyzing molecular and morphologic changes across 3D space. By leveraging Xenium, CosMx, Visium, Visium HD, and CODEX platforms, we interweave data at varying resolutions and biomarker coverage depth, overcoming important limitations inherent to single-platform analyses. Using this new approach, we reveal mechanisms underlying the progression of DCIS to intraductal carcinoma (IDC) in breast cancer and the transition from normal glands to Gleason pattern 3 (GP3) in prostate cancer. We have identified differentially expressed genes (DEG), spatial relationships, and tumor microenvironment (TME) features integral to epithelial cell state transitions. Furthermore, we have provided functional and mechanistic insights into the potential involvement of some of these genes in the key transitions. In addition to technical pipelines relevant to other cancer types, this study offers a blueprint for understanding breast and prostate cancer progression and suggests potential processes for therapeutic intervention. Results Breast and Prostate Cancer Transition Study Cohort Overview We profiled 319 tumor and normal sections (2D) and blocks (3D) from 51 cases, encompassing breast cancer (112 assays, 21 cases) and prostate cancer (207 assays, 30 cases) as part of the NCI Human Tumor Atlas Network (HTAN; Fig. 1B ; Supplementary Tables S1–S3). The samples were divided into three cohorts based on the assay method and analysis strategy: stacked 3D, native 3D, and 2D cohorts. The stacked 3D cohort comprised 233 assays, including 76 assays from breast cancer and 157 from prostate cancer. Five spatial omics platforms (Xenium, CosMx, Visium, Visium HD, and CODEX), together with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) imaging, were used to reconstruct 3D tumor structures and investigate molecular markers associated with the transition from noninvasive to invasive states (Supplementary Tables S2–S5). We also added additional 2D sections to form a nonserial 2D analysis cohort to increase sample size for DEG analyses, which included a total of 305 sections from 47 cases. Additionally, we performed native 3D assays using fluorescent lightsheet microscopy (FLSM) to trace the glandular structures in 3D and directly observe the transition from noninvasive to invasive states in both breast and prostate cancers. Volumetric Lightsheet Microscopy Reveals Tumor Architecture To investigate the architecture of precancerous and invasive tumor volumes within intact samples, we utilized FLSM to image cleared and immunostained tumor tissues ( Fig. 2A and B ). This analysis included five samples from two patients with breast cancer and nine samples from two patients with prostate cancer ( Fig. 2A , “Methods”). Cytokeratin-5 (CK5) and pan-cytokeratin (PanCK) were used to label basal cells and epithelial cells, respectively, enabling the delineation of normal, precancerous, and invasive lesions in both breast and prostate cancer tissues ( Fig. 2C and D ). Figure 2. Volumetric lightsheet microscopy reveals 3D tumor architecture. A, Lightsheet cohort information. Samples used for the following detailed analysis were highlighted in pink and blue for breast and prostate tumors, respectively. B, Schematic of the experimental workflow for lightsheet microscopy. Tumor samples (“Methods”) were tissue-cleared and antibody-labeled before imaging by lightsheet microscopy. C, 3D view of the breast cancer sample HT944B1. D, 3D view of the prostate cancer sample HT957Z1. E, Two representative regions of DCIS were observed in a given breast cancer sample, surrounded by IDC and normal ductal structures. Regions are indicated in C . Scale bars, 100 μm. F, Fraction of PanCK-positive regions that are IDC (yellow) vs. DCIS (blue) across the whole structure in ROI1. G, 3D surface reconstruction of ROI1 in E . Scale bars, 300 μm. H, Selected region ROI3 of HT957Z1 in D , with HGPIN (blue dotted curves) to GP3/4 (yellow dotted curves) transitioning in prostate cancer sample. The IDC-P region is highlighted with orange dotted curves. Scale bars, 100 μm. I, Ratio between CK5-positive and PanCK-positive area decreases with the invasive transition across Z. J, 3D reconstruction of the high-grade PIN to GP3/4 transition in H . Scale bars, 200 μm. IDC-P, IDC of the prostate. In all images, CK5 is in white and PanCK is in red. ( B, created with Biorender.com .). To investigate the differences between DCIS and IDC architectures, we focused our analysis on HT944B1 with confirmed IDC and DCIS features by pathologist’s review. This 7 mm by 2.5 mm by 1 mm sample (Supplementary Mov. S1) was filled with large but scattered regions positive with PanCK staining but little to no CK5 staining on the periphery, indicative of IDC and a discontinuous or absent basal layer ( Fig. 2C , yellow arrowhead in E ; Supplementary Mov. S2 and S3). Although IDC regions seem separated and scattered on a 2D section, they are interconnected throughout the tumor sample and can span large volumes (Supplementary Mov. S1, S2, and S4; Supplementary Fig. 1A), consistent with a pattern of invasion and uncontrolled growth in the 3D space. There are also six distinct PanCK-positive areas with CK5 staining surrounding their periphery. Some regions feature a thin layer of PanCK staining within the CK5 boundary, indicative of normal ductal structures in which a single layer of basal epithelial layer surrounds a single layer of luminal epithelial layer ( Fig. 2E , green dashed line). Others feature an enlarged PanCK patch inside of the CK5 boundary, indicative of DCIS regions in which malignant luminal cells in the breast duct start to proliferate but the basal layer is still intact ( Fig. 2E , blue dashed line). DCIS morphology either resembles a large homogeneous mass [ Fig. 2E , region-of-interest (ROI)1] or an enlarged ductal structure ( Fig. 2E , ROI2). For example, the DCIS structure highlighted in ROI1 spans more than 750 μm in the z-dimension, which is the direction perpendicular to the sections ( Fig. 2F ). The regions with intact CK5 + basal layers seem to retain the CK5 layer throughout the volume we observed, which leads us to hypothesize that the invasive lesion exists outside of the sampled region. Nonetheless, DCIS regions can be embedded within IDC regions ( Fig. 2G ; Supplementary Mov. S4). Lastly, we observed one region with multiple DCIS-like areas nested into a single larger structure, with strong CK5 staining interwoven with PanCK-stained precancer cells (Supplementary Fig. S1B and S1C; Supplementary Mov. S5). We propose that the observed structure is a breast lobule filled with neoplastic cells. As lobular carcinoma in situ was not indicated by our pathologist, we hypothesize that the cancer cells originated from DCIS regions outside of the sample but invaded through the ductal system. To investigate differences between high-grade PIN and invasive prostate tumor structures, we focused our detailed analysis on HT957Z1 that has coexisting normal glandular structures, high-grade PIN, and invasive adenocarcinoma. The pathology report of this patient indicates prostatic acinar adenocarcinoma with a Gleason score of 4 + 3. We observe bright but unspecific staining of spherical structures throughout many prostate samples, which we suspect originate from antibodies trapped by corpora amylacea ( Fig. 2D ; Supplementary Fig. S1D and S1E; Supplementary Mov. S6). We postulate that this reflects the overall inflammatory status of the patient. Similar to breast cancer samples, normal prostate ducts and acini are marked by an outer layer of CK5 and a thin inner layer of PanCK (Supplementary Fig. S1E). Some ductal structures feature an enlarged inner PanCK layer (25–50 µm thick rather than the typical ∼10 μm thick) with an intact CK5 boundary, suggestive of high-grade PIN structures ( Fig. 2H , blue dashed line). These high-grade PIN structures are adjacent to, and seemingly connected to, disordered PanCK+ branching structures without CK5 on the periphery, consistent with the invasive pattern of Gleason score 4 ( Fig. 2H , yellow dashed line, and Supplementary Mov. S7). Indeed, the CK5 to PanCK ratio decreased with the transition from 0.4 to 0.1 ( Fig. 2I ). This observed transition offers a detailed view of the architectural changes during the neoplastic transition ( Fig. 2J ; Supplementary Mov. S8). In addition, we observed ductal structures with strong CK5 staining on the basal layer and a lumen filled with PanCK-positive cells, similar to the DCIS morphology observed in breast cancer. These could be IDC of the prostate ( Fig. 2H ; Supplementary Fig. S1F orange dashed line). In summary, FLSM of intact breast and prostate tumors revealed that regions appearing disconnected in 2D are in fact highly interconnected in 3D, with DCIS and high-grade PIN lesions embedded within and/or transitioning into invasive carcinoma. These analyses highlight how basal layer integrity and epithelial expansion define architectural shifts, providing a direct volumetric view of noninvasive and invasive morphology. Gene Discovery Serial Section Workflow and Computational Framework To understand the molecular drivers associated with the structural transition, we devised a multimodal workflow integrating spatial assays across different platforms. Although the archetypical 2D section is blind to transition dynamics in the third dimension, it does provide large amounts of data, thanks to lower imaging costs. With a view to optimizing 2D tradeoffs of cost versus the limited field-of-view provided by 2D spatial assays, we developed an experimental and computational framework for volumetric integration of 2D sections from a tissue block using five platforms, namely H&E, Xenium, CosMx, CODEX, and the Visium family (Supplementary Fig. S2A). The data from the intermingled sections are computationally combined, furnishing a comprehensive view of spatial and structural variations (Supplementary Fig. S2B). Briefly, sections are cut at specific intervals and optimally arranged on slides according to the respective imaging area of each platform. Following imaging, sections are spatially registered using a keypoint workflow, enabling precise computational alignment across sections (arXiv:1511.01154), and the resulting data are annotated for gene discovery (“Methods”). The product is a block-specific atlas of computationally registered sections that can be examined for precancer-to-cancer transitions and interconnected tumor volumes. Single-platform 2D sections are generally unable to fully characterize transitions, unless the transition region is both sufficiently linear and there is a serendipitous match between it and the section orientation (Supplementary Fig. S2B). The computationally registered multisections in our method capture both linear and nonlinear transition regions within the section area, leaving no topologically disconnected image fragments of the transition region. The integration of platform data and the respective genes they cover support further computational inferences of the transition continuum by proximal correlations of expression (Supplementary Fig. S2C). The approach is used here for finding ROI level DEGs associated with cancer transition in volumetric tumor blocks. Effectively, this allows regions, for example, DCIS, microinvasion (MI), and IDC in breast cancer, to be examined holistically along a spatial continuum. We developed two methods to discover genes associated with these interconnected transition regions: path-based and morphology-based (“Methods”). Briefly, in the path-based method, we calculated a single correlation value across multiple spatial platforms within each interconnected 3D volume. The regression was run on expression values for each region along the path of the transitioning epithelial structure. In the morphology-based method, all regions morphologically annotated as noninvasive (e.g., DCIS) were compared WITH the all invasive regions (e.g., IDC) within the same platform. We also supplement these 3D ROI-level DEGs with 2D approaches that involve assessing regions’ myoepithelial intensity using basal layer markers. Using these markers, we are able to assign each region an invasiveness score, which is an indication of the basal layer marker gene abundance for the region and serves as a continuous metric reflecting the degree of morphologic and molecular progression along the transition axis within each ROI. This score was then correlated with gene expression, allowing the identification of cohort-level genes associated with myoepithelial integrity (“Methods”). Transitionary regions in all ROIs were reviewed and validated by board-certified pathologists. Biomarkers for DCIS-to-IDC Transition in Breast Cancer First, we applied our methodology to ascertain biomarkers correlated to the DCIS-to-IDC transition in breast cancer. Nine tissue samples were serially sectioned (“Methods”). Two samples having greater sectioning depths (460 and 120 µm) were selected for ROI-based analysis, as their increased depths enabled visualization of more pronounced morphologic changes along the Z-dimension of the tissue blocks. HT704B1, a 450-µm deep breast carcinoma specimen with regions of DCIS and IDC, was analyzed using five spatial platforms: Xenium ( n = 6), CODEX ( n = 12), H&E ( n = 20), CosMx ( n = 4), and Visium HD ( n = 2; Fig. 3A ; Supplementary Mov. S9 and S10). The 3D analysis of these sections revealed that regions separated in 2D space by more than 5 mm were in fact interconnected in the Z plane ( Fig. 3B ; Supplementary Table S6), underscoring the value of serial sectioning for understanding true morphologic relationships. We analyzed two regions of interest, ROI1 and ROI2, and identified common metabolic, epithelial integrity, and proliferation modules associated with the transition from DCIS to MI and to IDC ( Fig. 3C–E ; Supplementary Mov. S11 and S12). For example, DCIS in ROI1 demonstrated sustained expression of HMGCS2 (R 2 = 0.79, P = 0.003: path-based) and TFF1 (R 2 = 0.82, P = 0.002: path-based), which was lost in the interconnected IDC volume ( Fig. 3D ). Additionally, DCIS in ROI2 demonstrated strong expression of PLAT that significantly decreased at the site of MI ( Fig. 3E ). Both TFF1 and PLAT may play a role in maintaining epithelial integrity, potentially limiting neoplastic cell migration and invasiveness ( 14 – 18 ). HMGCS2 facilitates ketogenesis, enabling the production of lipid-derived energy ( 19 ), possibly enhancing precancerous cells' survival under hypoxic conditions often present in DCIS regions ( 20 ). In IDC, we observed upregulation of two genes involved in cell proliferation, TCIM (FC = 0.60: morphology-based on Xenium; ref. 21 ) and MKI67 (FC = 0.47: morphology-based on Xenium), in ROI1, and angiogenic factor VEGFA (R 2 = 0.74, P ≤ 0.001; path-based; ref. 22 ) in ROI2 ( Fig. 3D and E ). TCIM , acting through the activation of Wnt/β-catenin pathway ( 21 ), may play a role in inducing invasive cancer cell proliferation marked by MKI67 . Figure 3. 3D DCIS-to-IDC transition in breast cancer. In HT891Z1, we analyzed two ROIs, ROI1 and ROI2, that capture the transition from a normal gland, through HGPIN, to GP3 morphology (Supplementary Mov. S17 and S18). In HT891Z1 ROI1, the transition showed distinct differences in gene expression along the normal–HGPIN–GP3 axis ( Fig. 4C ). In less invasive and normal regions, we observed higher expression of FAS (R 2 = 0.53, P = 0.026; path-based). FAS , encoding the Fas cell surface death receptor that promotes apoptosis via the formation of the death-inducing signaling complex, initiates a cascade of caspases, culminating in programmed cell death ( Fig. 4D and E ; refs. 35 , 36 ). Conversely, along the normal to GP3 transition, we observed upregulation of GDF15 (R 2 = 0.68, P = 0.006; path-based) and MYC (R 2 = 0.58, P = 0.016, path-based) , whose expression also goes up as breast cancer progresses ( Fig. 4E ). GDF15 , a member of the TGF-β superfamily, has been implicated in bone metastasis and progression to castration-resistant prostate cancer ( 37 ) but not in earlier stages of prostate cancer. Notably, in section Z290 of ROI1, we observed a striking dichotomy between normal and HGPIN expression patterns on the same section. On the right side of the gland, FAS was detected, whereas the left side exhibited elevated expressions of MYC and GDF15 . SERPINA3 has been implicated in a variety of processes, including mediating apoptosis, autophagy, and aerobic glycolysis, thereby affecting cell survival and metabolic pathways ( 39 ). Additionally, in melanoma, high SERPINA3 expression has been associated with extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling, increased invasion, metastasis, and poorer overall survival, suggesting a similar proinvasive role ( 40 ). Finally, we identified pathways shared across multiple ROIs that may help to drive the normal-to-GP3 transition ( Fig. 4F ; Supplementary Fig. S4 and S5C). Impact of the TME on Malignant Transition in Breast and Prostate Cancers In addition to epithelial cell markers, we explored changes in the TME that might facilitate the transition from normal to more invasive epithelial cells. We identified two TME cell types potentially involved in this transition: tumor-associated macrophages (TAM) and cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAF). Using our 2D automated gene discovery workflow ( Fig. 5A ), we identified two markers, SPP1 and MS4A6A , that distinguish TAM populations across different morphologic regions in non-TNBC breast cancer ( Fig. 5B ). In HT704B1 ROI1, we analyzed the expression of SPP1 and MS4A6A throughout the z-dimensional section stack, in which there is a clear association of MS4A6A + TAMs infiltrating DCIS regions, whereas SPP1 + TAMs are more prevalent within IDC regions ( Fig. 5C and D ; Supplementary Fig. S6A and S6B). Interestingly, only luminal cell-of-origin breast tumors displayed this relationship, whereas sections from basal tumors differed in that their SPP1 + and MS4A6A + TME expression was associated with noninvasive morphology. Similarly to TNBC, in prostate cancer, we observed localization of MS4A6A + TAMs with noninvasive morphology. To further evaluate this association in three dimensions, we performed an analysis using all Xenium sections from HT704B1. For each TAM, we computed the shortest 3D distance to the nearest epithelial region. We then quantified the basal-layer intensity score of the corresponding epithelial region as a measure of invasiveness. Across five of the six sections analyzed, SPP1 + TAMs were preferentially associated with more invasive epithelial regions characterized by lower basal-layer integrity scores, whereas MS4A6A + TAMs were more frequently localized near less invasive regions with higher basal-layer integrity scores (Supplementary Fig. S6C). In non-TNBC breast sections, we observed upregulation of key stromal genes around invasive regions— MFAP5 and ASPN —that contribute to tumor progression ( Fig. 5B and E ). MFAP5 , a fibroblast-secreted ECM glycoprotein, facilitates cancer cell invasion by remodeling the ECM and activating PI3K/AKT and TGF-β signaling pathways, which drive the EMT ( 54 – 56 ). The juxtaposition of these immune and stromal programs with transitioning epithelial cells suggests that malignant invasion arises from coordinated epithelial–microenvironmental interactions.
