Xen-Spat: An Analysis Pipeline for Imaging-Based Spatial Transcriptomic Data to Quantify Cellular Colocalization in the Tumor Microenvironment 1. Introduction  In recent years, spatial transcriptomics (ST) has emerged as a cutting-edge tool to measure RNA transcripts at single-cell resolution while maintaining their spatial context [ 1 ]. This allows us to visualize the gene expression patterns within cells of the tumor/stromal tissue and visualize distinct neighborhoods that make up the heterogeneous microenvironment [ 2 ]. Imaging-based platforms such as Xenium and CosMx now measure hundreds of transcripts in individual cells within intact tissue sections at subcellular resolution [ 3 ].  As with many new technologies, the ability to generate ST datasets has outpaced the ability to meaningfully analyze them. Several software packages have been developed in both the R and Python (v3.11) environments, including Seurat [ 4 ], Scanpy [ 5 ], Squidpy [ 6 ] and Giotto [ 7 ]. These packages include systematic pipelines including data pre-processing, normalization, data reduction, and clustering to analyze data at single-cell resolution and annotate individual cell types. Additional methods such as Cell2location [ 8 ], Ficture [ 9 ], and SMaSH [ 10 ] use gene expression and spatial data to generate fine-grained cell type labels in an automated fashion. Using these cell labels, downstream spatial data analyses can be performed, including cell–cell interactions between different cell types, cellular and immune niche analysis, spatial hotspot detection, spatially variable gene analysis, domain detection, and cell–cell communication [ 11 ]. Even as the number of options for analysis grows, users must piece together these pipelines to generate meaningful data that can be used to predict response or estimate potential biomarkers for patient stratification.  Tumor heterogeneity is a critical factor that impacts the development of cancer at both intertumoral and intratumoral levels. Tumor heterogeneity holds significant clinical relevance, as it affects crucial aspects of tumor initiation, disease progression, and treatment outcomes [ 12 ]. The tumor microenvironment (TME) is composed of mixed cell types, including tumor, stromal and immune cells, which communicate through complex ligand-receptor interactions [ 13 ]. The spatial relationships between multiple cell types within the tumor microenvironment can be quantified using several methods that include pairwise distance metrics [ 14 ], Pearson correlations [ 15 ], sliding window approaches [ 16 ] or graph-based approaches. To quantify the enrichment of a specific cell type in the tumor and its surrounding stromal tissue, niche analysis of ST data is a valuable tool. The objective of niche analysis is to identify spatially contiguous regions with a recurring multicellular composition that can be compared within and across samples. Methods using both cell-based and gene-based approaches have been utilized to identify niches [ 17 ].  In addition to niche analysis, spatial enrichment analysis can be performed more broadly, using the pairwise distance between specific cell types; defining an optimal distance from the tumor tissue or tumor cells helps us to understand the spatial colocalization between different cell types. Similarly, SpottedPy (v1.9.3) is a Python package (v3.11) designed to identify spatial hotspots and generate interaction maps within the tumor ecosystem [ 18 ]. Beyond just compiling and comparing analysis pipelines, here we present a new way of defining regions of interest in ST data. A hotspot is a region of tissue in which there is a high density of a specific cell type. Methods to identify spatial hotspots include k-means clustering, the box-counting method, and Delaunay triangulation [ 19 ]. Here, we compare different methods for defining a niche, compile these methods into a packaged pipeline, and demonstrate how these methods can be leveraged to address biological questions. In total, we are presenting a custom-built analysis pipeline to analyze spatial transcriptomics data to generate both single-cell analysis output, which can be combined with spatial data to estimate cell type colocalization using the Morisita index [ 20 ], spatial niches using BuildNicheAssay [ 21 ], cellular hotspot colocalization using geospatial analysis, and spatial enrichment analysis using pairwise distance to quantify tumor heterogeneity in the tumor microenvironment.  Although each of these approaches addresses one aspect of tissue organization, they are typically implemented in separate packages that differ in their inputs and in how cell types are labeled. Several gaps remain for users who wish to combine them. Tumor and stromal compartments are usually defined by pathologist annotation or a manually drawn region of interest, which is difficult to apply consistently across a cohort. Hotspot methods identify where a cell type is concentrated but do not quantify the area over which the hotspots of two cell types overlap. Finally, because proximity, niche and hotspot measurements are generated separately, it is difficult to follow a single observation from one measurement to the next. Xen-Spat addresses these gaps by assigning tumor and stromal niches automatically, quantifying pairwise hotspot overlap as an area, and reporting all measurements on a single set of uniform cell type labels.    2. Materials and Methods   2.1. Patient Tissue Samples  Fresh-frozen tissue samples (n = 6) from patients with primary breast cancer were obtained from Duke University Hospital. All six tumors were HER2-positive; four were estrogen receptor (ER) and progesterone receptor (PR) positive, one was ER low positive (10%) and PR negative, and one was ER and PR negative. Five tumors were grade 3, one was grade 2, and clinical stage ranged from IA to IIIA ( Table S1 ). Tissue was collected from patients identified in the medical oncology clinics at Duke University Medical Center, Durham, North Carolina, USA, under the tissue banking protocol given in the Institutional Review Board Statement. The tissue bank study population included patients undergoing ultrasound-guided or stereotactic-guided biopsies of mammographically and ultrasound-detected abnormalities at Duke University Breast Imaging Clinics. All six samples were core needle biopsies obtained before any treatment. Eligibility requirements for the study included age > 18 years, mammographically and ultrasound-detected abnormalities, and permission from the subject’s attending physician or radiologist. The tissue bank was open to all genders and racial and ethnic groups. The collected samples were sectioned at 5 µm thickness and mounted onto Xenium slides. The mRNAs in the tissue were profiled using a predesigned 280-gene Xenium Human Breast gene expression panel together with a 50-gene custom panel using the Xenium (10x Genomics, Pleasanton, CA, USA) In Situ platform ( Table S2 ). Processing steps were performed following manufacturer protocols by the Duke Molecular Genomics Core. The processed tissue sections were run on the 10x Xenium Analyzer (Xenium Onboard Instrument software version 1.9.2.0; Analysis software version 1.9.0.0).    2.2. Single Cell Analysis Pipeline for 10x Xenium RNA Data  An overview of the Xen-Spat pipeline is shown in  Figure 1 . The raw gene count matrix from the Xenium Onboard Analysis output was analyzed using the Scanpy pipeline (v1.9.3). The raw counts were converted to AnnData format, combining both single-cell and spatial data, and downstream analysis was performed. The single-cell analysis pipeline, including data filtering, normalization, dimension reduction, UMAP clustering, and cell type annotation, was performed using the Scanpy analysis package in a Python environment (v3.11). Transcripts with a quality score below 20 were excluded by the Xenium Onboard Analysis before generation of the count matrix. To retain the high-quality cells for further analysis, we filtered out the cells with ≤5 expressed genes and ≤ 10 transcripts. Cells with an unusually low or high number of detected genes were then removed, using the 2nd and 98th percentiles of the number of genes detected per cell as limits; the number of cells remaining after each filtering step is reported for each sample in  Table S3 . The filtered data were log-normalized, and all genes were used for further analysis. Principal component analysis was performed on the normalized data, and a neighborhood graph was constructed from the first 20 principal components using 10 neighbors. Leiden clustering was performed on this graph with a resolution of 0.25 for major cluster identification, and resolutions between 0.15 and 0.3 were used for subset clustering to maximize separation based on gene expression profiles. UMAP embeddings were computed from the same graph and were used for visualization only. Both the main cluster and the subset clusters were combined to generate uniform labeled cell type clusters. Integration of the six samples was evaluated separately and is described in the  Supplementary Materials .    Figure 1   Overview of the Xen-Spat pipeline. ( a ) Input data from the discovery cohort (six HER2+ breast cancer biopsies) and the independent validation cohort. ( b ) Quality filtering of the discovery cohort. ( c ) Two-tier cell type annotation performed on each sample separately: major clusters are annotated from differentially expressed and canonical marker genes, clusters with markers of more than one lineage are subset and reclustered, and the resulting labels are merged and mapped to a uniform set of cell types. Integration is optional and is described in the  Supplementary Materials . ( d ) All four spatial modules read the uniform label file. Modules are arranged from the regional to the cellular scale; for each, the spatial relationship measured, the scale and the main parameters are shown. The steps applied to each cohort are listed in  Table S9 . Created in BioRender. Crosby, E. (2026)  https://BioRender.com/afpa92i  (accessed on: 10 October 2026).                     2.3. Cell Type Annotation  Cell types were annotated in two tiers. First, major clusters (Leiden resolution 0.25) were annotated using the top 10 differentially expressed genes for each cluster, identified with the rank_genes_groups function (Wilcoxon rank-sum test), together with canonical marker genes for each cell type. Second, major clusters that contained marker genes of more than one lineage (T cell, mixed immune cell, lymphoid and myeloid clusters) were subsetted and reclustered at resolutions between 0.15 and 0.3 to resolve individual cell types. The major and subset cluster labels were then combined and mapped to a uniform set of cell type labels shared across all samples. The marker genes used for each label are listed in  Table S4 . The annotation workflow is illustrated for sample 046 in  Figure 2 . The metadata file containing cell coordinates and the cell type labels, along with cell ID and other details, was saved as the uniform labeled metadata file (CSV format) and used to perform all the spatial analysis. The detailed cell type labels and their uniform labels are shown in  Table S5 . For the validation cohort, the cell type labels released with that dataset were used without reannotation. Those labels are specific to each section, and the cells counted as tumor cells are those carrying the tumor label specific to each section concerned: tumor cells together with proliferative tumor cells in S1_TOP and S4_TOP, and epithelial and tumor cells in S3_TOP, where the released annotation does not separate carcinoma from benign epithelium. The tumor compartment of S3_TOP should therefore be read as an epithelial compartment that contains the carcinoma rather than as carcinoma alone. S2_TOP, which is normal breast tissue, carries no tumor label of any kind, so no tumor compartment is defined for it, and this serves to demonstrate what the readout will look like with no tumor present.    Figure 2   Xen-Spat cell type annotation workflow for sample 046. ( a ) UMAP plot of Xenium single-cell data colored by cell types of major clusters. ( b ) UMAP plot of Xenium single-cell data colored by cell types of subset clusters selected from major clusters.  (c ) UMAP plot of Xenium single-cell data colored by cell types of combined clusters. ( d ) UMAP plot of Xenium single-cell data colored by cell types of uniform clusters. ( e ) Dot plot showing the key marker gene expression used to annotate the uniform cell types. The integrated data are shown in  Figure S10 .                     2.4. Conversion of AnnData Object to Seurat Object  To perform spatial niche analysis, we used the BuildNicheAssay function in Seurat (v5). In this paper, we used samples 097 and 100 as example data to perform both the single-cell and spatial analyses to generate the main figures. To perform the spatial niche analysis, the AnnData object from the Python environment needs to be integrated with the Seurat object. To achieve this, 10x Xenium output was loaded into the Seurat R environment using ReadXenium, and the spatial coordinates were integrated into the Seurat object. Using sctransform, the single-cell data were normalized and scaled, and the normalized gene count matrix was generated. Once the gene count matrix was generated, the usual single-cell analysis pipeline of dimension reduction, UMAP clustering, and cell type annotation was not followed. The cell type labels from the uniformly labeled metadata file generated from the Scanpy object were integrated into the Seurat object as Leiden clusters by matching the cell ID for the corresponding samples. Cell IDs that were filtered out during the Scanpy single-cell analysis process were labeled as not-assigned in the Seurat object and excluded from further analysis. The resulting Seurat object was used by the BuildNicheAssay function for further processing.    2.5. Terminology for Spatial Relationships  Throughout this manuscript, we use four terms to describe spatial relationships between cell types. Proximity refers to the measured distance between individual cells and is quantified in the distance-based enrichment analysis ( Section 2.10 ). Colocalization refers to the presence of two cell types in the same tissue region, either within the same quadrat (Morisita index,  Section 2.6 ) or within the same hotspot ( Section 2.8 ). Spatial overlap refers to the area of intersection between the hotspot contours of two cell types ( Section 2.8 ). For comparison between samples, it is expressed as a fraction of the smaller of the two hotspot areas. Interaction is reserved for functional communication between cells, such as direct contact or ligand-receptor signaling, which is not measured by any of the Xen-Spat modules. The spatial measures described here identify cell type pairs for which such interactions are plausible and can be tested by other methods.    2.6. Cell–Cell Spatial Proximity Analysis Using Morisita Index  Morisita proposed that the index of overlap between communities can be calculated as:   (1)      C  λ   =     2     ∑    i  =  1     s       x  i    y  i          λ  x  +    λ  y     XY         
where λ is Simpson’s index of diversity   (2)       λ    x    =        ∑   i  =  1    s        x    i          x    i    −  1      X    X  −  1            (3)       λ    y    =        ∑   i  =  1    s        y    i          y    i    −  1      Y    Y  −  1           To generate the Morisita overlap index across all samples, the image was divided into a 10 × 10 grid of equal quadrats (grid size of 10). Because the number of quadrats is fixed, the physical size of each quadrat depends on the dimensions of the tissue section and ranged from 604 to 966 µm in width and 291 to 651 µm in height in the discovery cohort ( Table S6 ). A grid size of 10 was chosen so that most quadrats contained enough cells of each type for Simpson’s index to be estimated reliably; finer grids produce many empty quadrats for less abundant cell types. The effect of grid size on the Morisita index is shown in  Figure S1 . A higher Morisita value indicates that the two cell types are distributed across the same quadrats. At this scale, the index measures colocalization at the level of tissue regions rather than contact between individual cells, which is assessed with the distance-based analysis ( Section 2.10 ). Multi-Cellular Neighborhood Niche Analysis  To estimate the distribution of the neighborhood niches of different cell types across the samples, we used the BuildNicheAssay function in Seurat (v5.0.0), which defines niches based on the cell type composition of each cell’s spatial neighborhood. For each cell, the neighborhood was defined as its 25 nearest neighboring cells (neighbors.k = 25), which corresponds to a median radius of 29 to 39 µm in these samples, and the neighborhood compositions were clustered by k-means into a number of niches equal to the number of unique cell types in the sample (niches.k). Niches for samples 097 and 100 are shown in  Figure 4 . To assign niches to the tumor or stromal compartment, we calculated the Dice coefficient between the cells of each niche and the tumor cells. The Dice coefficient was calculated from the cell-level labels as twice the number of tumor cells assigned to the niche divided by the sum of the number of tumor cells and the number of cells in the niche. Within each sample, the niche or niches above the largest gap between consecutive sorted Dice coefficients were assigned to the tumor compartment, and the remaining niches were combined to form the stromal compartment. Because the assignment depends on the gap within each sample rather than on a fixed value, no threshold needs to be set for a new dataset. The rule assumes that the Dice coefficients within a sample separate into two distinct groups. The pipeline therefore reports, for every sample, the Dice coefficient of each niche in rank order, the gap below each rank, the largest and second-largest gap, and the partition that the second-largest gap would have produced. We define the gap ratio as the size of the largest gap divided by the size of the second-largest gap. A large gap ratio indicates a distinct break between tumor-associated and stroma-associated niches, whereas a ratio near 1 indicates that the coefficients are distributed smoothly and that the position of the split is set by small differences between adjacent niches. In the six discovery biopsies, the gap ratio was 3.9 to 28.5. In the validation sections, which are whole resection faces rather than core biopsies and contain niches of intermediate tumor content, the ratio was 1.2 to 1.7. Taking the split at the second-largest gap instead of the first largest gap would move one or two niches between compartments ( Table S8, Figure S2 ). Where the gap ratio is near 1, we recommend reporting the Dice coefficient as a continuous measure of tumor association rather than converting it to a binary label, repeating the downstream comparison at the second-largest gap as a sensitivity check, or fixing a threshold in advance and stating it. A second check is independent of the gap ratio. If every niche in a section has a low Dice coefficient, which happens when the section contains little tumor, the largest gap can fall among small values and assign most niches to the tumor compartment although none of them overlaps the tumor substantially. In this case, the lowest coefficient above the split is also reported; across the sections analyzed here, it was 0.45 or higher. A section in which no cells are annotated as tumor cells, such as the normal breast tissue in S2_TOP (8 niches, 277,906 cells), admits no partition: with zero tumor-labeled cells, the Dice coefficient of every niche is 0.000 by construction, which is itself informative: uniformly zero coefficients indicate an absence of detectable tumor rather than a failure of the gap rule, and this case is excluded from the lowest-coefficient-above-the-split statistic reported above. Spatial Hotspot Detection Using Geospatial Analysis  To automatically identify regions of high-density cell clusters (hotspots) within the tissue of each sample, we used the geospatial analysis packages in R (v4.4.3), spatstat (v3.3-3), sp (v2.2-0), spdep (v1.4-2) and sf (v1.0-21). Hotspots were identified using the Getis-Ord Gi* statistic [ 22 , 23 ] in R. For the proof of concept, synthetic data were created, mimicking a cell type that is closely packed in the tissue and a cell type that is more dispersed, and these were combined into a single point pattern object using cell coordinates; the window size was estimated using the minimum and maximum x and y coordinate values from the synthetic data ( Figure S2a ). The spatial point pattern object created for each cell type was kernel-smoothed using the density function. Here we used a smoothing sigma value of 0.5 µm for all the cell types for uniform smoothing ( Figure S2b ). Because this bandwidth is smaller than a raster pixel, the smoothing step effectively assigns cell counts to the raster pixels. The intensity-smoothed image was converted into a raster image, and an sf point object was generated from a 128 × 128 raster with a single layer (the default). Because the raster has a fixed number of pixels, the physical size of each pixel depends on the dimensions of the tissue section and ranged from 47 to 75 µm in width and 23 to 51 µm in height in the discovery cohort ( Table S6 ). Using the coordinates from the sf point object, the spatial neighborhood was estimated using the knn2nb function with k = 8 as the number of neighbors. On a regular grid, the eight nearest neighbors of each pixel are the eight immediately adjacent pixels (queen contiguity), which is the conventional neighborhood definition for the Gi* statistic on gridded data [ 23 ]. The spatial weights were calculated using nb2listw, and the Gi* was calculated using the spatial neighborhood and the spatial weights. Hotspot Sensitivity Analysis  To cross-verify the hotspot region generated using the Getis-Ord Gi* statistic, we used the quadratcount function on the synthetic data point pattern object. The quadratcount function divides the spatial point pattern object into windows of a defined size and counts the number of data points in each window. For visualization purposes, we generated count data for the synthetic data using a downscaled window size of 32 × 32 ( Figure S4i ) instead of the original 128 × 128 sf point object generated above, compared this with the Gi* z-score output plot ( Figure S4j ), and mapped the hotspot region onto the quadrat count output data ( Figure S4k ). The contour-covered (red) hotspot regions mapped onto the quadrat count output correspond to regions of high cell counts relative to the remainder of the field.  To understand the effect of adjusting the number of spatial neighbors k on the hotspot count and changes in the spatial overlap intersection area of the contours generated for different cell types, we adjusted k in steps of 2^n, where n varies from 1 to 6. Major cell types, including tumor cells, B cells, fibroblasts, and T cells, were analyzed in sample 097 to estimate the change in hotspot number with varying k. The changes in the spatial overlap intersection area between tumor cells and T cells are shown ( Figure S4l –q). To estimate the changes in spatial overlap area, we kept k = 8 for tumor cells and adjusted k for the other cell types listed above. The number of hotspots was high at low k values and reached an approximate plateau when the k value exceeded 16 ( Figure S4r ).    2.10. Estimation of Cell Type Enrichment for Integrated Data  Distances between cells were calculated within each sample. For every cell, the Euclidean distance from its centroid to the centroid of the nearest tumor cell was calculated, and cells were labeled near (less than 25 µm), margin (25 to 75 µm) or far (more than 75 µm). Cell type enrichment in each distance category was calculated separately for each sample. For this analysis and the comparison of macrophages below, cell type labels were taken from the integrated object described in the  Supplementary Materials , so that the same cell type categories were available in all six samples. Tumor cells were the three tumor clusters of the integrated object (GATA3, TACSTD2/HER2 and TOP2A); the cluster annotated as stroma was not included. To compare gene expression between macrophages near tumor cells and macrophages at the margin, transcript counts were summed across cells within each patient and distance category (pseudobulk), giving one near and one margin profile per patient. Differential expression was tested with PyDESeq2 (v0.5.4) using a design that included patient as a covariate, with Benjamini–Hochberg correction. Because transcripts from tumor cells can be assigned to adjacent cells during segmentation, we plotted the counts of epithelial transcripts ( EPCAM ,  KRT7 ,  KRT8 ,  KRT19 ,  CDH1 ,  GRHL2 ,  DSP ,  AR ,  ESR1 ,  ERBB2  and  VTCN1 ) per cell against distance to the nearest tumor cell, in macrophages and, as a non-phagocytic comparison, in fibroblasts. Genes with more than twofold higher mean expression in tumor cells than in macrophages located more than 50 µm from any tumor cell, in at least four of the six samples (72 genes;  Table S7 ), were considered susceptible to this spillover, and the differential expression analysis was repeated with these genes removed.     3. Results   3.1. Single-Cell Analysis Pipeline to Analyze Breast Cancer ST Data  Breast cancer is a complex disease with each tumor exhibiting significant cellular and molecular heterogeneity. Recent advances in ST analysis have opened the possibility to dissect distinct niches within each tumor to better understand the spatial context and immune landscape. Different analysis methods created for different spatial technologies are rapidly being developed. Here we present a pipeline combining multiple analysis methods for comprehensive characterization of 10x Xenium data using six HER2+ breast cancer biopsy samples ( Figure 1 ;  Table S1 ).  The spatial transcriptomics breast cancer samples were analyzed individually to fully capture the heterogeneity in the spatial distribution of different cell types across samples. All spatial analyses were performed on each sample separately, and cell type labels were harmonized across samples ( Table S5 ) so that the results could be compared across the cohort. Using Scanpy, we performed data filtering, normalization, dimension reduction, clustering and cell type annotation. After standard data preprocessing and quality control filtering, a range of 18,002–120,038 high-quality cells were retained for further analysis in each sample. At this stage, we performed graph-based clustering of data using the top 20 principal components. Clusters were visualized using uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP).  Annotation of cell types of the UMAP clusters is a critical step, often requiring multiple iterations of clustering at different resolutions to fully capture the true number of cell types. We began by annotating the major cell types in the individual samples using the differentially expressed transcripts that were segmented into the cell-pseudo boundary generated by the Xenium analyzer ( Figure 2 a). After this step, several major clusters still contained mixed marker genes for several different cell types, requiring further sub-clustering to achieve the resolution needed to identify clean clusters of individual cell types ( Figure 2 b). The gene panel was designed to target analysis of immune cells, so those were focused on for specific subset annotations. Subset analysis was performed across all samples on the myeloid cell, lymphoid cell, mixed immune cell, T cell, and macrophage clusters. The major and subset clusters were combined ( Figure 2 c) and uniformly labeled ( Figure 2 d) to compare the cell types across all the samples and to perform downstream spatial analysis; a dot plot shows the key marker genes used for annotation ( Figure 2 e). The cell types identified across all six samples include: Tumor cells (TUM), basal epithelial cells (BEC), endothelial cells (EC), fibroblasts (FB), adipocytes (AC), myoepithelial cells (MEC), macrophages (MP), dendritic cells (DC), CD8 T cells (CD8), T cells (TC), Tregs (TR), NK cells (NK), B cells (BC), and mast cells (MC). For easier identification, uniformly labeled cell types are shown in consistent colors throughout the manuscript. Not all cell types were present in all samples, as is expected given the heterogeneity of the samples. Some cell types were present across all the samples (TUM (32.31% ± 11.27), MP (16.05% ± 8.79), FB (15.11% ± 11.52) and EC (7.83% ± 3.06) while immune cell types were especially variable. This is demonstrated by the distribution and number of each different cell type in each sample, as shown in the UMAP clustering data from all biopsies ( Figures S5–S9 ).  We also evaluated integration of the six biopsies into a single object. Integration is not required for any of the spatial analyses in Xen-Spat, each of which operates within a single tissue section, and mixing between samples after integration was limited, as expected for tumors from different patients. The integration procedure and its assessment are therefore described in the  Supplementary Materials (Figure S10 ), and all results that follow were generated from the individual samples, with the exception of the distance-based enrichment analysis ( Section 3.5 ), which used the cell type labels assigned in the integrated object so that the same categories were available in every sample.    3.2. Estimating Cell Type Colocalization in the Tumor Microenvironment  Once cell types are accurately assigned, the spatial relationships between different cell types can be assessed. To quantitatively measure the spatial proximity between different cell types as a metric to assess their potential for interaction, we utilized a method borrowed from geospatial analysis. The spatial distribution of individual organisms in ecology, whether clustered, dispersed, or random, can be analyzed using spatial point pattern analysis. Spatial point pattern methods usually use quadrat-based counting methods, distance-based methods and density-based methods to measure spatial distribution [ 20 ]. Here we used the Morisita index, which measures the spatial colocalization between pairs of cell types present in the tumor microenvironment. The Morisita index is a quadrat-based method to measure the spatial distribution of different cell types in each sample. To calculate the Morisita index of the spatially colocalized paired cell types, we used the spatial coordinates and the cell type labels previously defined in the uniformly labeled metadata file. Note that the Morisita index does not incorporate ligand-receptor information. Here we focus on two of the samples, 097 with a high amount of T cell infiltration and 100 with low T cell infiltration. These samples demonstrate the range in immune infiltration and showcase how the Morisita index can be used to direct downstream analysis by identifying cell types that occupy the same regions of the tissue. The Morisita index value varies from 0 to 1, with 0 indicating no colocalization and 1 indicating strong spatial colocalization of the cell types ( Figure 3 a,b). Quadrat maps were generated using a grid size of 10, which partitions the whole image into a 10 × 10 grid and estimates the Morisita index between each pair of cell types, showing the areas of low (yellow) and high colocalization (red). Dendritic cells versus T cells in sample 097 showed a large area of colocalization across the sample, reflected in a high Morisita value of 0.96. In sample 100, tumor cells and macrophages were in close proximity, highlighted by the dark red quadrats in the quadrat map, with a Morisita value of 0.81 ( Figure 3 c,d). Projection of selected cell types based on Morisita values back onto the tissue confirms the spatial proximity predicted by this metric ( Figure 3 e,f). Similar analyses for the remaining four samples are also shown, highlighting the diversity of patterns observed in different samples ( Figures S11 and S12 ). As the Morisita index also depends on the abundance of each cell type, raw values indicate relative colocalization within a sample and should not be compared directly between cell type pairs of very different abundance or between samples; the values quoted above for samples 097 and 100 are therefore illustrative. Because the Morisita index is calculated on a square grid, the resulting value is sensitive to grid size. To assess the effect of grid size on the estimated Morisita values, we increased the grid size in steps of 10; the resulting values are shown in  Figure S1 . One drawback to this method is that cell types with small frequencies can have artificially inflated metrics when they are in close proximity to another cell type and widely distributed across the sample. This is in contrast to cell types that are highly colocalized within only small regions of the sample, which is reflected in a low Morisita score.    3.3. Automated Identification of Multi-Cellular Enriched Niches  In addition to pairwise measurement of cell distance, cell types can be projected back into their spatial context, allowing for the assessment of cellular niches ( Figure 4 a,d). Here, we again highlight a sample with high immune infiltration and a sample with low immune infiltration in the main text to demonstrate the spectrum and its impact on the analyses. To quantify the spatial distribution of the different cell type niches and the cell types that share them, we performed neighborhood niches analysis using the BuildNicheAssay function in Seurat ( Figure 4 b,e). The size of each niche and the total number of niches were dependent on the number of cells and distinct cell types in a particular sample. The cell composition and proportion for each niche are shown, demonstrating that some niches had a clear predominant cell type and others were more mixed ( Figure 4 c,f). In the highly immune-infiltrated sample 097, B cells and T cells were present in every niche, indicative of the widespread immune infiltration throughout the tissue ( Figure 4 c). In sample 100, several niches were composed predominantly of a single cell type, including Niche 3 (fibroblasts), Niche 9 (basal epithelial cells), Niche 6 (endothelial cells), and Niche 10 (adipocytes) ( Figure 4 f). Niche plots are a useful, quantifiable way to quickly identify different patterns of immune infiltration across samples/patients ( Figures S13 and S14 ).  Of particular interest is the automated identification of niches that significantly overlap the tumor region, which allows the distribution of immune and other cell types to be quantified separately in the tumor vicinity and in the stroma. To do this, we identified the tumor cells ( Figure 4 g,j), spatially overlaid each niche in turn onto the tumor cells, and estimated the Dice coefficient for each niche. In every sample, a single niche had a Dice coefficient well above all others (0.60 to 0.83, compared with 0.22 or lower for all other niches) and was labeled the tumor niche; the remaining niches were labeled stromal niches ( Figure S2 ). We also visually confirmed that the tumor niche overlapped well with the tumor cells. The Dice coefficients for every niche in all six samples are given in  Table S8 . Examples of tumor and stromal niches are shown ( Figure 4 h,k;  Figures S13 and S14 ). This allows for the binning of niches as tumor or not for the evaluation of the composition and gene expression of these niches within and across samples ( Figure 4 i,l). This is a particularly valuable aspect of the pipeline for tissues that do not have a clearly defined structure or tumor margin, or for samples that have not been carefully annotated by a pathologist. Automated niche assignment is intended as a reproducible alternative when pathologist annotation is unavailable or impractical at the scale of a cohort, rather than a replacement for it, and comparison with blinded pathologist annotation is a direction for future validation. Assessing tumor-prevalent niches leverages the spatial component without relying on clear biologic structures or manual annotation to define the region of interest.    3.4. Hotspot Detection Using Geospatial Analysis  While niche analysis provides an unbiased way of dividing the sample into distinct neighborhoods, it does not directly measure hotspots within individual cell types or the spatial overlap of hotspots between specific cell types of interest. To address this, we created a pipeline that borrows from geospatial analysis to label areas of high cell density for individual cell types, termed hotspots. Hotspots represent regions of tissue where cells are highly clustered together. Here we used the Getis-Ord Gi* statistic to identify regions of high-density cell clusters against a null hypothesis of random distribution. The z-scores and  p  values generated by comparing the distribution of cell types against a uniformly spaced spatial grid allow us to identify statistically significant hotspots and cold spots. Hotspots and cold spots identified using this method represent regions of high and low cell concentration, respectively, and are not attributable to chance. Once we have identified the hotspot regions of individual cell types, we can determine the regions of spatial colocalization between different cell types. We designed this automated pipeline using tools available in the geospatial analysis toolbox. Tools from the R packages spatstat and sp were used to generate the contour plot needed to outline the hotspot and the spatial colocalization regions. First, the x and y coordinates were converted into spatial point pattern objects (PPO) for tumor cells and T cells from sample 097 ( Figure 5 a,e). Next, the Getis-Ord Gi* method was applied to the PPO, and significant hotspots were determined for each cell type ( Figure 5 b,f). A contour plot was created based on the Getis-Ord Gi* statistic using the contourLines function in the sp package ( Figure 5 c,g). Finally, a contour cutoff was selected to define hotspot regions. This procedure was repeated for all cell types in each sample ( Figures S15 and S16 ). Using the selected contour area, cell type pairs (e.g., tumor cells vs. T cells or CD8 T cells) were chosen, and their corresponding subset contour plots ( Figure 5 d,h) were superimposed on each other to identify the regions of spatial colocalization ( Figure 5 i–k). In the overlap plot, the regions of spatial colocalization are highlighted in yellow ( Figure 5 k). The bar plot can be used to summarize the hotspot area of tumor cells and T cells individually in the tissue as well as the spatial colocalization area ( Figure 5 l). To demonstrate the utility in a sample with low total immune infiltration, similar analysis was performed on sample 100 ( Figure 5 m–x). Here we see that there is a relatively small population of CD8 T cells; however, 67% of the CD8 T cell hotspot area (4.56 of 6.80 mm 2 ) overlapped with a tumor cell hotspot (total tumor cell hotspot area, 7.76 mm 2 ). This is consistent with what we show in  Figure 3 , where CD8 T cells and tumor cells show close spatial proximity. Overall, this new tool allows for a quantifiable way to compare the overlap of two specific cell types across tissue sections. This pipeline can automatically identify both hotspot areas for a single cell type and areas of meaningful colocalization between different cell types of interest in an unbiased manner. Distance-Based Cell Type Enrichment Analysis  Here we have manually defined the spatial distance between the different cell types ( Figure 6 a,b). Three distinct regions were isolated: cells at a distance of <25 µm from the tumor cells were defined as near cells, cells between 25 µm and 75 µm as margin cells, and cells > 75 µm away as far cells ( Figure 6 c,d). These distances were chosen based on near (<25 µm) being approximately one to two cell diameters, a distance at which contact-dependent or short-range paracrine interaction between two cells is plausible [ 24 ]. We measured the cell type enrichment in terms of percentage of cells at each distance relative to the total count of the corresponding cell type across all six samples ( Figure 6 e). We then calculated the fold change for each cell type near tumor cells compared to the margin, focusing on immune cells to define the immune microenvironment around tumor cells ( Figure 6 f). We observed that some cell types, like Tregs and B cells, have distinct patterns across samples, with a subset of patients enriched in the margin and the other enriched near tumor cells. Application of Xen-Spat Analysis Pipeline on Independent Cohort  To validate the feasibility of applying the Xen-Spat analysis pipeline to an independent dataset, we ran our pipeline on a publicly available Xenium dataset [ 26 ]. This is a breast cancer dataset that used Xenium in situ technology on 12 FFPE human breast tissue sections (8 ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS), 3 invasive ductal carcinoma and 1 normal breast) obtained from commercial biobanks, using a 280-gene custom panel, with paired H&E images. Specimen type and treatment history are not reported for these samples. Of the sections analyzed here, S1_TOP is DCIS with normal-adjacent regions, S1_BOTTOM is comedo-type DCIS, S2_TOP is normal breast tissue, and S3_TOP consists predominantly of columnar cell hyperplasia and usual ductal hyperplasia with a DCIS component [ 26 ]; S4_TOP is listed as invasive ductal carcinoma in the sample annotations released with the dataset. Pathologist annotations of the H&E images for different tissue regions are shown in  Figure 7 a. The different regions include normal duct, dilated ducts, ductal hyperplasia, solid DCIS, DCIS-comedo, and tumor region with immune infiltrates. The Xenium data included the cell type labels that were generated by the original authors for all the samples. Because these published labels were used without reannotation, the quality filtering and annotation steps of Xen-Spat were not applied to this cohort ( Table S9 ). Here we used the Xenium output files and the annotated cell type files to run Xen-Spat on one of their samples (S1_TOP). First, we calculated the Morisita index between the different cell types identified in this sample ( Figure 7 b). The analysis output shows that the macrophages and T lymphocytes are highly colocalized. Next, we performed the niche analysis using the 11 different cell types identified and the 25 nearest neighbors of each cell to generate different niches ( Figure 7 c). The cell type composition of each niche is shown in  Figure 7 d. The niche analysis output shows several different regions with distinct niches characterized by the distribution of different cell types. Next, we applied hotspot detection to measure the area of colocalization between proliferative tumor cells and T cells ( Figure 7 e–g). We included quantification of the area of overlap, which demonstrates very little spatial overlap between T cells and tumor cells in this sample ( Figure 7 h). The original paper describing this dataset (sample: S1_Bottom) reported differential expression of  MMP11  within different ducts, positing that MMP11 could be a biomarker for tumor invasiveness. Because the validation sections gave the lowest gap ratios of any sections analyzed (1.3 to 1.7;  Figure S2 ), we asked what the compartment boundary chosen in each of them corresponds to in the published annotation. In S1_TOP, the tumor compartment comprises two niches with Dice coefficients of 0.75 and 0.46 and contains 41.9% of the cells in the section; 93.7% of those cells carry a tumor label, and the compartment captures 92.6% of all tumor-labeled cells. The partition given by the second-largest gap retains only the higher-scoring niche and is marginally purer (96.5%) but captures only 61.8% of all tumor-labeled cells, so the selected partition is the better description. The two niches differ in composition: the first is 89.9% tumor cells and the second 58.6% proliferative tumor cells and 29.9% tumor cells ( Figure S3a ), so the niche added by the larger gap is a proliferative tumor niche rather than stroma.  In S3_TOP and S4_TOP, the comparison is less favorable to the selected partition. There, the rule assigns a single niche to the tumor compartment, giving purities of 91.3% and 89.5% but capturing only 66.0% and 48.5% of the tumor-labeled cells, whereas the partition at the second-largest gap captures 94.0% and 92.8% at purities near 68% ( Figure S3b ). Across the three sections, the two candidate partitions result in a tradeoff between capturing more of the tumor compared to capturing a more pure tumor compartment, and the largest-gap rule consistently selects the higher-purity option. This is the practical consequence of a gap ratio near 1, and it is the reason we recommend reporting the Dice coefficient as a continuous score, or repeating the downstream comparison at the second-largest gap, when the ratio is low ( Section 2.7 ).     4. Discussion  The use of spatial transcriptomic data at single-cell resolution offers a powerful lens through which to examine the tumor microenvironment. In this study, we developed and applied a comprehensive pipeline to analyze 10x Xenium data from HER2+ breast cancer biopsies, enabling the identification of distinct cellular niches and patterns of cell type colocalization. We have packaged this workflow with detailed documentation on GitHub.  One of the central challenges in ST analysis is deciding whether to integrate samples or analyze them independently. Kumar et al. constructed a comprehensive Human Breast Cell Atlas by integrating all samples at single-cell resolution to create a normal breast tissue, cell type, and cell state atlas [ 27 ]. We demonstrate that both approaches have advantages and disadvantages. While integration facilitates cross-sample comparisons, it may obscure biologically relevant heterogeneity. In contrast, individual analysis may preclude the identification of patterns shared across patients in a cohort. In Xen-Spat, integration is optional. Each spatial module operates within a single tissue section, and comparison across samples relies on a harmonized set of cell type labels rather than a shared expression space. In our cohort, integration of six biopsies from different patients resulted in limited mixing, and clusters in the integrated object were partly driven by the patient of origin. Subclustering an integrated object can be an efficient way to identify minor populations shared across patients when integration performs well, whereas a population present in only one patient is more reliably resolved in that patient’s own data.  Cell type annotation remains a critical and iterative step in spatial transcriptomic analysis. Despite the use of canonical marker genes and differential gene expression profiling, several clusters required sub-clustering to resolve mixed cell populations. This highlights the limitations of current clustering algorithms and the need for refined resolution strategies, particularly in heterogeneous tissues like breast tumors. Newer methods, including the additional cell segmentation cocktail available with the Xenium workflow, will improve this process. The variability in immune cell infiltration across samples further underscores the importance of accurate annotation. For example, the consistent presence of tumor cells and macrophages across all samples contrasted with the sporadic appearance of T cells and dendritic cells, highlighting the differential immune engagement that may have implications for prognosis and therapy. Throughout the manuscript, we have compared each analysis tool with a highly immune-infiltrated and a low immune-infiltrated sample to demonstrate this point.  To quantify cell–cell interactions, Salié et al. performed permutation test-based interaction analysis at the single-cell level on immune cell subset populations in distinct immune neighborhoods to predict the interaction between different cell types enriched in different neighborhoods [ 28 ]. Hickey et al. used a grid-based approach in CODEX multiplex images to generate distinct cellular neighborhoods (CNs) in tumor tissue, with specific groups of cell types enriched in different CNs [ 16 ]. Co-correlation analysis between cell types in these distinct neighborhoods predicted the cell–cell interactions. Here, we used a Morisita index-based approach to quantify cell type colocalization without ligand-receptor information. This method allowed us to assess the co-distribution of cell types within each sample and to compare these patterns across samples.  The Morisita index and the hotspot analysis both summarize cell positions on a grid, whereas the distance-based enrichment analysis uses the coordinates of individual cells. Coordinate-based methods such as Ripley’s cross-K function [ 29 ], the pair correlation function [ 30 ] and neighborhood enrichment tests [ 6 , 31 ] avoid an arbitrary partition of the tissue and express colocalization as a function of distance, which makes the spatial scale explicit. However, they require edge correction and inhomogeneous null models [ 32 ] in tissues with irregular boundaries, and they are more sensitive to small errors in cell position. Grid-based methods are computationally simple, produce a map of where colocalization occurs, and tolerate positional error at the scale of cell segmentation, but their results depend on the size and placement of the grid, a limitation known as the modifiable areal unit problem [ 33 ]. For this reason, we report the physical size of each grid ( Table S6 ) and use the Morisita index as a regional screen, with the distance-based analysis providing the cell-scale measurement. Because the Getis-Ord Gi* statistic can be calculated for any set of spatial units, the hotspot analysis could also be extended to three dimensions using voxels from serial sections.  Our geospatial hotspot analysis provided a framework for identifying regions of high-density cellular colocalization. By adapting ecological spatial point pattern methods, we were able to delineate high-density regions using the Getis-Ord Gi* statistic and quantify overlap between key cell types, such as tumor cells and CD8 T cells. This approach offers a scalable and unbiased method to assess spatial relationships and may be particularly useful in identifying immune exclusion zones or regions of active immune surveillance. This differs from the hotspot analysis implemented in SpottedPy, which operates on Visium spot data at approximately 55 µm resolution, where a single spot may contain on the order of ten cells of different types. Xen-Spat instead operates on cell type labels at single-cell resolution, so hotspots are defined for individual cell types rather than for spots grouped into epithelial (EPI) and epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) categories. This resolution allows the spatial overlap between any pair of cell types to be quantified directly, both as the area of intersection and as the number of separate regions in which that overlap occurs, and it distinguishes T cells lying within the tumor mass from those immediately adjacent to it. This work provides an analysis roadmap for users to employ while pointing out critical decision points. This packaged workflow and associated datasets provide an illustrative demonstration of the range of immune infiltration into tumors and a variety of ways to quantify and compare these differences. Together, these analyses underscore the value of integrating spatial, single-cell, and geospatial methodologies to unravel the complexity of the TME and guide future therapeutic strategies.  Xen-Spat contains some established components, and we make no claim that these individual pieces are new. Its contribution is the combination, and three capabilities in particular are, to our knowledge, not available together in an existing package. First, the tumor and stromal compartments are defined automatically. Rather than requiring a pathologist-annotated tumor margin or a manually drawn region of interest, Xen-Spat overlays each niche on the tumor cell mask in turn and assigns it by Dice coefficient, so that compartment-resolved composition and differential expression can be obtained for tissues with no clear architecture and for cohorts too large to annotate by hand. Second, hotspot colocalization is quantified as an area rather than as a distance. Getis-Ord Gi* contours are computed for each cell type at single-cell resolution and intersected pairwise, returning both the area of overlap and the number of distinct regions in which that overlap occurs for any pair of cell types the user selects. Third, all four modules read from a single uniform cell-label object, so proximity, niche membership, hotspot overlap and distance-binned expression are reported on the same cell type vocabulary and are directly comparable within a sample and across a cohort. In practice, this is what allows a pattern first seen in the Morisita index to be followed through to a niche, to a hotspot overlap area, and finally to differential expression in the cells concerned, as we have done here for macrophages and tumor cells.  The automatic definition of the tumor and stromal compartments depends on the Dice coefficients forming two separable groups within a sample, and the application of this rule in highly heterogeneous tissue deserves additional comment. In the six core biopsies analyzed here, the break was unambiguous, with the largest gap between consecutive sorted coefficients 3.9 to 28.5 times the next largest. The whole resection faces of the validation cohort gave ratios between 1.2 and 1.7, because those sections contain niches of intermediate tumor content, and in each of them a split taken at the second-largest gap would move one or two niches between compartments ( Figure S2 ). This is the expected behavior in diffusely infiltrative or heavily admixed tissue, where tumor and stroma interdigitate below the scale of a niche and tumor content varies continuously across niches rather than dividing into two groups. In that type of sample, the split is also sensitive to the segmentation and to the number of niches requested. A second failure mode is independent of the gap ratio: when every niche has a low Dice coefficient, as in a section that contains little tumor, the largest gap can fall among small values and place most niches in the tumor compartment although none of them overlaps the tumor substantially. The lowest coefficient above the split should therefore be inspected alongside the gap ratio; across the sections analyzed here it was 0.45 or higher. The two cohorts here also differ in what the assignment is used for. In the discovery biopsies, where the gap ratio was 3.9 or greater in every sample, the compartments carry the comparisons of cell type composition and gene expression between tumor and stromal niches ( Figure 4 i,l;  Figures S13 and S14 ). In the validation sections, the compartment assignment is reported to show that the rule transfers to data labeled by other investigators, and none of the results described in  Section 3.6  depend on it, so the weaker separation in those sections does not affect any conclusion drawn from them. More generally, the pipeline reports the gap profile for every sample, and we recommend inspecting it before accepting a binary assignment. Where the separation is weak, the Dice coefficient remains informative as a graded score of tumor association; downstream comparisons should be repeated at the second-largest gap as a sensitivity check, and an independent anchor such as a pathologist outline of the tumor bed on the matched section is valuable if available. A section containing no tumor cells, such as the normal breast tissue in S2_TOP (8 niches, 277,906 cells), has no tumor compartment to define: every niche’s Dice coefficient is 0.000 in this case, which is itself diagnostic: a sample in which every niche scores zero is not missing a partition; it is signaling the absence of tumor, and it is excluded from this step rather than forced into a partition.  Xen-Spat is distributed as a documented workflow with worked examples rather than as a single installable package, and it spans the Python and R environments rather than unifying them. Its proximity and colocalization metrics screen for candidate interactions on the basis of spatial arrangement; they do not establish ligand-receptor signaling, and they are complementary to, rather than a replacement for, communication-focused methods. Finally, it has been demonstrated only on imaging-based platforms at single-cell resolution in breast tissue; application to spot-based platforms such as Visium would require aggregation choices the pipeline does not currently make.  Finally, we have applied this pipeline directly to an independent, publicly available dataset confirming its functionality. We were also able to verify biologic findings described in the original manuscript using independent niche analysis methods. The verification further serves to highlight the power of this technology to identify transcriptional differences in regions that were indistinguishable by a pathologist. This is particularly meaningful as we study DCIS and endeavor to better understand and predict which lesions will progress to invasive disease and which will remain indolent. The application of these types of spatial technologies and analysis pipelines like the one we have created could provide critical insights into the biology of disease.    5. Conclusions  Xen-Spat provides a sequential route from single-cell annotation of imaging-based spatial transcriptomic data to four quantitative descriptions of tissue organization: regional colocalization by the Morisita index, multicellular niches, geospatial hotspots and their pairwise overlap, and distance-binned cell type enrichment with the associated differential expression. Applied to six HER2+ breast cancer biopsies and to four samples from an independent Xenium cohort, it recovered the expected range of immune infiltration, separated tumor from stromal compartments without manual annotation, and reproduced a previously reported difference in  MMP11  expression between spatial niches. The workflow, its parameter sensitivity analyses and worked examples are available on GitHub. We anticipate that the automated compartment assignment and the hotspot overlap module will be the most transferable to other tumor types and to larger cohorts. DeSpaST: deconvoluting spatial transcriptomics signals to cell-level resolution using histology images. Advances in spatial transcriptomics (ST) technologies enable spatially resolved gene expression profiling, yet most platforms remain limited to spot-level resolution, where each measurement aggregates signals from multiple cells and obscures cell-specific programs and microenvironmental interactions. Existing computational approaches either provide limited sub-spot refinement or rely on matched single-cell RNA sequencing references that are costly and difficult to obtain. Here, we present DeSpaST (Deconvoluting Spatial Transcriptomics Signals to Cell-Level Resolution Using Histology Images), a dynamic edge-conditioned graph convolutional network that deconvolves spot-level ST data into cell-level gene expression profiles using only paired histology images. DeSpaST extracts nucleus-level morphological features, constructs directed cellular interaction graphs, and integrates spatial and transcriptional information through message passing. Validated across four cancer datasets with orthogonal Xenium, immunofluorescence, ablation, and interslice evaluations, DeSpaST enhances spatial resolution, facilitates downstream cellular-level analyses, and provides deeper insights into tissue biology. Background  Spatial transcriptomics (ST) technologies have made significant progress in transitioning transcriptomic research from the cell level to a 2D spatial cell system. This transition is crucial for investigating cell–cell communication, tissue heterogeneity, and the tumor microenvironment, offering new insights into intricate biological processes. In contrast to single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq), which requires tissue dissociation, ST technologies profile gene expression and preserve the spatial composition of cells within the native tissue environment [ 1 ]. ST technologies (e.g. 10× Genomics Visium [ 2 ], Nanostring GeoMx DSP [ 3 ], HDST [ 4 ], and Slide-seq [ 5 ]) utilize unique spatial barcodes to label the spatial locations and capture the gene expression at thousands of barcoded spatial locations (referred to as spots) within one experiment [ 6 ]. While these methods achieve high detection efficiency, their spatial resolution is inherently limited. The barcoded spot area (Spot diameter: 10× Genomics Visium: 55 μm, Nanostring GeoMx DSP: 10 μm [ 7 ], and Slide-seq: 10 μm [ 8 ]) encompasses a diverse population of cells, ranging from a few cells up to 200 cells [ 9 ]. To accurately distinguish the mixed-cell populations and uncover biological inferences from the ST data, it is essential to develop computational models that can enhance the resolution of ST data.  Several computational methods have been developed to improve the spatial resolution of ST data. Bayesian-based methods such as BayesSpace [ 10 ] refine gene expression to sub-spot resolution, only yielding modest improvement. Deep-learning-based approaches such as SPOTlight [ 11 ], Tangram [ 12 ], cell2location [ 13 ], and CARD [ 14 ] integrate ST data with scRNA-seq data, mapping related gene expression cells to ST coordinates or reconstructing the ST landscape from various cell combinations. However, the reliance on scRNA-seq data significantly raises the experimental costs and introduces constraints, including limited cell types and potential biases in spatial reconstruction accuracy.  Instead of relying on the scRNA-seq data, integrating histology images with ST data presents a more feasible and promising way to enhance ST resolution. Most ST platforms, such as Visium and HDST, typically provide corresponding histology images, like hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining images, which offer high-resolution morphological and spatial information for individual cells across the tissue sections. Deep-learning-based methods such as TESLA [ 15 ], XFuse [ 16 ], and iStar [ 17 ] have been developed to integrate the histology image with ST data to enhance ST resolution. However, these methods primarily enhance resolution at the pixel level but fall short of achieving cell-level gene expression resolution. Furthermore, these methods focus on extracting pixel level histological features [e.g. pixel intensities in red, green, blue (RGB) channels], neglecting true cell features and cell–cell interactions, which compromises model accuracy. A specialized model that directly incorporates actual cell-level features is necessary to improve the biological application of ST data.  Many fundamental biological questions—including the delineation of cell-type boundaries, characterization of the tumor microenvironment, and inference of cell–cell communication—inherently require cell-level resolution. However, true single-cell spatial assays such as Xenium or MERFISH remain expensive, limited in gene panel size, and not universally available, making spot-level ST the dominant modality in practice. Moreover, matched scRNA-seq data from the same tissue, which several existing deconvolution methods depend on, is not always obtainable and may introduce additional biases when tissue dissociation alters cell-type composition. A computational approach that can reliably infer cell-level expression directly from spot-level ST data and routine histology images therefore addresses a practical and widely encountered gap in the field.  In this work, we developed an innovative model called DeSpaST (Deconvoluting Spatial Transcriptomics Signals to Cell-Level Resolution Using Histology Images), which incorporates the cell level features from histology image with ST data using dynamic edge–conditioned graph convolution neural network ( Fig. 1 , and  Supplementary Fig. S1 ). Starting with a histology image, we perform cell segmentation and explicitly extract cell morphological and spatial interaction features, followed by constructing the cellular graphic interaction structures of the tissue. We then build a graph deconvolution model that combines ST data with these morphological features and interaction structures to deconvolute spot-level gene expression into cell-level gene expression profiles. In contrast to the previous methods that primarily rely on pixel-level information and use convolutional neural network (CNN)-like structures to encode the features, which often failing to capture cell–cell interaction information. DeSpaST leverages the graph convolutional networks (GCNs) to fully capture the cellular interaction topologies by constructing cellular interaction graphic structures. Unlike conventional CNNs, GCNs operate on non-Euclidean data structures, enabling comprehensive modeling of diverse cellular interaction topologies. DeSpaST offers several practical advantages. First, it does not require scRNA-seq references, reducing experimental cost and avoiding dependence on matched dissociated-cell datasets. Second, it leverages morphology and local tissue architecture to improve spatial localization and denoising within spots, which is particularly valuable in heterogeneous tumors where boundaries and niches vary over short distances. Third, DeSpaST’s inferred cell-level expression supports downstream analyses that are difficult at spot resolution, such as cell-type mapping at cellular granularity, spatial domain characterization, and trajectory inference. In our experiments, these advantages manifest as improved agreement with orthogonal measurements (e.g. Xenium), clearer spatial patterns, and improved recovery of spatial domains, with robustness supported by ablations demonstrating that performance depends on both transcriptional input and morphology rather than visual cues alone. Together, these considerations motivate DeSpaST as a practical and interpretable approach for cell-level resolution inference from spot-based ST, while clarifying the conditions under which it is most reliable.    Result   Overview of the DeSpaST model  DeSpaST requires only two inputs: a histology image and ST data ( Fig. 1a ). Histology images offer the individual cell spatial organization and morphology characterization, while the ST data provide gene expression at the spot level. To explicitly extract the cell spatial and organization characterizations from the histology image, we first employed the HD-staining deep-learning algorithm [ 18 ,  19 ] to segment and classify the cell nucleus from the tissue image. Alternatively, other methods for cell or nuclei segmentation could also be applied at this step. We then extracted the morphology features for each cell to construct the cellular graphic structures (see  Fig. 1a  and  Method  section for details). DeSpaST builds the graphic convolution networks by performing the four following steps: (i) extract image patches based on the spot coordinates in the ST data; (ii) construct a directed cellular graphic structure for each patch using nearest neighbors based on the Euclidean distance from a cell to its neighbors; and (iii) derive features from the directed cellular graphic structures to incorporate the spatial and morphology information of the cells into the graph convolutional network. Each node in the graph represents a cell. Node features include cell size, shape, and other morphological features. Edges denote spatial and morphological relationships between cells. Edge features include cell spatial proximity, cell connectivity angle, and interaction edge categorization ( Supplementary Fig. S2 ) [ 4 ]. The model is then constructed using two convolutional layers and one fully connected layer ( Supplementary Fig. S1 ). All cell nodes are updated through a message passing from all neighboring nodes in each convolutional layer, which incorporates both morphological and cell–cell spatial interaction features of neighboring cells. In this study, we demonstrate DeSpaST’s ability in accurately capturing cell-level gene expression to overcoming spatial resolution limitations in ST data, using breast, lung, and ovarian cancer datasets as examples. DeSpaST offers a new convenient tool for advancing biomedical research, with broad applicability to diverse spatial transcriptomics datasets.    DeSpaST effectively enhances gene expression resolution  To assess the efficacy of DeSpaST, we applied the model to a well-studied breast cancer 10× Visium dataset [ 20 ]. We then conducted a comparative analysis of DeSpaST’s performance against the TESLA model [ 15 ], which is a machine-learning framework designed to enhance gene expression to pixel-level resolution [ 15 ]. DeSpaST demonstrated notable advancements in elucidating gene expression patterns. To illustrate, we present two marker genes,  MS4A1  and  ERBB2 , as representative examples ( Fig. 1b ). The  MS4A1  gene encodes the surface molecule CD20, which serves as a widely recognized marker indicative of B-cell lineage [ 21 ].  ERBB2  encodes the human epidermal growth factor receptor-2 (HER2) protein [ 22 ], which is used as a tumor marker in breast cancer diagnosis [ 23 ,  24 ]. For each gene, the cell-level gene expression profile from DeSpaST, spot-level gene expression pattern from Visium ST data, and the pixel-level gene expression patterns from TESLA ( Fig. 1b ), iStar, and XFuse ( Supplementary Fig. S3a  and  b ) were plotted separately. Compared to Visium, TESLA, iStar, and XFuse, DeSpaST showed the gene expression profiles with highest clarity and precision for both genes, successfully enhancing the gene expression resolution. Notably, the gene expression patterns from DeSpaST correlated well with the pathologist-annotated regions. DeSpaST high  ERBB2  gene expression cells closely matched the pathologist-annotated tumor regions. Also, the DeSpaST high  MS4A1  expressed cells were well aligned with the annotated immune cell regions. In contrast, Visium, TESLA, iStar, and XFuse did not achieve the same level of visual clarity as DeSpaST in these regions. The  MS4A1  gene expression profile is particularly noteworthy because it is nearly imperceptible in the Visium ST data and in the reconstructions produced by TESLA ( Fig. 1b , right), iStar, and XFuse ( Supplementary Fig. S3b ), whereas DeSpaST accurately discerns the  MS4A1  gene expression pattern and immune cell regions.  Remarkably, DeSpaST’s cell-level gene expression predictions demonstrate its capability and reliability in distinguishing between different cell layers. In three specific areas ( Fig. 1c  and  d , and  Supplementary Fig. S4 ), pathologists meticulously annotated the invasive carcinoma and immune cell regions to delineate their boundaries in the H&E images. The gene expression patterns predicted by DeSpaST effectively differentiated between these immune cell and tumor cell regions. DeSpaST accurately captured the elevated expression of ERBB2 in tumor regions and the elevated expression of MS4A1 in immune cell regions. The distinct gene expression patterns of MS4A1 and ERBB2 predicted by DeSpaST ( Fig. 1c  and  d  ,  and  Supplementary Fig. S4b ) precisely delineated the tumor and immune boundaries. In contrast, Visium, TESLA, iStar, and XFuse could not accurately delineate these cell layers and boundaries ( Supplementary Fig. S3a  and  b ); instead, they only provided ambiguous patterns, which indicates a lack of precision in defining the regions. Moreover, as shown in  Supplementary Fig. S4c , DeSpaST demonstrated exceptional potential in precise cell type annotation. Beyond the highly expressed ERBB2 tumor region, DeSpaST identified an additional layer outside the tumor region with abundant MS4A1 expression, which had not been previously annotated. Upon closer examination of the H&E image by the pathologist, the layer was found to be a lightly stained layer, containing fibrous connective tissues interspersed with inflammatory cells, crucial for restricting tumor expansion. This finding of interspersed immune cells is consistent with the MS4A1 gene expression pattern predicted by DeSpaST.    DeSpaST accurately predicts cellular-level gene expression  The above comparison between pathology annotation and DeSpaST highlights the resolution enhancement power of DeSpaST. To further evaluate the model’s performance, we conducted a direct and comprehensive comparison of cellular-level expression for individual genes. In addition to the Visium spot-level gene expression measurement, Janesick  et al . [ 25 ] also measured the cellular-level gene expression of hundreds of genes through the Xenium experiment. We applied DeSpaST to this breast cancer Visium dataset from Janesick  et al . [ 25 ], segmented and classified the cell nucleus from the H&E image ( Supplementary Fig. S5 ), and deconvolving spot-level ST signals into cell-level gene expression profiles. Despite the inherent limitations of adjacent-section comparisons (e.g. local distortion, cell displacement, and microenvironmental differences), DeSpaST showed strong concordance with Xenium in spatial distribution patterns. For example, for the breast cancer marker gene  CCND1  [ 26 ,  27 ] ( Fig. 2a ) and T-cell marker gene  CD69  [ 28 ,  29 ] ( Fig. 2b ), DeSpaST accurately predicted the gene expression patterns, in agreement with the observed patterns in the Xenium. Both Visium and TESLA failed to resolve these patterns adequately, especially in the complex tissue regions. Consider the top of the tissue section ( Fig. 2c  and  Supplementary Fig. S6a ) where intricate tumor and immune cell domains are present. Only DeSpaST successfully captured gene expression within intricate microenvironments ( Fig. 2d  and  e ), accurately reflecting the patterns observed in the Xenium experiment. Conversely, TESLA and Visium failed to capture these spatial variations in gene expression, resulting in unclear expression patterns. In the case of the  CD69  gene ( Fig. 2b ), the Visium ST data are noisy and lack a clear expression pattern. Although TESLA reduces some noise, it fails to capture the inherent gene expression patterns accurately. In contrast, DeSpaST effectively eliminates noise and accurately discerns the true gene expression pattern.    Figure 2   Evaluation of DeSpaST in cell-level gene expression prediction.
