With the gene pattern identified by DeSpaST, our next step involves a quantitative assessment of the performance enhancement achieved by the DeSpaST model. To facilitate this assessment, spot-level gene expression was reconstructed by taking the average expression of cells inside each spot. For quantitative comparison across methods, we reconstructed spot-level expression by averaging the predicted cellular expressions within each Visium spot and then computed gene-wise Pearson correlations against Xenium for DeSpaST, raw Visium, TESLA, iStar, and XFuse ( Supplementary Fig. S3 ). DeSpaST exhibits a stronger correlation to Xenium ( r  = 0.754 for  CCND1  gene and  r  = 0.665 for  CD69  gene) than both Visium ( r  = 0.477 for  CCND1  gene, and  r  = 0.239 for  CD69  gene) and TESLA ( r  = 0.720 for  CCND1  gene, and  r  = 0.424 for  CD69  gene) ( Fig. 2f  and  Supplementary Fig. S3c ). Similar enhancements in clarity and noise reduction in gene expression patterns were observed in other genes as well, such as the  ERBB2  and  MS4A1  genes ( Supplementary Fig. S7 ). DeSpaST demonstrated strong consistency with Xenium experiments for both of these genes, achieving a correlation of  r  = 0.850 for the  ERBB2  gene and  r  = 0.610 for the  MS4A1  gene ( Supplementary Fig. S7c  and  d ). In addition to the above genes, to assess transcriptome-wide generalizability, we computed spot-level Pearson correlations for all examined Xenium genes and summarize the overall trend using correlation density plots ( Fig. 2g ;  Supplementary Fig. S3c ): DeSpaST achieves higher overall agreement with Xenium (median  r  = 0.518) than Visium (median  r  = 0.198) and TESLA (median  r  = 0.479), and the top 20% highest-density region summary consistently favors DeSpaST, indicating systematic improvement beyond a small set of marker genes.  To address the concern that histology-guided models might rely on visual cues and to validate key graph-construction hyperparameters, we performed a comprehensive set of ablation and sensitivity analyses ( Supplementary Fig. S8 ). First, randomizing the input transcriptional counts (“Random count”) caused a substantial collapse in performance—gene-wise correlation with Xenium dropped (CD69:  r  = 0.188; CCND1:  r  = 0.379), the overall summary decreased (top 20% high-density mean correlation: 0.174), and downstream spatial domain agreement deteriorated (NMI: 0.033; ARI: 0.0196)—demonstrating that accurate transcriptional signals are essential and that morphology alone cannot recover meaningful spatial expression. Second, randomizing morphology features (“Random image info”) also reduced performance relative to the full model (e.g. CD69:  r  = 0.423 versus 0.665; top 20% high-density mean: 0.202 versus 0.582; NMI: 0.169 versus 0.194; ARI: 0.0910 versus 0.1167), indicating that morphology provides complementary information but is not solely responsible for DeSpaST’s gains. Finally, we evaluated the robustness of the k-nearest-neighbor (kNN) cell-graph parameter by varying        on the breast dataset: extreme values were suboptimal (e.g. top-20%-density mean correlation = 0.161 at        and 0.220 at       ), while intermediate values (      –12) consistently achieved higher performance (0.58–0.64) and stable domain-detection agreement, supporting our choice of        as a balance between locality and connectivity ( Supplementary Fig. S8 ). Together, these analyses show that DeSpaST integrates both transcriptional and morphological information and that its performance is stable across a biologically reasonable range of neighborhood sizes.  To further test whether the deconvoluted outputs preserve biologically meaningful spatial structure beyond individual marker genes, we evaluated each method using a downstream spatial domain detection task on the breast cancer 10× Visium dataset [ 20 ]. As shown in ( Supplementary Fig. S9 ), we used the manually annotated domains as ground-truth labels. For each tool, we took the predicted cell-by-gene expression matrix together with per-cell spatial coordinates as input, constructed (i) an expression kNN graph in PCA space and (ii) a spatial kNN graph in 2D coordinate space, fused them into a hybrid connectivity matrix, and inferred domains using Leiden community detection (parameters reported in Supplementary Information). We then quantified concordance with manual annotations using NMI and ARI ( Supplementary Fig. S9b ; higher is better). DeSpaST achieved the best agreement with manual labels (NMI = 0.194; ARI = 0.117), outperforming iStar (NMI = 0.182; ARI = 0.056), XFuse (NMI = 0.033; ARI = 0.011), and TESLA (NMI = 0.143; ARI = 0.031), indicating that DeSpaST’s deconvolution better preserves domain-level organization for downstream spatial analyses.  Supplementary Fig. S9c  further visualizes the inferred domains from each method, where DeSpaST produces domain boundaries that are qualitatively more consistent with the expert annotations.  The remarkable cell-level resolution achieved by DeSpaST creates new possibilities for examining cell–cell communications within a spatial context. For instance, within the cellular milieu surrounding the breast ducts ( Supplementary Fig. S10 ), we detected elevated expressions of breast cancer marker genes  CCND1  and  ERBB2  ( Supplementary Fig. S10a  and  c ). In contrast, immune cell marker genes  CD69  and  MS4A1  ( Supplementary Fig. S10b  and  d ) exhibited high expression in the outside layer adjacent to the tumor cells. The gene expression patterns predicted by DeSpaST align with the Xenium gene panel, while TESLA failed to predict them accurately. DeSpaST’s findings suggest possible interactions between immune and tumor cells, highlighting its potential for further studies on the tissue microenvironment and cell–cell communication.    DeSpaST accurately captures the cell-level protein expression  As products of gene expression, protein expressions are generally correlated with differentially expressed mRNAs [ 30 ,  31 ]. Next, we evaluate whether the gene expression patterns obtained by DeSpaST could reflect protein expressions at the cell level [ 25 ]. We plotted and compared the  MS4A1  and  ERBB2  gene expression patterns with the corresponding HER2 and CD20 protein immunofluorescence (IF) signals ( Fig. 3a  and  b ). Interestingly, the gene expression patterns predicted by DeSpaST closely align with protein expression profiles, while Visium and TESLA are not able to capture them. We calculated the correlations between predicted  MS4A1  gene expression and Xenium IF CD20 protein signals. DeSpaST exhibits superior performance compared to TESLA and Visium with higher correlation ( r  = 0.622 for DeSpaST versus  r  = 0.420 for Visium and  r  = 0.401 for TESLA;  Fig. 3c ). DeSpaST also demonstrated a notably higher correlation of ERBB2 gene expression with HER2 protein expression ( r  = 0.839) when compared to Visium ( r  = 0.821) and TESLA ( r  = 0.660), as illustrated in  Fig. 3d . Although Visium and TESLA also showed good correlations with the HER2 IF signals, DeSpaST significantly outperformed them in predicting fine-grained details gene expression patterns ( Supplementary Fig. S11 ). Notably, only DeSpaST accurately captured the comprehensive pattern of ERBB2 gene expression, depicting the tumor’s shape around the breast duct in alignment with IF protein signals. In contrast, Visium and TESLA predicted a vague outline of ERBB2 expression, lacking finer details and failing to depict a clear pattern. Application of DeSpaST for cell type identification  Given the highly precise cell-level gene expression predicted by DeSpaST, we employed DeSpaST for downstream analysis. This involved leveraging the predicted cell-level gene expression to delineate the spatial distribution of various cell types. Unlike ST data, where one spot may contain multiple cells, DeSpaST’s cellular-level resolution offers a superior depiction of cell-type distribution. Utilizing DeSpaST’s gene expression predictions as input, we applied the cell-type identification algorithm ScType [ 32 ] to assign the cell type to each single cell. The resulting cell-type profiles were mapped back onto the spatial location and detected locations for tumor cells, lymphocytes, fibroblasts, and macrophages ( Supplementary Fig. S12a ). To validate the cell-type distribution by DeSpaST, we implemented the ScType algorithm with the Xenium data and plotted the cell-type distribution in  Supplementary Fig. S12b . The spatial distributions of annotated cell types from DeSpaST closely resemble the cell types obtained from Xenium, which further substantiate the accuracy of DeSpaST. To reveal the tumor’s immunological response, we specifically focus on tumor cells and immune cells ( Fig. 4a  and  b ). Both DeSpaST ( Fig. 4a ) and Xenium panel ( Fig. 4b ) delineated similar tumor and immune cell regions. Heterogeneous areas are found at the upper and middle portion of the tissue where tumor and immune cells closely interact, which indicates the recognition and attack of activated immune cells that impede tumor spread. In contrast, tumor regions at the lower portion of the slides appear less confined, forming dense and more aggressive tumor areas where there is a lack of immune cell control. Both Xenium and DeSpaST accurately classify these complex cell environments. While Xenium served as a valuable reference here, DeSpaST exhibits greater potential and offers the flexibility to include more marker genes for cell type classification analysis. Unlike Xenium's panel of 306 genes, DeSpaST can leverage the transcriptomic level gene expression data from ST data. This enables the inclusion of a wider range of cell-type markers, leading to more accurate classification.    Figure 4   Application of DeSpaST in spatial cell-level downstream analysis. Application of DeSpaST in uncovering pseudo temporal trajectories of tumor progression  Following the annotation of cancer cells, we calculated the pseudo-trajectories timeline of tumor development based on the inferred cell level gene expression predicted by DeSpaST. The partition-based graph abstraction (PAGA) method was used to construct the topological graph and a cluster with high expression of cancer stem cell marker  ALDH1A 3 [ 33 ,  34 ] was selected as the root node ( Supplementary Fig. S13 ). Pseudotime values were estimated and mapped back to each cell's spatial location to infer the dynamic trajectories of tumor progression ( Fig. 4c ). Interestingly, the clusters of early pseudotime cancer cells and late pseudotime cancer cells occupy markedly distinct regions in the tissue section. These distributions align precisely with the DCIS (ductal carcinoma  in situ ) and invasive tumor regions annotated by expert pathologists ( Fig. 4d ). Tumor cells with early pseudotime exhibit a denser and more uniform composition characterized with reduced variability in size and shape, corresponding to DCIS regions ( Fig. 4d ). In contrast, late pseudotime tumor cells, located in the invasive tumor region, show increased invasivenexss and a more loosely organized structure.    Utilization of DeSpaST across diverse tissue datasets  In addition to the above two breast cancer datasets, DeSpaST can be broadly applied to various tissue types and datasets. We further applied DeSpaST to Visium datasets from human ovarian cancer ( Fig. 5 ) and human lung cancer ( Supplementary Fig. S16 ). DeSpaST extracted the cellular morphology features from the H&E image and deconvoluted the cell-level gene expression for all the Visium genes across each cell. For the human ovarian cancer dataset, we selected the ovarian cancer marker gene  BRCA1  [ 35 ,  36 ] ( Fig. 5b ) and ovarian normal tissue marker  FOXL2  [ 37 ,  38 ] ( Fig. 5c ) as illustrative examples. DeSpaST significantly improved gene expression pattern resolution compared to the Visium spot-level expression ( Supplementary Fig. S14b  and  c ). High  BRCA1  expression ( Fig. 5b ) corresponds with dark-purple regions in the H&E-stained image, which were annotated as tumor cells, while high  FOXL2  expression corresponds to pink color areas indicative of normal ovarian tissue ( Fig. 5c ). We zoomed in on five specific regions to showcase the resolution of DeSpaST’s output and highlight the differences in gene expression ( Fig. 5d–f ,  Supplementary Fig. S15 ). DeSpaST  BRCA1  and  FOXL2  exhibit distinct gene expression patterns between tumor and normal ovarian tissue regions. Similar cell-level resolution improvement of DeSpaST is also observed in the human lung cancer Visium dataset ( Supplementary Fig. S16 ). We illustrated three marker genes as examples of the resolution improvement compared to the Visium spot level resolution ( Supplementary Fig. S17 ): cancer marker gene  EGFR  [ 39 ], T lymphocyte marker  CD4  [ 40 ], and fibroblast maker  SFRP2  [ 41 ]. DeSpaST further clarified and enhanced the resolution of these patterns ( Supplementary Fig. S16 ). As depicted in  Supplementary Fig. S16e , DeSpaST accurately demonstrated high EGFR expression in tumor regions and elevated SFRP2 expression in fibroblast areas. Regions like  Supplementary Fig. S16f  and  g  illustrate the tumor microenvironment with interactive immune cell and tumor cell regions. DeSpaST successfully distinguished immune cells and tumor cells with high EGFR expression in tumor regions, as well as elevated CD4 expression in corresponding immune cell regions. The strong agreement between DeSpaST’s output and pathological annotations in both ovarian and lung cancer tissues supports its accuracy and reliability in uncovering cell-level gene expression from spot-level ST data for multiple tissues.  Finally, to assess cross-region generalizability, we spatially split the Visium spots into training and held-out subsets. On the held-out portion, DeSpaST maintained substantially higher agreement with Xenium than raw Visium (e.g. CD69 Pearson r: 0.653 versus 0.192; CCND1 Pearson r: 0.614 versus 0.208;  Supplementary Fig. S18 ), confirming that the model generalizes beyond the training region.     Discussion  In this paper, we presented DeSpaST, which is a graphic deconvolution model that integrates the cell morphology features from histology images with spatial transcriptomic data to predict the cellular resolution gene expression for cells across the tissue section. Unlike other methods that only enhance the ST resolution, DeSpaST stands out as the first model to directly infer cell-level gene expression from histology images and ST data. DeSpaST is innovative and beneficial in that it takes advantage of the histology images and explicitly models the spatial organization of cells. By constructing the cellular graphic structure, cell morphology and interaction information from histology images were successfully input to the GCN model as nodes and edges, respectively. GCN, with its capability to handle complex non-Euclidean structures, enables deconvolution at cell-level resolution by well aligning with the diverse and intricate cellular interaction topologies. We demonstrated the high accuracy, resolution, robustness, and efficacy of DeSpaST in this paper. This model can be easily applied to diverse types of tissues and ST data.  The cellular-level gene expression inferred from DeSpaST offers powerful support to many biomedical applications. In this study, we applied DeSpaST’s output to the spatial cell type annotation and inferred the pseudotime trajectories of tumor development. DeSpaST offers the cellular resolution for cell type identification compared to traditional spot-level cell type identification. DeSpaST clearly illustrates the cell types for individual cells, enabling the revelation of cell–cell interaction in the tumor microenvironment and providing valuable insights into tumor immunology studies. Pseudotime analysis further uncovers the pseudo-temporal trajectories of tumor progression, revealing distinct clusters of early- and late-stage cancer cells. The high precision of DeSpaST establishes a reliable foundation for subsequent spatial transcriptomics analyses, such as deriving differentially expressed genes and exploring cell–cell communication inference.  A key limitation of our evaluation is that the Xenium measurements used for validation are obtained from an adjacent FFPE section, rather than the exact same section profiled by Visium. Although adjacent-section validation is often necessary in practice because assays are destructive or mutually exclusive, it is inherently imperfect: consecutive sections can exhibit local tissue distortion during sectioning and mounting, cell displacement, partial-volume differences, and subtle microenvironmental heterogeneity (e.g. immune infiltration near boundaries). These factors can weaken strict quantitative comparability even when broad spatial trends remain visually similar. Therefore, the agreement we observe between DeSpaST predictions and Xenium should be interpreted primarily as qualitative and semi-quantitative evidence that DeSpaST recovers coherent spatial gene-expression patterns and microenvironmental structure, rather than as an absolute quantitative ground truth at single-cell resolution. To mitigate this limitation, we emphasize evaluations that do not require one-to-one cell correspondence across sections—such as region-level pattern concordance, marker-consistent localization, and spot-level correlations computed after aggregating predicted cells within each Visium spot—and we further assess whether predicted cell-level signals support consistent tissue organization using downstream spatial domain analyses.  Beyond the cross-section validation constraints discussed above, several additional limitations should be noted. First, DeSpaST’s accuracy depends on the upstream nucleus segmentation step; segmentation errors such as missed nuclei, over-segmentation, or misclassification propagate to the graph construction and deconvolution. Second, genes with very low or near-zero expression in the Visium data are inherently difficult to deconvolve, as there is minimal transcriptional signal to distribute among cells. Third, standardized simulation frameworks that jointly model realistic histology with spatially structured single-cell expression are not yet available, and matched single-cell spatial datasets with paired Visium and H&E inputs remain scarce, precluding direct ground-truth validation at single-cell resolution. Despite these limitations, DeSpaST demonstrates consistent improvements across multiple complementary evaluation criteria and tissue types.  In addition to uncovering cellular gene expression in ST data, DeSpaST holds the potential for deconvoluting cellular protein expression in spatial proteomics. Recently, numerous spatial proteomic methods have been developed to enable the direct detection of protein molecules with spatial variability. However, the resolution remains limited, typically operating at spot sizes around 20–100 μm [ 42–45 ]. The application of DeSpaST to improve the resolution of spatial proteomics encourages further exploration of spatially cellular protein expression.  DeSpaST is designed for broad applicability, leveraging histology images and ST data as input to uncover cellular-level expression. Its capabilities can be further extended by incorporating additional data sources. For example, if single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data are available from the same tissue or a similar sample, DeSpaST can integrate it as a cell type constraint, potentially improving the deconvolution accuracy. This is particularly valuable when dealing with very weak sequencing signals in ST data, as scRNA-seq offers higher sequencing depth. An additional enhancement for DeSpaST could involve its extension to 3D spatial transcriptomes. Recently, spatially resolved transcriptomic atlases in high-dimensional data have emerged to revolutionize the understanding of cell interaction and gene regulation within the organ. Organ-level 3D spatial transcriptomics [ 46–48 ] or proteomics [ 49 ] were reconstructed from serial 2D tissue sections. DeSpaST, with a potential 3D GCN version, could leverage these data’s complexity to learn 3D spatial cell features and deconvolute gene expression. This is particularly relevant as current 3D spatial transcriptomes often miss data between sections. DeSpaST can potentially address this gap and provide a more complete picture of the 3D spatial transcriptomic landscape.    Method   Datasets   Human breast cancer datasets 1  Two human breast cancer datasets were employed for constructing and validating the DeSpaST model. The first human breast cancer dataset consists of Visium ST data for DCIS and Invasive Carcinoma FFPE human breast cancer tissue. This dataset contains 2518 spots, with 5244 median genes per spot and a sequencing depth of 32 524 reads per spot.    Human breast cancer datasets 2  The second human breast cancer dataset is associated with a recently released Xenium  in situ  platform [ 25 ]. This research conducted a comprehensive analysis with three complementary technologies (Chromium, Visium, Xenium) on a single breast-cancer FFPE tissue. The Visium output ST data were used to deconvolute the cell-level gene expression using DeSpaST, which contains 4992 spots, with 5712 median genes per spot and 40 003 mean reads per spot. The Xenium panels were used as a reference standard to evaluate DeSpaST’s cell-level resolution prediction. Additionally, IF staining was performed after Xenium to assess the expression profiles of HER2 and CD20 proteins. The results from both the Xenium panel and the subsequent IF staining were then used to verify the effectiveness of DeSpaST.    Human ovarian cancer dataset  The human ovarian cancer dataset is obtained from 10× Genomics and contains 4674 spots, with 8792 median genes per spot.    Human lung cancer dataset  The human lung cancer dataset is obtained from 10× Genomics and contains 6195 spots, with 10 087 median genes per spot.     Spatial transcriptomics data preprocessing and image feature extraction  Spatial transcriptomics data were first preprocessed prior to analysis. Gene expression values in the spot barcode profile matrix were normalized to counts per million (CPM). To mitigate the impact of outliers, the normalized CPM values were scaled to the 95th percentile.  The cell morphology features were extracted from H&E images using HD-Staining (Histology-based Digital Staining of Pathology Images) [ 18 ], which is an automatic deep-learning model that simultaneously segments and classifies cell nuclei, as well as provides morphology information about each identified cell nucleus. The extracted morphological features encompassed the centroid position, cell area, convex area, eccentricity, extent, filled area, major axis length, minor axis length, orientation, perimeter, solidity, and probability. In addition, we further enriched DeSpaST by incorporating 1024-dimensional intermediate box features and 256-dimensional mask features derived from the HD-Staining model. These cell morphological features were incorporated into the construction of DeSpaST.    Cellular graphic structure construction  We initially divided whole-slide H&E images into 250 × 250-pixel patches centered on the Visium spots. In total, we generated 2518 patches for the 10× Visium human breast cancer dataset, 4992 patches for the Janesick  et al . [ 25 ] human breast cancer dataset, 4674 patches for the human ovarian cancer dataset, and 6195 patches for the human lung cancer dataset. For each patch, we first obtain each cell location by performing cell segmentation, then construct a directed graph structure by connecting the cells based on their spatial proximity. This graph structure was designed to incorporate at least eight nearest neighbors. Pairwise Euclidean distances between cell coordinates were computed to identify the nearest neighbors. For those patches with very low cell density (<8 cells), DeSpaST dynamically resized the patch to include at least eight neighboring cells. These directed graph structures captured the spatial relationship and connectivity among cells in the tissue.  Each graph structure consisted of two main components: nodes and edges. Nodes represent morphological features extracted through HD-Staining for individual cells. These node features have undergone global scaling as part of the preprocessing. Edges store information on edge categorization and edge spatial representation ( Supplementary Fig. S2 ). Edge categorization is determined based on the types of cells connected by each edge, which provides insight into the type of interactions between the connected cells. Here, we included a total of 49 combinations of edge categorizations across seven cell types ( Supplementary Fig. S2a ). Edge spatial representation refers to the spatial aspects of cell interactions, including the Cell Connectivity Angle and Spatial Proximity. Cell Connectivity Angle indicates the connectivity between neighboring cells and the directionality of these connections. Spatial Proximity reflects the physical distance between cells. Both nodes and edges collectively constitute the cellular graphic structure, which synergistically contributes to the definition of complex cellular relationships. Image registration and result comparison   Immunofluorescence image and Xenium panel registration to hematoxylin and eosin images  In order to register the IF image and Xenium panel to the Visium corresponding H&E images and facilitate the comparison to the protein/RNA expression experiment, we employed skimage.transform package for image transformation. To achieve a precise and efficient registration, we systematically tested various combinations of angles and scales between the IF and H&E images. Subsequently, we fine-tuned the registration using the original scale.    DeSpaST model validation  We validate DeSpaST through the assessment of RNA expression and protein expression by utilizing data from the Xenium panel and IF images, respectively. Using the spatial information from Visium spot locations, we reconstructed the spot-level expression for DeSpaST, TESLA, Xenium panel, and IF protein expression. The accuracies of Visium ST data, TESLA, and the DeSpaST model were evaluated using the Pearson correlation coefficient with the Xenium panel and IF image.     Cell type analysis  To assign cell types to each predicted single cell, we adopted a fully automated cell-type identification algorithm, ScType [ 32 ], which utilizes the Xenium-tested marker gene as the selected cell markers. The cellular level gene expression predicted by DeSpaST was used as input. The Seurat package was used to normalize the data with the default LogNormalize method. We then use the Seurat FindNeighbors function with parameter dims = 1:50 and FindClusters function with resolution = 0.9, which results in 23 clusters. ScType was also applied with Xenium Breast Cancer Cell Marker panel. Each cluster was assigned to the cell type with the highest score, and clusters assigned the same cell type were merged into larger clusters.    Pseudotime analysis  The gene expression of tumor cells predicted by DeSpaST was extracted for pseudotime analysis. We first reduced the gene expression dimension using principal component analysis (PCA). Then, cell clustering was performed using the Leiden algorithm, which is a fast approach to ensure that all cells are well connected for downstream optimal trajectory inference [ 55 ]. Partition-based graph abstraction (PAGA) [ 56 ] is used to construct a topological graph based on the cell partitions. The cluster with high expression of  ALDH1A 3 [ 33 ,  34 ], a gene marker of cancer stem cells, was selected as the trajectory root node. The Diffusion Pseudotime (DPT) method [ 57 ] was then applied to estimate pseudotime values, which represented the tumor cell dynamics. All analyses were performed using the SCANPY [ 58 ] Python packages.    Spatial domain detection  To assess whether each deconvolution method preserves biologically meaningful spatial structure at the domain level, we performed downstream spatial domain detection using the predicted cell-by-gene expression matrix together with per-cell spatial coordinates as inputs. For each method, we first constructed two neighborhood graphs: (i) an expression kNN graph in a low-dimensional transcriptomic space, obtained by PCA on the predicted expression matrix and kNN graph construction using Scanpy, yielding an expression connectivity matrix       ; and (ii) a spatial kNN graph in the 2D coordinate space using Euclidean neighbors, yielding a symmetric binary adjacency matrix       . We then fused these graphs into a hybrid connectivity matrix via a linear combination,        where       balances spatial proximity and transcriptional similarity. Finally, we applied Leiden community detection on       to infer spatial domains for each tissue section, using identical processing across methods; all parameters are reported in the Supplementary Information. Domain assignments were benchmarked against manual domain annotations (when available) using Normalized Mutual Information (NMI) and the Adjusted Rand Index (ARI).    Key Points    DeSpaST introduces a dynamic edge-conditioned graph convolutional network for deconvolving spot-level ST data into true cell-level-resolution gene profiles.    DeSpaST integrates spatial and morphological features from histology images to model cell–cell organization and improve accuracy.    Extensively benchmarked across multiple cancer datasets, outperforming existing methods in resolution and precision.    DeSpaST enables diverse applications, including cell-type annotation, tumor trajectory analysis, and cell–cell communication discovery, demonstrating its potential to provide new insights in various biological contexts. title: Cell-resolved spatial mapping of antibody-drug conjugate targets in breast cancer.

evidence_text:
Cell-resolved spatial mapping of antibody-drug conjugate targets in breast cancer.

Background

Antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) activity and target-dependent on-target/off-tumor toxicity depends in part on which cells express the target antigen, a feature that bulk assays cannot resolve.

Methods

We analyzed a publicly available whole-transcriptome CosMx breast tumor dataset including 154,816 cells and 18,934 genes. Eleven clinically relevant ADC targets were profiled across seven annotated lineages. Findings were contextualized using TCGA-BRCA bulk transcriptomes (1,097 tumors and 114 normal tissues) and assessed in two public Xenium breast cancer specimens.

Results

HER2 (ERBB2), TROP2 (TACSTD2), HER3 (ERBB3), NECTIN4 and MUC1 were enriched in tumor epithelium. B7-H3 (CD276) was highest in endothelial and myoepithelial cells, with similar mean expression in stromal and tumor cells. PSMA (FOLH1) was enriched in endothelium. TCGA-BRCA tumor-normal differences did not identify these cellular sources. No overall-survival association remained after multiple-testing correction or covariate adjustment. HER2 and TROP2 tumor enrichment recurred in both Xenium specimens, whereas EGFR was not tumor restricted.

Conclusions

Cell-resolved spatial profiling separated ADC targets enriched in tumor epithelium from those expressed in vascular and stromal compartments. B7-H3 and PSMA localization was consistent with prior immunohistochemical reports and is confirmatory. These RNA-level results do not establish surface-protein abundance, ADC response, or clinical toxicity. Low-abundance microenvironmental findings remain based on a single discovery specimen and require protein-level validation. Protein-level confirmation, and correlation with ADC efficacy and toxicity, are required before these maps can inform clinical decisions. Antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) link a target-specific antibody to a cytotoxic payload and are now central to breast-cancer treatment [ 2 ]. Trastuzumab emtansine established the class in HER2-positive disease [ 3 ], extending median progression-free survival from 6.4 to 9.6 months and median overall survival from 25.1 to 30.9 months relative to lapatinib plus capecitabine. Trastuzumab deruxtecan and the TROP2-directed agents Sacituzumab govitecan and datopotamab deruxtecan have since broadened their use across breast cancer subtypes [ [4] , [5] , [6] , [7] ]. In the long-term DESTINY-Breast04 analysis, investigator-assessed median progression-free survival was 8.8 versus 4.2 months (hazard ratio, 0.36), and median overall survival was 22.9 versus 16.8 months (hazard ratio, 0.69), with trastuzumab deruxtecan versus treatment of the physician's choice in HER2-low advanced breast cancer [ 4 ]. In the final ASCENT analysis, Sacituzumab govitecan improved median progression-free survival to 4.8 versus 1.7 months (hazard ratio 0.41) and median overall survival to 11.8 versus 6.9 months (hazard ratio 0.51) in metastatic triple-negative breast cancer [ 5 ]. HER3, NECTIN4 , folate receptor-α, B7-H3, MUC1 and CEACAM5 are among the additional targets in clinical development [ [8] , [9] , [10] ]; the molecular alterations of MUC1 and their therapeutic exploitation have been reviewed recently [ 11 ]. For an ADC, tissue-level abundance is not enough. The target must also be located on the relevant cells. Expression in stroma, vasculature or normal epithelium can contribute to target-dependent on-target/off-tumor toxicity, but ADC toxicity is multifactorial and also reflects payload cytotoxicity, platform-related properties, and host factors [ 12 ]. The clinical burden can nonetheless be substantial. In the updated DESTINY-Breast04 analysis, adjudicated drug-related interstitial lung disease or pneumonitis occurred in 12.1% of patients receiving trastuzumab deruxtecan, including 1.1% grade 5 events [ 4 ]. In the final ASCENT analysis, the most common grade 3 or higher treatment-emergent adverse events with Sacituzumab govitecan included neutropenia (52%) and diarrhea (12%) [ 5 ]. Conversely, target-negative tumor cells may escape direct binding, although a membrane-permeable payload can affect neighboring cells through a bystander effect [ 13 ]. Bulk assays and tissue-averaged immunohistochemistry do not resolve the cellular source of a target signal. The broader importance of tissue architecture extends beyond ADCs to other tumor-directed delivery platforms, including nanocarriers influenced by vascular permeability and retention, as well as stimuli-responsive nanoparticles under development for breast cancer [ 14 , 15 ]. Cell-resolved target assessment is already used in the chimeric antigen receptor T-cell field to anticipate on-target/off-tumor effects [ 16 ]. For ADCs, bulk surveys have catalogued target expression across tumors and normal tissues, including a 54-target pan-cancer analysis [ 17 ]. A post-mortem breast cancer series also compared metastases with matched normal organs [ 18 ]. In high-grade serous ovarian cancer, dissociated single-cell RNA sequencing identified clinical ADC targets that were most often restricted to cancer cells [ 19 ]. Spatial profiling has therefore been proposed as a means of interpreting target availability in tissue context [ 20 ]. Breast single-cell atlases have examined heterogeneity in ERBB2 and TACSTD2, but primarily within the malignant epithelial compartment [ 21 ]. Few studies have spatially identified multiple ADC targets across malignant and non-malignant compartments in breast cancer. Imaging-based transcriptomics can provide this information while preserving histological structure [ [22] , [23] , [24] , [25] ]. We therefore mapped 11 ADC targets in a publicly available whole-transcriptome breast cancer specimen, examined the recurrence of selected patterns in two public Xenium specimens, and compared the findings with TCGA-BRCA bulk transcriptomes. The study is descriptive. Its purpose is to identify which cells contribute to each target transcript and to show where tissue-level abundance may obscure that source. Materials and methods Single-cell spatial dataset We used the public CosMx Spatial Molecular Imager Human Whole Transcriptome FFPE breast dataset (Bruker Spatial Biology, "breast discovery" release, sample S0) [ 22 ]. The dataset contains one tumor specimen, which served as the discovery sample. Selected findings were examined in two additional public Xenium specimens (the cross-specimen Xenium analysis). We obtained the cell-by-gene matrix, cell metadata, and cell polygons from the public repository. The complete dataset contained approximately 645,000 cells. To make the analysis tractable using standard hardware, we drew a reproducible random subsample (seed = 1) and retained cells with at least 50 detected RNA molecules. This yielded 154,816 cells. Removing negative-control and system-control probes left 18,934 genes. Global coordinates were converted from pixels to micrometers using a scale of 0.12028 µm per pixel. We also split the retained cells into two random halves and compared cell-type mean target-expression matrices to assess sensitivity to subsampling. Clustering, annotation and differential expression Analyses were performed in R 4.5.2 with Seurat 5.5.1 [ 26 ]. Counts were log-normalized to counts per 10,000, then subjected to a natural-log transformation. We scaled the 2,000 most variable genes and used 30 principal components to construct a shared-nearest-neighbor graph. Louvain clustering was run at resolution 0.5, followed by UMAP embedding. Clusters were assigned to seven lineages using module scores for canonical markers and established breast cell-type signatures [ 27 ]. The lineages were tumor epithelial, fibroblast/stromal, myeloid, B/plasma, T, myoepithelial, and endothelial. One-versus-rest Wilcoxon rank-sum tests identified positive cell-type markers, with at least 10% detection, a minimum log2 fold-change of 0.25, and at most 500 cells per group. P values were adjusted by the Benjamini-Hochberg method. These cell-level tests treat cells from one specimen as independent observations. We therefore used them to describe within-sample marker specificity and placed greater weight on effect sizes than on nominal P values. ADC-target analysis We examined eleven clinically relevant ADC targets: ERBB2 (HER2), TACSTD2 (TROP2), ERBB3 (HER3), NECTIN4, FOLR1 (FRα), CEACAM5 (CEA), CD276 (B7-H3), MUC1, MET, EGFR and FOLH1 (PSMA). For each cell type, we calculated mean log-normalized expression and the number and fraction of cells with detectable expression. Per-cell expression was also mapped in tissue coordinates. Cross-platform single-target detection comparison To describe cross-platform differences in single-target detection, we compared ERBB2 and TACSTD2 between the whole-transcriptome CosMx dataset and a 313-gene Xenium breast panel [ 23 ]. For each dataset, we calculated the fraction of tumor cells with zero counts for the target gene. The assays were applied to different specimens and used different chemistries and panel sizes; this descriptive comparison was not designed to isolate a platform or panel-design effect. Receptor subtype, spillover control and spatial organization For each target, we report the number and fraction of expressing cells, along with the mean expression. This provides cellular support for findings in low-abundance microenvironments. To assess whether FOLH1 and CD276 enrichment could reflect transcript spillover across cell boundaries, we built a k-nearest-neighbor graph (k = 10) from cell centroids. We calculated the proportion of tumor-epithelial neighbors for each cell, then compared expression in the enriched lineage between cells with few (<25%) and many (>50%) tumor neighbors. The receptor phenotype was inferred from tumor-cell expression of ESR1, PGR, and ERBB2 , with GATA3 and MKI67 as context. This RNA-based classification is not equivalent to immunohistochemical receptor status. Cell-type neighborhood enrichment followed the approach implemented in Squidpy [ 28 ]. For each ordered cell-type pair, we compared the observed number of graph edges with a null distribution from 100 permutations of cell-type labels and expressed the result as a z-score. Bulk transcriptomic contextualization (TCGA-BRCA) TCGA-BRCA gene-level expression (log2(normalized count + 1)) and clinical data were obtained from the UCSC Xena TCGA hub [ 29 , 30 ]. Sample barcodes identified 1,097 primary tumors and 114 solid-tissue normals. In this dataset, NECTIN4 is recorded under its alias PVRL4 and was mapped accordingly. Tumor-versus-normal differences were tested for each target by the Wilcoxon rank-sum test with Benjamini-Hochberg adjustment. Overall survival was derived from vital status and time to death or last follow-up. The full survival cohort contained 1,080 patients. For each target, we fitted a univariable Cox model using continuous expression and performed a median-split log-rank test. We interpreted these P values in the context of the 11 tested targets and did not search for additional endpoints and subgroups. Multivariable Cox models were fitted separately in the 808 patients with complete data for age, pathologic stage, and PAM50 intrinsic subtype. Cross-specimen validation on Xenium We analyzed two additional public Xenium breast cancer specimens: the Human Breast invasive ductal carcinoma sample and the breast cancer reference block [ 23 ]. The invasive ductal carcinoma specimen came from a different patient. Public metadata did not establish patient-level independence of the reference block. We used the vendor-supplied graph-based clusters and assigned cells to the same lineages by marker scores. Four ADC targets were represented in the Xenium panel: ERBB2, TACSTD2, MUC1, and EGFR . For each target, we compared detection fractions between tumor epithelial and non-tumor cells. Detection fraction was chosen because absolute expression is not directly comparable across platforms with different panel sizes and sequencing depths. Results A seven-lineage single-cell spatial map of the breast tumor Unsupervised clustering produced 15 clusters, which were assigned to seven cell types ( Fig. 1 ). Tumor epithelium was the largest compartment (95,803 cells; 61.9%). Fibroblast/stromal and myeloid cells each accounted for 10.3%, followed by B/plasma cells (6.9%), T cells (5.3%), myoepithelial cells (2.7%), and endothelial cells (2.6%). Quality-control distributions are shown in Supplementary Fig. S2. These populations occupied coherent tissue regions, with tumor epithelium forming contiguous fields and glandular structures ( Fig. 1 B). One-versus-rest testing identified 4,449 positive markers. The leading markers matched the assigned lineages, including PIP, SERHL2, and MLPH in the tumor epithelium; COL1A1, LUM, and POSTN in the stroma; and EGFL7, PLVAP, and FLT1 in the endothelium ( Fig. 2 ; Supplementary Table S4). The same correspondence was seen for myeloid ( APOE, LYZ, C1QC ), B/plasma ( IGKC, IGHA1, JCHAIN ), T ( GNLY, GZMA, ITGAE ) and myoepithelial cells ( ACTA2, MCAM, CSPG4 ). Fig. 1 Single-cell spatial map of the breast tumor. (A) Uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) of 154,816 analyzed cells from one CosMx breast tumor specimen, colored by seven annotated cell types. (B) Spatial distribution of the same cells using tissue coordinates in micrometers. Each point represents a cell centroid. The same cell-type color key is used in both panels. Fig. 2 Cell-type marker expression in the discovery specimen. The five positive one-versus-rest markers with the largest average log2 fold change are shown for each of seven cell types. Dot color represents mean log-normalized expression across all cells in the indicated lineage, including zero-count cells. Dot size represents the fraction of cells with a nonzero gene count. The size-key values are fractions: 0.25, 0.50 and 0.75 correspond to 25%, 50% and 75%, respectively. Expression was normalized to 10,000 counts per cell and transformed using ln(1 + x). Marker-test results are provided in Supplementary Table S4. ADC targets show tumor-enriched and microenvironment-enriched patterns The eleven ADC targets followed two broad patterns ( Fig. 3 ). MUC1 (mean log-normalized expression 0.82), HER2/ ERBB2 (0.68), NECTIN4 (0.60), TROP2/ TACSTD2 (0.52) and HER3/ ERBB3 (0.39) were highest in tumor epithelium. Their mean expression in non-malignant compartments was 0.14 or lower. Spatial maps showed that HER2 and TROP2 expression were associated with the tumor-epithelial regions of the section ( Fig. 4 ). Fig. 3 ADC-target expression across cell types. Dot plot of 11 antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) targets in the CosMx discovery specimen. Dot color represents mean log-normalized expression across all cells in each lineage, including zero-count cells. Dot size represents the fraction of cells with a nonzero gene count; size-key values of 0.1-0.4 correspond to 10%-40%. Expression was normalized to 10,000 counts per cell and transformed using ln(1 + x). MUC1, HER2, NECTIN4, TROP2 and HER3 had their highest mean expression in tumor epithelium. B7-H3 was highest in endothelial and myoepithelial cells, and PSMA was highest in endothelium. Cell counts and detection fractions are provided in Supplementary Table S1. These measurements concern RNA expression. Fig. 4 Spatial expression of representative ADC targets. Per-cell expression of HER2 (ERBB2, upper left), TROP2 (TACSTD2, upper right), PSMA (FOLH1, lower left) and B7-H3 (CD276, lower right) in the CosMx discovery specimen. Each point represents a cell centroid. The four panels use the same tissue coordinates and a common expression color scale. Expression was normalized to 10,000 counts per cell and transformed using ln(1 + x). The maps show transcript localization and do not establish surface-protein abundance. Other targets were expressed preferentially outside the tumor compartment. B7-H3/ CD276 was highest in endothelial (0.35) and myoepithelial cells (0.31), followed by fibroblast/stromal and tumor cells (both 0.16). PSMA/ FOLH1 was concentrated in endothelium (0.47), whereas mean tumor-cell expression was 0.05. This distribution agrees with the reported localization of PSMA to tumor-associated neovasculature rather than breast carcinoma cells [ 31 ]. FOLR1 and CEACAM5 remained low across all cell types in this specimen (≤0.10). The microenvironmental findings were supported by the number of cells expressing (Supplementary Table S1). PSMA was detected in 20.0% of endothelial cells (817 of 4,076) and 3.2% of tumor cells. B7-H3 was detected in 16.0% of endothelial cells, 12.9% of myoepithelial cells, and 9.5% of tumor cells. Low PSMA expression in tumor cells argues against tumor-derived transcript spillover as the main explanation for endothelial enrichment. In the neighborhood analysis, endothelial cells with fewer than 25% tumor neighbors still had a mean PSMA expression of 0.39 (n = 2,282), compared with 0.05 in tumor cells. B7-H3 enrichment in stroma, endothelium and myoepithelium was also retained in cells located away from tumor epithelium (Supplementary Table S2). Single-target detection differed between platforms and specimens In the CosMx whole-transcriptome specimen, 60% of tumor cells had zero ERBB2 counts, and 68% had zero TACSTD2 counts. In the targeted 313-gene Xenium specimen, the corresponding fractions were 3.5% and 11%. Because the assays were applied to different tissue specimens and used different chemistries and panel sizes, these differences cannot be attributed solely to assay design. They nevertheless caution against interpreting a zero count as absence of target expression over spatial transcriptomic platforms. Tumor receptor phenotype and spatial organization Among tumor cells, ERBB2 was the most highly expressed receptor gene (mean 0.68; detected in 36.6% of cells). ESR1 (0.09; 5.8%) and PGR (0.04; 2.7%) were low. This RNA profile is compatible with, but not diagnostic of, a HER2-enriched or hormone-receptor-negative phenotype. The HER2 and TROP2 findings should therefore be interpreted in the context of these receptors. Neighborhood analysis showed strong self-association of the tumor epithelium (z = 507) and negative associations with all non-malignant cell types. The largest negative values were observed in myeloid cells (z = -308) and fibroblast/stromal cells (z = -294). Among non-malignant populations, fibroblasts co-localized most strongly with myeloid cells (z = 131), whereas endothelial cells co-localized most strongly with myoepithelial cells (z = 137; Supplementary Fig. S3). Subsampling had little effect. Two random halves of the retained cells produced nearly identical cell-type mean target-expression matrices (Pearson r = 0.998). HER2 and TROP2 tumor enrichment recurs in additional Xenium specimens Both Xenium specimens were public datasets distinct from the CosMx discovery sample, although only the invasive ductal carcinoma specimen was known to come from a different patient. We therefore assessed cross-specimen recurrence without treating the reference block as a separate patient-level replicate (Supplementary Fig. S4, Supplementary Table S3). Because panel content and sequencing depth differed, the comparison used detection fractions. Ranking cell types by mean expression gave the same ordering. Tumor epithelium had the highest HER2/ ERBB2 and TROP2/ TACSTD2 expression in all six specimen-by-target comparisons. In the invasive ductal carcinoma specimen, for example, TROP2 was detected in 84% of tumor cells and 26% of non-tumor cells. MUC1 showed the same pattern where it was included in the panel. EGFR differed. In both Xenium specimens, EGFR was detected as often as or more often in non-tumor cells, with the highest levels in myoepithelial cells. Bulk tumor-versus-normal expression In TCGA-BRCA (1,097 tumors and 114 normal tissues), six targets were higher in tumor tissue: CEACAM5 (log2 fold-change +4.1), MUC1 (+2.1), CD276 (+0.85), ERBB3 (+0.85), NECTIN4 (+0.75) and ERBB2 (+0.54). All adjusted P values were below 0.001 ( Fig. 5 ; Supplementary Table S5). TACSTD2 did not differ between groups (log2 fold-change -0.29; P = 0.06). Four targets were lower in tumors: FOLR1 (-3.8), EGFR (-3.5), MET (-2.4) and FOLH1 (-1.6). These bulk contrasts are influenced by tissue composition and do not identify the cell type expressing the gene. B7-H3 illustrates the distinction, as it was higher in bulk tumor tissue but arose mainly from endothelial, myoepithelial and stromal cells in the spatial data. Fig. 5 ADC-target expression in TCGA-BRCA tumors and normal tissues. Box plots show log2(normalized count + 1) expression of 11 ADC-target genes in primary tumors (n = 1,097; red) and solid-tissue normal samples (n = 114; blue). The center line is the median, boxes span the 25th-75th percentiles, and whiskers extend to the most extreme values within 1.5 times the interquartile range. Points beyond the whiskers are outliers. The y-axis range differs between gene panels. Two-sided Wilcoxon comparisons and Benjamini-Hochberg-adjusted P values are reported in Supplementary Table S5. No ADC target shows a strong association with overall survival Among the 1,080 patients with survival data, no univariable association remained significant after correction for eleven targets. The lowest nominal P values in this full cohort were observed for NECTIN4 in the continuous Cox model (P = 0.040) and the median-split log-rank test (P = 0.053; Supplementary Fig. S1; Supplementary Table S6). The complete-covariate subset contained 808 patients. In this subset, CEACAM5 had a nominal univariable association (P = 0.019), which weakened after adjustment for age, pathologic stage, and PAM50 subtype (hazard ratio 1.22; P = 0.071; Benjamini-Hochberg-adjusted P = 0.478). No target was associated with overall survival after covariate adjustment (Supplementary Table S7). These analyses do not support a strong single-gene prognostic effect, although the unselected cohort and limited event count constrain the inference. Discussion At the RNA level, the eleven ADC targets separated into two expression patterns in the discovery specimen. HER2, TROP2, HER3, NECTIN4 and MUC1 were concentrated in tumor epithelium. Among these, MUC1 had the highest mean expression, consistent with its long-standing status as a tumor-associated antigen and with continuing efforts to exploit MUC1 alterations therapeutically [ 11 ]. B7-H3 and PSMA were more prominent in stromal or vascular compartments. Bulk and tissue-averaged assays cannot resolve this difference in cellular source. Recovery of the established PSMA neovascular pattern provides an internal check on the cell assignments. These data do not estimate the therapeutic index, which also depends on surface protein abundance, internalization, expression in vital normal tissues, and payload and linker chemistry. Localization alone does not indicate whether a compartment contains sufficient antigen to affect treatment. PSMA is a useful caution. We detected FOLH1 in 20% of endothelial cells, but quantitative immunohistochemistry found PSMA staining in only a small minority of breast-cancer neovessels [ 32 ]. Those authors questioned the viability of PSMA-directed theranostics in this disease. A cell type can therefore be the dominant source of a low-abundance transcript without presenting a clinically meaningful antigen burden. Our study locates the RNA signal but does not quantify surface protein or predict efficacy or toxicity. The bulk and spatial examinations answered different questions. TCGA-BRCA identified targets whose total expression differed between tumor and normal tissue. It could not show whether the signal came from malignant cells. B7-H3 was higher in bulk tumor tissue but mapped mainly to endothelium, myoepithelium, and stroma in the spatial specimen. This is not a contradiction. Tumor-versus-normal contrasts are influenced by tissue composition, so we do not interpret bulk upregulation as evidence of tumor-cell specificity. Prior work defines the limits of the study's novelty. Single-cell surveys have already been used to identify non-malignant expression of CAR-T targets [ 16 ]. ADC-target catalogues are available for pan-cancer and breast cancer tissues [ 17 , 18 ], and dissociated single-cell data have been used to assess ADC target restriction in ovarian cancer [ 19 ]. B7-H3 expression in tumor endothelium and fibroblasts has been reported [ 33 ], as has PSMA expression in breast cancer neovasculature [ 31 , 32 ]. Our contribution is narrower. We assign 11 ADC-target transcripts to cell types in intact breast tissue, including the myoepithelial compartment, and assess selected targets in 2 additional specimens using another platform. The recovery of the known B7-H3 and PSMA localizations supports the approach but does not constitute a new biological discovery. Tumor epithelium occupied spatially segregated regions, apart from stromal, immune, and vascular populations (Supplementary Fig. S3). Together with the neighborhood control, this pattern makes simple transcript spillover an unlikely explanation for the B7-H3 and PSMA findings. The discovery tumor had low ESR1 and PGR expression and comparatively high ERBB2 . HER2 and TROP2 localization should therefore be interpreted within the context of their respective receptors rather than generalized across all breast cancer subtypes. Cross-specimen support was strongest for HER2 and TROP2. Their enrichment in tumor epithelium recurred in both Xenium specimens and on a second imaging platform. The invasive ductal carcinoma specimen came from a different patient, but the public metadata did not establish patient-level independence for the reference block. The evidence therefore represents recurrence across three specimens and two platforms, not three independent patients. EGFR was highest in myoepithelial cells in both Xenium specimens, showing that tumor restriction cannot be assumed for every target. B7-H3 and PSMA were absent from the targeted panel, so their localization remains based on the discovery specimen. The survival analyses provide no evidence that any target is an independent prognostic marker. Nominal associations differed between the full cohort and the complete-covariate subset and did not survive correction for or adjustment for covariates. This null result should not be read as proof that the target expression has no prognostic relevance in any subgroup. The cohort was unselected, the number of events was limited, and we deliberately avoided exploratory analyses by subtype or alternative endpoints. Translating these transcript-level maps into clinical decisions will require protein-level measurement and direct correlation with ADC efficacy and toxicity. We regard this as the central next step, rather than a peripheral caveat. A practical sequence would begin with multiplexed immunofluorescence or imaging mass cytometry on matched tissue sections, using the lineage markers applied here to reproduce the cell assignments alongside antibodies directed against the ectodomains engaged by ADCs. Simultaneous RNA and protein co-detection on the same section would then allow the transcript-to-protein relationship to be assessed cell-by-cell rather than assumed. Compartment-resolved quantitative scoring, as applied to PSMA in breast-cancer neovasculature [ 32 ], could subsequently convert localization into an estimate of antigen burden within each compartment. Clinical correlation would require complementary study designs. For efficacy, pretreatment tumor blocks from patients subsequently treated with a defined ADC could be scored separately for tumor-cell and microenvironmental target protein expression and related to objective response and progression-free survival. Assessment of toxicity would require additional evidence from relevant normal tissues and organ-specific adverse events in ADC-treated cohorts, because protein expression within the tumor microenvironment alone cannot establish on-target/off-tumor toxicity. Only outcome-linked studies of this kind can determine whether compartment-specific expression patterns such as those reported here for B7-H3 and PSMA have measurable clinical consequences. The spatial framework may also be relevant beyond ADCs. Nanoparticle and other tumor-directed delivery systems are influenced by vascular permeability, stromal barriers, and the organization of the tumor microenvironment [ 14 , 15 ]. Although these mechanisms differ from antigen-dependent ADC targeting, they reinforce the broader value of resolving delivery-relevant compartments within intact tissue. Until protein-level and outcome-linked data become available, however, the present findings should be interpreted as a hypothesis-generating guide to where such validation should be directed, not as evidence of ADC efficacy or safety. Limitations The whole-transcriptome discovery analysis is based on one tumor. HER2 and TROP2 were examined in two additional public Xenium specimens, but only one was clearly documented as a different patient. B7-H3 and PSMA were not present in the targeted validation panel. Their low-abundance stromal and vascular patterns, therefore, require confirmation in larger, patient-level cohorts across breast cancer subtypes. Cell annotations were marker-based rather than reviewed against matched histopathology. Differential expression tests also treated cells from a single specimen as independent units, which can inflate statistical confidence. Effect sizes and marker identity are more informative here than nominal cell-level P values. Public metadata did not consistently provide specimen-level sex and gender information, and these variables were not analyzed. Whole-transcriptome imaging was sparse for individual genes, limiting per-cell quantification. The bulk and survival analyses were based on a single cohort, and no signal of survival remained after adjustment. Most importantly, every target measurement was messenger RNA. ADC binding depends on the availability of an accessible cell-surface protein, whose RNA abundance cannot be measured directly. We did not assess protein localization, internalization, drug response, or toxicity. The findings are therefore descriptive and hypothesis-generating. Conclusion Single-cell spatial transcriptomics separated ADC targets enriched in tumor epithelium from targets expressed in stromal and vascular cells. HER2 and TROP2 showed the most consistent tumor enrichment across the three profiled specimens, whereas EGFR did not. These RNA-level findings should inform the design of protein-level, multi-patient validation studies. They cannot substitute for direct measurement of surface antigen or ADC activity. Compartment-resolved protein confirmation, followed by correlation with ADC response and toxicity in treated cohorts, is the necessary next step before any of these observations is applied clinically. Ethics approval and informed consent This study used only publicly available, de-identified datasets and involved no direct participant contact or new data collection. Ethical approval and informed-consent procedures for the source studies were reported in the original dataset publications. No additional ethics approval or informed consent was required for this secondary analysis. Data and code availability All analyzed datasets are publicly available. The discovery dataset was the CosMx SMI Human Whole Transcriptome FFPE breast dataset (breast discovery release, sample S0; Bruker Spatial Biology; https://nanostring.com/products/cosmx-spatial-molecular-imager/ffpe-dataset/ ). The validation datasets were the Xenium Human Breast invasive ductal carcinoma specimen (Xenium_V1_FFPE_Human_Breast_IDC_With_Addon) and the Human Breast Cancer reference block (Xenium_FFPE_Human_Breast_Cancer_Rep1) from the 10x Genomics Datasets portal ( https://www.10xgenomics.com/datasets ). TCGA-BRCA gene expression and clinical data were obtained from the UCSC Xena TCGA hub ( https://tcga.xenahubs.net ). evidence_text:
Molecular characterization of large cell neuroendocrine carcinoma of the lung by multilayered omics analysis. Large cell neuroendocrine carcinoma (LCNEC) is a rare type of lung cancer with a very poor prognosis, and its underlying molecular features remain elusive. Here, multi-omics analysis of 27 LCNEC cases along with seven small cell lung carcinomas is performed. The genomic and epigenomic alterations as well as the correlation of the genomic mutations with the pathological subtypes are characterized, which are not always consistent. Spatial omics analyses are also conducted, and most of the cases are successfully grouped into a high ASCL1 neuroendocrine (NE) subtype and high ASCL2 or YAP1 non-NE subtypes; however, an ambiguous state is observed for some specimens, which shows the simultaneous expression of NE and non-NE lineage markers. The findings of this study indicate that LCNEC may transit toward the NE or non-NE directions. By controlling the transcriptional regulatory networks of such elasticity, a new approach may be contemplated to overcome the pleiotropic therapeutic responses of LCNEC. Introduction  Lung cancer accounts for a large fraction of the high cancer mortality rate worldwide. To eradicate lung cancer, molecular characterization has rapidly progressed not only at the genome level, but also at the transcriptome, epigenome, and proteome levels. For the major subtypes, such as lung adenocarcinomas, mutations in driver genes have been identified, and molecular targeted drugs have been developed  1  . Immune cell-targeting approaches have also been established for the major cancer types  2  , including detailed clinical regimens for immune checkpoint blockage (ICB). Given the advances in treatment, the prognoses of lung cancer patients have markedly improved, particularly for those having drug-matched driver mutations or immune cell “hot” tumors, including tumors exhibiting a high tumor mutational burden (TMB) and tumors infiltrated with highly active immune cells  3  . Nonetheless, a large number of patients with lung cancer still lack rational therapies because the molecular pathology remains unclear.  Large cell neuroendocrine carcinoma (LCNEC) is a minor lung cancer type. It has a very poor prognosis with a 5-year survival rate of 17–57%  4 , 5  . Although it is relatively rare, it accounts for nearly 3% of total lung cancer cases; however, its molecular features are largely undefined. This lack of molecular data for each of the phenotypes hinders their precise diagnosis and optimal treatment, which render chemotherapy the standard treatment  6  , although the association between the genomic mutation patterns and the pathological phenotypes is unclear.  Some pioneering studies have been conducted for small cell lung carcinomas (SCLCs), which also belong to the same high-grade neuroendocrine carcinomas (HGNECs) along with LCNEC. SCLC also has a poor prognosis, with a 5-year survival rate of 5%  4  . Clinically, SCLCs are classified into neuroendocrine (NE) and non-neuroendocrine (non-NE) subtypes. Pathologically, the NE and non-NE subtypes may be further subdivided on the basis of the immunostaining patterns of lineage-associated transcription factors and activators, including the  ASCL1  and  NEUROD1  subtypes in NE and the  POU2F3  and  YAP1  subtypes in non-NE (designated as SCLC-A, SCLC-N, SCLC-P, and SCLC-Y subtypes)  7 , 8  . Some SCLC subtypes are also classified by inflammation patterns. SCLC-I may respond to ICB therapy because a large amount of immune cell infiltration is observed, which indicates that immunotherapy will show high efficacy  9 , 10  . The tumors of SCLC-I also exhibit high expression levels of epithelial–mesenchymal transition-related genes and various differentiation phenotypes. Recent studies have suggested that SCLC-I may overlap primarily with SCLC-Y  11 , 12  .  Based on the knowledge obtained from SCLC, several attempts have been made to characterize LCNEC at a molecular level, but only a limited number of studies have been published. This may be partly due to not only because LCNEC is a rare cancer subtype but also because the rate of cancer progression is so rapid that surgery is not an option for the majority of cases. Nevertheless, George et al.  13  , successfully generated the first dataset of LCNECs, in which the cases were classified in accordance with mutation patterns, with Type 1 having a  TP53  mutation only and Type 2 having  TP53  and  RB1  mutations. Another subtype, namely Type SCLC, is also defined by considering the expression patterns of a group of marker proteins. The first attempt was made to associate these types with the pathological (NE or non-NE; ASCL1, NEUROD1, POU2F3, or YAP1 types) subtypes, which were similarly defined as a case of SCLC; however, its correlation with clinical phenotypes remains unclear. In addition, the genomic mutational patterns may be even more complex, leaving a substantial number of relevant genomic features overlooked, such as large structural variants (SVs) and mutations occurring in repetitive regions  14 , 15  . Thus, extensive long-read whole-genome sequencing (WGS) analysis is necessary  16 – 18  , in which the DNA methylation status can be determined  19  .  The transcriptome knowledge of LCNEC remains even poorer, although transcriptome subtyping of LCNEC is expected to yield important information to reveal highly heterogeneous or versatile changes of their cancer cell phenotypes. Notably, LCNEC can display different expression profiles. The co-occurrence of lung adenocarcinoma or lung squamous cell carcinoma has been observed in approximately 12% of the cases  20  , indicating that parts of LCNEC may originate from a subgroup of these cancers, possibly through trans-differentiation. After emergence, the elastic nature of the transcriptome programs may be retained, thereby enabling a wide variety of phenotypes. To precisely understand the gene expression changes in LCNEC, further in-depth analysis of omics features is necessary, including those of the surrounding stromal and immune cells.  To elucidate the heterogeneous transcriptomic profiles of tumors in general, various spatial transcriptome technologies have been recently developed  21 – 23  . Using these spatial transcriptome techniques, various gene expression profiles are associated with tumor cell proliferation, and their changes into more malignant phenotypes in the complex tumor microenvironment (TME) have been established. Moreover, new insights into these phenotypes have been obtained, which cannot be clarified solely by analyzing their genomic mutations. The key factors influencing heterogeneous tumor phenotypes have been identified  24 , 25  . For LCNEC, such an approach will enable the precise molecular characterization of the genomic and multi-omics aberrations in LCNEC. Furthermore, this approach will provide insights into the biology of HGNEC.  Here, we show a series of systematic multi-omics studies of LCNEC, including WGS for 34 HGNEC specimens (27 and seven cases of LCNEC and SCLC, respectively). Moreover, 21 cases (LCNEC) were further subjected to long-read WGS analysis for SV and DNA methylation analyses. Spatial RNA profiling using Xenium in situ hybridization was conducted for all 34 HGNEC cases. Using the Xenium data, each cancer cell, even within a single case, was classified into one of the aforementioned subtypes. A similar characterization was also conducted for the surrounding stromal and immune cells. For network level analyses, sequence-based approaches were used, which included single-nucleus RNA-seq (snRNA-seq), Visium, and STOmics. The transcriptome profiles of tumor cells were also elucidated at the whole transcriptome level.    Results   Study design  Multi-omics analysis was conducted for 34 HGNEC cases (27 LCNEC and seven SCLC cases; Fig.  1a ). Based on pathological analysis using immunohistochemistry (IHC), these cancers were classified into four subtypes: 16, 3, 10, and 5 cases of ASCL1-positive (A-type), NEUROD1-positive (N-type), POU2F3-positive (P-type), and YAP1-positive (Y-type) subtypes, respectively (Supplementary Table  S1 ). Long-read WGS analysis (average sequencing depth of 58.5×; N50 read length of 14.5 kb in tumor genomes) was also conducted for 21 LCNECs (Supplementary Table  S2 ). The spatial gene expression data were collected for all 34 cases using Xenium (version 1 using the custom panel of 302 genes, Supplementary Table  S3 ). To validate the expressions of key genes, 13 cases were also analyzed by Xenium 5 k (Supplementary Table  S4 ). Visium analysis was conducted for 19 of the cases (Supplementary Tables  S5 ). The datasets of short-read WGS (average sequencing depth of 91.1× in the tumor genomes) and parts of the spatial omics analysis, which have been obtained for our previous study  26 , 27  , were also used. The statistics for the generated datasets are described in the supplementary information.    Fig. 1   Characterization of the LCNEC genomes.   a  Overview of the study.  b  OncoPrint of the point mutations and SVs for 21 cases. The samples in the plot are arranged by four subtypes (ASCL1, NEUROD1, POU2F3, and YAP1). TMB is shown above the plot. The percentages shown to the right of the plot indicate the mutation rate for the 21 samples. Genes were selected from highly mutated genes associated with cancer or reported in previous studies  13 , 91 , 92  . Gray squares indicate no mutation. Point mutations are all one colored square, but SV is displayed shorter than the point mutation.  c  Lollipop plots showing the locations of the mutations in the ADAMTS family. Blue, red, and green lollipops indicate a frameshift with deletion, nonsense mutations, and missense mutations, respectively. The vertical axis represents the number of mutations.  d  Mutations and IHC scores for cases classified by the George et al. subtype (G-subtype)  13  . The upper part shows the  TP53 ,  RB1 ,  STK11 , and  KEAP1  mutations, whereas the lower part shows the IHC score for ASCL1, NEUROD1, POU2F3, and YAP1. Gray squares indicate no mutation. The higher the IHC score, the darker the purple color. Type 1 was classified as a case with mutations in  TP53  and  STK11/KEAP1  and expressing NE markers. Type 2 was classified as a case with mutations in  TP53  and  RB1  but not expressing NE markers. Type SCLC was classified as a case with  TP53  and  RB1  mutations and expressing NE markers, and the others were classified as “Others”.  e  IHC scores of TTF-1 and ASCL1 by cases classified by the G-subtype. TTF-1 is shown in green, and ASCL1 is shown in red bar plots. Source data are provided as a Source Data file for ( e ).                     Genomic mutational features of LCNECs  Using the WGS data of the 21 LCNEC cases, their mutation patterns were characterized. Short and long-read datasets were used for detecting mainly point mutations and SVs, respectively. Overall, the average number of detected point mutations was 15.4 per Mb, which is far higher compared with other lung cancer subtypes (Supplementary Fig.  S1a )  28  . This difference may be partly due to the fact that most patients with LCNEC (20 cases, 95%) have a smoking history, which is further supported by the observation that their mutational signatures showed a high proportion of tobacco-related signatures, including SBS4, ID3, and DBS2 (Supplementary Fig.  S1b ).   TP53  and  RB1  mutations are present in 90% (19 cases) and 57% (12 cases) of the cases, respectively (Fig.  1b , Supplementary Fig.  S1c ), which is consistent with a previous study  13  . The long-read data were also used to detect mutations that were not covered by short-read data. For example, a 46.5-kb duplication was detected in  RB1 , and a 37.7-kb deletion included the  STK11  region. In the present study,  RB1  mutations were detected in all P-type cases. Mutations in other tumor-suppressor genes, such as  STK11  (five cases), were spread across the subtypes. Interestingly, a series of mutations was detected in the ADAMTS family genes as frequently as those in the LCNEC signature genes (76%, Fig.  1c , Supplementary Fig.  S1d ).  ADAMTS12  was previously reported as a frequently mutated gene in LCNECs  13  . The  ADAMTS20  gene was also mutated in six cases, followed by three cases containing  ADAMTS9  and  ADAMTS12  mutations, thereby indicating their potential application as marker genes for this cancer subtype. Moreover, all three  ADAMTS12 -mutant cases were classified as A-type tumors. This gene family encodes a metalloprotease, and it is associated with anti-tumor immunity and inflammation  29  . Several studies have indicated that this gene family may have a functional role in lung cancers (also see below section of the in vitro assays)  30  .  Among all LCNEC cases, the overall mutation rate was highly variable. The total number of mutations in protein-coding genes showed no significant difference between the NE and non-NE subtypes (Supplementary Fig.  S1e ). A case of the highest mutation rate (tkbhgnec6) involved a patient who received neo-adjuvant therapy, which could be explained by the effects of the anti-cancer drug. Two of the cases (tkbhgnec10 and tkbhgnec13), which showed low mutation rates, involved younger patients. Compared with other cases, no  TP53  mutation was detected in these two cases. One of the cases, tkbhgnec10, harbored a  KRAS  G12 mutation, which is a well-known driver mutation for lung cancers  31 , 32   but very rare in LCNEC.    Relationship of genomic mutations with clinical or pathological subtypes  In this study, the relationship between the clinical/pathological subtypes and the observed mutational patterns was precisely examined. Based on George et al. classification scheme  13   (referred to as the “G-subtype” in this study), the 21 LCNEC cases were classified into Type 1 (NE type:  TP53  [and  STK11/KEAP1 ] mutation-positive and  RB1  mutation-negative) and Type 2 (non-NE type:  TP53  mutation-positive and  RB1  mutation-positive). In this study, only two and five cases were categorized as Type 1 and 2, respectively (Fig.  1d ). Five cases were classified as Type SCLC with NE properties. The remaining nine (43%) cases were unclassified.  The relationship between the IHC profiles of the representative diagnostic markers and the subtypes was also examined. The results showed that Type 1 cases overlapped with the NE type and exhibited a high expression of ASCL1. The expression level of TTF-1/NKX2-1 was also high (Fig.  1e ), which is consistent with a previous report indicating that TTF-1 is involved in the maintenance of NE properties (Supplementary Fig.  S1f ,  g )  33  . However, no TTF-1/NKX2-1 expression was detected in Type 2 LCNEC cases, which belong to the non-NE type. Most of the P-type cases belonged to Type 2, whereas all of the Type SCLC tumors exhibited TTF-1/NKX2-1 expression along with ASCL1 expression. Overall, no significant correlation was observed between ASCL1 and TTF-1/NKX2-1 expression (Pearson’s correlation coefficient = 0.10, Fig.  1e ), indicating that these two networks may be under distinct regulatory programs. Interestingly, in several cases, IHC showed a double-positive (DP) pattern for ASCL1 and YAP1 (Fig.  1d ), although their expression was supposed to be mutually exclusive as subtype markers (see spatial transcriptome analysis below for further details on this issue). These patterns have also been reported in other studies  10 , 34  .    Long-read data detects complex genomic structures in the LCNEC genome  We hypothesized that the patterns of the SVs or aberrant DNA methylation as detected by the long reads may be useful for the classification of LCNECs. For SVs, LCNEC genomes harbored a large number of rearranged regions compared with other lung cancer types analyzed in previous studies  16 , 18  . In addition, the SV patterns were distinct from that of point mutations for each subtype (Fig.  2a ). The N-type tumors harbored significantly lower numbers of SVs ( P  < 0.05; Welch’s  t -test, Fig.  2b ), whereas the Y-type tumors contained a larger number of SVs compared with other subtypes ( P  = 0.11; not statistically significant, Fig.  2b ). Moreover, in many cases, the SVs were associated with repetitive regions, including long interspersed element 1 (L1, LINE-1), which is a mobile repeating element in the human genome. Abnormal L1 retrotranspositions have been identified in several tumors, and they may cause the deletion of tumor-suppressor genes, complex structural abnormalities, and oncogenes amplifications  35 , 36  . For example, a large number of L1 insertions were detected in tkbhgnec8 (a case categorized as “Others” in the above-mentioned G-subtype classification), indicating that L1 transposition became active at a certain phase of tumor progression (Fig.  2c ). Using the single breakend SV module of Nanomonsv  37  , which enables repeat-associated ambiguous alignments, candidate SVs were successfully detected in a comprehensive manner (Fig.  2d ). SVs frequently overlapped with known cancer-related genes. In tkbhgnec3 (another case of “Others”),  NF1  was disrupted by a rearrangement occurring at the repetitive region (Fig.  2e ). The disruptions in  PTEN  were detected in two cases, which were both non-NE tumors (Fig.  2e ). For tkbhgnec8, which contained the largest number of L1-associated SVs,  PTEN  translocations with chromosome 2 were detected. A partial human L1 sequence was inserted into the breakpoint, indicating that the L1 transposition event may have initiated cancer progression.
