Long-read analysis also detected the LCNEC genomes, which occasionally harbored a large number of high copy number regions, including extrachromosomal DNAs (ecDNAs). ecDNA is a recently characterized class of copy number aberrations, in which a particular genomic region is dissected from the chromosome and forms an independent replication unit  38 , 39  . Seven ecDNA candidates were detected in five cases that were assigned to only A- or P-types (Fig.  2f , Supplementary Fig.  S2a , Supplementary Table  S6 ). For example, in jichihgnec28, a 1.5-Mb region, including the  MYCN  gene, was detected as a candidate ecDNA (left, Fig.  2f ). In tkbhgnec2, a 476-kb region, including the  MYB  gene, was detected as a region of heavy amplification (CN = 12.07; right, Fig.  2f ). The transcription factor  MYB  and its amplification/overexpression promoted cell proliferation  40  . Several ecDNA candidates were also detected as homogenously staining regions (HSR) located within chromosomes (Supplementary Fig.  S2b ). To validate these ecDNA, fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) analysis was conducted. Furthermore, the  MYC  ecDNA candidate in jichihgnec25 was verified (Fig.  2g ). Compared with the control (jichihgnec23 without  MYC  aberrations), significant  MYC -amplified signals were detected in tumor cells of jichihgnec25 (Fig.  2h ).    DNA methylation patterns in the LCNEC genome  The DNA methylation features were also characterized (Fig.  3a , Supplementary Fig.  S3a ). We found that hypo-methylation occurred in most cases (Fig.  3b ). In particular, five cases exhibited lower methylation patterns. No significant difference was detected in the genome-wide methylation pattern among the four subtypes (Supplementary Fig.  S3b ). No significant correlation was also observed between the degree of hypo-methylation and mutation frequency (Fig.  3c ), although genome-wide hypo-methylation has been frequently associated with genomic instability in other cancer subtypes  41 , 42  . The degree of DNA methylation was most diverse in the non-NE type, as the most relevant hypo-methylated and hyper-methylated cases were identified in the Y-type (tkbhgnec1, “Others”) and P-type (jichihgnec28, “Type 2”) groups, respectively (Fig.  3b ). Association of genomic and epigenomic patterns with pathological subtypes  Despite intensive analysis of the obtained genomic DNA data, the association between the revealed genomic features of LCNECs and the pathological subtypes remained unclear. The point mutation patterns were not significantly different among subtypes, except for  RB1  mutations. Regarding SVs, a larger number, particularly those associated with repeat elements, were enriched in Y-type cases, whereas ecDNA candidates were detected in A-type or P-type cases; however, those features were not always decisive. Alternatively, most of the differences, which render this cancer type distinct from other lung cancer types, were not clearly evident from these analyses.    Diverse transcriptome features in LCNEC tissues  The transcriptome of the specimens was examined to determine whether they were associated with various pathological subtypes. Using Xenium equipped a full custom 302-gene panel  18  , data for 37 tissue sections representing 34 HGNECs (27 LCNEC and seven SCLC cases; Supplementary Table  S3 ) were successfully generated. A total of 14,110,579 cells were classified into 34 clusters and assigned to 14 cell types (Fig.  4a , Supplementary Fig.  S4a ). Immune and stromal cells were readily separated from tumor cell clusters. A total of 8,190,322 epithelial cells were extracted and assigned to NE and non-NE tumor cells along with normal epithelial cells. The tumor cells showed specific expression profiles among the patients, particularly those belonging to different subtypes (broken line, Fig.  4b ). On the contrary, the microenvironmental stromal and immune cells showed diverse expression patterns, but they were not separated by the patients (left side, Fig.  4b ). For a more precise classification, particularly for epithelial cells consisting of tumor cells, a second round of clustering was conducted, in which 26 sub-clusters were identified (Fig.  4c ). A clearer association was observed compared with genomic DNA analysis between the pathological and molecular subtypes (Supplementary Fig.  S4b ). Most of the A- and N-types were assigned to the NE type (highly  ASCL1 -expressing cells were defined as the NE type because  NEUROD1  probes were not included in the custom Xenium panel; see further discussion in Supplementary Fig.  S5 ), whereas the P-type cells were assigned to non-NE tumors. Y-type tumor cells exhibited diverse patterns depending on the case, with clusters located in the bridging area of other clusters. Notably, for some of the Y-type cases, although YAP1 is related to the non-NE epithelial lineage, tumor cells expressing NE markers, such as  CALCA , were also identified (Supplementary Fig.  S4c ). A series of validation analysis for the v1 panel was conducted using the 5 k panel from a viewpoint of the wider variety of genes (Supplementary Fig.  S6 ).  In general, non-NE tumors were divided into two subtypes based on the expression of  YAP1  and  ASCL2  (the  ASCL2  gene was utilized instead of  POU2F3  because the  POU2F3  gene was not included in the Xenium panel; however, the gene expression patterns mostly overlap with  ASCL2   45 , 46  . The overlapping expression pattern of  POU2F3  and  ASCL2  is shown in Supplementary Figs.  S5 ,  S6 ). When we examined the clustering pattern, some sub-clusters showed a neutral pattern between the NE and non-NE type tumor cells (in purple; Fig.  4c, d ). In addition, the cells expressed NE ( ASCL1 ) and non-NE ( YAP1  or  ASCL2 ) marker genes (designated “DP” type). Five cases contained these DP-type tumor cells as a large proportion of the total cells (Supplementary Fig.  S4d ). For example, for tkbhgnec6, which was classified into Y-type cases,  ASCL1  was also expressed in addition to  YAP1  (Fig.  4e ). A significant amount of  ASCL1/YAP1-  or  ASCL1/ASCL2 -DP cells were detected in the DP cases (Fig.  4f ). To validate the presence of DP cells, snRNA-seq was conducted using strictly dissociated cells for representative cases (Fig.  4g , Supplementary Table  S7 ). Again, the simultaneous expression of NE and non-NE marker genes within a single cell was observed in these cases. Even in some cases in which the tumor cells were categorized as NE, some cells contained these DP features but to a lesser extent.  To characterize DP cases, genes in which mutations were over- and under-represented in DP cases were detected (Supplementary Fig.  S4e ). First, DP cases did not harbor any  RB1  mutations (Fig.  4d ). On the contrary, six genes, including  STK11 , were highly mutated in DP types. In a previous study  13  , cases having  STK11  mutations were classified into Type 1 LCNECs. They reported that Type 1 LCNECs shared mutation profiles with lung adenocarcinomas and squamous cell carcinomas. The fact that DP types overlapped with Type 1 LCNECs and harbored evident non-NE profiles should be in line with the previous study. No obvious driver (gain-of-function) mutation was found in this subtype, which was attributed to the observed ambiguous phenotype of DP cases. The lack of evident drivers in the DP type, together with the  STK11  mutation, may allow the multi-faceted activation of the pathways, which are activated occasionally in adenocarcinomas or squamous cell carcinomas. The DNA methylation patterns of the DP cases were also re-examined, which exhibited low DNA methylation levels in the promoters and enhancers of the  ASCL1  and  YAP1  genes. This pattern may result in the transcriptional activation of both genes in these cells (Supplementary Fig.  S4f ).  In addition, other six sections (five cases) contained pure NE and non-NE tumor regions in the same tissue section (Fig.  4d , Supplementary Fig.  S4g ; designated as “Mixed” type). It is highly unlikely that these two regions originate from independent cancers based on the genomic mutation profiles (Supplementary Fig.  S4h ,  i ). We also validated that these tumors arouse from the single origin by conducting multiregion genome sequencing (Supplementary Fig.  S7 ; the detailed analysis of the data will be published elsewhere). It is rather more likely that these cases also represent the highly dynamic nature of the transcriptome in this cancer subtype. To further clarify this hypothesis, the expression profiles of the NE and non-NE regions of these mixed cases were examined. Based on the Xenium trajectory (Fig.  5a, b ), the NE and non-NE tumors were primarily included within the overall clusters of the respective groups, although they did not reside in the cluster core. These results indicated that the LCNEC cells could be differentiated into the NE and non-NE types through transcriptome changes. Transcriptional network changes in LCNEC tumor cells  The mechanism by which the tumor cells may go back and forth between the NE and non-NE states was further characterized by altering their transcriptome programs, with the DP type residing between them and the Mixed type as a developed form in both directions. Based on transcriptome trajectory analysis, we found that, starting from a normal alveolar epithelial cell as the root, the differentiation states of the tumor cells were primarily bifurcated  46   to the NE and non-NE directions (Fig.  5a, b ; Supplementary Fig.  S4j  for SCLC cases). For the non-NE trajectory, the normal  YAP1 -positive epithelium progressed to high  YAP1  tumors and further changed into high  ASCL2 -expressing tumor cells. On the contrary, the NE type tumors were separately mapped onto the trajectory at the opposite side of the non-NE branch. The DP-type sub-clusters branched out from various states of the NE and non-NE tumors. Although highly indicative, limitations were still evident, as this trajectory was only derived from the 302-gene Xenium panel. In addressing such limitations, trajectory analysis was also performed using the snRNA-seq data, indicating the bifurcate trajectory similar to that of Xenium (Supplementary Fig.  S5j ).  To characterize the more comprehensive transcriptomic features of the versatile differentiation of the tumor cells at a network level, the whole transcriptome data was analyzed. For this purpose, Visium analysis was conducted for 19 LCNEC cases using freshly frozen specimens (Supplementary Fig.  S5a ,  b , Supplementary Table  S5 ). A total of 35,688 spots were analyzed, including 23,917 epithelial cell spots, which showed similar bifurcation patterns in the case of Xenium analysis.  To comprehensively understand the transcriptome features, a Waddington-like landscape for the cells was generated (Fig.  5c ) as described previously  47   (see “Methods” for the detailed procedure). We found that the lineages for the DP cases were located adjacent to the Y-type and A-type cases (at the position indicated by a white circle). A substantial number of the cells of the Mixed type resided in the neighboring region, indicating that DP may be an intermediate in the transition from either the NE or non-NE type to the Mixed type. On the other side of the landscape, a group of tumor cells belonging to the non-NE type were found. These cells were primarily derived from  ASCL2  tumors. Mixed cells residing nearby were also found; however, no DP-type cells were observed. In this lineage, the transition state of DP may have been unstable; thus, it rapidly developed into a mixed state. In either of the cases, this landscape should represent the elastic nature of the transcriptome program of LCNEC. To observe the Mixed state of the cells, the prognosis of the patients with or without those cell types was examined. The results showed that the patients with the Mixed type exhibited poor prognosis among LCNEC as well as overall HGNEC, including SCLC cases (Fig.  5d ). To further evaluate the differentiation directions of LCNEC cells, we considered that the Mixed subtypes should appear as the corresponding ends of the trajectory paths of the NE and non-NE (Supplementary Fig.  S8 ). The Mixed types were widely and continuously positioned in the trajectories of the NE and non-NE paths. Notably, in Mixed cases with Ad/Sq-like and NE-like tumors, the NE cells were resided outside of the core trajectories of NE, which may have allowed these cells to flexibly differentiate to the YAP1-positive Ad/Sq direction. Collectively, these results indicated that the boundary between NE and non-NE cells should not always be decisive. The same trend was observed in Xenium 5 k analysis as well (Supplementary Fig.  S9 ).  In this study, we aimed to understand the nature of the transcriptome network for the respective states. Using network construction based on the weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA)  48 , 49  , 20 co-expression networks were identified for the tumor cells of the NE, non-NE, and DP cells (Fig.  5e ). Two network modules were uniquely activated in DP cells (Fig.  5e , Supplementary Fig.  S10 ). The upregulation of these module genes in DP cells was also validated by the snRNA-seq and STOmics data, which is a spatial platform strictly for single-cell resolution (Supplementary Fig.  S10c ,  S10d , Supplementary Table  S8 ). Module 13 was identified as a highly activated module in tkbhgnec11, including  CALCA , which is a typical NE marker. All DP cases activated Module 17. This module contained enriched Gene Ontology terms, including “Response to Endoplasmic Reticulum Stress (GO:0034976)” and “Cytokine Activity (GO:0005125)”, which indicates that cells with high Module 17 may be exposed to intense inflammation. It also included  FGL1 , which has been reported as the LAG3 ligand and is considered an immunosuppressive factor  50  . The cells with a transition status, such as DP cases, may be sensitive to ICB therapy, which reactivates the surrounding immune cell activity. A strategy to induce the de-differentiation/trans-differentiation of LCNEC cells to this DP state may render the cells more vulnerable to drug treatment for this difficult cancer subtype. The same strategy may be considered for a wider variety of subtypes. At present, a series of epigenome-targeting drugs are being developed  51 , 52  , which may be used to control the differentiation of the cells in a designated direction. Chromatin status, which is represented by DNA methylation, may also provide an important clue for this purpose.    Validation analysis of the possible transition of the lineage using cell lines  To validate the observed possible lineage transition from the NE to non-NE state, we conducted a series of in vitro experiments. For this, we conducted a timelapse gene knockdown (KD) analysis of  ASCL1  using two cell lines of LCNEC. Three independent siRNAs, having different KD efficacies, were introduced for the KD experiment (Supplementary Fig.  S11 ). Cells were collected after 0, 24, 48, 72, and 96 h of the transient transfection of the siRNAs. Those cells were subjected to single-cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq) conducted by 10× Flex (a probe-based scRNA-seq analysis), and the data was obtained with approximately 1000 cells per sample (62,885 and 92,878 mean reads per cell in VMRC-LCD and H810, respectively; Supplementary Table  S9 ). We expected that this dataset should represent timelapse features at different time points at different KD efficacy, and diversities inherent to each cell.  In VMRC-LCD, after 72 h KD, clear eventual activation of  YAP1  was observed (Fig.  5 f,  g ; also see Supplementary Fig.  S11  for further details). We further analyzed the pseudotime lineage eventually reaching the  YAP1  activation and found that there are roughly three stages, which were designated as “early”, “middle” and “late” transition states. The characteristic genes and the modules, which appeared at the “ambient” state in clinical specimens, gradually appeared from early, middle, to late states. At the module level analysis, the transition pattern of the DP-associated module, Module 17, which is mainly consisted of stress response genes, were similar with that of clinical samples (Supplementary Fig.  S11g ). At the gene-level analysis, we found that, in the middle state, the transition of  DLL3 , which is a downstream target of  ASCL1  and is a down-regulator of  NOTCH1  mRNA was relevant, suggesting, at this stage, the feedback regulation of  DLL3  may have been overcome at this stage. Interestingly, the above path was the most relevant in the KD series of  ASCL1  siRNA (siASCL1) #1, in which the KD efficacy was the largest. In the series of siASCL1 #2 and #3, giving a lower KD efficacy, a different path was more relevant, suggesting that lineage determination is dependent on the expression levels of  ASCL1 .  From the analysis of H810, the lineage transition was less diverse (Supplementary Fig.  S12 ). Most of the cells did not reach the full activation of  YAP1 , although genes expression changes similar with the middle state were observed. It should be also noted that the cell death rate in H810 was higher than that of VMRC-LCD, suggesting that the lineage determination is also dependent on the initial state of the cellular expression profile.  Taken together, these results clearly showed that the LCNEC cancer cells have inherent potential for the lineage transition, which should be very likely to occur in vivo. Also interestingly, we observed that the expressions of the ADAMTS family genes were induced towards the middle to late stage of the transition (Supplementary Fig.  S11p, q ). These genes are reported to play a role in lineage transition including EMT via their ECM remodeling function, thereby involved in the Notch signaling being regulated by the TGF-β signaling  53 – 55  . The mutations detected from the clinical samples might represent the functional role of these genes in this functional context.    Microenvironment statuses in each LCNEC subtype  To further pursue the possibility of ICB therapy for the LCNEC subtype, the status of the surrounding stromal cells, including immune cells, was characterized. ICB therapies are shown to be effective for a fraction of SCLC cases, particularly for the inflammatory subtype (SCLC-I subtype)  56  . Based on the Xenium data, a significantly large proportion of stromal cells, including fibroblasts and endothelial cells, were found in non-NE ( YAP1 ) types, including Mixed and DP-type cases (Fig.  6a ), compared with the other types. This finding indicates that their microenvironments may be generally distinct from the other types. Such a difference was particularly relevant for immune cells, with the non-NE ( YAP1 ) type exhibiting the largest population (Fig.  6b ). Several studies suggested that this Y-type has similar properties to SCLC-I  10 , 11  ; thus, ICB therapies are likely to be effective. Immune cell infiltration was also generally higher in the Mixed and DP types, indicating a similar potential for ICB therapies. If the treatment can be conducted before the DP and Mixed cases are consolidated for more difficult types, or if the transcriptional state can be induced back to these states, then more relevant ICB effects may be expected. The compositions of the neighboring cells were considered, and their patterns were classified into 20 CNs (Fig.  6c, d , Supplementary Fig.  S13b ). When we focused on immune cell-related CNs, CN2 appeared as a plasma-cell-rich niche. This CN2 was particularly associated with DP and non-NE subtypes but was less relevant in the NE subtypes (Fig.  6e  and Supplementary Fig.  S13c ). Despite the active immune potential, such tumors were immunosuppressive, which is the important feature of DP and non-NE subtypes. In particular, in DP-type cases,  FGL1  expression was relevant in tumor cells, allowing the escape from immune cell attacks. Such a plasma cell signature is reported as a predictive marker of the outcomes of PD-L1 blockage  57  . Immunotherapies may be effective for the DP subtype.  For the other subtypes, a similar level of immune cell filtration was observed. For example, three cases (tkbhgnec2, tkbhgnec24, and tkbhgnec19) harbored a large amount of infiltrating T cells (Fig.  6b ). This microenvironmental signature was identified as CN13, which is a T-cell-rich niche (Fig.  6f ). These cases consisted of tumor cells representing the non-NE type ( ASCL2 ; sub-cluster Non-NE-p-2 in Fig.  4c ) with high expression of immune response-related genes (Supplementary Fig.  S13d ). In these cases, tumor cells showing high expression levels of immunosuppressive genes, including  CD274  (PD-L1) and  IDO1 , may enable the cells to escape immune cell attack despite a large number of CD8+ cytotoxic T cells in the surrounding regions (right panel; Fig.  6g ). Given this molecular feature, the T cells were located only in the adjacent region, and they could not infiltrate into the tumor region (left panel; Fig.  6g ). Genomic mutation analysis of tkbhgnec2 revealed the amplification of the region with PD-L1 in addition to the PD-L2 and JAK2 regions. This amplification was reported as a potential marker for ICB efficacy  58 , 59  . This mutation may attract and eliminate immune cells. In many other cases, immune cell levels remained low despite belonging to the same subtype. In fact, the same profiles were also found from SCLC cases (Supplementary Fig.  S13e ). By inducing the transcriptional program before drug treatment to take advantage of the elastic nature of LCNECs, an altered microenvironment may be obtained to improve therapeutic effectiveness, including that of ICB therapeutics.  For further understanding lineage transition state in TME, we conducted the analysis of cell-cell interaction inference. We found that the enhanced signals of TGF-β mediated interaction, which is a representative indicator of de-differentiation, were detected for more than a half of the cases. Interestingly, these interactions appeared to be the most relevant in the tumor cells in the DP or Mixed (in particular, combined with Ad) cases (left, Fig.  6h  and Supplementary Fig.  S14 ). Interaction mediated by the Notch signaling, which is a representative marker for the non-NE differentiation and actually found from the cell assays, was also found, again suggesting that these interactions should play an important role in the lineage transition (right, Fig.  6h  and Supplementary Fig.  S14 ). A precise way to control the lineage transition, if found, should be clinically important. In fact, recently, a novel drug treatment strategy is being conducted where the cancer cells should be firstly converted to those of the lineage which is more vulnerable by a combinatory use of multiple drugs, such as those of EZH2-targeting drugs and the PI3K/AKT inhibitors (i.e., capivasertib) for triple negative breast cancer  60  . The features observed here may give an important clue to contemplate the treatment strategy for this difficult cancer type.     Discussion  In this study, genomic DNA and spatial transcriptome analyses of LCNECs were conducted. For this subtype, the clinical or pathological features could not be clearly represented solely by WGS sequencing, either by short or long-read sequencing. However, spatial transcriptome analysis provides new insights into the diverse behavior of this cancer. In fact, we unexpectedly found that the transcriptomic profiles were elastic, thereby enabling the stable existence of an intermediate status between the NE and non-NE subtypes and showing the DP and Mixed types. The observed diversity may be derived from a fluctuation in transcriptome regulation. The results of spatial analysis should be considered a complementary approach to genome-centered diagnosis. Moreover, when we characterized the characteristic profiles of surrounding cells, especially those of the immune cells, we found that the immune cell states were occasionally and significantly different even among the cases sharing the same transcriptome patterns and belonging to the same subtype. If an effective strategy can be designed to control the status of these elastic cancers, then we may have a wider choice of therapeutic strategies, including ICB therapies.  The identified molecular features of LCNECs would be associated with patient prognosis. As mentioned previously, mutation statuses alone were difficult to predict their survival rates. For example, focusing on ADAMTS family genes (the detailed multilayered omics features of these genes are shown in Supplementary Fig.  S15 ), no significant differences were found between mutant and non-mutant cases (Supplementary Fig.  S16a  in the George et al. public dataset  13  ). On the contrary, the DP-associated module in which some LCNEC cases showed a particularly high level would be a prognostic factor. The high group showed a significantly better prognosis in their dataset in the same manner as DP types in our dataset (Supplementary Fig.  S16b–d ).  Precisely, in this study, seven SCLC cases were included to the analysis as a common member of HGNEC. SCLC cells were exclusively mapped to either NE or non-NE branches (Supplementary Fig.  S4j ). Unlike LCNECs, no cases represented DP (Fig.  4d , Supplementary Fig.  S4b ), which made SCLC different from LCNEC. All the DP cases in LCNEC had no  RB1  mutations, unlike SCLC, which generally harbor  TP53  and  RB1  mutations  61  . Furthermore, a very recent publication of LCNEC analysis  62   reported that NSCLC-like LCNECs showed  FGL1  overexpression. This gene was included as a core member in the DP-specific co-expression module so that DP cells harbored molecular features similar to those of NSCLC cells. However, some common molecular features were found between LCNEC and SCLC. For example, the T-cell-rich stromal niche was observed in LCNEC and SCLCs. The non-NE-p-2 tumor sub-cluster (high PD-L1 and IDO1 expressions), which was involved in this niche, included one LCNEC and three SCLC sections.  This study provides a foundation for a comprehensive understanding of the molecular background of diverse tumor subtypes and their progression mechanisms in LCNEC, thereby leading to the identification of vulnerable points in the tumors, which are therapeutic targets for each subtype.    Methods   Clinical samples  A total of 34 cases of SCLC or LCNEC diagnosed at Tsukuba University Hospital (Ibaraki, Japan) and Jichi Medical University Hospital (Tochigi, Japan) between 2010 and 2023 were retrospectively enrolled. All cases involved surgically resected lung specimens. A histopathological evaluation was independently performed by three pathologists (K.A., R.M., and D.M.) in accordance with the 2021 World Health Organization classification of thoracic tumors. Clinical information was retrieved from the patients’ medical records. All samples were obtained with the appropriate informed consent at the University of Tsukuba Hospital and Jichi Medical University Hospital. This study was approved by the institutional ethics committees at the University of Tsukuba, Jichi Medical University, and the University of Tokyo. Specimens from both males and females were used in this study. As information regarding sex or gender was not the focus of this study, it was not taken into account in the statistical analysis.    Immunohistochemistry  Immunohistochemical staining was conducted on FFPE sections with a 3-μm thickness. The representative sections for each case were stained with the following primary antibodies: ASCL1 (556604, BD Pharmingen), NEUROD1 (ab213725, Abcam), POU2F3 (HPA01652, Sigma-Aldrich), YAP1 (ab52771, Abcam), and TTF-1/NKX2-1 (IR056, Agilent).  The immunostaining intensity was evaluated as 0 (negative), 1+ (weak), 2+ (moderate), or 3+ (strong). The percentage of tissue area displaying each intensity level was estimated for the entire section. An H-score was derived using the following formula:  H-score = [0 × (% at 0) + 1 × (% at 1 + ) + 2 × (% at 2 + ) + 3 × (% at 3 + )].    FISH  Automated SureFISH (Agilent Technologies) was performed using Dako Omnis (Agilent Technologies), which is an automated staining platform. In detecting  MYC  amplification, a set of SureFISH 8q24.21  MYC  294 kb P20 and SureFISH Chr8 CEP 635 kb P20 (Agilent Technologies) oligo probes was used. These probes were obtained from Dako Omnis and synthesized using oligo-based SureFISH technology (Agilent Technologies). The probes were mixed with IQFISH Fast Hybridization Buffer 900 (Agilent Technologies) at a ratio of 2:9. The deparaffinized and rehydrated sections were heated at 97 °C for 15 min in ISH Pretreatment Solution (Agilent Technologies) and subsequently incubated with ISH Pepsin (Agilent Technologies) at 32 °C for 18 min. Denaturation was performed at 66 °C for 10 min, followed by hybridization at 45 °C for 120 min. The sections were washed with ISH Stringent Wash Buffer (Agilent Technologies) at 61 °C for 10 min. After automated staining on the Dako Omnis, all specimens were manually coverslipped using Fluorescence Mounting Medium (Agilent Technologies) containing DAPI.    Long-read WGS  High-molecular-weight (HMW) DNA samples were extracted from FF tissues using the MagAttract HMW DNA Kit (Qiagen). Library preparation was performed using the Ligation Sequencing Kit (SQK-LSK114, ONT) in accordance with the manufacturer’s protocol. Sequencing was conducted with R10.4 flow cells (FLO-PRO114, ONT) using PromethION (ONT).    Short-read WGS  Using the extracted HMW DNA, library preparation was conducted using the TruSeq Nano DNA Library Prep kit (Illumina). Sequencing was conducted using NovaSeq 6000 (Illumina).    Multiregion WGS  For conducting multiregion WGS, regions of interest with different subtypes were marked by a pathologist on hematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-stained sections. The corresponding regions were dissected from 10 µm FFPE sections using the AVENIO Millisect system (Roche). Genomic DNA was extracted using the QIAamp DNA FFPE Tissue Kit (Qiagen) according to the manufacturer’s protocols. DNA concentration was assessed using the Agilent 2100 Bioanalyzer (Agilent Technologies). Library preparation was conducted from 50 ng of genomic DNA using the NEBNext UltraShear FFPE DNA Library Prep Kit (New England Biolabs). Sequencing was performed using NovaSeq X (Illumina) with 2 × 150 bp paired-end reads.    In situ RNA expression profiling by Xenium  For Xenium v1 analysis, the samples were prepared using the Xenium Slides & Sample Prep Reagents (PN-1000460, 10× Genomics). FFPE tissue blocks were sectioned at 5-µm thickness and placed on the Xenium slide (10× Genomics), followed by a 3-h incubation at 42 °C, in accordance with the manufacturer’s instructions ( CG000578 , Rev A, 10× Genomics). Deparaffinization and decrosslinking of the sectioned tissues were performed in accordance with the manufacturer’s instructions ( CG000580 , Rev A, 10× Genomics). Further preparation was conducted according to the instructions for “Xenium In Situ Gene Expression” ( CG000582 , Rev A, 10× Genomics). The pre-designed probes (302 genes reported in a previous report  18  ) were hybridized at 50 °C overnight. Post-hybridization wash, ligation, and amplification were also performed. Autofluorescence quenching and nuclei staining were performed in the dark. The Xenium run was performed using Xenium Analyzer (10× Genomics).  The similar protocols were employed for Xenium 5 k analysis. The pre-designed (5001 genes, Xenium Prime 5 K Human Pan Tissue & Pathways Panel) and custom add-on panels (98 genes and two boosted genes) were used. For cell segmentation, multimodal cell segmentation staining was performed according to the manufacturer’s instruction.    snRNA-seq  FF tissues were dissociated using the Chromium Nuclei Isolation Kit (PN-1000493, 10× Genomics) according to the user guide ( CG000505 , Rev A, 10× Genomics). The extracted nuclei were subjected to library preparation using a Chromium GEM-X Single Cell 3′ Kit v4 (PN-1000691, 10× Genomics) based on the manufacturer’s instructions ( CG000731 , 10× Genomics). The constructed library was sequenced using NovaSeq 6000 (Illumina).    Spatial transcriptome sequencing by Visium  For Visium analysis, FF tissues were sectioned at a 10-µm thickness, and the sections were placed on the Visium slide (10× Genomics). Fixation, H&E staining, and imaging were performed according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Tissue permeabilization was performed with a 12-min incubation. After the tissues were permeabilized, cDNA synthesis, amplification, and sequencing library preparation were conducted using Visium Spatial Gene Expression Reagent Kits (10x Genomics). Sequencing was conducted using NovaSeq 6000 (Illumina).    Spatial transcriptome sequencing by STOmics  For STOmics preparation, each step was conducted according to the manufacturer’s instructions. FF tissues were sectioned at 10-µm thickness, and the sections were placed on a STOmics chip (1 cm × 1 cm). Tissue fixation and fluorescent staining of single-stranded DNA were performed. Imaging was performed using a Leica DM6 B microscope. Tissue permeabilization was conducted for 12 min. Reverse transcription and tissue removal were conducted, and the cDNA samples were collected. After cDNA purification and amplification, library preparation was performed. Sequencing analysis was conducted using DNBSEQ-T7 (MGI).    KD assays and scRNA-seq by Flex for cell lines  VMRC-LCD cells and H810 cells were obtained from JCRB and ATCC by the catalog numbers of JCRB0814 and CRL-5816, respectively. VMRC-LCD was cultured using EMEM (M4655, Sigma-Aldrich) with 10% FBS, MEM Non-essential Amino Acid Solution (M7145, Sigma-Aldrich) and Antibiotic-Antimycotic (15240062, Gibco). H810 was cultured with DMEM/F-12 medium supplemented with 5% FBS, 0.005 mg/mL insulin (090-06481, Wako), 0.01 mg/mL transferrin (T0665, Sigma-Aldrich), 30 nM sodium selenite (196-10841, Wako), 10 nM hydrocortisone (088-02483, Wako), 10 nM β-estradiol (S1709, Selleck) and additional 2 mM L-glutamine (25030081, Gibco). Both cell lines were cultured in an incubator at 37 °C maintained at 5% CO 2 . For the  ASCL1  KD analysis, transfections were conducted using Lipofectamine RNAiMAX Transfection Reagent (13778150, Invitrogen) by a standard protocol provided by the manufacturer. The pre-designed siRNAs (Silencer Select Pre-designed: s1656, s1657, s1658 for  ASCL1 , Silence Select Negative Control No. 1 siRNA for negative control) were purchased for the experiment. The KD efficacy was evaluated by standard real-time RT-PCR procedures (RR096A, TaKaRa) using Roche LightCycler 96 System (Roche). The real-time PCR primers were designed as follows:  ASCL1  forward 5′-GGTGCGAATGGACTTTGGAA-3’,  ASCL1  reverse 5′- TCTCAGGCATGCCTCGCTTA-3′,  ACTB  forward 5′- TGGCACCCAGCACAATGAA-3′, and  ACTB  reverse 5′- CTAAGTCATAGTCCGCCTAGAAGCA-3′.  The cells were collected at the presented KD time points, and the fixation was made in 4% formaldehyde for 1 h at room temperature according to the manufacturer’s protocol ( CG000782 , Rev D, 10× Genomics). The fixed cells were subjected to the Flex analysis using GEM-X Flex V2 Reagent Kits ( CG000834 , Rev B, 10× Genomics). For the constructed libraries, sequencing was conducted using the AVITI24 platform (Element Biosciences) with 28/90-bp paired-end reads at the sequence statistics as indicated in Supplementary Table  S9 .    Detection of point mutations and SVs  Short-read WGS data were mapped to the human reference genome hg38 using BWA mem (version 0.7.17)  63   after adapter trimming and PCR duplicate removal. Point mutations, including SNVs and short indels, were detected by using GATK (version 4.1.3.0)  64   Mutect2, and then filtered using FilterMutectCalls. Annotation was added for each mutation by using ANNOVAR (version 2018Apr16)  65  .  Base calling of long read WGS data was conducted using Guppy (version 6.4.6 and 6.5.7, ONT). The sequencing data were mapped to the human reference genome hg38 using minimap2 (version 2.24)  66  . Somatic SVs were detected by Nanomonsv (version 0.7.2) using the normal counterpart sample as a control. In addition to detecting canonical SVs, analysis using the single breakend SV module of Nanomonsv was also conducted.  The mutation data were summarized and visualized using the maftools  67   R package based on the results of ANNOVAR.    Detection of CNVs  Copy number profiles were calculated using FACETS (version 0.6.2)  68   with “cval = 75, snp.nbhd = 5000, and ndepth = 5” for the preProcSample function and “cval = 800 and min.nhet = 25” for the procSample function.    Mutational signature analysis  Mutational signatures were extracted for somatic point mutations, copy number aberrations, and SVs. Then, the extracted signatures were decomposed into COSMIC mutational signatures (v3.3)  69   using SigProfilerExtractor (version 1.1.4)  70  .    Clone analysis  Clone numbers were estimated using the VAFs for point mutations by PyClone-VI (version 0.1.1)  71   with the option -c 40 -d beta-binomial -r 10. The number of variant tags counted by Mutect2 and the information on the copy numbers and cellularity calculated by FACETS were used as input.    Mutation detection using multiregion WGS data  Sequencing reads were aligned to the hg38 human reference genome with BWA mem (version 0.7.17) after conducting adapter trimming using fastp (version 0.23.2). Following the alignment, samtools (version 1.15) was used for coordinate sorting and indexing, and PCR duplicates were flagged with Picard MarkDuplicates (version 2.26.11). Mutations in  TP53  and  RB1  were evaluated at their respective loci by manual inspection on the Integrative Genomics Viewer (IGV) (version 2.17.4).    Detection and validation of ecDNA structures  The candidates of ecDNA were constructed using CoRAL (version 1.0)  72  . The regions with a copy number of ≥6 were set as the seed regions. The number of supporting reads was set to five or more as a prerequisite for creating the breakpoint plot to ensure the reliability of the breakpoints. Only cancer-related genes, which were included in the Bushman lab cancer-related gene list, were considered. To predict the generation mechanism, the ecDNA candidates were classified using the AmpliconClassifier (version 1.2.1)  73  . In addition, HSR and its candidate loci, where the ecDNA was integrated, were identified using CoRAL with the hsr option.    DNA methylation  To analyze the genome-wide DNA methylation status, the methylation status at each CpG site was initially aggregated from the modBAM file using the pileup module of modkit (version 0.3.1). Then, the entire human genome region was divided into 50-kb windows, and the methylation rate in each window was calculated. To calculate the methylation rate, the CpG sites supported by three or more reads in normal tissues and six or more reads in tumor tissues were analyzed. The methylation rate within each window was calculated by dividing the number of methylated CpG sites in the region by the number of reads at all CpG sites, and the methylation status of the entire genome was quantitatively assessed by the rate. The methylation rate for each 50-kb window was visualized as a heat map using IGV (version 2.17.4)  74 , 75  . To compare the DNA methylation status among LCNEC subtypes, the median methylation rate of the entire genome was calculated for each case.  To assess the methylation status of the transposons, RepeatMasker data obtained from the UCSC Table Browser were used. For LINE-1, the methylation rate was calculated for sequences containing regions with a length of 6 kb or more, which were likely to have transfer activity. In addition, the methylation rates of Alu and SVA elements were evaluated. To evaluate the methylation rate, the same criteria as in a similar way to the above were applied to the analysis of CpG sites supported by three or more reads in normal tissue and six or more reads in tumor tissue.  To analyze the methylation of the regions related to transcriptional regulation, the methylation rates for the CGI, CGI shore, promoter, and enhancer regions were calculated. Each area was defined as follows: The CGI region obtained from the UCSC Data Integrator was used for the analysis, and 2000 bp upstream and downstream of the CGI were defined as the CGI shore region. Based on the position of the transcription start site (TSS) obtained from Ensembl Biomart, a total of 2000 bp from 1000 bp upstream to 1000 bp downstream of TSS was designated as the promoter region. To define the enhancer region, public ChIP-seq data (Acc. DRA001860  76  ; H3K27ac: DRR017154, H3K4me1: DRR017151, control: DRR017155) were initially used for histone-modified H3K27ac and H3K4me1, which are the enhancer markers of VMRC-LCD, an LCNEC cell line. Then, the acquired fasta sequence data were mapped to the human reference genome hg38 using Bowtie2 (version 2.5.3)  77  . After mapping, the reads mapped to multiple locations were removed using samtools (version 1.19)  78  , and only unique map reads were extracted. Subsequently, the protein-binding regions of H3K27ac and H3K4me1 were detected using MACS3 (version 3.0.1)  79  , and the read enrichment regions identified by peak call were defined. Furthermore, the union of the peak regions of H3K27ac and H3K4me1 was calculated using the merge subcommand of bedtools (version 2.31.1)  80  . Finally, using the bedtools intersect subcommand, the area excluding the promoter region was defined as the enhancer region. The methylation rates were calculated for these four regions in a similar manner as described above, and comparative analyses were performed for each subtype.    Computational analysis of the Xenium data  Visualization was performed using Xenium Explorer (version 3.0.0, 10× Genomics). Further analyses were conducted using Seurat (version 5.0.3)  81  . Cells with >10 RNA counts were used.  To analyze the merged data for all sections, Seurat sketch-based analysis  82   was conducted as follows: (1) 5000 cells per section (185,000 in total) were subsampled using the SketchData function after normalization using Seurat; (2) using the subsampled cells, scaling and dimensional reduction by PCA were performed followed by clustering by the FindClusters function with a resolution of 1.0 using 30 PCs; (3) all of the cell data were projected onto the subsampled data. Cell-type annotation for each cluster was conducted on the basis of marker gene expression patterns.  To analyze each cell-type group in detail, the subsampled cells in each of the cell-type groups were extracted and re-scaled. Then, clustering was conducted by FindClusters with a resolution of 0.8 using the first 20 dimensions. Cell-subtype annotation for each sub-cluster was conducted according to the marker gene expression patterns in tumor and epithelial cells. Pseudotime trajectory analysis was conducted using Monocle 3 (version 1.3.7)  83   using the subsampled data of epithelial sub-clusters.    Computational analysis of the snRNA-seq data  The expression count matrix was generated using Cell Ranger (version 9.0.1, 10× Genomics). Further analyses were conducted using Seurat (version 5.0.3). The thresholds were set to nFeature_RNA > 250, nFeature_RNA < 6000, and percent.mt <10. Then, the data were log-transformed using NormalizeData and scaled using ScaleData. Clustering was conducted by FindClusters using the first 30 dimensions of PCA. Tumor cell clusters were defined based on the tumor and normal epithelial cell marker genes. For  ASCL1 ,  ASCL2 , and  YAP1  expression, the cells with a log-normalized count >0.25 were considered positive. In visualizing of all snRNA-seq datasets, cells from six samples were integrated by Harmony integration  84  .  Pseudotime trajectory analysis for all snRNA-seq datasets was conducted using Monocle 3 (version 1.3.7). Batch correction between samples was performed using the align_cds function. The percent of mitochondrial genes was also considered for data integration.    Computational analysis for Visium data  Mapping, the generation of the expression count matrix, and H&E image alignment were performed using Space Ranger (version 1.3.1, 10× Genomics). Further analyses were conducted using Seurat (version 5.0.3). All spots in the 19 cases were merged, and the count matrix was normalized and scaled. Integration was conducted by IntegrateLayers using the HarmonyIntegration  84   option. Clustering was performed using the first 30 dimensions of harmony reduction. All clusters were manually annotated according to cell-type marker expression.  The trajectory inference was conducted using Slingshot (version 2.10.0)  85   to detect simple differentiation paths in LCNECs considering intermediate phases. Only tumor cell spots were used. Harmony integration was performed to visualize the UMAP plot.  To construct gene co-expression networks, tumor and epithelial spots were extracted. Co-expression networks were constructed using hdWGCNA (version 0.3.3)  48 , 49  . Metaspots were created with the option min_spots = 25. The soft power threshold was automatically set to 10 for network construction. To extract modules upregulated in DP-type cases, differential module eigengene analysis was conducted using the FindDMEs function and the Wilcoxon rank-sum test.    Computational analysis of the STOmics data  STOmics data were processed by SAW (versions 5.4.0 and 6.0.0) using default parameters. The count data were converted using stereopy (version 0.7.0)  86  . The bin50 data were further analyzed using Seurat (version 5.0.3). Normalization was conducted using SCTransform. To determine the co-expression module activities, scores were calculated using the expression levels of the module member genes (kME >0.4) by the AddModuleScore function.    Computational analysis of the Xenium 5 k data  Visualization was performed using Xenium Explorer (version 5.0.0, 10× Genomics). The downstream analyses were conducted using Seurat (version 5.4.0). To merge the data of all 13 sections, 5000 cells per section were subsampled using Seurat SketchData function. Clustering was performed by Seurat FindClusters function with a resolution of 1.5. Cell-type annotation for each cluster was conducted on the basis of marker gene expression patterns. Trajectories were constructed using Monocle 3 (version 1.3.7) using the subsampled epithelial cells.    Computational analysis of the Flex scRNA-seq data  The expression count matrix was generated using Cell Ranger (version 10.0.0, 10× Genomics) from the  ASCL1  KD and control Flex scRNA-seq datasets of VMRC-LCD and H810 cell lines. The obtained matrix was analyzed using Seurat (version 5.3.1). For quality control, cells with the percentage of mitochondrial genes of ≤15% were retained. Cells with 4000–10,000 and 4000–11,000 detected genes were used for VMRC-LCD and H810, respectively. After filtering, the data were normalized, scaled with regression of cell-cycle scores, and subjected to dimensional reduction by PCA, UMAP visualization, and clustering. Pseudotime trajectory analysis was performed using Slingshot (version 2.14.0) with setting the initial-state cluster (0 h) as the starting point.  To extract expression changes in NE-to-non-NE transitions from VMRC-LCD data, cell populations showing major transcriptional changes after  ASCL1  KD were extracted for re-clustering and pseudotime trajectory analysis. Genes whose expression changed along the pseudotime were identified using tradeSeq (version 1.20.0). For this analysis, genes expressed in ≥20 cells were used, and mitochondrial and ribosomal genes were excluded. From the tradeSeq results, genes satisfying an adjusted  P -value < 0.05 and an expression range along the pseudotime (expr_range) ≥0.5 were extracted. Among them, the top 1000 genes with the highest test statistics were used for clustering based on the smoothed expression patterns along the pseudotime. To verify whether the obtained pseudotime-associated gene clusters were also present in the actual clinical specimens, the gene clusters were mapped to the UMAP plot of Xenium 5 k data.    Kaplan–Meier analysis  For our dataset, the differences in survival were calculated with the Peto-Peto modification of the Gehan-Wilcoxon test using the survdiff of the survival package of R. Significance level was tested at 5%. Kaplan–Meier curves were plotted using the ggsurvplot of the survminer package. With regard to the George et al. dataset (Supplementary Fig.  S10a, c ), the  P -values in survival analysis were calculated using the log-rank test.    Waddington-like landscape  A Waddington-like landscape  87   was generated using Visium data. The Visium spots were integrated by harmony integration using Seurat (version 5.2.1). PHATE coordinates were determined using the harmonized expression data (version 1.0.11, PHATE)  88  . Valley-ridge (VR) scores were calculated by adding the 0.9 valley and 0.1 ridge components. Valley components were determined using entropies, which were calculated by the CCAT algorithm (CompCCAT function, ppiA=net17Jan16.m) using SCENT (version 1.0.3)  47 , 89  . Ridge components were calculated by multiplying the inverse RNA velocity and spot centrality distance. RNA velocity was determined as the average displacement vector to the nearest neighbors ( k  = 5) based on the Euclidean distance. Landscape was visualized by Houdini (version 20.5.557, SideFX) using the PHATE coordinates and VR scores.    Niche analysis  Cellular niche analysis of microenvironmental cells was performed using the Xenium data, considering the compositions of the neighboring cells. A niche matrix (patterns of 25 surrounding cells) in each case was constructed using the Seurat BulildNicheAssay function (version 5.0.3). Then, the niche matrices of all the cases were merged and re-clustered by using K-means clustering ( k  = 20). All the microenvironmental cells were classified into 20 CNs.    Ligand-receptor analysis for cell-cell communication inference  Visium and Xenium 5 k data were used for inferring cell-cell communications. Using Visium data, ligand-receptor interactions of the “Secreted Signaling” were extracted using CellChat (version 2.1.2). The parameters were set to type = “truncatedMean” and contact.range = 100 for the computeCommunProb function.  Using Xenium 5 k data, the “Cell-Cell Contact” interactions were also considered in addition to the “Secreted Signaling” using CellChat (version 2.2.0.9001). The parameters were set to type = “truncatedMean”, scale.distance = 1, and contact.range = 10 for the computeCommunProb function, and min.cells = 500 for the filterCommunication function.    Statistics and reproducibility  No statistical method was used to predetermine sample size. No data were excluded from the analyses. The experiments were not randomized. The Investigators were not blinded to allocation during experiments and outcome assessment. For Xenium, 37 datasets from 34 cases were analyzed. For Visium, 19 representative cases were analyzed. For snRNA-seq, six representative cases were analyzed, particularly focusing on the DP type. For STOmics, two independent experiments were conducted for each of two cases. For Xenium 5 k, 13 representative cases were analyzed. A Reproducible CD36-Enriched Lipid-Associated Macrophage State in Lung Adenocarcinoma and Its Spatial Relationship to Exhausted CD8+ T Cells 1. Introduction  Lipid accumulation in the tumor microenvironment (TME) is increasingly recognized as a determinant of antitumor immunity [ 1 , 2 ]. Lipid uptake, synthesis and oxidation regulate the effector capacity of tumor-infiltrating CD8 +  T cells and can, in principle, be modulated pharmacologically [ 3 , 4 ], and among myeloid cells, lipid metabolism has been reported to shape tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) toward phenotypes that support tumor growth [ 5 ]. Lipid-handling macrophages are therefore of interest in lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD), including as potential targets for combination with immune checkpoint blockade (ICB). Single-cell studies have mapped the cellular composition of LUAD and changes in intercellular communication across disease stages [ 6 , 7 , 8 ]; however, it is not known whether a lipid-handling macrophage state in human LUAD is reproducible across patients and cohorts or how such a state is positioned relative to exhausted CD8 +  T cells.  CD36, a class B scavenger receptor and long-chain fatty acid transporter that binds oxidized low-density lipoprotein and cholesterol [ 9 , 10 , 11 ], is of particular interest because pharmacological CD36 inhibitors already exist and have shown preclinical activity in combination with anti-programmed cell death protein 1 (anti-PD-1) therapy [ 12 , 13 , 14 ]. Across several tumor compartments, CD36 blockade or genetic deletion has been reported to restore antitumor immunity in mouse models: CD36 inhibition synergizes with anti-PD-1 by relieving CD8 +  T-cell lipid peroxidation and ferroptosis [ 14 ]; CD36 blockade acts additively with anti-PD-1 in regulatory T cells without disrupting systemic immune homeostasis [ 12 ]; and myeloid-specific CD36 deletion suppresses tumor growth [ 13 ]. In non-small cell lung cancer, CD36 has been linked to tumor-cell lipid metabolism, macrophage reprogramming and T-cell function [ 15 ]. However, these findings were obtained in mouse models or in cell types other than human LUAD macrophages, and whether a reproducible CD36-expressing macrophage population exists in human LUAD and how it is positioned relative to exhausted CD8 +  T cells in situ have not been examined.  We therefore set out to characterize, in primary LUAD, (i) the identity and cross-cohort reproducibility of a lipid-associated macrophage (LAM) population with relative CD36 enrichment (CD36-enriched LAM) using cell- and patient-level analyses of two single-cell cohorts, together with candidate transcriptional regulators inferred from expression data; (ii) its spatial relationship to exhausted CD8 +  T cells in a single-cell-resolution spatial dataset and, under a pre-specified plan, in an independent spatial specimen; and (iii) candidate ligand–receptor interactions predicted from dissociated cells in order to derive experimentally testable hypotheses. We additionally performed drug-target Mendelian randomization (MR) using CD36 cis-expression quantitative trait loci (cis-eQTLs). This analysis addresses a different question from the tumor-microenvironment analyses—whether genetically determined systemic CD36 expression is associated with LUAD risk—and was used to delimit, rather than to support, the rationale for targeting CD36.    2. Materials and Methods   2.1. Data Sources  Data sources, platforms and analytic purposes are summarized in  Supplementary Table S1 . Single-cell RNA-sequencing data were obtained from GSE131907 (primary lung tumors) [ 6 ]; an independent replication cohort used GSE189357, which comprises nine patients with adenocarcinoma in situ (AIS), minimally invasive adenocarcinoma (MIA) or invasive adenocarcinoma (IAC) (three of each) [ 16 ]. Single-cell-resolution spatial transcriptomic data were obtained from a publicly available 10x Genomics (Pleasanton, CA, USA) dataset (Experiment 2: Xenium Prime 5K In Situ Gene Expression with Cell Segmentation, formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded (FFPE) human lung adenocarcinoma, Xenium Prime 5K Human Pan Tissue and Pathways Panel, Xenium Onboard Analysis v3.0.0; 278,328 cells), released under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0) license [ 17 ]. An independent spatial specimen from a different donor was obtained from the 10x Genomics Visium HD Spatial Gene Expression dataset of fixed-frozen human lung adenocarcinoma (CytAssist; Visium Human Transcriptome Probe Set v2.0; Space Ranger 3.1.1; CC BY 4.0) [ 18 ]. The commercially sourced, de-identified tissues used for these datasets were processed and released by 10x Genomics; no tissue was collected by the present authors. Bulk RNA-sequencing data from The Cancer Genome Atlas LUAD cohort (TCGA-LUAD) were used for an exploratory survival analysis of a barrier signature ( Supplementary Note S1 ). Anti-PD-1 cohorts GSE135222 (discovery) and GSE126044 (small independent supportive cohort) [ 19 ] were used for exploratory immunotherapy-response analyses. Genetic analyses used eQTLGen (CD36 cis-eQTL exposure data;  n  = 31,684) [ 20 ], the International Lung Cancer Consortium/Transdisciplinary Research in Cancer of the Lung (ILCCO/TRICL) LUAD genome-wide association study (outcome data; dataset ieu-a-984; 11,245 cases and 54,619 controls), FinnGen (independent replication cohort; 571 cases and 218,221 controls) [ 21 ] and Genotype-Tissue Expression (GTEx) v8 (tissue-specific eQTLs) [ 22 ]. No cell lines were used in this study, and no new human or animal samples were collected; all analyses used publicly available, de-identified secondary data, and no additional ethical approval was therefore required, as stated in the Institutional Review Board Statement.    2.2. Single-Cell and Spatial Transcriptomic Analysis  Only primary lung tumor cells from GSE131907 were retained. Quality-control thresholds were 200–7000 detected features per cell, a mitochondrial read fraction ≤20%, and genes detected in ≥3 cells. Following normalization, selection of 2000 highly variable genes (vst method), scaling and principal component analysis (30 components), Harmony batch correction [ 23 ] was applied using sample identity as the grouping variable. Clustering and uniform manifold approximation and projection used the first 20 Harmony dimensions (resolution 0.5 for all cells; 0.6 for myeloid subclustering). LAM program scores (CD36, TREM2, APOE, FABP5, GPNMB, SPP1, LPL, LGALS3, CTSB, CTSD, FABP4, PLIN2, ACP5, CD9, NUPR1) and immunosuppressive/M2 program scores (MRC1, CD163, IL10, ARG1, MARCO, TGFB1, CCL18, SPP1) were computed with the Seurat AddModuleScore function, which compares the mean expression of a gene set with that of expression-matched control genes [ 24 ] and is widely used to define macrophage states in single-cell data; because such scores can be influenced by dropout and baseline expression, cluster-level results were confirmed with the rank-based UCell method [ 25 ]. CD36-enriched LAM (clusters 0 and 3) was defined operationally by integrating CD36 detection, LAM program scores and myeloid subclustering, with MARCO + FABP4 +  alveolar macrophages (high LAM score, low CD36) serving as an internal comparator; the name denotes relative, not uniform, CD36 expression. In the patient-level, replication and transcription-factor leave-out analyses, CD36-enriched LAM was compared with other non-alveolar myeloid cells. Differentially expressed marker genes were identified using FindMarkers (only.pos = TRUE, min.pct = 0.25, logfc.threshold = 0.25) and, at patient level, by paired pseudobulk analysis ( Section 2.5 ). Exhausted CD8 +  T cells were identified primarily from the cell-subtype annotations provided with GSE131907 [ 6 ] and cross-validated using module scores for PDCD1, HAVCR2, LAG3, TIGIT, CTLA4, TOX, ENTPD1 and LAYN.  In the replication cohort, myeloid cells were reclustered with the same workflow. Clusters whose mean alveolar score (MARCO, FABP4 and MCEMP1; AddModuleScore) exceeded the larger of 0.3 and the across-cluster mean plus 0.5 standard deviations were classified as alveolar macrophages and excluded; among the remaining clusters, the one with the highest sum of the ranks of the fraction of cells with detectable CD36 and of the mean TAM-LAM program score (CD36, TREM2, APOE, SPP1, GPNMB, PLIN2, C1QA and C1QB) was taken as the candidate population (cluster 2). Because the features used for this selection overlap with those that would otherwise be used to judge similarity, replication was assessed with four criteria that do not depend on the selection genes; these criteria were defined post hoc after the replication cohort had first been analyzed. They were (i) presence of the candidate population in each patient; (ii) discrimination of the candidate population from other non-alveolar myeloid cells, overall and within each patient (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, AUC), by a held-out signature consisting of the top 50 discovery markers after removal of all 25 genes used for scoring or cluster selection (the union of the LAM, TAM-LAM, immunosuppressive and alveolar gene sets), scored with UCell, together with the reverse test (replication-derived signature scored in the discovery cohort); (iii) genome-wide concordance of patient-level log2 fold changes between cohorts; and (iv) projection of replication cells onto the discovery atlas by Seurat reference mapping [ 26 ]. To examine the lower CD36 detection rate in the replication cohort, discovery counts were binomially down-sampled to the median transcript depth of the replication cohort (20 draws), CD36 detection was compared with that in monocytes, and enrichment was tabulated by patient and lesion stage.  For the Xenium section, a gene was considered detected when at least one transcript was assigned to the cell. T cells were defined by CD3E; CD8 +  T cells additionally required CD8A or CD8B with CD8A + CD8B ≥ CD4; macrophages were non-T cells with CD68, CD163, MRC1 or ITGAX; and epithelial cells were EPCAM +  cells that were neither T cells nor macrophages. Spatial CD36-enriched LAM were defined as CD36-positive macrophages additionally positive for TREM2 or PLIN2; exhausted CD8 +  T cells were defined as CD8 +  T cells positive for ≥2 of 7 exhaustion markers (HAVCR2, LAG3, PDCD1, TIGIT, CTLA4, TOX, ENTPD1). Neighborhood analysis used each cell’s 10 nearest spatial neighbors. The number of CD36-enriched LAM–exhausted CD8 +  T-cell neighbor pairs was compared with null distributions from 1000 label permutations in which labels were shuffled either across all cells or only within the relevant compartment (LAM label among macrophages, exhausted label among CD8 +  T cells); in post hoc sensitivity analyses, the compartment-restricted shuffles were further stratified by deciles of transcript depth, by 250 × 250 μm tiles, or by 500 μm tiles combined with depth tertiles. Nearest-neighbor distances were compared between exhausted and non-exhausted CD8 +  T cells using the Wilcoxon rank-sum test; the exhausted fraction of CD8 +  T cells was tabulated by distance to the nearest CD36-enriched LAM, tested with the chi-squared test for trend in proportions and compared with that obtained with an equal number of randomly drawn CD36-negative macrophages (50 draws); the fractions of exhausted and non-exhausted CD8 +  T cells within 20, 30 and 50 μm of a CD36-enriched LAM were compared with Fisher’s exact test; and logistic models of exhaustion on log distance were adjusted for log transcript count, the numbers of CD8 +  T cells and macrophages within 50 μm, distance to epithelium and distance to CD36-negative macrophages, with 95% confidence intervals from a 6 × 6 spatial block bootstrap (500 resamples).  For the Visium HD specimen, an analysis plan specifying bin-classification rules and a primary endpoint was written before the expression data were loaded ( Supplementary Note S2 ). The primary unit was 8 μm bins with ≥20 unique molecular identifiers (UMIs), with 16 μm bins (≥50 UMIs) as a sensitivity analysis. CD8 bins required CD3E, CD3D or CD2 and CD8A or CD8B counts (CD8A + CD8B ≥ CD4); exhausted CD8 bins required ≥2 of the same seven exhaustion markers; macrophage bins required absence of T-cell transcripts and ≥2 counts of CD68, CD163, C1QA, C1QB, C1QC, MRC1, CD14 or MS4A7; and CD36-enriched LAM bins required ≥1 CD36 count and ≥2 counts of TREM2, APOE, GPNMB or APOC1 (core genes that replicated at patient level in both single-cell cohorts), with the Xenium rule as a sensitivity definition. The primary endpoint was the compartment-restricted permutation test, with replication declared if the observed/expected ratio exceeded 1 with one-sided  p  < 0.05; distance gradients and adjusted logistic models were secondary endpoints.    2.3. Functional Enrichment, Transcription-Factor Activity and Cell–Cell Communication Analysis  Gene Ontology and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes over-representation analyses and gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) of the Hallmark collection were performed with clusterProfiler [ 27 ] (Hallmark gene sets [ 28 ]); GSEA was repeated after excluding alveolar macrophages. Transcription-factor activity was inferred using decoupleR (univariate linear model; minimum regulon size = 5) with the DoRothEA regulon network (confidence levels A–C) [ 29 , 30 ], and differences between groups were tested with the Wilcoxon test and Benjamini–Hochberg correction; a small curated network of lipid-related transcription factors was used as an additional sensitivity analysis. To quantify the circularity that arises when regulon targets overlap with population-defining genes, the DoRothEA analysis was repeated in both cohorts after removing the 25 population-defining genes from all regulons (LO-1) and after additionally removing the top 100 discovery markers (LO-2); patient-level activity differences were tested with exact paired Wilcoxon tests. Cell–cell communication was analyzed with CellChat v2 and CellChatDB.human [ 31 ], retaining communication groups with ≥10 cells and calculating communication probability with population size accounted for. Because CellChat infers communication potential from ligand and receptor expression in dissociated cells, the inferred interactions are not spatially resolved. Sender specificity was quantified as each sender group’s share of the summed communication probability to exhausted CD8 +  T cells.    2.4. Drug-Target Mendelian Randomization and Colocalization  Two-sample drug-target MR [ 32 ] was performed with the TwoSampleMR package [ 33 ]. The exposure comprised CD36 (Ensembl gene ID ENSG00000135218) cis-eQTL instruments from eQTLGen ( p  < 5 × 10 −8 ; clumped at r 2  = 0.1 within a 250-kb window; F-statistic >10) [ 20 ]. The outcome was the ILCCO/TRICL LUAD genome-wide association study (dataset ieu-a-984). The primary analysis used the inverse variance-weighted (IVW) method, supplemented by weighted-median and MR–Egger analyses, heterogeneity and pleiotropy tests, leave-one-out analysis, an independent cis-instrument sensitivity analysis (r 2  < 0.001), reverse-direction MR (LUAD liability as exposure and CD36 expression as a continuous outcome, reported as β) and FinnGen replication; reporting follows the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology using Mendelian Randomization (STROBE-MR) guidelines [ 34 ]. Colocalization was analyzed separately from MR with coloc.abf (3861 single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) within ±500 kb of CD36; priors p1 = p2 = 1 × 10 −4  and p12 = 1 × 10 −5 , with p12 varied from 1 × 10 −6  to 1 × 10 −4  as a sensitivity analysis) [ 35 ]. To assess lung-specific instruments, significant CD36 cis-eQTLs were retrieved from GTEx v8 [ 22 ] and looked up in the European linkage disequilibrium (LD) reference panel and in the LUAD summary statistics.    2.5. Statistical Analysis  All statistical analyses were performed in R (version 4.4.3; R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria) using the Seurat (version 5.5.0), harmony (1.2.4), UCell (2.10.1), DESeq2 (1.46.0), clusterProfiler (4.14.6), GSVA (2.0.7), decoupleR (2.12.0), CellChat (2.2.0.9001), TwoSampleMR (0.7.8) and coloc (5.2.3) packages. Two groups were compared with the Wilcoxon rank-sum test and more than two groups with the Kruskal–Wallis test; proportions were compared with Fisher’s exact test or the chi-squared test for trend; correlations were assessed with Spearman’s rank correlation; survival was compared with the log-rank test and Cox regression; and the AUC was used to describe discriminative performance. Cell-level differential expression used Seurat FindMarkers; multiple-testing correction used the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure. Because cells are nested within patients, the major single-cell comparisons were repeated at patient level: counts were aggregated per patient and group, paired pseudobulk differential expression was performed with DESeq2 (design ~ patient + group; patients with ≥20 cells in both groups) [ 36 , 37 ], and patient-level program scores and transcription-factor activities were compared with exact paired Wilcoxon tests. For spatial analyses, the statistical unit is cells (Xenium) or bins (Visium HD) within a single specimen (one patient per platform); spatial  p  values therefore describe structure within that specimen and do not generalize to patients. Permutation  p  values are one-sided and based on 1000 permutations; the smallest attainable value (1/1001) is reported as  p  = 0.001. Statistical power for the Mendelian randomization analysis was approximated post hoc from the standard error of the IVW log odds ratio (normal approximation; alpha = 0.05, two-sided) to obtain the minimum detectable effect at 80% power and the power to detect specified odds ratios. Null MR findings are interpreted throughout as absence of evidence rather than evidence of absence. Unless otherwise indicated, tests were two-sided and  p  < 0.05 (or adjusted  p  < 0.05) was considered statistically significant.     3. Results   3.1. A CD36-Enriched Lipid-Associated Macrophage State Is Identified in the LUAD Single-Cell Atlas  Reclustering of myeloid cells from primary LUAD tumors (11 tumors; 8793 myeloid cells) identified a macrophage population (clusters 0 and 3;  n  = 2593) that we term CD36-enriched LAM ( Figure 1 A). In paired pseudobulk analysis against other non-alveolar myeloid cells, the most strongly up-regulated genes were the resident-like macrophage markers SLC40A1, SELENOP and FOLR2 (log2 fold change 2.2–3.1), together with a lipid-handling and lysosomal program that included APOE, GPNMB, PLTP, PLA2G7, NR1H3, APOC1, CTSD, TREM2 and ABCA1 (log2 fold change 0.8–2.0) ( Figure 1 C;  Supplementary Table S6 ), resembling the TREM2 +  lipid-associated macrophage program originally defined in non-tumor tissues [ 38 ]. FABP5 and PLIN2 were moderately up-regulated (log2 fold change 0.87 and 0.77), whereas SPP1 was not (−0.05). The population therefore combines lipid-associated and resident-like macrophage features. The alveolar macrophage markers MARCO and FABP4 marked a separate cluster with a high LAM score but low CD36 detection, which served as an internal comparator ( Figure 1 C,D). CD36 transcripts were detected in 40.9% of CD36-enriched LAM versus 17.4% of other non-alveolar myeloid cells (pseudobulk log2 fold change 1.05; adjusted  p  = 1.0 × 10 −6 ), with enrichment in 10 of 11 patients ( Figure 2 F); CD36 was also detected in 29.4% of monocytes. Because droplet-based assays under-detect moderately expressed transcripts, detection rates are lower bounds; the name CD36-enriched LAM is an operational label for relative, not uniform, CD36 expression, and the population was defined by the joint LAM program rather than by CD36 alone. The LAM program score co-localized with CD36, TREM2 and APOE expression ( Figure 1 B), and CD36-enriched LAM and alveolar macrophages had the highest scores among myeloid subclusters ( Figure 1 D); cluster rankings were concordant between AddModuleScore and the rank-based UCell method (Spearman ρ = 0.97;  Supplementary Table S9 ). Of the 773 cell-level markers (FindMarkers), 650 (84%) remained significant at patient level ( Supplementary Table S6 ). CD36-Enriched LAM Is Recovered in an Independent Cohort by Selection-Independent Criteria  In the replication cohort (GSE189357; nine patients with AIS, MIA or IAC, three of each [ 16 ]; 17,366 myeloid cells), cluster 2 ranked highest on the composite CD36-detection/TAM-LAM score after exclusion of alveolar macrophages and was taken as the candidate population ( n  = 2109;  Figure 2 A). Because the features used to select this cluster overlap with those that define the population, replication was judged by criteria that do not depend on the selection genes ( Section 2.2 ). (i) The candidate population was present in all nine patients (43–335 cells per patient) and in all 11 discovery tumors (52–765 cells) ( Supplementary Table S5 ). (ii) A held-out discovery signature from which all 25 selection genes had been removed ranked cluster 2 first of 16 clusters (AUC 0.91 against other non-alveolar myeloid cells), with alveolar macrophages ranking second ( Figure 2 B); the signature discriminated the population in each patient (per-patient AUC 0.84–0.98), and a replication-derived held-out signature scored in the discovery cohort gave an AUC of 0.82 (per-patient 0.63–0.93) ( Figure 2 C). (iii) Patient-level log2 fold changes were correlated between cohorts across 10,226 genes (Spearman ρ = 0.61), 612 genes were up-regulated in both cohorts, and 41 of the top 100 held-out markers were shared (1.8 expected; hypergeometric  p  = 1.7 × 10 −48 ) ( Figure 2 D;  Supplementary Table S6 ). (iv) Reference mapping assigned 57.5% of cluster-2 cells to CD36-enriched LAM but also 52.6% and 62.8% of the cells in clusters 3 and 13, so in the replication cohort, this state is not confined to a single cluster ( Figure S3A; Supplementary Table S5 ). Consistent with this, cluster 2 ranked only fourth (AddModuleScore) or fifth (UCell) of 16 replication clusters on the 15-gene LAM program score ( Supplementary Table S9 ). The concordant core comprised APOE, APOC1, GPNMB, TREM2, CTSB, CTSD, ACP5, PLTP, ABCA1, NR1H3, the C1Q genes, FOLR2, SELENOP and SLC40A1, which were up-regulated in at least 10 of 11 discovery patients and in all 9 replication patients ( Supplementary Table S5 ). Not all features replicated: FABP5 and PLIN2 were not significantly up-regulated in the replication cohort, and SPP1 was strongly up-regulated in the replication cohort (log2 fold change 3.2) but not in the discovery cohort ( Figure 2 D).  CD36 itself was the least reproducible feature. In the replication cohort, CD36 was detected in 19.2% of CD36-enriched LAM, 15.3% of other non-alveolar myeloid cells and 27.1% of monocytes, and its patient-level enrichment was not significant (log2 fold change 0.64; adjusted  p  = 0.09). Down-sampling discovery cells to the transcript depth of the replication cohort reduced CD36 detection only from 40.9% to 35.4% ( Figure 2 E), so sequencing depth accounts for about one quarter of the difference between cohorts. The replication data also combine 10x Chromium v2 and v3 chemistries and include pre-invasive lesions; CD36 enrichment was seen in all three IAC cases but in only three of six AIS/MIA cases (two of six when cells were labeled by reference mapping) ( Figure 2 F;  Supplementary Table S5 ). With nine patients, these observations cannot separate technical from biological contributions, and the cause of the lower CD36 detection rate remains unresolved. We therefore regard CD36 enrichment as a relative and cohort-dependent feature of this population, which is reflected in its name.    3.3. Genes Up-Regulated in CD36-Enriched LAM Are Enriched for Lipid-Metabolism, Phagocytosis and Lysosomal Programs  Functional enrichment of genes up-regulated in CD36-enriched LAM ( Figure 3 ,  Supplementary Table S2 ) identified Gene Ontology terms for receptor-mediated endocytosis, lysosome organization, membrane lipid metabolism, lipid storage and steroid metabolism ( Figure 3 A) and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes pathways including lysosome biogenesis (adjusted  p  = 7 × 10 −42 ), phagocytosis, efferocytosis, cholesterol metabolism (CD36, APOE, ABCA1) and ferroptosis ( Figure 3 C). These results show that genes associated with lipid uptake, lipid handling and lysosomal processing are transcribed together in this population; they do not show that lipid uptake or lysosomal processing occurs or that these steps operate as a connected pathway because neither lipid content nor lysosomal function was measured. After excluding intrinsically lipid-rich alveolar macrophages, GSEA Hallmark analysis ( Figure 3 B,D) showed significant positive enrichment of fatty acid metabolism (normalized enrichment score = 1.57, adjusted  p  = 0.016), adipogenesis and peroxisome gene sets, and significant negative enrichment of interferon-α/γ response and inflammatory signaling. The latter is in line with a report that CD36 dampens type-I interferon signaling in tumor-associated macrophages in mouse models [ 13 ], but here it reflects transcriptional enrichment only. These enrichment analyses were performed in the discovery cohort only ( Supplementary Table S11 ).    Figure 3   Functional enrichment of genes up-regulated in CD36-enriched LAM. LXR (NR1H3) Is a Candidate Regulator of the CD36-Enriched LAM Program  Transcription-factor activity inferred with decoupleR and DoRothEA regulons was higher for NR1H3, which encodes the liver X receptor (LXR) isoform LXRα, in CD36-enriched LAM than in other non-alveolar myeloid cells (activity difference +1.58; rank 2 of 271 transcription factors in the discovery cohort; +1.01, rank 13, in the replication cohort), with smaller increases for NR1H2 (LXRβ) and lower SREBF2 activity ( Figure 4 A). Because target-based inference is partly circular when regulon targets overlap with the genes used to define a population, we repeated the analysis after removing all population-defining genes from every regulon (LO-1) and after additionally removing the top 100 discovery markers (LO-2). The NR1H3 difference fell to +0.31 (rank 21) and +0.10 (rank 64) in the discovery cohort and to +0.29 (rank 72) and +0.09 (rank 133) in the replication cohort ( Figure 4 A,B;  Supplementary Table S8 ). By contrast, the myeloid lineage factor SPI1 remained among the 10 highest-ranked factors after both leave-outs in both cohorts, and in the replication cohort, MAFB and CEBPB also ranked above NR1H3 after leave-out (ranks 11 and 12 after LO-2;  Figure 4 A). Of the 12 NR1H3 targets, only APOE is a population-defining gene, so removing APOE alone accounted for the fall from rank 2 to rank 21. The direction was largely consistent across patients: after LO-1, NR1H3 activity was higher in all 11 discovery patients and in 8 of 9 replication patients (exact paired Wilcoxon  p  = 0.001 and 0.008), and after LO-2, in 8 of 11 and 8 of 9 patients ( p  = 0.07 and 0.03). Expression data gave support that does not rely on target-based inference: NR1H3 mRNA was up-regulated at patient level in both cohorts (log2 fold change 1.78 and 1.93), and an LXR-target program that excludes all population-defining genes (ABCA1, ABCG1, MYLIP, PLTP, SREBF1, SCD, LPCAT3, APOC1, NR1H3, ABCG4) was higher in 11 of 11 and 9 of 9 patients ( Figure 4 C,D). SREBP2-target scores were lower in all 11 discovery patients but not consistently in the replication cohort (higher in 5 of 9). Inferred activities also depended on the regulon resource: with the curated lipid-related network used as a sensitivity analysis, the NR1H3 difference was +0.38, MAFB showed the largest difference and PPARG changed sign, and some of the highest-ranked factors in the full DoRothEA analysis (for example ESR2) are implausible in macrophages. Together, these data identify LXR as a candidate regulator suggested by concordant expression and inferred-activity data; they do not establish that LXR is the main regulator of this program, a larger inferred-activity difference does not imply a larger functional role, and LXR involvement would require perturbation experiments.
